Foreword

The “foreword” to a book or other works of literature, in contrast to the “preface,”
is usually written by someone other than the authors or editors. An expert, a prominent figure in the field, or someone who because of previous experience or publications on the subject is chosen to review the book. I am flattered that Drs. Markiewicz
and Yates asked me to write this foreword as I have been interested in first and second pharyngeal arch deformities for almost 50 years. The role of the foreword writer
is to provide a short (hence foreword) objective assessment and overall summary of
the work to help the potential audience decide whether to buy and read the book.
Presumably, the foreword will be laudatory, give the book credibility, and recommend it to the readers. In contrast, a preface is usually written by the authors to
explain why they chose the subject, the aims of the book, the learning goals, and a
summary. In the craniomaxillofacial surgery literature, a preface is attached to
works more commonly than a foreword. It should be noted that the correct spelling
is “foreword,” not “forward,” and this has been called the most frequently misspelled word in the English language.
Often, the authors or editors of a book are experts in the particular subject(s).
Searching the literature using the terms hemifacial microsomia (HFM), craniofacial
microsomia, first and second pharyngeal arch deformities, branchial arch deformities, Treacher Collins syndrome (TCS), Nager syndrome, facioauriculovertebral
syndrome, ocular-auriculo-vertebral spectrum, and lateral-facial dysplasia, among
others. does not produce significant contributions by the editors of this book.
Exploring how these two editors became interested in craniomaxillofacial deformities is informative for department chairs, program directors, and oral and maxillofacial surgery (OMS)faculty. It demonstrates how exposure during the early phases of
dental education can have a profound effect on students and their career choices.
I first met Michael Markiewicz as a 2nd or 3rd year dental student during his
observational visits to the craniofacial clinic at Boston Children’s Hospital, where
he often witnessed the interactions between myself and Dr. John Mulliken on children with complicated deformities. He had an interest in research and he participated in projects with Dr. Tom Dodson at Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH).
Markiewicz was then accepted to the Harvard School of Public Health for an MPH
vii

viii

Foreword

under the tutelage of Dr. Dodson who was the director of the MGH OMS Center for
Advanced Clinical Investigation. These two experiences started him on his path to
an academic career in OMS with a special interest in craniomaxillofacial deformities. Similarly, David Yates, as a student on a 2-month mission trip in Mexico, was
exposed to patients with craniofacial deformities, many of whom had cleft lip and
palate. Oral and maxillofacial surgeons were performing reconstructive operations
for underserved children in poverty. In addition, he was inspired by the book Ships
of Mercy which describes the work of Dr. Gary Parker, an OMS who has treated
many children with congenital facial deformities and who served as the chief medical officer on these floating “ships of mercy.” These experiences motivated Yates to
become an OMS. He applied and was accepted in dental school and completed his
residency in OMS at the University of Texas Southwestern, Parkland Hospital. He
recalled: “One of my first weeks there, Dr. Sinn did two craniosynostosis patients…
I was hooked!” He completed the residency and then a fellowship in cleft-craniofacial surgery.
Dr. Markiewicz and Dr. Yates are now well trained, board certified surgeons concentrating on craniomaxillofacial and cleft deformities with a career commitment to
treating these patients. As young surgeons looking for guidance in the literature,
they found that there is no central repository to be used as a resource for diagnosis
and management of children and adults with first and second pharyngeal arch deformities. Hence, they decided to recruit a group of experts in this field to produce an
authoritative text for clinicians. The result is: Comprehensive Management of
Craniofacial Microsomia and Treacher Collins Syndrome by Michael Markiewicz
and David Yates (editors).
When I began my career in the early 1970s, there was no unified concept of the
asymmetric and symmetric first and second pharyngeal arch deformities. The
patients were often treated in isolation by various specialists: otolaryngologists
worked on hearing issues, plastic surgeons on soft tissue deficiencies, both on the
problem of microtia, orthodontists on the teeth, oral and maxillofacial surgeons on
the jaws and skeletal contour asymmetries, and speech pathologists on speech.
Many patients also had cleft lip and palate. Hemifacial microsomia was considered
a unilateral deformity without consideration of the effects of the primary defect on
the adjacent and contralateral facial skeleton. There was very little coordination of
care and no road map for the timing and sequence of treatment. Much progress has
been made over the past 50 years. There is a better, although not complete, understanding of the etiopathogenesis, epidemiology, sequence of growth, and effects on
the adjacent and contralateral facial skeleton. In addition, the majority of patients
are now treated in specialized multidisciplinary craniofacial centers with input from
all the relevant specialists. There have been considerable advances in imaging for
diagnosis, individualized virtual treatment planning, and corrective surgery using
personalized cutting guides and fixation hardware. However, because these are rare
conditions and there are few large series from single institutions, many challenges
remain. The optimal timing and sequence for surgical procedures, the role of
growth-modifying dental orthopedics, the management of facial nerve, hearing, and
soft tissue deficits, to mention a few, are yet to be determined using prospective

Foreword

ix

controlled studies with high-quality data. As a practical matter, a comprehensive
evidenced-based text serving as a resource to help students, residents, fellows, and
practicing clinicians caring for these patients would be a significant contribution.
This is the goal of Comprehensive Management of Craniofacial Microsomia and
Treacher Collins Syndrome.
It is a tribute to their credibility in craniomaxillofacial surgery and their dedication to this subject that Drs. Markiewicz and Yates have been able to assemble a
large group of credible experts to accomplish this comprehensive text. There are 26
chapters; the first 12 are devoted primarily to craniofacial microsomia/hemifacial
microsomia (HFM) with some material also on TCS (Chaps. 9 and 10) as it relates
to hearing and external ear deformities that occur in both syndromes. Chapters 13,
14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, and 26 are primarily dedicated to TCS, and
Chap. 20 reviews the use of alloplastic temporomandibular joint placement (TMJR)
in both HFM and TCS. There are 70 listed contributors representing multiple specialties, geographic locations, and a broad range of ages and years of experience.
Perusing the list of contributors one can infer that the book does not represent a
specific or consistent conceptual philosophy or point of view. Rather, it is a general
encyclopedic treatise on multiple aspects concerning HFM and TCS. In addition,
there is a good deal of repetition and overlap of general information in the chapters.
Recognizing these inherent issues with multi-authored textbooks covering a broad
subject area, the editors bring both parts of the book to closure in Chaps. 12 and 26,
the overviews for HFM and TCS. A chapter worth mentioning, “Etiology and
Anatomical Variation in Treacher Collins,” by FJ Smith, begins with an enlightening and inspirational personal perspective on this condition, as the author has
Treacher Collins syndrome.
The variety of authors and specialties involved in this book provide a real-life
template on how to think and work collegially on these complicated patients, appreciating the contributions of each area of expertise. This is an example of interdisciplinary collaboration, the model for how these patients should be managed. In
addition, the book brings to the reader a comprehensive resource under one cover
with background, historic perspective, and multiple points of view with references.
It will help students, residents, fellows, and young and older surgeons understand
the complexity of these deformities and provide high-quality patient care.
Leonard B. Kaban
Walter C. Guralnick
Department of Oral & Maxillofacial Surgery
Harvard School of Dental Medicine
Massachusetts General Hospital
Boston, MA, USA

Preface

The premise of this book is simple. When searching for a comprehensive resource
on the management of patients with craniofacial microsomia and Treacher Collins
syndrome, we found that this text did not exist. In fact, we were surprised when we
realized that there were no definitive texts, on either subject. Given the common
management and procedures utilized to manage patients with both Craniofacial
Microsomia and Treacher Collins Syndrome, we felt that both entities would be best
addressed in the form of a sequential two volume text.
As two early career cleft and craniofacial surgeons, we were immediately confronted with patients suffering from these difficult and rare conditions. The majority of which had undergone multiple procedures – most of which did little to
improve their cosmetic appearance, functional outcomes, or quality of life. This
was certainly not due to the honorable intentions by the previous treating surgeons.
In fact, most patients had been operated on by multiple surgeons from various specialties in an attempt to improve the life of these patients. These patients suffer
significant functional limitations related to speech, mastication, breathing, hearing,
and vision. In addition, they have cosmetic concerns including facial deformities
and microtia, resulting in a significant psychological burden. When we turned to
the literature on these topics, we found an abundance of information, but it appeared
to be disjointed and incomplete. Most importantly, there was no definitive text that
delivered a comprehensive approach for managing patients with these challenging
conditions.
We wanted to compose a book which addressed the diagnosis and management
of all aspects of these two entities, a manual by which a practitioner could open the
first page, read through the chapters, and upon completion be provided with a roadmap on how to treat these rare conditions. Therefore, we compiled a list of necessary and pertinent subject matter, and engaged expert level authors to address these
topics in a comprehensive evidence based manner. This book is multidisciplinary in
nature and takes a comprehensive look at craniofacial microsomia and Treacher
Collins syndrome, specifically with regards to surgical management.
This book has been a labor of love and its content has already changed the way
in which we manage our own patients. We are very grateful to the authors who have
xi

xii

Preface

contributed and the content they have offered. Our hope is that this text will provide
guidance to young and experienced surgeons alike so that we may optimize the
management of these patients who entrust us with their lives and care.
El Paso, TX, USA
Buffalo, NY, USA

David M. Yates

Part I

Craniofacial Microsomia CFM

Chapter 1

Etiology and Anatomical Variance
in Craniofacial Microsomia
Ashley Manlove, Brian Mitchell, and Shelly Abramowicz

Introduction
Craniofacial microsomia (CFM) is a condition that includes a spectrum of phenotypic craniofacial anomalies that result from abnormal development of the first and
second branchial arches. The term CFM is often used interchangeably with other
names, most commonly hemifacial microsomia (HFM). Historically there has been
a variety of nomenclature used to describe the different phenotypical anomalies
associated with CFM including HFM, Goldenhar syndrome, oculoauriculovertebral
dysplasia, oromandibular dysostosis, as well as others. The degree of overlap (or
lack thereof) of phenotypic characteristics has led some experts to believe CFM is a
spectrum. The term oculoauriculovertebral spectrum has been used as an encompassing term for these variable phenotypes and has also been used interchangeably
with CFM or HFM [1].
CFM occurs in 1:3000 to 1:5000 live births [2, 3]. Most cases are sporadic, but
there are rare familial cases [4]. CFM does not have definitive diagnostic criteria,
such as a genetic test, but consists of a spectrum of phenotypic presentations with
underdevelopment of the various parts of facial skeleton and underlying soft tissues.

The orbits, zygomatic arch, maxilla, mandible, ears, facial nerves, and facial muscles may be affected. These anomalies can cause airway compromise, feeding
issues, facial paralysis, hearing challenges, and malocclusion. Therefore, a child
with CFM is best treated by a multidisciplinary team and followed from birth to
adulthood. This chapter will discuss pathogenesis, classification, and clinical presentation of CFM.

Pathogenesis
The first and second pharyngeal arches form around the 4th week of embryologic
development when the migration of neural crest cells from the neural tube begins
the development of branchial arch ectomesenchyme [5, 6]. Each branchial arch has
three layers (endoderm, mesenchyme, and ectoderm) which produce the four primordial components – muscle, artery, nerve, and cartilage [6]. These arches give
rise to the structures of the face innervated by cranial nerves V and VII. The first
branchial arch gives rise to the maxilla, mandible, zygoma, trigeminal nerve, muscles of mastication, and the anterior portion of the ear (tragus, root, and superior
helix) as well as the malleolus and incus. The second branchial arch gives rise to the
hyoid bone, the styloid process and facial nerve, the facial muscles and most of the
ear (helix, antihelix, antitragus, and lobule), as well as the stapes [7]. For these
structures to fully form, the mesenchymal cells of the arches must maintain continuous tissue-to-tissue communication to support the development of the skeletal, muscular, and neural components [8]. Disruption of this communication can result in
hypoplasia or aplasia of the affected structure [2].
The pathogenesis of CFM has not been definitively proven; however, etiology is
presumed to be due to abnormalities in the development of the first and second
branchial arches [9]. There are two prevailing theories in which the disruption of
branchial arch development causes subsequent malformation of craniofacial structures and, thus, CFM forms (1) vascular abnormalities and hemorrhage and (2)
abnormal cranial neural crest cell migration.

Vascular Abnormalities and Hemorrhage
In 1948 Braithwaite and Watson initially suggested that abnormal development or
the absence of the stapedial artery in utero could lead to ischemia and necrosis of
developing tissue, thus resulting in the phenotype of CFM [2]. The stapedial artery
is a transient structure within normal fetal development that arises around the 33rd
day in utero. It provides the vascular distribution to supply the primordia of the first
and second branchial arches and is the dominant blood supply to the face. It later
connects the future external carotid artery to the internal carotid artery. The

1

Etiology and Anatomical Variance in Craniofacial Microsomia

5

stapedial artery regresses by the 45th day of development [10]. Poswillo led a wellknown study in 1973 consisting of mice and M. irus monkey models with the first
and second branchial arch anomalies. The animals had similar findings to CFM. He
evaluated the embryos throughout their development and identified small areas of
hemorrhage and hematoma formation shortly following the anastomosis of vessels
that form the stapedial arterial stem. The bleeding affected the first and second branchial arches [2]. This theory also explains the variable nature of CFM, as a varying
amount of hemorrhage would produce different sizes and shapes of hematomas,
thus resulting in damage to local developing tissues in differing ways. This could
result in a wide spectrum of phenotypic variability [10].

Abnormal Cranial Neural Crest Cells
Anomalies or deficiencies in migration, proliferation, and differentiation of neural
crest cells (NCCs) have also been proposed as a possible mechanism for CFM [11,
12]. The neural crest cells are a migratory cell population specific to vertebrates that
originate from the developing neural tube. The cells delaminate and migrate to different regions of the embryo where they differentiate into a broad range of cell
types, stimulating local tissue growth during development [5, 12]. The migration of
neural crest cells also gives rise to the branchial arch ectomesenchyme around the
4th week in utero. In the cranial region, NCCs generate odontoblasts, cartilage,
bone, connective tissue, and smooth muscle, playing a key role in the development
of a large portion of the structures of the face and anterior neck [12, 13]. Given that
most craniofacial structures involved in CFM are derivatives of cranial NCCs, direct
disturbances of the migration, proliferation, and differentiation of cranial NCCs
have been suggested to be the origin of the developmental deformities found in
CFM. Giving support to this idea, NCCs have been shown to form the basis of craniofacial, vertebral, CNS, cardiovascular, and urogenital anomalies, which have all
been frequently observed in the CFM population [14, 15]. The abundance of extracraniofacial anomalies in CFM patients suggests that the NCCs could be the source
of the anomalies. Phenotypic variability in CFM could be explained by the extent of
the neural crest cell loss, leading to varying degrees of severity of the facial malformations [11]. There have been several transgenic mouse models described in the
literature in which neural crest problems appeared to cause the first and second
branchial arch anomalies, although these models have not perfectly mirrored the
constellation of findings in CFM [16].
There are extrinsic and intrinsic pathogenic factors that can cause vascular
abnormalities and hemorrhage as well as lead to abnormal neural crest cell migration. Teratogenic drugs such as thalidomide, alcohol, and retinoic acid have shown
CFM-like phenotype in animal models [11]. And intrinsic factors such as diabetes
and second-trimester bleeding are also correlated as major risk factors for CFM
(Table 1.1) [17, 18].

Classification
The wide variance in presentation of patients with CFM has led to many different
classification systems as well as different names. The term CFM is often used interchangeably with hemifacial microsomia (HFM), first and second branchial arch
syndrome, and otomandibular dysostosis. Goldenhar syndrome, or oculoauriculovertebral syndrome, may be used interchangeably but is more commonly discussed
as being on the CFM “spectrum” [9]. Goldenhar syndrome and oculoauriculovertebral syndrome are variants of CFM that include extracranial anomalies in addition
to those found in CFM including epibulbar dermoids (benign congenital eye tumors)
as well as vertebral and rib anomalies such as incomplete formation, fusion, or
missing ribs [1]. The classification systems attempt to make it easier to communicate among providers, predict future growth, and plan surgical interventions. The
two most commonly used classification systems are Kaban-Pruzansky and OMENS/
OMENS Plus. Most agree that the mandibular deformity is the foundation of the
classification system and best determines the overall deformity and treatment.

Kaban-Pruzansky Classification
In 1969 Pruzansky described three mandibular deformities associated with hemifacial microsomia patients. However, Pruzanksy did not consider the position of the
condyle relative to the glenoid fossa. Kaban et al. analyzed patients with HFM
three-dimensionally and classified them by the mandibular deformity [19]. Kaban
et al. modified the classification system in their article in 1988 breaking down Type
II into Type IIA and Type IIB to clarify the degree of condylar deformity and position
of the condyle with relation to the glenoid fossa. These observations were important
since the surgical treatment differs greatly between patients with Type IIA and Type
IIB. Kaban et al. report that neither the soft tissue ear deformity nor the cranial nerve
involvement correlates with the severity of the mandibular skeletal deformity [20,
22]. In contrast, Vento et al. found a positive association between mandibular hypoplasia and the severity of associated facial deformity [21]. These observations
resulted in Kaban-Pruzansky classification (Table 1.2).

OMENS Classification
The OMENS classification system was developed to include the major manifestations of HFM in a comprehensive and succinct fashion. Veneto et al. developed the
classification system to be comprehensive and allow for evaluation and analysis of
each deformity independently [21]. This classification system evaluates the patient
for (O) orbital distortion, (M) mandibular hypoplasia, (E) ear deformity, (N) nerve
involvement, and (S) soft tissue deficiency [21]. Within each subgroup, each manifestation is numerically classified by the level of deformity from zero (normal) to
three (most severe) (Table 1.3).

 M1: Mandible and glenoid fossa are small with shortened ramus
 M2: Mandibular ramus is short and abnormally shaped
   M2A: Glenoid fossa is in relatively normal position compared with contralateral side
   M2B: Temporomandibular joint is inferior, medial, and anteriorly displaced with
hypoplastic condyle
 M3: Complete absence of ramus, glenoid fossa, temporomandibular joint

 E0: Normal ear
 E1: Mild hypoplasia and cupping with all structures present
 E2: Absence of external auditory canal with variable hypoplasia of concha
 E3: Malpositioned lobule (usually inferior and anterior) with absent auricle

 N0: No facial nerve involvement
 N1: Upper facial nerve involvement; temporal and zygomatic branches

OMENS Plus Classification
The OMENS Plus classification system was developed and published in 1995 after
an editorial critique of the OMENS system. The suggestions were that the classification should include non-craniofacial anomalies to strengthen the system [23, 24].
OMENS Plus includes anomalies such as cardiovascular, renal, central nervous system, skeletal, GI, and pulmonary [15]. When extracranial findings are present, it is
reported as OMENS+ X system, where X is the number of anomalies in that system.
If more than one system is involved, it is reported at OMENS+ X system, Y system.
For example, if only one system is affected but multiple anomalies occur within that
system, it is documented at OMENS+ 2 skeletal (1 = C2–C3 fusion, 2 = scoliosis).
If two systems are affected, it would be documented as OMENS+ 1 cardiac
(1 = VSD) and 2 CNS (1 = hydrocephalus, 2 = Chiari malformation).

Clinical Features

soft tissues and neural and muscles [9, 25] (Table 1.4). The phenotypic expression

observed [7, 25] (Fig. 1.2a, b). At birth, the defect often appears mild; however the

asymmetry becomes more distinct with growth of the child and progressive development of the normal side [3].
While there are no official diagnostic criteria, most craniofacial experts agree
that mandibular and soft tissue deficiencies are necessary features for diagnosis of
CFM [20, 25]. Mandibular hypoplasia has been described as the cornerstone of
CFM, with a correlation demonstrated between the severity of mandibular hypoplasia and other defects [21]. Mandibular deficiency can vary from minimal
underdevelopment of the condyle to the absence of the ascending ramus and condyle with underdevelopment of the horizontal ramus. The entire temporomandibular joint (TMJ) can be involved, including the glenoid fossa of the temporal
bone [3].
Macrostomia, a transverse facial cleft, is a rare defect believed to be causes by
failure of mesodermal migration and merging within the maxillary and mandibular
prominences of the first branchial arch [26]. Macrostomia presents as a 1- to 2-cm
extension lateral to the normal position of the oral commissure [3]. It can occur
alone but is frequently associated with deformities of the structures developing from
the first and second branchial arches [27–29].
Auricular defects can range from mild to severe (Fig. 1.3). A mild deformity
would present as preauricular skin tags with or without cartilage or a preauricular
sinus with a normal inner ear [3]. Anomalies of the auricle and middle ear ossicles
can be present [25]. The most severe deformity consists of underdevelopment of all
parts of the external ear (auricle and external auditory canal) and middle ear (tympanic membrane, tympanic cavity, auditory ossicles, mastoid antrum, mastoid cells,
and Eustachian tube).
The maxilla, zygoma, temporal bone, and orbit may also be affected in CFM [9].
Maxillary underdevelopment is evidenced by decreased width from the midline
palatal raphe to the lingual surface of the teeth on the affected side [3]. An underdeveloped zygoma consists of flat malar eminence and shortened span of the zygomatic arch, contributing to the decrease in length of the canthal-tragal line on the

affected side (Fig. 1.4) [3]. The temporal bone does not have its origin in the first
and second branchial arches, but its development is intimately related to these visceral arches. Potential temporal bone abnormalities include underdevelopment or
the absence of the zygomatic and mastoid processes. Dissections of the temporal
bone in autopsy have shown that any part of the temporal bone other than the petrous
portion which houses the inner ear might be underdeveloped [3]. The orbit may
demonstrate vertical displacement (Fig. 1.5: 18 mos. with left vertical orbital dystopia). Coloboma of the upper eyelid and/or iris may be found. Microphthalmia or
anophthalmia is rare but has been observed [6].
The muscles innervated by the fifth and seventh cranial nerves may be underdeveloped, with possible paresis. Patients may have sensorineural hearing loss and
impairment of extraocular movements [3].
Extracraniofacial anomalies may be present in 55% of patients with CFM [29].
Patients with bilateral CFM are more likely to develop extracraniofacial anomalies
[14, 29]. These anomalies most often present in the vertebrae, ribs, circulatory system, CNS, urogenital tract, and gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Vertebral anomalies may
be found in cervical/lumbar/thoracic spine and/or ribs as hemivertebrae, block vertebrae, and/or scoliosis. These anomalies can range from asymptomatic to severe,
some causing significant health consequences [29]. CNS anomalies in CFM can
include hydrocephaly, ventriculomegaly, intracranial cysts, Arnold-Chiari malformations, or spinal cord anomalies. Circulatory system anomalies include ventricular or atrial septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, and valve malformations. GI
tract anomalies consist of inguinal/umbilical hernia, imperforate anus, or esophageal atresia. Urogenital anomalies may include renal aplasia, undescended testis, or
hydronephrosis. Respiratory tract anomalies are possible but rare, such as laryngomalacia, tracheomalacia, or lung hypoplasia [14, 29].

Conclusions
CFM has a variable presentation that can range from mild ear deformity and asymmetry to near-absent auricle and agenesis of the ramus and condyle. The two prevailing pathogenic models of CFM include vascular abnormalities in the developing
embryo and abnormalities with cranial NCC migration. Given the extreme phenotypic variation, numerous classification systems have been proposed with the two
most common being Kaban-Pruzansky and OMENS Plus. Careful analysis and
diagnosis by a multidisciplinary team is important to be able to provide appropriate
care to patients with CFM from infancy to adulthood. The multidisciplinary team is

Introduction
Craniofacial microsomia (CFM, OMIM 164 210) is the term used to describe a
developmental disorder with a spectrum of congenital abnormalities that affect anatomical structures derived from the first and second branchial arches. Multiple
names have been used to describe this aberrant embryologic development; CFM can
also be known in the literature as:

Otomandibular dysmorphogenesis [7]

Due to the significant variability in the presentation of the spectrum and the fact
that bilateral involvement is observed in 5–30% of the cases [11, 17], the term craniofacial microsomia is now preferred, and these entities are accepted to exist within
a continuum. From the Greek words micros (small) and sōma (body), microsomia
refers to the main phenotypical characteristics of a hypoplastic and malformed unilateral affected side of the craniofacial skeleton. It most commonly affects the external ear, middle ear, mandible, temporomandibular joint, muscles of mastication,
facial muscles, and other facial soft tissues of one side of the craniofacial region.
Other facial structures, such as the orbit, eye, nose, cranium, or neck, may be
involved [18]. When the entity is bilateral, it is usually an asymmetric
presentation.
In addition to craniofacial anomalies, there may be cardiac, vertebral, central
nervous system, genitourinary, and renal defects. As mentioned in the previous
chapter, the phenotype is highly variable as the expression varies from microtia to a
near complete agenesis of the affected side of the mandible and overlying soft
tissues.
This chapter compiles the many classification schemes and patient variations in
anatomic expression of craniofacial microsomia to provide a roadmap for patient
evaluation at various stages of patient presentation. The initial evaluation naturally
leads to further investigation of possible extracraniofacial abnormalities and guides
treatment sequencing for the patient’s life. Standardized evaluation of patients with
craniofacial deformities leads to better communication among clinicians and inevitably better treatment outcomes for patients.

Craniofacial Microsomia Classification Systems
Several classification systems have been developed since 1969 in an attempt to better differentiate the complex and variable phenotypical expression. Auriculofacial
defects are the predominant and pathognomonic features of CFM, and it is generally
agreed upon that its diagnosis requires the presence of at least one hypoplastic structure derived from the first or second branchial arches. However, the presence of
isolated microtia, preauricular skin tags, or macrostomia without other CFM features would be arguable to not fit criteria for establishment of a CFM diagnosis.

2

Initial Evaluation of a Patient with Craniofacial Microsomia

19

Because there is lack of consensus on the diagnostic criteria for this condition, its
prevalence, classification, and defined treatment protocols are not fixed. The literature today presents the medical community with multiple classification systems to
score the severity and guide treatment planning.
The mandible is the “keystone” to the skeletal deformities of CFM [19] and
therefore the basis in which the classification systems have been developed. Cousley
suggested the guidelines for minimum diagnostic criteria for CFM [20]. These criteria are not definitively accepted, despite their widely accepted use:
1. Ipsilateral mandibular and auricular defects (external or middle ear)
2. Asymmetric mandible or auricular defects (external or middle ear) with either:
(a) Involvement of two or more indirectly associated anomalies
(b) Positive family history of CFM

Skeletal Deformity Classifications
The purpose of the Pruzansky Mandibular Deformity Classification system is to
organize the severity of mandibular hypoplasia (Table 2.1). Kaban’s Modification to
Pruzansky’s Original Classification intends to include the glenoid fossa and TMJ
development based on radiological findings (Table 2.2). Surgical treatment strategies will vary based on the category, and this will be further discussed in the following chapters.

the mandible is strikingly different in size and shape from normal
Grade III Mandible is severely malformed, ranging from poorly identifiable ramal components
to complete agenesis of the ramus
[7]

[21, 22]

N. Fürchtgott et al.

Treatment of types I, IIA, and some IIB mandibular deformities can be accomplished by osteotomy (with or without bone grafting) or by distraction osteogenesis.
Treatment of many type IIB and all type III deformities requires total construction
of the ramus condyle unit and, in some cases, the glenoid fossa.

Auricular Deformity Classification
The Meurman grades of microtia was first described in 1957 to expand on classification systems of microtia. This system has been incorporated into more inclusive
classification systems seen later in this chapter. The severity of microtia starts with
hypoplasia of the auricle but with retained anatomic structures but then advances to
complete aplasia of crucial components. Grade I is classified as a malformed auricle
of smaller than normal size but retaining characteristic features. Grade II expands
with having a lack of fundamental features that may consist of a low, oblong elevation hook formed at the cranial end corresponding to the helix. Grade III is characterized with a more defective auricle with a malformed lobule and the rest of the
pinna being totally absent [23].

Soft Tissue Deformity Classifications
The Murray Grading of Severity of Soft Tissue Deformities was developed in 1984.
This system evaluates primarily microtia, CN deficits, and presents of clefts (Table 2.3).
The degree of soft tissue hypoplasia is directly proportional to the severity of the mandibular deformity. Muscles of mastication may be absent or reduced to fibrous tissue.

Multisystem Deformity Classifications
SAT Classification System
The SAT Classification System is an alphanumeric coding system based on the
TNM classification of malignant tumors. It combines elements of the Pruzansky’s
mandible classification, Meurman’s microtia staging, and Murray’s soft tissue
deformity grading (Table 2.4).

OMENS Classification (Vento, 1991)
The OMENS Classification is much more comprehensive than its predecessors, as
it includes elements of the previous classifications, but it separates orbital and mandibular defects into separate categories, as well as soft tissue and CN VII function
(Table 2.5) [26].
Horgan et al. described the importance of including extracraniofacial anomalies
in this system, after they found that the frequency of patients with CFM and other
organ system involvement was 55.4%. The classification system has been enhanced
to OMENS Plus (+), where the + sign and a number are added at the end of the
acronym to designate the presence and quantity of extracraniofacial findings [27]
Phenotypic Assessment Tool for Craniofacial Microsomia
The Phenotypic Assessment Tool for Craniofacial Microsomia (PAT-CFM) is a
comprehensive pictorial classification system that allows for standarization of the
assessment of patients with CFM (Fig. 2.1). The pictorial representation of the
OMENS+ classification was developed by Gougoutas et al, and further expanded to
include laterality and minor anomalies by the Craniofacial Clinic at Seattle
Children’s Hospital.

Patient Evaluation and Diagnosis
As with any other craniofacial condition, a multidisciplinary team approach for the
management of these patients is ideal. Here, qualified professionals from a myriad
of health disciplines work in a coordinated effort to deliver proper and consistent
medical, dental, and psychosocial care. The team should include a pediatrician,
audiologist, speech-language pathologist, orthodontist, pediatric dentist, oral maxillofacial surgeon, plastic surgeon, and otolaryngologist with access to neurosurgeon,
ophthalmologist, radiologist, social worker, psychologist, geneticist, orthopedic
surgeon, cardiologist, cardiothoracic surgeon, and urologist.
Although CFM is the second most common craniofacial congenital disorder, its
multidisciplinary team approach is not as well outlined as the management of patients
with cleft lip and palate. Table 2.6 contains a comprehensive list of anomalies commonly found in craniofacial microsomia. Due to the wide breadth of physical

anomalies, patients should always have a thorough physical exam at initial presentation to guide screening tests. Given the wide phenotypic diversity, creating evidencebased guidelines for screening and care is difficult in this patient population [38].

Prenatal Period
Prenatal diagnosis of sporadic cases has been reported with the use of fetal ultrasound; however, this is still very infrequent. It is more likely to detect a severe
malformation with these studies, and with the evolution of 3D scanning, some
milder cases of microtia, preauricular tags, and mandibular hypoplasia have been
identified [29].

2

Initial Evaluation of a Patient with Craniofacial Microsomia

27

Prenatal and birth history should aim to determine any maternal-fetal factors.
Medications and substances that have been linked to CFM due to their ability to
cause vascular abnormalities and hemorrhage, damage to Meckel’s cartilage, and
abnormal development of neural crest cells include thalidomide, triazene, retinoic
acid, pseudoephedrine, methotrexate, and heavy alcohol consumption.
Environmental factors also linked to CFM include hypoxia, ionizing radiation, and
hyperthermic stress [39–42].
Maternal intrinsic factors such as multiple gestations, diabetes, hypothyroidism,
and bleeding in the second trimester are major risk factors [29, 43].

Neonatal Period
The main goal during this time is to assure adequate respiratory support and address
any feeding difficulties. Additionally, extracraniofacial findings must be ruled out,
particularly those requiring emergent cardiothoracic surgical management.
Symptoms associated with respiratory distress include tachypnea, stridor, cyanosis, retractions, and episodic upper airway obstruction with apnea. If there are respiratory concerns due to airway obstruction, a surgical consultation for airway
management is necessary [44–46].
Some life-threatening congenital cardiac defects will require immediate repair.
Therefore, a chest x-ray, electrocardiogram, and echocardiogram are indicated as
part of the work-up in this age period.
Lactation consultants and speech-language pathologists can assess and provide
parents with necessary techniques to modify nursing and feeding times. Specialized
feeding bottles, nasogastric feeds, and even gastrostomy feeds might be necessary
for severe cases.
Work-up testing should also include a newborn hearing screening and renal
ultrasound. Strict monitoring of weight, height, and development is to be carried out
by the pediatricians.
Oral and mandibular abnormalities are identified within the first few hours of
life. An examination by the craniofacial surgeon should occur not only for the
assessment of respiratory support adequacy but also for parent education and establishment of an initial relationship for the long-term treatment plan.
Cervical/spinal and renal abnormalities can occur in up to 15% of patients with
CFM; however, routine neonatal screening is not definitively recommended. A retrospective review of 514 patients with isolated microtia or aural atresia without
facial asymmetry demonstrated that initial screening was inconsistent among the
cohort population. Of those screened, only 2% of the patients had renal abnormalities on ultrasound, and none of the patients had cervical or spinal abnormalities.
Routine screenings for renal or cervical/spinal abnormalities lack in consistency
and insurance approval and, more importantly, fail to capture true abnormality rates.
Routine screens with renal ultrasounds and spinal x-rays may not be warranted at
this stage unless clinically indicated [38, 47].

28

N. Fürchtgott et al.

0–12 Months
Ideally, an appointment will be made for initial visit with the craniofacial team prior
to discharge from hospital care after birth. The pediatrician can also trigger this
referral, and the first appointment should happen within the first weeks of life.
At the first craniofacial team visit, reassurance and educational resources are
given. This is an opportunity for the parents to meet with all members of the team
and determine barriers to care as well as to obtain referrals for pending studies.
It is important to establish a complete history and physical examination. This
should include a review of systems aiming to consider meeting developmental milestones, obstructive sleep apnea symptoms, difficulty with swallowing and feeding,
speech development, and a psychosocial assessment. Polysomnography, audiograms, and swallow evaluations by a speech-language pathologist could be indicated based on these symptoms.
The pediatrician is key to continue the patient’s close follow-up for monitoring
of continued development, weight gain, and growth charting.
Photography is used to document facial appearance throughout the patient’s
growth, starting at the initial visit and throughout the treatment process. Traditionally,
posteroanterior cephalograms have been the gold standard for assessment of facial
asymmetry. Nowadays, the use of cone-beam computerized tomography and the
ability to obtain three-dimensionally reconstructed images in a relatively low-dose
radiation study has gained popularity.
Since CFM is most commonly a simplex case with unknown etiology, risk recurrence estimates are empiric. It is estimated that the sibling recurrence risk is estimated to be 2–3%, assuming normal chromosomes and no family history. No
specific genetic testing is available, and only a few cases have demonstrated de novo
chromosome abnormalities. The identification of subtle clinical manifestations in a
patient’s relatives is important, as well as a three-generation family history. The
family history must inquire about other relatives with facial asymmetry, ear tags, ear
pits, hearing loss, vertebral malformations, eye abnormalities, abnormalities of
extremities, and cardiac or urogenital malformations [29, 48].

Childhood and Adolescence
During this phase, serial multidisciplinary evaluations must take into account the
improvement of facial symmetry and management of malocclusion, maximize hearing and communication, and support psychosocial needs.
An important consideration that is commonly overlooked is that airway problems that appear in infancy worsen with adolescence [49, 50].
It is not the purpose of this chapter to elaborate on the details of surgical management required for these patients, as they will be discussed further. However, this
excellent timeline elaborated at the Craniofacial Center at Seattle Children’s
Hospital can be a useful guide (Fig. 2.2).

Differential Diagnosis
Clinical findings overlap with other syndromes that have identifiable causative
genes, such as Treacher Collins syndrome, Townes-Brocks syndrome, CHARGE
syndrome, branchiootorenal spectrum disorders, and mutations of EFTUD2 [29].
Other entities for differential diagnosis include a traumatic postnatal deformity,
Parry-Romberg syndrome, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, unilateral condylar hyperplasia, Nager acrofacial dysostosis syndrome, and Pierre Robin sequence.

Summary
The initial evaluation of patients with craniofacial microsomia can be complex due
to a wide range of potential facial and extracraniofacial deformities. A methodical,
step-wise approach to patient evaluation with the help of the many classification
schemes available can guide clinicians to find not only the correct diagnosis but also
the corresponding steps to patient care. In evaluating these complex patients, it is
always helpful to standardize the initial evaluation to maintain consistency in reporting and diagnosis.

Introduction
Craniofacial microsomia (CFM) includes a spectrum of malformations primarily
involving structures derived from the first and second branchial arches.
Characteristics of this condition can include the following:
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•

Mandibular hypoplasia/micrognathia.
Facial asymmetry.
Ear malformations that can include microtia, anotia, or aural atresia.
Preauricular or facial tags.
Hearing loss.
Feeding/swallowing disorders.
Cleft lip and/or palate.
Extra craniofacial malformations can include vertebral, renal, cardiac, and limb
involvement.

The primary anomalies of CFM include the airway, oropharynx, and auditory
structures [1]. The goals of treatment for CFM are to optimize breathing, feeding/
swallowing, hearing, communication, facial symmetry, dental occlusion, and quality of life [1]. Intervention is age-dependent, time-sensitive, and dependent on the
stage of craniofacial development.

Breathing
Mandibular hypoplasia is one of the most common features in patients with CFM
[1, 2]. This upper airway obstruction places children with CFM at a high risk for
obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) with symptoms of snoring, increased work of breathing, and apnea in the neonatal period [2, 3]. Significant obstructive sleep apnea can
result in failure to thrive, pulmonary hypertension, and even death [2, 4]. Sleep-­
disordered breathing in this population can be associated with one or more of the
following sites of airway obstruction: glossoptosis, micrognathia, adenotonsillar
hyperplasia, midface hypoplasia, nasoseptal deviation, and rhinitis [1]. Patients
with more severe mandibular and orbital deformities seem to be at a greater risk for
obstructive sleep apnea [5]. Breathing patterns in patients with OSA can include
increased work of breathing, tachypnea and/or gas exchange abnormalities [6].
Obstructive sleep apnea has been defined as complete cessation of airflow for
more than two breaths or 10 seconds, and hypopnea is characterized by a >50%
reduction in ventilation with decrease in oxygen saturation (i.e., >3%). OSA can
range from mild to severe, and the classification and severity of obstructive sleep
apnea (OSA) are traditionally based on apnea-hypopnea index (AHI). Although
some definitions vary, the most commonly accepted definition in pediatric OSA is
as follows: ≤1 event/hour is normal, 1–5 is mild, 5–10 is moderate, and >10/hour is
severe OSA [2, 5, 7, 8].
Infants with difficulty breathing due to upper airway obstruction undergo monitoring by pulse oximetry, overnight polysomnography, and potentially direct laryngoscopy and/or bronchoscopy [1]. A Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire (PSQ) could be
completed by the parents and includes questions regarding sleep-disordered breathing and sleep habits [3]. Interventions can be nonsurgical or surgical. Nonsurgical
treatments for upper airway obstruction include prone positioning, positive pressure
(nasal, mask), nasal decongestants, and intubation. Surgical treatments for upper
airway obstruction include tongue lip adhesion, adenotonsillectomy, tongue base
reduction, septorhinoplasty, mandibular distraction, skeletal expansion, maxillary
advancement, and tracheotomy [1, 5, 9].
If the upper airway obstruction is severe and adequate respiration is not achieved
by positive pressure or surgical intervention, a tracheotomy may be performed. A
tracheostomy bypasses the upper airway and is the most effective intervention for
severe OSA. The goal of a tracheostomy is for eventual decannulation when a child
can adequately achieve respiration through the upper airway with surgical intervention or maturation. When a patient has a tracheostomy with or without ventilator
dependence, a speech/language pathologist (SLP) can evaluate the infant or child’s
ability to orally feed and to tolerate application of a speaking valve. A speaking
valve can allow for inhalation to occur through the tracheostomy tube and exhalation to occur through the nose and mouth, which allows for voicing and speech.
However it is important to note that an infant or child who has a tracheostomy due

3

A Look at Breathing, Feeding/Swallowing, and Speech Impairment in Patients…

35

to upper airway obstruction may not be able to tolerate a speaking valve due to
compromised airway patency. The otolaryngologist, SLP, and/or respiratory therapist (RT) could measure transtracheal pressure via manometry in order to determine
airway patency or the ability for the child to exhale adequately through the nose and
mouth [10].

play a role in swallowing and include V (trigeminal), VII (facial), IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (accessory), and XII (hypoglossal) (Table 3.2). Typical duration for the oral phase of swallowing is 1–2 seconds, and duration of the pharyngeal
phase is <1 second [13].
Historically, it was believed that only the brainstem centers were responsible for
controlling swallowing; however, later studies emphasized the importance of the
cerebral cortex during this action [14, 15]. The oral, pharyngeal, and esophageal
phases of swallowing are controlled by central pattern-generating circuitry of the
brainstem and peripheral reflexes. The central pattern generators of the brainstem
control the timing of swallowing, and the peripheral involvement depends on sensory feedback through reflexes of the pharynx and esophagus. The brainstem nuclei
that mediate the oral, pharyngeal, and esophageal phases of swallowing include the

3

A Look at Breathing, Feeding/Swallowing, and Speech Impairment in Patients…

39

trigeminal nucleus, reticular formation, nucleus tractus solitarius, nucleus ambiguous, dorsal motor nucleus, and ventromedial nucleus [16].

Oral Phase
During the oral preparatory phase of the swallow, labial compression reduces anterior spillage and promotes oral containment. Labial compression is important for
spoon clearance, labial rounding for straw drinking, and retraction/compression
movement during mastication.
Next, tension in the buccal musculature closes off the lateral sulcus and prevents
food particles from falling laterally into the sulcus between the mandible and the
cheek [11].
The tongue is divided into the oral portion and the pharyngeal portion, and the
oral tongue is under cortical and voluntary neural control [11]. The sensory receptors in the tongue control sensation of the bolus and taste. Tongue movements
include tongue cupping (important for bottle feeding), as the sides of the tongue seal
against the lateral alveolus for bolus holding. The oral cavity is sealed anteriorly by
elevation of the tongue tip and posteriorly by the soft palate and tongue contact. The
tongue elevates anteriorly and posteriorly to propel the bolus to the pharynx. As
food viscosity increases, the pressure of the tongue against the palate increases.
Adequate oral strength and range of motion help ensure that there is limitation to no
oral residue remaining in the oral cavity after swallowing [11, 17].

Pharyngeal Phase
Two critical roles of the pharyngeal phase of swallowing are to (1) generate enough
pressure to propel the bolus through the pharynx and upper esophageal sphincter
(into the esophagus) and (2) airway protection, closure of the larynx to prevent penetration or aspiration. Laryngeal penetration is when liquid or food enters the airway but does not move below the vocal cords. Aspiration occurs when food or
liquid passes below the vocal cords into the trachea. During the pharyngeal stage,
the soft palate elevates and contacts the lateral and posterior walls of the pharynx,
closing the nasopharynx at about the same time that the bolus head comes into the
pharynx. Soft palate elevation prevents bolus regurgitation into the nasal cavity. The
base of the tongue retracts (involuntary control from the brainstem but also can be
placed under some volitional control) to contact the bulging posterior pharyngeal
walls. The pharyngeal constrictor muscles contract sequentially from the top to the
bottom, squeezing the bolus downward, and the larynx elevates and the epiglottis
protects the airway [11, 17].

40

L. Brooks and S. Goudy

There are several airway protective mechanisms preventing aspiration of the foreign materials to the trachea before or during swallowing. The vocal folds close to
seal the glottis, the arytenoids tilt forward to contact the epiglottic base, the hyoid
bone and larynx are elevated and pulled anteriorly upward and forward, and the
epiglottis tilts backward to seal the laryngeal vestibule [11, 17].
Opening of the upper esophageal sphincter (UES) is essential for the bolus entry
into the esophagus. The UES is closed at rest during respiration and opens during
swallowing due to relaxation of the cricopharyngeus muscle, hyolaryngeal excursion, and pressure of the descending bolus [11].

Esophageal Phase
The esophagus is a muscular tube from the lower part of the UES to the lower
esophageal sphincter (LES). The UES is tensed at rest and opens during the swallow
to allow for passage of the bolus from the pharynx into the esophagus. The lower
esophageal sphincter is also tensed at rest to prevent regurgitation from the stomach,
relaxes during a swallow, and allows the bolus passage to the stomach. The cervical
esophagus (upper one third) is mainly composed of striated muscle, but thoracic
esophagus (lower two thirds) is smooth muscle. Through peristalsis the bolus moves
through the esophagus. Material moves from the UES to the LES within 8–20 seconds by a peristatic wave, regulated by the autonomic nervous system. Gravity
assists peristalsis in upright position [11, 17].

 eeding/Swallowing for Patients with Craniofacial
F
Microsomia (CFM)
Dysphagia is a feeding/swallowing impairment that includes any phases of the
swallow (oral, pharyngeal, or esophageal). Children present with dysphagia from
one or more of the following etiologies:
1. Neurologic (i.e., prematurity, central nervous system conditions)
2. Respiratory and other conditions (i.e., respiratory syncytial virus, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, cardiac disease)
3. Anatomic abnormalities of the aerodigestive tract (i.e., craniofacial abnormalities, vocal fold hypomobility, laryngeal cleft)
4. Gastrointestinal (i.e., reflux)
5. Other or unknown [18–23]
Children with dysphagia are at increased risk for developing respiratory compromise, failure to thrive, feeding refusal, and stressful interactions with their caregivers [18]. The goals for feeding/swallowing treatment are to implement evidence-based

adverse event (i.e., aspiration or pneumonia) [24].
The prevalence of feeding/swallowing difficulties in patients with CFM ranges
from 42% to 83% [25]. Anatomic anomalies of the jaw, palate, and cranial nerves in
patients with CFM can contribute to oropharyngeal phase dysfunction [26]. Children
with CFM with and without a cleft can present with impaired bolus control, delayed
swallowing initiation, nasopharyngeal regurgitation, post-swallow stasis/residue,
and aspiration in VFSS [26]. In addition, some children with CFM can have extra
cranial anomalies including CNS, cardiac, gastrointestinal, kidney, or skeletal.
Given these risk factors, it is important that an infant or child with CFM be closely
monitored for dysphagia (Table 3.3).
Given the wide phenotypic presentation associated with CFM, the assessment
and treatment of feeding/swallowing are highly individualized. If concerns arise a
speech/language pathologist should be consulted for an assessment and intervention
for impaired latch or extraction of fluid from bottle nipple, coughing with oral feeds,
instability with oral feeds, prolonged feeding times, and stridor/gulping with oral
feeds. Below are characteristics that may be present in a child with CFM and
descriptions of how that could impact feeding/swallowing (Table 3.4).

Mandible
Mandibular hypoplasia is present in 89–100% of patients with CFM [26]. More
severe hypoplasia showed more difficulty to form an appropriate bolus than less
severe hypoplasia, which can result in premature spillage of the bolus and possible
aspiration [26]. Structural anomalies such as mandibular hypoplasia can impact

At 12 months of age, the child transitions to intake of regular solids. Mastication

Poor Coordination of Respiration/Swallowing
Upper airway obstruction seen in patients with CFM can compromise oral feeding
[2]. Babies with CFM may present with tachypnea, stridor, and increased work of
breathing due to difficulty adequately breathing during the challenging task of oral
feeding. The ideal rhythm for bottle feeding is suck-swallow-breathe (SSB), occurring approximately once every second or 60 times a minute during bottle feeding.
Impaired coordination of breathing and swallowing can result in oxygen desaturations or bradycardia during feeding, and the baby may benefit from strategies such
as pacing/regulation [28, 29].
Some patients require high-flow nasal cannula support for respiratory compromise or noninvasive positive pressure ventilation which can increase pressure from
above and could compromise the child’s ability to close the airway adequately during a swallow resulting in misdirection of part of the bolus into the airway [30]. A
patient may require enteral feeding at that time which can include nasogastric tube,

3

A Look at Breathing, Feeding/Swallowing, and Speech Impairment in Patients…

43

orogastric tube, or gastrostomy tube. If there is a concern for emesis, the feeding
tube could bypass the stomach to the jejunum. Once a patient is oral feeding, quality
of the feeding is critical. Volume is a by-product of a “quality feeding” where there
is physiologic stability, good state regulation, and endurance [28, 29].
Infants and children who have been intubated (prolonged or emergent) may present with airway swelling, vocal cord injury, or tracheal injury which can compromise oral feeding [24]. Palate remodeling could also result, leading to velopharyngeal
incompetence [31, 32]. The clinician must consider the following: Was the intubation emergent? Were there multiple attempts to achieve successful intubation? Did
the patient self-extubate? Was intubation prolonged?

 isdirection of the Bolus into the Airway: Laryngeal
M
Penetration and Aspiration
Laryngeal penetration is defined as material entering the airway but does not pass
below the vocal cords. Aspiration is defined as passage of material below the vocal
cords [11]. Misdirection of the bolus into the airway (penetration or aspiration) is a
symptom of a physiologic swallowing impairment [33], and aspiration can occur
before the swallow secondary to oral control impairment or impaired timing/coordination, during the swallow secondary to incomplete closure of the laryngeal vestibule, or after the swallow secondary to weakness/impaired range of motion
(associated with residue). Thin liquids flow quickly through the oropharynx and can
be challenging to swallow safely for patients with dysphagia. Thus, liquids are the
most frequently aspirated material in children, and greater than 90% of the time
aspiration is silent [34]. If there is a concern that a patient has dysphagia and strategies during bedside treatment are not successful, an instrumental swallow examination could be performed to allow for visualization of the structures and swallowing
physiology. The two instrumental swallowing assessments are Videofluoroscopic
Swallow Study (VFSS)/Modified Barium Swallow Studies and Fiberoptic/Flexible
Endoscopic Evaluation of Swallowing. VFSS allows for views of the oral, pharyngeal, and esophageal phases of the swallow, whereas the VFSS assesses anatomy
and physiology of the nasopharynx, hypopharynx, and larynx (Figs. 3.1, 3.2,
and 3.3).
Strategies are used during VFSS and FEES to help guide the thin liquid bolus
away from the airway and into the esophagus, and the strategies will vary depending
on the type/etiology of the dysphagia. These strategies can include changing the
flow rate, bolus size, and positioning (i.e., side-lying, chin down, head turn, head
tilt) (Fig. 3.4).
When strategies are not successful in eliminating aspiration, thickened liquids (if
proven to be swallowed safely) may be recommended. Thickening liquids slows
oropharyngeal transit time while creating a more cohesive bolus, which makes the
liquid easier to control and minimizes the risk of aspiration before the swallow [35].
In addition, thickening can increase timing/duration of UES opening and amount of

44

Fig. 3.1 VFSS

Fig. 3.2 FEES

hyolaryngeal movement [12, 36]. However, there can be negative consequences
associated with thickened liquids, including refusal leading to dehydration, cost of
the thickening agent, accessibility of commercial thickeners, inconsistent achievement of target viscosity, and a negative impact on the child’s immature digestive
tract [37].

Pharyngeal Weakness
Movement of the lateral pharyngeal wall of the affected side can be reduced in
patients with CFM [25]. Decreased pharyngeal constriction can result in ineffective
bolus propulsion and/or pharyngeal residue, which can place the patient at risk for
aspiration after the swallow. The speech/language pathologist can confirm if the
residue is unilateral or bilateral by switching from lateral to anterior-posterior view
during a VFSS and then implement strategies to improve swallow function (Fig. 3.5).

46

L. Brooks and S. Goudy

Fig. 3.5 VFSS A–P view

Cleft Palate and Nasopharyngeal Regurgitation
Patients with CFM with a cleft lip/palate have been shown to have a higher likelihood of nasogastric feeding tube dependence at some point, which can impact
development of swallowing [26]. Suction strength/intraoral pressure can be severely
impaired if the patient also has a cleft palate. For bottle feeders, there are a variety
of nipple and bottle shapes, sizes, and characteristics that can help facilitate efficient
oral feeding. Specialty bottle nipples allow for extraction of fluid from up/down
movement of the jaw, rather than suction, and squeeze bottles to allow for the feeder
to compensate for the infant’s inability to extract fluid independently. Nasopharyngeal
regurgitation is present in a patient with a cleft palate, and approximately 20% of
children will require a secondary intervention for velopharyngeal insufficiency
post-cleft palate repair [38]. Infants with nasopharyngeal regurgitation may benefit
from a more upright feeding position [39].

3

A Look at Breathing, Feeding/Swallowing, and Speech Impairment in Patients…

Extracranial Anomalies That Impact Swallowing
Patients with CFM can present with extracranial anomalies including CNS, cardiac,
gastrointestinal, kidney, or skeletal involvement. Patients with cardiac involvement
might present with tachypnea that can compromise the ability to coordinate suck-­
swallow-­breathe [40]. Infants with cardiac abnormalities can also present with
fatigue and poor endurance during oral feeding. After cardiac repair the patient
could present with vocal cord impairment if the recurrent laryngeal nerve was compromised during surgery. Patients with gastrointestinal issues may have reduced
interest in oral feeding. Patients with reflux can place a patient in discomfort after
feed or, worse, risk for secondary aspiration of emesis.

Normal Speech and Language Development
The first 3 years of a child’s life are critical in the developmental of speech and
language skills. In infancy, babies are exposed to various stimuli, including sounds,
sights, and speech/language from others. Communication occurs early on in infancy,
such as crying to communicate a need, engaging or making eye contact, and reacting to certain sounds heard in the environment. While children may vary in their
development of speech and language, there is a typical progression or timetable of
speech and language skills that children follow (Table 3.5).

Speech and Language Development for a Child with CFM
Children with CFM have anomalies and comorbidities that can increase their risk
for speech, language, communication deficits, and neuropsychological deficits [41,
42]. Approximately 75–80% of children with CFM have some degree of hearing
impairment, most commonly conductive hearing loss, although sensorineural hearing loss can also be noted in approximately 10% of children with CFM [43, 44].
Children with features of CFM can demonstrate variable anomalies associated
with hearing loss including external ear abnormalities, aural atresia, and Eustachian
tube dysfunction [43]. Although most children with microtia have unilateral external ear malformations, they are at risk for bilateral hearing loss [1, 43]. Children
with CFM should have a comprehensive hearing assessment within the first
6 months of age to identify hearing loss and assess the type and severity of hearing
impairment [1]. Amplification options should be tailored to the degree of hearing
loss, nature, and laterality of hearing loss. Amplification can be beneficial for

3

A Look at Breathing, Feeding/Swallowing, and Speech Impairment in Patients…

49

children with even a mild hearing loss, and academic accommodations can be
implemented [45].
Severe to profound hearing loss can be associated with higher prevalence of
delays in speech articulation, receptive and expressive language delay, learning disabilities, and poorer communication and social skills [43]. Whether or not mild or
unilateral hearing loss can impact speech and language development is debatable [43].
In addition to the risk of delay with hearing loss, children can present with delays
or impairment due to facial nerve palsy, asymmetric soft palate movement, orofacial
clefting, malocclusion, tongue anomalies, and/or muscular deficiencies [42, 44, 46,
47]. These structural factors may impact articulation, speech intelligibility, vocal
quality, and/or resonance [42].
Children with CFM may present hypernasality and nasal emissions due to velopharyngeal dysfunction (VPD) associated with one or more of the following categories: structural deficits (cleft palate), physiologic (neuromotor), or mislearning of
articulation [38]. A submucous cleft palate can result in VPD if the velum is too
short to adequately contact the posterior pharyngeal wall [38]. A speech/language
pathologist can address accurate articulatory placement for speech sounds and correct errors associated with mislearning.
Children with CFM can be at higher risk of delayed language and neurodevelopmental milestones, particularly for patients with combined microtia and mandibular
hypoplasia [41, 48, 49]. Deficits can be particularly noted in receptive vocabulary
[47]. Children with CFM have complex healthcare needs and ongoing speech, language, and hearing monitoring throughout development [42].

Case Studies
Case Study #1
ZG was born at 34.4 weeks gestation with Goldenhar syndrome characterized by
microtia (no external auditory canal), mandibular hypoplasia on R side, cleft lip,
high arched and short palate, right sided macrostomia, R ear moderate to severe
conductive hearing loss on newborn hearing screening and ABR. Her ECHO,
RBUS, spinal films were normal. She presented with oxygen desaturations after
delivery so she was intubated for 1 day and then placed on supplemental O2 via
NC. PSG revealed 19 obstructive, 45 central, and 3 mixed apneas. There were 44
obstructive and 0 central hypopneas, giving an overall Apnea/Hypopnea Index
(AHI) of 19.1 events/hour. The Obstructive AHI was 11.4 events/hour. The Central
AHI was 7.7 events/hour. She also had tracheobronchomalacia and laryngomalacia
and underwent a supraglottoplasty which resolved the stridor but did not help with

50

L. Brooks and S. Goudy

her O2 desaturations. Five months later she had jaw surgery (rib graft, expanded
jaw), and her oxygenation improved and desaturations resolved. She also underwent
placement of gastrostomy tube (G-tube) at that time. Swallowing improved after
surgery as well, and her subsequent VFSS revealed no aspiration with thin liquids.
She fed best with the Dr. Brown’s specialty feeder (compression extraction) with a
preemie nipple. After so much time without oral feeding, she had difficulty with
interest and endurance, and given her G-tube feeding schedule, her mother felt that
she did not have an appetite. G-tube feeds were adjusted/compressed, and she has
more interest now in orally feeding. Foods and drinks were offered prior to her
bolus feeds when her appetite was the greatest.

Case Study #2
ES is a 7- month-old fraternal twin born at 36.3 weeks of gestation with craniofacial
microsomia which was not diagnosed prenatally (perinatologist noted a “recessed
chin” only). After birth she presented with features of CFM including with L microtia (L hearing loss) and mandibular hypoplasia. The lip and palate were intact without clefting. She had increased work of breathing with suprasternal retractions
requiring supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula. She had stridor concerning for
laryngomalacia, but endoscopy was compromised by her narrow airway (the epiglottis and tongue compromising the view of her larynx). Supraglottoplasty was
planned several times under sedation but discontinued, and given that her breathing
and stridor improved over time, she did not require surgical intervention. After
admission to the NICU, she presented with oxygen desaturation during oral feeding,
so she relied on an orogastric feeding tube for nutrition and hydration. She transitioned from continuous enteral feeding to bolus feeds, but given emesis the feeds
ran over 2 hours Q3. She was discharged home with OG tube taking small-volume
expressed breast milk, 5 ml, for practice. She had a gastrostomy tube placed at
10 weeks of age. She had an apnea monitor at home but did not have any events.
PSG showed OSA AHI of 16.6, and pulmonology put her on oxygen during the day
and night. A tracheostomy was discussed, but she was able to avoid that surgery
with improvement from supplemental O2. Follow-up PSG was normal, and she was
able to wean from O2, with only a home pulse ox to monitor oxygen saturations.
She received outpatient SLP through the craniofacial clinic and advanced oral intake
to 70 ml in 20 minutes via Dr. Brown’s specialty feeder (compression extraction)
using preemie nipple. At 4 months of age, she regressed and became significantly
aversive to oral. Weight gain was a challenge, and her enteral feeds were closely
monitored. Nutrition increased her calories from 20 kcal to 22 kcal. She started to
have worsening emesis at ~5 months of age, and G-tube schedule was changed to
continuous feeds overnight and bolus during the day. She is currently practicing oral
feeds of expressed breast milk via Dr. Brown’s specialty feeder with level 1 nipple
and has not initiated intake of purees. She has not yet had an instrumental swallow
study. She is less verbal than her twin sister and is starting early intervention soon.

Extracraniofacial Manifestations
of Craniofacial Microsomia
Jessica S. Lee and Paul W. Kloostra

Introduction
Craniofacial microsomia (CFM) represents a spectrum of congenital malformations of
the craniofacial structures in the first and second branchial arches, with 5–30% of
patients manifesting with asymmetric bilateral involvement [1, 2]. Although the term
craniofacial microsomia suggests that the affected structures solely pertain to the structures of the head and neck, many extracraniofacial manifestations are associated with
CFM and are important to recognize for accurate diagnosis and management. As with
many other craniofacial anomalies, patients with CFM require longitudinal care by a
multidisciplinary craniofacial team consisting of craniofacial surgeons (oral and maxillofacial surgery, otolaryngology, and/or plastic surgery), neurosurgeons, nursing, nutritionists, oral and maxillofacial surgery and otolaryngology (when either is not the
primary craniofacial surgeon), orthodontists, pediatric dentists, pediatricians, psychologists, social workers, and speech pathologists. This chapter provides an overview of the
extracraniofacial systems that may be involved, the associated diagnoses within each
system, physical exam findings, and imaging available to initiate a workup, or rules out
a suspected diagnosis. However, it is beyond the scope of this chapter to discuss the
various nuances of each diagnosis and its management but should be used to direct the
reader toward the many other resources available for a more in-depth discussion.

Etiology
Several theories have been proposed to explain the etiology of CFM, including the
disturbance of vascular development within the first and second branchial arches
during the first 6 weeks of gestation, teratogen exposure, and/or an error in migration of neural crest cells responsible for the formation of craniofacial structures.
With the use of a mouse model, Poswillo demonstrated some of the phenotypic
anomalies seen in CFM by causing vascular disruption of the stapedial artery in
utero resulting in the destruction of local and regional differentiating craniofacial
tissues [3–5]. Exposure to teratogens, such as thalidomide and retinoic acid, has
been documented to produce craniofacial anomalies similar to that of CFM, including extracraniofacial manifestations [6, 7]. Accutane (13-cis-retinoic acid) is known
to destroy neural crest cells and disrupt their migration resulting in craniofacial
anomalies resembling CFM and Treacher Collins syndrome, based on timing of
gestational exposure [6, 8, 9]. A study by Lammer et al. (1985) demonstrated a
characteristic pattern of anomalies in 21 infants exposed to isotretinoin during the
first trimester involving craniofacial, cardiac, thymic, and central nervous system
structures [10], suggesting a deleterious effect on cephalic neural crest cell activity
observed in patients with CFM.
A genetic basis for CFM has also been well documented in the literature where
autosomal dominant and recessive patterns of transmission have been described in
families with features of CFM with a large case series reporting a positive history of
50% of patients. Variability in penetrance and expression along with heterogeneity
is likely the reason for the wide phenotypic spectrum observed in CFM [11].
The exact etiology of CFM remains a subject of debate and is likely secondary to
a multifactorial process including both genetic and environmental factors resulting
in a wide spectrum of phenotypic variability.

Classification of Craniofacial Microsomia
Several classification systems of CFM have been proposed. In 1969, Pruzansky
classified mandibular anomalies of CFM into three types, I through III, based on the
severity of hypoplasia of the ramus and condyle [12]. This classification system was
later modified by Kaban et al. (1988) where type II was subdivided to IIA and IIB,
to clarify the degree of mandibular function and location of the temporomandibular
joint apparatus, which would then determine the necessary surgical correction, if
any [13]. This modified classification of mandibular anomalies was included in the
OMENS classification system, first conceived by Vento et al. (1991), to include
other craniofacial manifestations of CFM in which each letter represents one of the
five major manifestations: O for orbital distortion, M for mandibular hypoplasia, E

4

Extracraniofacial Manifestations of Craniofacial Microsomia

57

for ear anomaly, N for nerve involvement, and S for soft tissue deficiency [14].
Owing to the frequent association with cardiac, skeletal, and central nervous systems, the OMENS classification was modified by Horgan et al. (1995) to include
extracraniofacial manifestations of CFM and expanded to the OMENS+ (plus) designation [15].

 xtracraniofacial Anomalies Associated
E
with Craniofacial Microsomia
A review of the literature suggests that up to 55% of patients with craniofacial
microsomia demonstrate extracraniofacial differences [15–18]. Several studies have
demonstrated a higher rate of association between specific organ systems (e.g., skeletal, central nervous system, cardiac) and CFM, while other systems did not demonstrate as strong of an association (e.g., pulmonary, gastrointestinal) [15–17, 19].
Syndromologists typically consider an anomaly to be associated with a diagnosis if
it occurs in at least 10–15% of patients [15, 20]. Based on this definition, associated
extracraniofacial manifestations of CFM include vertebral (24.3–35.5%), cardiac
(18.5–33.1%), central nervous system (10.4–18.2%), developmental (8–73%), and
genitourinary (10.5–15.8%). Other organ systems, such as gastrointestinal and pulmonary, were less frequently associated, with a prevalence of only in 7–11.6% and
3–9%, respectively [15–17, 19] (Table 4.1). Given the common association of extracraniofacial anomalies with CFM, it is essential that CFM patients are screened
with a comprehensive history, prenatal imaging, and postnatal physical examination
with imaging.
