Vertebral and Central Nervous System
Vertebral anomalies are the most frequent extracraniofacial manifestations associated with CFM with a prevalence of 24.3–35.5% [15–17, 19]. The most common
anomalies include scoliosis, hemivertebrae, block vertebrae (Fig. 4.1), and rib
anomalies. Less commonly associated manifestations include vertebral agenesis,
failure of vertebral fusion, and cervical spine instability, such as atlanto-axial
subluxation.
The prevalence of central nervous system (CNS) anomalies is reported to be
between 10.4% and 18.2% [15–17, 19]. The most common structural anomalies of
the CNS include neural tube defects (e.g., encephalocele), agenesis or hypoplasia of
the corpus callosum, intracranial lipomas, Arnold-Chiari malformations, hydrocephaly, ventriculomegaly, cerebral hypoplasia, and microcephaly [15, 16, 18,

4

Extracraniofacial Manifestations of Craniofacial Microsomia

59

Fig. 4.1 3D ultrasound
demonstrating fused/block
vertebrae

21–31]. A higher prevalence of developmental disorders, such as intellectual disability, language, speech, or neuropsychomotor delay, has also been associated with
CFM when compared to the general population [32–34]. Some CNS anomalies may
be detected prenatally via α-fetoprotein (AFP) concentrations in maternal serum
and sonography which may detect such conditions as neural tube defects, hydrocephalus, and agenesis of the corpus callosum [35, 36].
Physical exam findings related to vertebral anomalies include torticollis, shortening, and/or decreased flexibility of the neck and asymmetric shoulder height. The
lower back should be examined for hypertrichosis, skin tags, dimples, sinus tracts,
and lipomas which are suggestive of underlying intraspinal anomalies. The thorax
should be examined for symmetry and rib size anomalies. In older children, the
spine and thorax should also be examined while the patient is bending forward to
evaluate for size and symmetry. The vertebrae should also be examined for deformities and disruptions in the curvature of the spine [37].
Physical exam findings significant for CNS anomalies include sacral dimples,
port wine stain, genitourinary, vertebral anomalies, and micro- or macrocephaly.
Sacral cutaneous dimple over the midline of the back (Fig. 4.2), dermal sinus, port

60

J. S. Lee and P. W. Kloostra

Fig. 4.2 Deep sacral
dimple

wine stain, focal hirsutism, lower extremity anomalies, and anal and genitourinary
anomalies may suggest the presence of an underlying neural tube defect [38, 39].
Patients with micro- or macrocephaly will demonstrate a head circumference greater
than two standard deviations from the mean. Head circumference should be measured and tracked with a centile growth chart [35]. Microcephaly should be monitored for developmental delay, while macrocephaly should be evaluated and
monitored for signs and symptoms of hydrocephalus including irritability, seizures,
somnolence, vomiting, loss of muscle strength, or tone.
A neurological exam should include evaluation of lower extremity reflexes, sensation, strength, and symmetry. Suspected limb atrophy should be further assessed
with limb length and calf circumference. Lower extremity findings may indicate the
presence of a long-standing neurologic anomaly, such as tethered cord syndrome or
diastematomyelia, which may respond to operative intervention [37]. The presence
of vertebral anomalies on clinical exam should raise suspicion for possible intraspinal pathology.
Imaging may be indicated in any patient with positive physical exam findings, as
well as for tracking growth over time and helping anticipate future progression [37].
Posteroanterior and lateral radiographs of the thoracolumbosacral spine, including
the pelvis, should be obtained with inspection of the entire spine for signs of pathology, as dysplastic vertebrae are often non-contiguous [37].
Suspicious findings on plain films should be further characterized with CT and/
or MRI. CT and MR imaging unfortunately possess inherent risks including ionizing radiation and possible need for sedation in young children, respectively.
However, vertebral anomalies are commonly associated with CFM; Buckley and
Guille (2010) reported a high risk of occult intraspinal anomalies, including tethered cords and diastematomyelia [37, 40, 41]. Trenga et al. (2016) also found a
higher incidence of spinal cord anomalies in patients with complex bony malformations (>2 vertebra involved) when compared to less complex bony malformations
[42]. Similarly, some CNS anomalies, such as agenesis of the corpus callosum or
intracranial lipomas, may not be apparent on clinical exam [26]. Renkema et al.
(2018) reported a notable disparity of the prevalence of CNS anomalies among
studies that routinely obtained CT or MR imaging (42–69%) and those that did not
(2–29%) [15, 16, 18, 21–31, 43].

61

4 Extracraniofacial Manifestations of Craniofacial Microsomia

Due to the high incidence of occult vertebral and CNS pathology, routine screening of CFM patients with CT and/or MRI seems warranted, especially for those not
previously evaluated, and investigation of concerning findings on history and physical exam. In addition, it is reasonable to include a complete view of the head, vertebrae, and spine when obtaining advanced imaging. As always, the prudent surgeon
should use his or her best clinical judgment to weigh the risk, benefits, and alternatives of additional imaging with each patient’s unique presentation.

Developmental Disorders
Screening for developmental disorders with timely diagnosis is crucial, as children
with CFM have a higher prevalence of intellectual disability (18–58%), language or
speech delay (8–68%), and neuropsychomotor delay (17–73%) [24, 26, 29, 44].
Screening for developmental delay in infants and toddlers from birth to age 5 should
be assessed with a standardized screening tool (e.g., Center for Disease Control
Milestone Checklist) which can assist with early detection, referral, and possible
intervention [45]. However, assessment of development and psychosocial health
cannot be limited to a single assessment and must be monitored regularly over time.
Table 4.2 provides a summary of the recommended measures for psychosocial
screening for children with craniofacial differences.

and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition (DSM-5) and the American
Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (AAIDD), which possess similar definitions of ID but differ in their definitions of severity [46].
Evaluation and management of speech and language delays in children include
determining whether an impairment in communication skills exists, specifying the
nature of any impairments, and initiate appropriate intervention strategies.
Development of speech and language can be assessed with standardized screening
tools, such as the CDC Milestone Checklist; however, caretakers should be aware
that each child’s developmental timeline may differ. If the child is not meeting
expected milestones for speech and language, a comprehensive developmental evaluation, in addition to a speech and language evaluation, may be warranted.
The American Cleft Palate – Craniofacial Association (ACPA) Standards of Care
require that all cleft and craniofacial teams have in place “a mechanism to initially
and periodically assess and treat, as appropriate, the psychological and social needs
of patients and families/caregivers and to refer for further treatment as necessary”
and that “the team uses a process to evaluate its own performance with regard to
patient assessment, treatment or satisfaction and to make improvements as a result
of those evaluations.” [47] The Americleft Psychosocial Group (APG) has identified
measures that can be used efficiently within the context of a routine cleft or craniofacial team visit and encourages the use of valid and reliable measures that would
allow for consistent assessment of psychosocial adjustment of children within teams
and allow for comparisons of outcomes across teams [48].
The APG has identified measures within three major categories to properly
address psychosocial needs of patients and families/caregivers which can be used
routinely in the context of a cleft or craniofacial team visit: (1) family risk, (2) psychosocial adjustment, and (3) quality of life. The recommended measures address
categories that are both generic (used with children with and without cleft and/or
craniofacial anomalies) and specific to children with cleft and/or craniofacial anomalies. Further, they have identified measures that allow for both children (patients)
to self-report and for their caregiver to report on these measures to include both
perspectives “Heppner CE, April 27, 2020, Clinical audit and psychosocial screening in cleft and craniofacial teams, Personal communication”.
Family risk measures can be assessed with the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory
Family Impact Module (PedsQL FIM) and the Psychosocial Assessment Tool-­
Craniofacial Version (PAT-CV) which are completed by caregivers and can be used
as screening for families.
Psychosocial adjustment measures include both child (patient) and caregiver
report instruments. The most widely used and internationally validated instrument
is the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) which provides caregiver report forms for
children 18 months of age into adulthood and self-report instruments beginning at
11 years of age. The Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System
(PROMIS®) also utilizes child and caregiver report instruments which evaluates
and monitors physical, mental, and social health in children and adults. This

4

Extracraniofacial Manifestations of Craniofacial Microsomia

63

National Institutes of Health (NIH) supported measurement tool is free of charge for
all users “Heppner CE, April 27, 2020, Clinical audit and psychosocial screening in
cleft and craniofacial teams, Personal communication”.
The third major category of assessment recommended by the APG is quality of
life. The Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) is a generic measure of quality of life, assessing physical, emotional, social, and school functioning, with caregiver proxy report available beginning in infancy and child self-report available
beginning at age 5. The CLEFT-Questionnaire (CLEFT-Q) is a cleft-specific measure completed only by the child beginning at age 8 and assesses the child’s perception of appearance, speech, psychological adjustment, social functioning, and
physical functioning in the area most likely to be affected by the cleft, drinking, and
eating “Heppner CE, April 27, 2020, Clinical audit and psychosocial screening in
cleft and craniofacial teams, Personal communication”.
Patients with facial differences, including CFM, are at risk for intellectual disability, speech and language delay, neuropsychomotor delay, poor self-esteem,
maladaptive or poor coping skills, and poor home and community interactions.
Ensuring our patients are treated within a multidisciplinary setting, screened early
and regularly for developmental, speech and language, and psychosocial development, is imperative. The ideal comprehensive cleft and craniofacial team will
include a social worker, speech language pathologist, and psychologist present at
team meetings, but all teams must, at the very least, have access to these services
when at-risk patients and/or families are identified with the aforementioned screening tools.

Cardiac
Cardiac anomalies are commonly observed in the CFM population with a prevalence rate of 18.5–33.1% [19]. The predominant cardiac anomalies include ventricular septal defects, atrial septal defects, valvular defects, patent ductus arteriosus,
and Tetralogy of Fallot. Less common anomalies include pulmonary valve stenosis,
transposition of the great arteries, and dextrocardia.
Diagnosis of cardiac anomalies may be possible with prenatal obstetric sonography, with the optimal age for screening being 18–22 weeks of gestation [49].
Advanced fetal echocardiography may be indicated if maternal risk factors such as
fetal cardiac or non-cardiac abnormalities are suspected on obstetric ultrasound,
such as increased nuchal translucency or congenital heart disease in a first-degree
relative of the fetus [50]. While the cardiac screening exam, consisting of the four-­
chamber and outflow tract views, is designed to maximize the detection of heart
anomalies during a second-trimester scan, some cardiac anomalies such as fetal
arrhythmias, valvular insufficiency, obstruction, or cardiomyopathy may not be
detected or present, until after 18–22 weeks of gestation [51–53]. A fetus diagnosed
with CFM should prompt a high index of suspicion for cardiac defects and consideration for fetal echocardiography. When a fetal cardiac anomaly is diagnosed with

64

J. S. Lee and P. W. Kloostra

fetal echocardiography, a referral should be made to a pediatric cardiologist before
delivery, to discuss pre- and perinatal management.
Newborn examination should include visual inspection, auscultation, pulse
oximetry, blood pressure, abdominal, and extremity exams. A newborn demonstrating central cyanosis should alert the physician to possible underlying congenital
heart disease (CHD). Cardiac auscultation may demonstrate abnormal heart sounds
(e.g., S3 gallop) or pathologic murmurs. Pulse oximetry should be used to screen for
CHD as some newborns may be asymptomatic. Pre- and post-ductal pulse oximetry
should be obtained to identify ductal-dependent lesions, as these infants are at
increased risk for significant morbidity and mortality [54]. Blood pressure discrepancies measuring ≥10 mmHg higher in the upper extremity compared to the lower
and diminished or absent pulses in the lower extremity are also suggestive of CHD
[55]. Hepatomegaly in newborns where the liver edge is palpated more than 3 cm
below the right costal margin may be seen in infants with heart failure secondary to CHD.
In the presence of a positive physical exam finding, screening should be continued with an electrocardiogram (EKG) and chest radiograph. While some lesions
such as tricuspid atresia and pulmonary stenosis may present with specific EKG
patterns, many cyanotic lesions will not be apparent on a neonatal EKG, and a high
index of suspicion should be maintained even with a negative EKG. A chest radiograph should be obtained for a newborn with cyanosis or respiratory distress, assessing for non-cardiac causes, such as pneumothorax, pulmonary hypoplasia, or
diaphragmatic hernia [56].
In the setting of positive physical exam findings, but negative EKG and/or chest
radiograph, newborn echocardiography should be obtained. This can provide a
definitive diagnosis of congenital heart defects with information on cardiac anatomy and function and should be performed in consultation with a pediatric cardiologist. An echocardiogram should be considered for first-line workup if signs and
symptoms of a critical cardiac anomalies are present, such as shock, cardiomegaly,
severe cyanosis, or respiratory distress concerning for pulmonary edema. The
necessity, timing, and frequency of follow-up echocardiogram assessment should
be made in conjunction with your pediatric cardiologist, guided by the nature and
severity of the cardiac anomaly, presence of heart failure, anticipated timing and
mechanism of progression, and the options available for intervention.

Extremity
Extremity anomalies are fairly common in CFM patients, with a prevalence rate of
11.6–20.7% [15, 16]. The most common include polydactyly, absent or anomalous
thumb with or without radial dysplasia, and congenital hip dislocation. Other
regions of the skeletal system may accompany extremity anomalies, such as the ribs
and vertebrae, including the cervical spine (see section on “Vertebral and Central
Nervous System”).

4

Extracraniofacial Manifestations of Craniofacial Microsomia

65

Prenatal detection of extremity anomalies may not be demonstrated on ultrasound until the end of the second trimester or beginning of the third trimester as
endochondral ossification occurs during the third trimester.
Physical exam of a newborn should include evaluation of height/length and
upper and lower extremity morphology and lengths, along with the number and
morphology of digits. Radial dysplasia encompasses a range of presentations from
a minor, such as an isolated thumb anomaly, to more severe, such as the complete
absence of the thumb and radius with severe ulnar bowing, elbow stiffness, and
humeral hypoplasia (Fig. 4.3) [57, 58]. A shortened, unilateral lower extremity may
be a sign of unilateral hip dislocation. The Ortolani and/or Barlow maneuvers may
be used to evaluate the stability of the hips, where a palpable “clunk” may be elicited in the affected hip [59].
The underlying skeletal morphology associated with polydactyly, first-digit
(thumb) hypoplasia, or first-digit agenesis with radial dysplasia can be assessed
with pain radiography. Depending on the severity, treatment may include occupational and/or physical therapy, splinting and/or casting, or surgery.
Ultrasonography is the first-line imaging for suspected congenital hip dislocation
in the first 4 or 6 months of life; however, it is technique sensitive. Radiographs are
helpful in infants older than 4–6 months, when the femoral head and acetabulum are

ossified. More advanced imaging such as CT or MRI are not typically useful in
making the diagnosis but may aid in the evaluation of postsurgical reduction [60].
Infants born with or suspected of extremity anomalies should be referred to an
orthopedic and/or plastic surgeon for further evaluation and management.

Genitourinary
Genitourinary anomalies occur in 10.5–15.8% of patients with CFM. The most
common include renal agenesis or aplasia, renal ectopia, hydronephrosis, ureteral
anomalies, vesicoureteral reflux (VUR), hypospadias, and cryptorchidism [15–
17, 19].
Initial diagnosis of congenital genitourinary anomalies is possible with routine
antenatal ultrasonography as fetal kidneys can be detected by the 12th to 15th week
of gestation [61]. However, the renal cortex and medulla may not be distinct from
each other until the 20th to 25th week of gestation [62]. Amniotic fluid volume can
be assessed at or beyond 20 weeks of gestation with decreased amniotic fluid (oligohydramnios) being a positive predictor of abnormal fetal renal function and indicates bilateral fetal renal dysfunction or a poorly functioning solitary kidney [63].
Postnatal evaluation should include an abdominal exam, where a palpable mass
may represent hydronephrosis secondary to obstructive uropathy. An enlarged bladder in a male infant, especially after voiding, is suggestive of bladder outlet obstruction (i.e., posterior urethral valves) [64]. A single umbilical artery is also associated
with an increased risk of congenital genitourinary anomalies, particularly VUR
[65]. Pulmonary evaluation in neonates with severe oligohydramnios is critical to
rule out pulmonary hypoplasia with severe cases often requiring intensive supportive care after birth [66].
Postnatal evaluation of the genitourinary tract with renal ultrasonography is recommended in infants with renal malformation detected on antenatal ultrasound
[67]. Routine ultrasonography should not be performed until after the infant returns
to their birth weight to ensure volume repletion and increased renal plasma flow,
glomerular filtration rate, and urine output, as this will avoid underestimating the
severity of hydronephrosis compared to renal ultrasonography completed within the
first 48 hours of life. In contrast, neonates with known bilateral renal involvement,
solitary kidney, or a history of oligohydramnios should have a renal ultrasound
completed within the first 24 hours of life due to their increased risk of severe renal
anomaly and need for intervention [67]. Additional diagnostic tests such as serum
creatinine and voiding cystourethrography (VCUG) may be obtained to assess renal
function in patients with bilateral renal anomalies as well as serial ultrasounds to
monitor renal growth and development. These findings should be discussed with a
pediatric urologist and/or pediatric surgeon for the appropriate timing and management of congenital urologic anomalies.

4

Extracraniofacial Manifestations of Craniofacial Microsomia

67

Gastrointestinal
Extracraniofacial anomalies involving the gastrointestinal (GI) system are relatively
uncommon with a prevalence of 7–11.6% in CFM patients [15, 16, 19]. The most
common GI anomalies reported include esophageal atresia (EA) with possible tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF), anorectal stenosis or atresia, imperforate anus, diaphragmatic hernia, and umbilical hernia.
Congenital GI anomalies may be first detected on a standard obstetric ultrasound
during the second or third trimester which may demonstrate polyhydramnios with a
small or collapsed stomach, suspicious for esophageal atresia [68–70]. However, it
may be difficult to diagnose esophageal atresia if it is associated with a tracheoesophageal fistula, which allows amniotic fluid to flow into the stomach, resulting in
relatively normal stomach and amniotic volumes [71]. Congenital diaphragmatic
hernias (CDH) may also be diagnosed via prenatal ultrasound with the majority of
cases detectable by 24 weeks of gestation, or later, detection prior to 24 weeks is
associated with greater severity and may require further workup and/or referral to a
fetal surgeon to prevent or reverse pulmonary hypoplasia and restore adequate lung
development for neonatal survival [72, 73].
Anorectal atresia may be identified as early as 12 weeks of gestation with dilated
loops of fetal bowel seen on prenatal ultrasound [74], but more recent studies demonstrate that the absence of a “target sign” on prenatal ultrasound may be the most
important sign of anorectal malformation [74–78].
The newborn abdominal exam should first evaluate overall size and appearance,
noting defects in the abdominal wall and assessing for distension. A scaphoid abdomen with the absence of breath sounds on the ipsilateral side is suggestive of a
congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Palpation of the abdomen should be completed to
assess for defects of the abdominal wall and abdominal masses, which require further workup.
Esophageal atresia (EA) is an interruption of esophageal continuity, often associated with tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) [79]. The classification of the various
relationships between esophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula was first
described by Vogt (1929) and modified by Gross (1953) (Fig. 4.4) [80, 81]. A neonate with isolated esophageal atresia (Gross Type A) generally present with excessive drooling, choking, and inability to feed. Gross Type B, C, and D represents a
combination of EA with TEF: EA with proximal TEF (Type B), EA with distal TEF
(Type C), or EA with proximal and distal TEF (Type D) [81]. These combinations
place the newborn at risk for aspiration of food, saliva, and/or gastric acid. Gross
Type E, also known as an H-type TEF, consists of an intact esophagus with TEF,
often less symptomatic and diagnosed later in life. Infants with a Type E anomaly
often present with a long-standing history of recurring aspiration and multiple episodes of pneumonia [82].
Finally, the anus should be inspected for presence and position. However, patency
cannot be assumed until verified by passing of meconium, usually by 48 hours of

68

J. S. Lee and P. W. Kloostra

Fig. 4.4 Gross classification of tracheoesophageal malformation

life, and failure to pass meconium in the setting of progressive abdominal distension, refusal to feed, and vomiting should be investigated for possible anorectal
atresia or stenosis [83]. Atresia or stenosis may not be apparent on initial exam in
infants with a normal external anus; however, it may be confirmed with inability to
pass a rectal temperature probe 2–3 cm from the anal verge. When anorectal atresia
or stenosis is suspected clinically in the setting of poor feeding or no passage of
meconium, plain radiographs of the abdomen should be obtained [84],

demonstrating colonic obstruction. If the diagnosis of an atresia or stenosis is suspected but not demonstrated on plain film radiography, a barium enema should be
obtained [85–87].
Suspected esophageal atresia can be confirmed by obtaining a chest radiograph
after attempting to pass a catheter into the stomach more than 15 cm. Gross Types
A–D (Fig. 4.5) will demonstrate the catheter curled in the proximal esophageal
pouch, whereas Type E, consisting of a continuous esophagus with TEF, will not.
The presence of air in the proximal stump of the esophagus is suggestive of Type A
(no fistula) or B (proximal fistula), and gastric air suggests the presence of a distal
fistula as in Type C or D. A barium swallow study with passage of contrast from the
esophagus into the tracheobronchial tree confirms the presence of a proximal fistula
(Type B, D, or E). Type E fistulas can be difficult to diagnose and may require
esophageal endoscopy and bronchoscopy. CT is generally not necessary; however,
three-dimensional virtual bronchoscopy may be beneficial for surgical planning [88].
Umbilical hernias are asymptomatic and spontaneously resolve within the first
5 years of life and may be observed if they demonstrate progressive decrease in
umbilical ring size. However, some hernias may interfere with feeding and become
incarcerated or strangulated if the hernia contains bowel, and, although rare, an
incarcerated umbilical hernia is a surgical emergency. Umbilical rings that are
greater than 1.5 cm in diameter and do not decrease in size, or elicit symptoms are
a relative indication for surgical repair [89, 90].
Suspected congenital diaphragmatic hernias (CDH) that have not already been
diagnosed in utero should be evaluated with chest radiography, which will demonstrate herniation of abdominal contents into the thoracic cavity (Fig. 4.6) [91]. If
undiagnosed CDH is suspected, radiographic evaluation should not be delayed, as

most patients develop respiratory distress. Severe cases often require endotracheal
intubation or even extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) [92–94].
Suspected or confirmed gastrointestinal anomalies should be followed up with a
pediatric otolaryngologist and pediatric gastroenterologist and/or surgeon for further workup with possible intervention.

Respiratory
Although fairly uncommon, respiratory system anomalies may accompany patients
born with CFM with a prevalence rate of 3–9% [15, 16, 19]. The most common
anomalies include pulmonary hypoplasia choanal atresia, laryngomalacia, tracheomalacia, and tracheal stenosis.
Prenatal ultrasound may confirm the presence of pulmonary hypoplasia, especially in the setting of congenital diaphragmatic hernia or oligohydramnios. Other
respiratory anomalies, however, are not well characterized with prenatal ultrasound.
Respiratory system anomalies may be apparent soon after birth. Many, including
pulmonary hypoplasia, present with non-specific signs and symptoms such as
tachypnea, retractions, respiratory distress, hypoxemia, and/or cyanosis. A newborn
in respiratory distress should be managed according to standard guidelines relative
to gestational age.

4

Extracraniofacial Manifestations of Craniofacial Microsomia

71

Children with choanal atresia may vary in presentation depending on the extent
of involvement, as they can present unilaterally or bilaterally. Those born with unilateral choanal atresia, which represent two-thirds of cases, typically present later in
life with unilateral nasal discharge and/or obstruction [95, 96]. Infants born with
bilateral choanal atresia typically present with noisy breathing, upper airway
obstruction, or cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying.
Choanal atresia should be suspected if a number 5 or 6 French catheter cannot be
passed through the nasal fossa into the oropharynx with a distance of at least
32 mm [97].
Laryngomalacia in a newborn will often manifest with intermittent, low-pitched,
“wet” inspiratory stridor and may be louder when feeding or sleeping [98, 99].
Tracheomalacia will present with different symptoms based on location and severity. Intrathoracic lesions typically present with a barking and croup-like cough,
whereas extrathoracic lesions will present with an inspiratory stridor. Tracheal stenosis may demonstrate an inspiratory stridor or expiratory wheeze refractory to
bronchodilator therapy [100].
Chest radiography is typically the first-line imaging modality obtained for infants
with a suspected respiratory anomaly, differentiating between cardiac and pulmonary causes such as pneumothorax, pulmonary hypoplasia, and/or diaphragmatic
hernia [56]. Infants with pulmonary hypoplasia may demonstrate a diffuse haziness
and coarse interstitial pattern on their chest radiograph, reflecting atelectasis or
inflammation, with low or normal lung volumes. Suspected choanal atresia can be
confirmed with CT, typically demonstrating narrowing of the posterior nasal cavity
at the level of the pterygoid plate [101]. Tracheal anomalies, however, are not well
visualized with plain film radiography or CT. While CT and MRI “virtual tracheobronchoscopy” have been reported as viable options for the assessment of tracheal
stenosis, a multidetector CT is needed to provide both end-inspiratory and end-­
expiratory images to demonstrate the dynamic change in tracheomalacia [101–105].
A child with suspected respiratory anomalies including choanal atresia, tracheal
stenosis, tracheomalacia, or laryngomalacia should be referred to a pediatric otolaryngologist for full endoscopic evaluation.

Conclusion
Extracraniofacial manifestations should be suspected in children born with craniofacial microsomia as up to 55% of patients are likely to demonstrate these findings.
A systematic approach to each extracraniofacial organ system is recommended to
work up or rule out various suspected diagnoses. As with the care for craniofacial
manifestations of CFM, multidisciplinary and longitudinal care is often required for
these extracraniofacial diagnoses as well.

Chapter 5

Management of the Mandibular Deformity
in the Growing Patient with Craniofacial
Microsomia
Cory M. Resnick and Bonnie L. Padwa

Treatment of the Growing Child
Craniofacial surgeons initially concentrated on the correction of end-stage deformities in older children and adults. Advances in anesthetic and surgical techniques and
in understanding the pathogenesis of craniofacial anomalies encouraged earlier
intervention for certain malformations during growth. The hypothesis was that
operative correction of a craniofacial malformation in the growing child would normalize the functional matrix, thereby optimizing future growth potential by placing
structures in a more anatomical position and improving function. In theory, this
would minimize secondary deformity and distortion by releasing restricted growth
of adjacent skeletal structures. Moreover, early intervention can improve appearance, body image, and socialization of the child.
The goal of treatment of CFM in childhood is to achieve improved function and
optimal facial symmetry and aesthetics when craniofacial growth is complete. The
treatment approach is dictated by mandibular skeletal type (Kaban types I, IIA, IIB,
and III), presence of a midface deformity (cant of the maxillary occlusal plane and
piriform rims), age (chronological, dental, skeletal), and psychosocial development

of the child. (Table 5.1 provides a summary of general assessment principles by age

In the growing child, the first goal is to surgically create an open bite on the
affected side by elongation and rotation of the mandible to the midline. The open
bite must be maintained and controlled to permit leveling of the occlusal plane by
vertical maxillary growth on the affected side. Success depends on the potential for
vertical growth of the midface and maxillary alveolus as the deciduous teeth are
shed and the permanent teeth erupt. Therefore, a child with CFM must be in the
mixed dentition to benefit from early management. The protocol is not applicable
after the permanent teeth have erupted because vertical midfacial and dentoalveolar
growth is essentially complete by this time.
Treatment should proceed in a stepwise fashion, conforming to a predictable
sequence with several sequential phases consisting of some or all of the following:
functional appliance treatment, early orthodontic treatment, early mandibular operation (including ramus and fossa construction if necessary), immediate postsurgical
dental appliance to support graft remodeling or regenerate consolidation, comprehensive orthodontic treatment, treatment of the end-stage skeletal deformity in non-­
growing patients, and soft tissue augmentation.

5

Management of the Mandibular Deformity in the Growing Patient with Craniofacial…

79

Functional Appliance Treatment
Impaired mandibular growth may be the result of absent or reduced condylar cartilage proliferation and reduced protrusive action of the condyle due to the absolute
or relative absence of lateral pterygoid muscle function on the condylar head. A
functional orthodontic appliance that enhances the neuromuscular environment,
promotes mandibular and maxillary growth, and expands the soft tissue envelope on
the affected side may be used in young patients with CFM. The appliance is a
removable acrylic orthodontic activator with guide planes and shields that is constructed to hold the affected side of the mandible in a lowered and protrusive position. The appliance stimulates bone apposition in the ramus-condyle unit and
coronoid process by substituting for the normal translatory and protrusive motion
produced by the lateral pterygoid muscle. The degree of deformity and patient compliance greatly affect the outcome of functional appliance therapy. Response to
functional appliance therapy has been shown to be beneficial in patients with
type I CFM.
A study of 15 type I CFM patients showed that, during treatment with a functional appliance, the affected side increased in size more than the unaffected side in
four children, by an amount equal to the unaffected side in four children, and slightly
less than the unaffected side in seven children. However, no significant mean difference between the groups in growth of the two sides in the sample occurred [2]. A
similar response was reported by Melsen et al. [3]
If the response to functional appliance therapy is good, then it may be possible to
avoid surgical lengthening of the mandibular ramus on the affected side in patients
with type I mandibles, provided the angulation of the maxillary occlusal plane is
acceptable. In type IIA CFM, a similar presurgical treatment phase may be beneficial [3, 4]. Advocates of presurgical orthopedic therapy are of the opinion that even
when a functional appliance does not avoid the need for mandibular lengthening
procedures, the appliance produces a soft tissue environment that has a reduced
tendency for postoperative skeletal relapse.

Early Orthodontic Treatment
In patients with CFM, there may be delayed tooth eruption and dental anomalies,
and crowding of the dentition is common [5]. Orthodontic treatment in childhood
focuses on control of tooth eruption and prevention or correction of dentoalveolar
adaptations to the asymmetrical position of the maxilla and mandible. The orthodontist should be actively involved in the treatment of children with CFM throughout their growth period.

80

C. M. Resnick and B. L. Padwa

 arly Mandibular Operation and Immediate Postsurgical
E
Dental Appliance
Operative correction of the mandibular skeletal deformity is indicated in some children. Mandibular lengthening and creation of an open bite on the affected side during the mixed dentition allow vertical growth of the midface on that side, permitting
the maxilla to meet the new position of the mandible. In turn, the secondary deformity of maxillary occlusal plane canting that occurs when interceptive treatment is
not employed may be decreased or avoided. This can theoretically prevent the need
for a Le Fort I osteotomy after completion of skeletal growth.
In type I, IIA, and some IIB patients, the mandible is elongated and rotated to the
correct midline. The mandible can be elongated using either conventional orthognathic surgical methods or by distraction osteogenesis (DO).
Conventional orthognathic techniques include a vertical ramus osteotomy, often
combined with a coronoidectomy on the affected side, or an inverted L osteotomy,
leaving the condyle on the affected side in position. The proximal and distal fragments are secured using rigid fixation. A compensatory releasing osteotomy may be
required on the unaffected side to allow the mandible to rotate passively to the new
position without excessive torquing of the condyle on the unaffected side; this is
usually not required in young children.
The standard procedure for distraction osteogenesis (DO) includes creation of a
mandibular ramus osteotomy. A distraction device is fixed to the lateral aspect of the
ramus and is secured to the bone on either side of the osteotomy. Numerous distraction devices are commercially available, all permitting a gradual separation of bone
fragments. The ideal device is technically easy to apply, completely buried (avoiding the cutaneous pin tracks associated with transcutaneously placed pins and externally located devices), and easily removed following the period of distraction and
retention. To obtain the most predictable outcomes, three-dimensional treatment
planning should be used to allow precise positioning of the osteotomy and proper
orientation and fixation of the device to the bony segments (Fig. 5.1).
a

b

Fig. 5.1 Three-dimensional plan for distraction osteogenesis of the right ramus using a semi-­
buried unidirectional device. Note the proximal segment in red. (Reproduced with permission
from: Resnick et al. [42])

Ilizarov [6] recommended a 5-day latency period to permit soft tissue healing
prior to the beginning of distraction, a principle extrapolated from the orthopedic
experience of distracting long bones. Animal models [7] as well as human studies of
mandibular distraction [8] have shown no difference in outcomes when the latency
period is eliminated. As such, many craniofacial surgeons have eliminated the
latency period from the DO protocol and instead begin the distraction phase immediately following osteotomy and device placement [9]. Distraction commences at a
rate of 1–2 mm per day, spreads over two to four activations, and continues until the
desired mandibular expansion is achieved. This end point is based on clinical examination and follow-up radiographs correlated with three-dimensional treatment
planning. Clinical examination ensures correction of the asymmetry and presence
of an open bite on the affected side. During the first 3–4 days of distraction, the
proximal fragment may move posteriorly and superiorly until it becomes fully
seated in the glenoid fossa or against a stop at the skull base; mandibular lengthening may not be appreciated on clinical examination at this stage. The distraction
period is then followed by a retention period of 6–8 weeks or at least two times the
number of millimeters of distraction in days, to allow the regenerate to consolidate
[10]. Ultrasonography can be used to assess bone consolidation during the retention
period, if desired [11, 12]. Following the consolidation period, the distraction device
is removed.
DO has a number of advantages compared to conventional techniques: mandibular lengthening occurs with minimal morbidity, need for bone grafting and donor
site morbidity are eliminated, operative time is decreased, and hospital length of
stay is shortened. Additionally, initial observational studies and animal models suggested that soft tissue expansion occurs simultaneously with bone lengthening [13,
14]. This provides a soft tissue environment that may permit greater long-term skeletal stability. However, several recent longitudinal follow-up studies have shown
that the mandibular asymmetry usually recurs over time and that additional operations to correct skeletal asymmetry are often necessary [15–18].
With both conventional osteotomies and DO, no operation is performed on the
maxilla in a growing child; an open bite created on the affected side is maintained
and regulated by the use of an orthodontic appliance to allow for eruption of the
teeth and vertical growth of the maxilla, thus leveling the maxillary occlusal plane
(Fig. 5.2) [19–22].
If the ramus has been lengthened by distraction, the appliance should be fitted on
the final day of distraction and worn throughout the period of consolidation. If the
ramus has been lengthened by conventional osteotomy or ramus construction, the
appliance should be fitted as soon as possible following the operation. The orthodontic appliance is first used as a bite block to maintain the open bite for 3–6 months
after the operation. Then eruption of the maxillary teeth and vertical growth of the
maxilla on the affected side are directed by gradually reducing the maxillary side of
the appliance over the next 1–2 years. Finally, the open-bite closure is completed by
active orthodontic movement of the maxillary teeth, thus leveling the maxillary
occlusal plane.

In many patients with type IIB and in all patients with type III deformities, there
is insufficient ramus available for the use of conventional osteotomies. Similarly,
DO cannot be used because this technique requires enough available bone to fix the
device and a glenoid fossa or flat surface at the skull base to act as a stop for movement of the proximal bone fragment. Therefore, the mandibular ramus and TMJ
must be constructed with an autologous graft or flap. Costochondral grafts or vascularized free fibula flaps are used most commonly for this purpose (Fig. 5.3). The
new TMJ is constructed to be symmetrical with the opposite joint, as lateral and
posterior as possible. The creation of an open bite and the use of an orthodontic
appliance to control maxillary growth and eruption of the maxillary teeth are otherwise the same.
Costochondral grafts have long been the gold standard for mandibular reconstruction in young patients [23, 24] because they have an excellent track record of
viability and stability [25]. A small cartilaginous cap is harvested with the costal
bone and used as the articulating surface. The long-term prognosis depends on symmetrical growth between the normal side and the constructed ramus-condyle unit.
Ramus-condyle units that have been constructed with costochondral grafts often
elongate during facial growth allowing symmetry to be maintained [26], though
overgrowth and undergrowth are possible [27, 28]. CCGs are primarily composed
of cortical bone and rely on recipient tissues for revascularization [29]. Postoperative
resorption, therefore, is common, and, in some cases, complete graft loss occurs
over time. Furthermore, the grafted bone is thin and does not respond well to

The free fibula flap is an alternative to CCG for mandibular construction [31].
The attributes of this flap include a large amount of available donor bone, a consistent bone shape allowing for osteotomies within the flap to create a more natural

5

Management of the Mandibular Deformity in the Growing Patient with Craniofacial…

87

shape, a robust blood supply, less resorption compared with grafts, and a favorable
response to future distraction osteogenesis if needed [31, 32]. The free fibula flap
may have growth potential in skeletally immature patients [5, 33]. The outcome of
free fibula flaps for ramus-condyle unit construction has variable results with observational studies suggesting a lack of growth potential [34, 35] and others showing
that the flaps do elongate during growth [36].
A disappointing complication that has been associated with construction using
free fibula flaps in patients with CFM is ankylosis. Resnick and colleagues reported
that 63% (5 of 8) of their patients with CFM (mean age 8.8 years) who had construction of the ramus condyle unit with a fibula developed ankylosis over a 7.3-year
follow-up [37]. The patients that developed ankylosis were skeletally immature at
the time of construction. This is in contrast to Santamaria et al.’s series of ten
patients with HFM who had a free fibula flap for ramus construction at a mean age
of 7.2 years [31]. None of their patients developed ankylosis over the 45.4 months
of mean follow-up period. The operative technique described is similar in both studies, except that Santamaria et al. did not use intermaxillary fixation intraoperatively.
One possible explanation for the significant difference in ankylosis rates between
the studies is that Resnick et al. attempted to improve symmetry and posterior facial
height by rotating the mandible to the midline and in a counterclockwise direction.
They established the best-fit dental occlusion and fixed this position intraoperatively
with intermaxillary fixation and an occlusal splint while the fibula was inserted. The
ramus lengthening and midline correction on the affected side might have caused
the fibula to be pushed superiorly into the fossa particularly in younger patients who
did not undergo a compensatory releasing osteotomy on the contralateral (unaffected) side. The lack of intraoperative intermaxillary fixation in the report by
Santamaria and colleagues indicates that they may not have repositioned the mandible and that the fibula may therefore have been placed in a passive position, exerting less pressure on the fibula against the fossa. The tight abutment of the articulating
surface of the fibula and the skull base in those patients in the Resnick series who
did not undergo contralateral releasing osteotomies may have contributed to their
high rate of ankylosis. When this construction is used, it is best to avoid close
approximation of the articulating flap surface and the skull base. This can be accomplished either by inserting the fibula in a passive position and planning to use distraction osteogenesis in the future to achieve symmetry and occlusal correction or
by creating a contralateral releasing osteotomy to allow the mandible to rotate while
minimizing upward pressure on the fibula at the time of the construction. Given the
variability in the growth of the fibula and the chance of ankylosis, these patients
should be followed closely for recurrent asymmetry and treated if necessary with a
secondary lengthening procedure.
The results of treatment of growing children with CFM using conventional methods are mixed. Kaban et al. at Boston Children’s Hospital reported 20 patients with
CFM who underwent treatment during growth [21]. They were separated into two
groups: group 1 (type I or IIA, n = 10) and group 2 (type IIB or III, n = 10). Group
1 patients were treated with a mandibular osteotomy with or without a bone graft to
lengthen the mandibular ramus and rotate the mandible to the midline, followed by

88

C. M. Resnick and B. L. Padwa

the use of an orthodontic appliance as discussed earlier. Group 2 patients had construction of the ramus-condyle unit and, as necessary the temporomandibular joint,
with costochondral grafts or iliac crest grafts with costochondral junctions. The
average follow-up was 50.9 months (group 1) and 45 months (group 2). In all children the midface grew vertically to close the surgically created open bite, and the
maxillary occlusal plane was leveled without an osteotomy. Of the patients with
type I or IIA (group 1), followed to completion of growth (n = 9/10), none required
a maxillary osteotomy or a second procedure to lengthen the mandible. Of the
patients with type IIB or III (group 2) who were followed to growth completion,
none required a maxillary osteotomy, but four required a second mandibular elongation procedure in the late mixed dentition or early teen years.
Padwa et al. at Boston Children’s Hospital retrospectively studied midfacial
growth in patients (n = 33) with type IIB and III CFM after early construction with
costochondral grafts [38]. Patients who had symmetrical growth of the constructed
ramus and condyle (42%) had leveling of the intergonial angles and occlusal planes.
Patients whose constructed rami grew but, at a diminished rate relative to the normal
side (42%), remained asymmetrical with some improvement in but not complete
leveling of the maxillary occlusal plane. Those who had minimal growth of the graft
(16%) had an increase in the maxillary and mandibular deformities (increase in
occlusal cant and intergonial angle).
Vargervik and Ousterhout at the University of California, San Francisco, reported
continued growth of the lengthened mandible in the majority of ten patients with
CFM followed until growth was completed [2]. In three of their patients, however,
growth of the affected side did not keep pace with the normal side and facial asymmetry recurred, requiring a second mandibular lengthening procedure that also
involved a maxillary osteotomy.
Longitudinal studies of CFM patients treated with DO in the mixed dentition
have demonstrated that the majority of patients experience recurrence of their facial
asymmetry and require additional procedures after the completion of skeletal
growth. Meazzini et al. studied eight patients with type I and II mandibular deformities who had DO at a mean age of 5.6 years [15]. By postoperative year 5, all
patients demonstrated recurrent asymmetry, with a mean return of 77% of the original asymmetry between the affected and unaffected sides.
In 2009 Nagy et al. published a meta-analysis which included 13 studies of early
mandibular DO for CFM and concluded that there was a lack of statistical evidence
to support DO as a single-stage treatment for the facial asymmetry associated with
CFM [39]. Recently, Pluijmers et al. published another meta-analysis of early CFM
treatment including bone graft construction and DO. In the patients who had a bone
graft, more than 50% experienced recurrent asymmetry [18]. While the study design
did not permit calculation of a relapse rate for patients who had DO, the analysis
found that most patients had recurrence of the asymmetry after DO. Not surprisingly, recurrent asymmetry occurred least frequently in patients with type I mandibles. The best long-term results were achieved in those patients who had early
grafting followed by distraction of the graft in adolescence. Some studies also suggested that early intervention can reduce negative psychosocial effects associated

5

Management of the Mandibular Deformity in the Growing Patient with Craniofacial…

89

with having facial asymmetry. Based on these observations, the authors of this analysis concluded that single-stage correction should be delayed until the completion
of skeletal growth and that a staged approach with both an early intervention and a
final correction at skeletal maturity should be considered in patients with type IIB
and III mandibles.
There has been a recent trend in the temporomandibular joint surgery community
to favor total alloplastic joint replacement over autologous reconstruction of
destroyed joints. As a result of the success of these alloplasts, this technique is
beginning to expand to pediatric and congenital mandibular construction. Initial
concerns about longevity of these joints and utility in young patients have been
quelled by emerging long-term evidence of their success [40]. Alloplastic constructs
have the advantages of complete customizability via virtual planning, ability to
achieve large vertical and horizontal changes, and predictable and stable mandibular
construction that allows precision in maxillary repositioning without the expected
settling and remodeling that occurs postoperatively in autologous constructs. In
growing patients, one must continue to consider the very long timeline of expected
use of this joint with still unknown longevity after 20 years and possible need to
upsize the condylar components during and after growth. Some surgeons have suggested performing an osteotomy in the native mandibular body to advance the mandible as necessary to compensate for growth asymmetry after an alloplastic joint has
been placed during growth, to avoid the need to exchange joint components for
larger versions [41].
In summary, it appears that early treatment should not be considered definitive
treatment for the facial asymmetry seen in CFM. Early intervention may be useful
as a component of a staged approach to asymmetry correction and may be indicated
to reduce the psychosocial burden of facial asymmetry during the childhood years.
Future advances in techniques and materials may improve outcomes.

Learning Aims
1. Understand hemifacial microsomia (HFM) relative to the nature of this
congenital deformity as well as the clinical, radiographic, and diagnostic
characteristics.
2. Realize the surgical treatment options that have been used to manage
HFM, particularly in reference to TMJ reconstruction.
3. Review the literature on application of techniques to reconstruct the TMJ
and correct the associated HFM dento-skeletal-facial deformity.
4. Be aware that patient-fitted total joint prosthesis provides superior outcomes relative to stability, function, and quality of treatment compared to
autogenous bone grafts for TMJ reconstruction in the HFM patient.
5. Know the surgical protocol and sequencing for surgical correction of the
severe HFM patient with patient-fitted total joint prosthesis in conjunction
with orthognathic surgery and facial augmentation.

Introduction
Hemifacial microsomia (HFM) is a specific condition of unilateral incomplete or
hypoplastic development of the facial soft tissues and skeleton. HFM is the second
most common facial birth defect after cleft lip and palate with an estimated occurrence rate of 1 in 5600 live births. It is also known as Goldenhar’s syndrome,
L. M. Wolford (*)
Clinical Professor of Oral and Maxillofacial Srugery and Orthodontics, Texas A&M
University College of Dentistry, Private Practice; Baylor University Medical Center,
Dallas, TX, USA

© Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2022
D. M. Yates, M. R. Markiewicz (eds.), Craniofacial Microsomia and Treacher
Collins Syndrome, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-84733-3_6

93

94

L. M. Wolford

oculo-­auriculo-­vertebral spectrum, otomandibular dysostosis, lateral facial dysplasia, and branchial arch syndrome. HFM occurs sporadically in most cases and can
be considered as a nonspecific symptom complex that is etiologically and pathogenetically heterogeneous. Extreme variability of expression is characteristic of this
disorder [1, 2].

Classification
There are several proposed classifications that identify the severity of this syndrome,
but for the purpose of this chapter, the classification system proposed by Pruzansky
in 1969 and later modified by Mulliken and Kaban in 1987 will be used [3]. This
assigns HFM patients to one of four categories based on size and function of the
temporomandibular joint (TMJ). Type I is a small mandible with normal TMJ morphology. Type IIa is a ramus with abnormal size and shape, but the glenoid fossa
maintains its position, whereas Type IIb is a ramus and TMJ with abnormal size,
shape, and function and is displaced outside of the plane of the contralateral side.
Type III describes an absent condyle, ramus, and TMJ. This classification system
may be the most useful to the surgeon in the preoperative evaluation, diagnosis, and
treatment planning because of its simplicity and inclusion of TMJ anatomy and
function.

Clinical and Imaging Features
The features of HFM patients, depending on the degree of expression, may include
some or all of the following characteristics: (1) unilateral hypoplasia or absence of
the mandibular condyle, ramus, and body; (2) retruded mandible and chin deviated
toward the ipsilateral side; (3) high occlusal plane angle facial morphology; (4)
hypoplasia of the ipsilateral maxilla, zygomatico-orbital complex, and temporal
bone including the absence of the zygomatic arch and glenoid fossa; (5) ipsilateral
soft tissue deficiency affecting the muscles, subcutaneous and glandular tissues,
nerves, and skin; (6) decreased ipsilateral facial height; (7) Class II skeletal and
occlusal relationship; (8) premature occlusal contact on the ipsilateral side; (9)
transverse cant in the occlusal plane and skeletal structures; (10) ipsilateral hypo-­
eruption of the teeth and partial anodontia; (11) eye, ear, and vertebral anomalies;
and (12) decreased oropharyngeal airway and sleep apnea in cases with significant
expression and mandibular retrusion (Figs. 6.1a–c and 6.2a, b). Facial deformity
and asymmetry usually worsen with growth. The contralateral TMJ articular disc
may become anteriorly displaced induced by the abnormal condylar rotation caused
by the mandibular asymmetry and the functional overload on the contralateral joint.
Typical TMJ symptoms may accompany the contralateral TMJ disc displacement
such as TMJ pain, headaches, myofascial pain, ear symptoms, clicking/popping, etc.

Less-involved HFM deformities with a healthy functional ipsilateral TMJ can
usually be treated with orthognathic surgery and facial augmentation if indicated.
However, HMF deformities commonly have a unilateral distorted, hypoplastic, or
absent TMJ structure requiring TMJ reconstruction in conjunction with orthognathic surgery to provide optimal stable and predictable functional and esthetic outcomes. There are two primary methods to reconstruct the TMJ: autogenous bone
grafts (i.e., costochondral graft, sternoclavicular graft) and alloplastic TMJ total
joint prosthetic devices. Understanding the nature of the HFM deformity, the timing

6

of reconstruction, the surgical treatment options including TMJ reconstruction and
orthognathic surgery, and the outcome predictability and stability will enable the
surgeon to apply this knowledge to optimally treat HFM and similar deformities.
This chapter will focus on the more complex HMF cases with absent TMJs that are
not amendable to conventional orthognathic surgery.

Autogenous Bone Grafts (ABGs)
The most common sources for autogenous bone grafts (ABGs) to reconstruct the
ipsilateral condyle in HFM are costochondral grafts (CCG, Fig. 6.3) followed by
sternoclavicular grafts (SCGs, Fig. 6.4). Vascularized fibula grafts could be

considered when bone and soft tissue deficiencies are severe requiring bone and soft
tissue replacement, but this is rarely indicated. For growth center transplants if
required in younger patients, CCG or SCG may provide growth potential, although
unpredictable. An additional method advocated by some to reconstruct the ipsilateral mandible is distraction osteogenesis.
Indications for condylar reconstruction using ABG include the following: (1)
non-functional TMJ related to deformed or absent TMJ condyle, (2) zero to one of
the previous TMJ surgeries (for free grafts), (3) good vascular bed (for free grafts),
(4) both hard and soft tissues are required (vascularized fibula graft), (5) growth
center transplant indicated (CCG or SCG), (6) custom-fitted total joint prosthesis
unavailable, (7) allergy to all metals in total joint prosthesis, (8) requires relatively
minimal repositioning of the dento-skeletal structures, and (9) patient preference.
Contraindications for free ABG include (1) multiply operated TMJ (two or more
previous failed TMJ surgical procedures), (2) connective tissue autoimmune disease
or systemic inflammatory disease, (3) previously failed TMJ allografts, (4) conditions causing decreased vascularization and prolonged healing, (5) polyarthropathies, and (6) concomitant TMJ and orthognathic surgery indicated, requiring
significant movement of the dento-skeletal structures.
Advantages of using ABG are (1) native bone readily available, (2) growth
potential (CCG or SCG), (3) articular disc attached to graft (SCG), and (4) vascularized fibula graft available for requirement of major hard and soft tissue replacement.
Disadvantages of ABG are as follows: (1) requires graft harvest significantly
increasing the operating time, (2) donor site morbidity, (3) grafts subject to physiological loading with possible subsequent bone remodeling or resorption, (4) grafts
can bend, warp, and fracture, (5) cannot predictably correct significant dento-­
craniofacial deformities, (6) unpredictable growth, and (7) difficult to control
occlusion.

Costochondral Grafts (CCGs)
CCG grafts (Fig. 6.3) for many years were the most popular and published ABG
technique to reconstruct the TMJ for HFM, ankylosis, or other TMJ pathologies
[3–8]. It is relatively easy to harvest and stabilize to the ramus. The costochondral
junction fits nicely into the glenoid fossa, if there is a fossa present. Often HFM
patients will not have an ipsilateral zygomatic arch or glenoid fossa. Some surgeons
suggest reconstructing the fossa with bone grafting in order to place the CCG into a
stable relationship [7]. This is usually not necessary if the CCG is placed on the
medial side of the ramus where it can articulate on the base of the skull, eliminating
the need for reconstructing a fossa. The CCG does have growth potential, but it is
very unpredictable. The CCG can exhibit no growth or commonly will demonstrate
significant over growth, as the CCG grows more like the rib than the TMJ. The
elasticity and flexibility of the CCG, often because of the thin cortex, present a
structure that when stressed or loaded excessively can bend, warp, or fracture

6

Surgical Management of Hemifacial Microsomia with Temporomandibular Joint…

99

resulting in the positional shifting of the mandible and occlusion, with larger skeletal movements increasing that risk. CCGs also have a significant risk of TMJ
ankylosis.
Kaban et al. [4] advocated early treatment of HMF patients with Type I, IIa, and
some Type IIb patients with mandibular osteotomies. The costochondral graft has
been popular for reconstruction of the ipsilateral TMJ in the young Type IIb and III
HFM patients due to the growth center at the costochondral junction and for reconstruction of the glenoid fossa [3–8]. However other articles demonstrated that rib
graft growth is unpredictable with either no growth or significant overgrowth, creating a deformity that required additional surgery [5, 6].
CCG grafts are falling out of favor as a recent international survey by Hawkins
et al. [9], in 2019 reported that 95.5% of responding surgeons prefer alloplastic TMJ
replacement for end-stage TMJ pathology over CCG.

Sternoclavicular Grafts (SCGs)
SCG may function better than CCG for autogenous reconstruction of the TMJ as it
has a very thick cortex, lots of medullary bone, and an articular disc attached to the
condylar head (Fig. 6.4a). The upper half of the clavicle is harvested along with the
articular disc attached to the upper head of the clavicle providing a more normal
functioning condyle. For Types IIb and III HFM patients with an absent fossa, the
SCG usually fits best by placement on the medial side of the ramus, articulating
beneath the skull base or positioned along the posterior border of the mandible if
there is a fossa present (Fig. 6.4b). The SCG grows more like a mandibular condyle,
when used as a growth center transplant, but growth is unpredictable. The SCG is
much stronger with minimal elasticity and flexibility as compared to the CCG, with
less susceptibility to excessive loading that could bend, warp, or fracture the graft,
thus providing better predictability and stability than CCG. However, it is susceptible to bony remolding when loaded as in large mandibular advancements that
could affect occlusal stability. The primary complication is post-surgical clavicle
fracture, as the donor site is significantly weakened by the harvest and may take a
minimum of 6 months to regain significant strength [10, 11].
Wolford et al. [10] in 1994 demonstrated the use of the sternoclavicular graft
(SCG) to reconstruct the HMF patient with the absent TMJ and to lengthen the
mandible on the affected side. The upper half of the clavicle and associated portion
of the articular disc were harvested (Fig. 6.4). The mandible was advanced as predetermined, and the graft was secured against the medial side of the residual ramus/
body secured with bone screws and the condylar head seated against the base of the
skull (see Case Presentation #1; Figs. 6.5, 6.6, 6.7, 6.8, and 6.9), or the graft was
positioned against the posterior border of the ramus (Fig. 6.4b) if a fossa is present.
This grafting system provided a better normal growth potential and stability as compared to a CCG. The graft will either grow relatively normally or exhibit deficient
growth, but has not been observed to overgrow. Wolford [10] recommended the use

Vascularized Fibula Grafts
Vascularized fibula grafts have been documented for use in HFM patients [12]. The
fibula graft can be a viable autogenous alternative where there is gross deficiency in
bone and soft tissue, vascularly compromised recipient site, and/or major volumes
of bone and soft tissue replacement are required. The fibula graft does leave an
unsightly scar and bony deformity at the donor site. Although this graft system has
been successful in some cases of HFM and for other conditions requiring mandibular reconstruction, there are significant risks with early and late morbidities including chronic donor site sensory disturbance (67%), chronic pain (26%), gait
disturbance (20%), chronic lower limb weakness (20%) such as limited walking or
stair climbing ability, limited toe mobility, donor site cosmetic deformity, and malocclusion (22%) [13]. Ankylosis is a major complication occurring in 63% of HFM
patients receiving these grafts [12]. These risks must be carefully weighed before
considering this method of HFM reconstruction.

patients treated with distraction at an average age of 7.3 years with 5–15 years of

with all requiring orthognathic surgery. The authors concluded that bone distraction

Patient-Fitted TMJ Total Joint Prosthesis
There are two TMJ total joint prosthesis (TJP) systems in the USA approved by the
Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for TMJ reconstruction: TMJ Concepts
(Ventura, CA, USA) and Biomet Microfixation (Jacksonville, FL, USA). For application to HFM, a patient-fitted prosthesis is superior to a stock device.

Biomet Microfixation System
The Biomet Microfixation TMJ replacement system is a stock device (off-the-shelf)
with several sizes to choose from for fossa and mandibular components. Biomet
patient-fitted devices are not FDA approved for use in the USA but are available in
other countries. Clinical trials for the stock device were initiated in 1995 and granted
FDA approval in 2005. The ramus component is composed of a chromium cobalt
alloy, but the side toward the ramus has a titanium coating to help with osseointegration. The ramus component is available in three lengths, 45, 50, and 55 mm, which
limit adaptation for HFM patients. There are three basic styles including standard,
offset, and narrow. The fossa component is composed of dense ultra-high-molecular-­
weight polyethylene (UHMWPE), with three fossa sizes to choose from including
small, medium, and large. This is metal-on-polyethylene articulation, which is the
gold standard in orthopedics. The mandibular component is stabilized to the ramus
with 2.7-mm-diameter screws, and the polyethylene fossa component is secured to
the lateral rim of the fossa with 2.0-mm-diameter screws. There is no osseointegration of the fossa component and no posterior stop in the fossa, rendering the standard stock prosthesis unsuitable for reconstruction of the HFM patient. The literature
has demonstrated good outcomes using the stock device for indicated TMJ pathology [20–25]. Aagaard [26] has shown success using the patient-fitted Biomet device
for TMJ reconstruction of end-stage TMJ pathology, but there are no reports on use
for the HFM patients. The patient-fitted prosthesis does have a posterior stop on the
fossa component, but no osseointegration. For HFM patients with the absence of the
zygomatic arch and glenoid fossa, where the fossa component must be adapted to
the temporal bone, this device is not recommended because of potential for screw
loosening related to the thin temporal bone, unfavorable anatomical morphology,
and lack of osseointegration of the device.

106

L. M. Wolford

TMJ Concepts System
Developed originally in 1989 by Techmedica, Inc. (Camarillo, CA, USA) and since
1997 manufactured by TMJ Concepts, Inc. (Ventura, CA, USA), this patient-fitted
TMJ total joint prosthesis is manufactured to meet the patient’s specific anatomical
requirements for TMJ reconstruction and mandibular repositioning. The fossa component is made of a commercially pure titanium (CPT) shell and four layers of CPT
mesh bonded to the shell. UHMWPE is bonded to the titanium mesh to function as
the articulating surface. The CPT mesh allows the fossa component to be fixated to
the zygomatic arch, or the temporal bone if the arch and fossa are missing, with
screws and provides a framework for osseointegration maximizing the long-term
stability of the fossa component. The fossa component has a posterior stop to provide a centric relation position for the condylar head of the prosthesis, which is
essential when the TMJ TJP is combined with orthognathic surgical procedures and
particularly for reconstruction of the HFM patient. The mandibular ramus component is made of titanium alloy with a condylar head of cobalt-chromium-­molybdenum
alloy. This device provides a metal-on-polyethylene articulation which is the gold
standard for orthopedic joint reconstruction. The titanium alloy composition of the
mandibular component provides osseointegration with the underlying bone of the
ramus. The TMJ Concepts TJP provides the ability to reconstruct the TMJ and
advance the mandible and concomitantly perform orthognathic surgery at the same
operation.

Virtual Surgical Planning (VSP)
Presurgery, a CT scan is acquired following the specific TMJ Concepts CT acquisition protocol. The CT data is sent to 3-D Systems (Littleton, CO) to develop a 3-D
computer model of the patient’s anatomical structures (Fig. 6.2a, b). The application
of computer-assisted surgical simulation with virtual surgical planning (VSP) for
cases requiring TMJ reconstruction with patient-fitted TJP and orthognathic surgery
has significantly improved treatment quality by decreasing the preoperative workup
time and increasing the accuracy of surgical preparation, and subsequent surgery.
VSP is performed on the computer model, placing the maxilla and mandible into the
planned final post-surgical position and occlusion (Fig. 6.2c, d). The indicated condylectomy (if any condylar remnant remains) and any necessary bony recontouring
of the fossa or ramus can be done virtually (Fig. 6.2d). A 3-D stereolithic model is
constructed with the maxilla and mandible in their final post-surgery position and
sent to TMJ Concepts to manufacture the patient-fitted TJP (Fig. 6.10a, b) [27, 28].
HFM patients may be missing the zygomatic arch and glenoid fossa. The fossa
component, therefore, can be designed to fit against the temporal bone where it can
be fixated with bone screws with subsequent osseointegration (Fig. 6.3a,b). Extreme
care must be exercised as the temporal bone in this area may be extremely thin,

1–2 mm. Drilling the holes for screw placement must be done very delicately to

Two weeks prior to surgery, the final dental models are prepared. This usually
requires one mandibular dental model and two maxillary models if the maxilla is to
be segmentalized (one sectioned and used to establish the surgical occlusion and an
uncut model). These models are sent to 3-D Systems for incorporation into the computer model for construction of the surgical splints. Two splints are produced: an
intermediate splint used to reposition the mandible into its final position for stabilization of the contralateral mandibular ramus sagittal split osteotomy and for placement of the ipsilateral TMJ TJP, and a final palatal splint to stabilize the segmented
maxilla (if indicated). Upon completion of manufacture by TMJ Concepts, the TMJ
prosthesis is forwarded to the hospital, and the dental models and splints are forwarded to the surgeon.

Surgical Management of HFM Patients
Presurgical orthodontic preparation is usually required to obtain the best occlusal
outcome.
The most consistently predictable treatment outcomes functionally and esthetically for the HFM (Type IIB and III) patients are achieved by reconstructing the
TMJs and advancing the maxillo-mandibular complex in a counterclockwise

108

L. M. Wolford

direction with a patient-fitted TJP and orthognathic surgery. The TMJ Concepts
system is the prosthesis of choice because of the material selection, patient-fitted
design to meet the patient’s specific anatomical requirements, presence of a defined
posterior stop in the fossa component, and osseointegration of the fossa and mandibular components (Fig. 6.10a, b). For the HFM patient, a contralateral mandibular
ramus sagittal split osteotomy is performed to aid in repositioning the mandible,
and the indicated maxillary osteotomies are completed as well as any other adjunctive procedures (turbinectomies, nasoseptoplasty, genioplasty, rhinoplasty, etc.).
All procedures can be done at one operation or separated into two or more operations if the surgeon prefers. Additional secondary reconstruction procedures to correct residual bony and soft tissue deficiencies may be necessary in more complex
HFM cases using bone grafts, synthetic bone, alloplastic implants, etc. to build up
the residual deformed skeletal structures as well as soft tissue reconstruction to fill
out the soft tissue defects using fat grafts, tissue flaps, free vascularized grafts,
and so on.

Surgical Sequencing
The surgical sequencing used by the author for treating HFM patients is outlined in
Table 6.1. Since HFM cases can usually benefit from counterclockwise rotation of
the maxillo-mandibular complex to get the best functional and esthetic outcome
[29–32], repositioning the mandible first with the TJP and contralateral sagittal split
osteotomy (before the maxillary osteotomies are performed) simplifies the model
surgery, and splint construction improves the accuracy of the patient’s surgery and
outcome as compared to the traditional orthognathic surgical sequencing of performing the maxillary osteotomies first [33]. Performing the counterclockwise rotation of the mandible first will create posterior open bites, being greater on the
ipsilateral side as the transverse cant of the mandibular occlusal plane is also corrected. If segmentalization of the maxilla is required to optimize the occlusion, a
palatal splint is indicated to stabilize the upper arch and allow maximum interdigitation of the occlusion as the maxilla is stabilized [32]. Any ancillary procedures are
then performed.
Patients with HMF commonly have sleep apnea issues as a result of the retruded
mandible, decreased oropharyngeal airway, and/or nasal airway obstruction.
Counterclockwise rotation of the maxillo-mandibular complex with advancement
of the mandible is highly effective and predictable in opening the oropharyngeal
airway. In conjunction with correcting any nasal airway obstruction (e.g., turbinectomies, nasoseptoplasty) post-surgery, these patients will have significant improvement in the airway and elimination of sleep apnea [34–36].

or preauricular incision
