functional and esthetic outcome

Surgical Protocol
The surgical procedures are done under general anesthesia with nasoendotracheal
intubation. The HFM surgical sequencing is outlined in Table 6.1. The patient is
prepared for surgery, and a Tegaderm dressing applied over the mouth and nose to
seal off while performing the TMJ procedures. For the HFM patients with a contralateral TMJ disc displacement, an endaural incision is made, and disc repositioned
and stabilized with the Mitek Mini Anchor (Mitek Products Inc. Westwood, MA)
technique [37, 38]. The ipsilateral side is approached via an endaural or preauricular
incision if the ear is present or adjacent to where the TMJ would be if the ear is
severely deformed, mal-positioned, or absent. The zygomatic arch may be absent as

110

L. M. Wolford

well as the glenoid fossa; therefore the dissection is carried down to the temporal
bone anterior to the internal meatus and extended medially beneath the cranial base
to develop a pocket and foundation to place the patient-fitted fossa component. The
superior aspect of the ramus is identified if present. A condylectomy is performed if
there is a remnant that would interfere with the placement of the prosthesis. A coronoidectomy is performed if present. If the coronoid is severely hypoplastic or
absent, the hypoplastic temporalis muscle, if present, is reflected from the remnant
of the coronoid process.
An ipsilateral submandibular incision is made to expose the hypoplastic ramus/
body, and the hypoplastic pterygo-masseteric sling is reflected off the mandible. A
subperiosteal tunnel is created over the ramus to connect to the base of the temporal
bone. The ipsilateral mandible is then mobilized so it can be repositioned downward
and forward to advance the mandible to its new position; this is a critical aspect for
the success of the surgery. If the mandible is not completely stripped of all its attachments and fully mobilized, an adequate position of the mandible may not be
achieved. The soft tissues surrounding the mandible (skin and muscles) will usually
stretch to accommodate large advancements. Any bony modifications to the fossa,
temporal bone, or ramus/body of the mandible are completed as determined from
the 3-D stereolithic model surgery workup.
The face is draped with sterile towels, Tegaderm incised, and oral cavity entered
to perform a contralateral mandibular ramus sagittal split osteotomy using Wolford’s
modified technique [39, 40]. The mandible is mobilized, and a prefabricated intermediate occlusal splint is placed to position the mandible into its final predetermined position. Maxillo-mandibular fixation (MMF) is applied; the contralateral
mandibular sagittal split osteotomy is stabilized with a bone plate and screws, and
the incision closed. The face is re-prepped and resealed with a Tegaderm dressing,
and the surgeon changes gloves and gown. The fossa component of the patient-fitted
TMJ Concepts prosthesis is placed through the endaural/preauricular or temporal
incision and secured to the lateral rim of the fossa if present or temporal bone with
4–5, 2-mm-diameter, 4-mm-length screws. The mandibular component is inserted
through the submandibular incision, and the condyle seated into the fossa component against the posterior flange and secured to the ramus/body with 8–9, 2-mm-­
diameter bicortical screws. Fat is harvested from the abdomen through an umbilicus
or suprapubic incision or from the buttock and packed around the fossa/condyle
articulating area to prevent heterotrophic bone and scar tissue formation [41–44].
The incisions are closed.
MMF and the occlusal splint are removed. Through a maxillary vestibular incision, the maxillary osteotomies are completed. The maxilla is down-fractured,
mobilized, and segmented when indicated, and palatal splint is secured in place.
Intranasal procedures such as turbinectomies and/or nasal septoplasty are performed
if indicated to eliminate pre-existing nasal airway obstruction. The new occlusion is
established and secured with MMF. Four bone plates and screws are used to stabilize the maxilla with at least two screws above and two screws below the osteotomy
site for each plate. Autogenous or synthetic bone grafts are placed into the osseous
gaps in the lateral maxillary walls. An alar base cinch suture is placed to redefine

6

Surgical Management of Hemifacial Microsomia with Temporomandibular Joint…

111

nasal width, and the incision closed in a V-Y fashion [45]. MMF is removed, and
light elastics applied to guide the occlusion and decrease stress on the muscles of
mastication. Adjunctive procedures such as genioplasty, rhinoplasty, and so on are
then completed. It is recommended that additional ipsilateral hard and soft tissue
augmentation be performed at a secondary operation.

Periarticular Fat Grafts
With any of the TMJ reconstruction procedures using ABG or the alloplastic TMJ
joint prosthesis, the placement of fat grafts around the articulating areas of the new
joint significantly improves the treatment outcomes. The rationale for placing autologous fat grafts around the ABG or TJP is to obliterate the dead space surrounding
the graft or prosthesis, thus preventing the formation and subsequent organization
of a blood clot. Creating this physical barrier, the fat grafts serve to reduce the differentiation of pluripotential cells and prevent the formation of extensive fibrosis
and heterotopic calcification at the TMJ articulation.
Wolford et al. [41–44] have previously reported a technique in which fat grafts
harvested from the abdomen or buttock were packed around the articulating components of the total joint prosthesis. This technique significantly decreased the postoperative incidence of peri-implant fibrosis and heterotopic/reactive bone formation.
Patients with fat grafts were shown to do better clinically with less pain and increased
jaw function compared to similar patients reconstructed without fat grafts. Prior to
the use of fat grafts, approximately 35% of patients with total joint prostheses
required additional surgery to remove heterotopic/reactive bone and dense fibrosis
that developed around the prostheses causing pain as well as limited TMJ and jaw
function. Using the fat grafts has reduced reoperation to less than 2% for heterotrophic bone and fibrosis. Wolford also described the use of fat grafts to replace the
deficient soft tissues in HFM patients on the ipsilateral side of the face [46].

Age of Surgical Intervention
The patient’s age and symptoms can affect the treatment protocol. For instance, a
HFM patient under the age of 12 years with severe hypoplasia and malformation or
absence of the TMJ may benefit from a growth center transplant, using a CCG [3–5]
or sternoclavicular graft [10, 11]. CCGs are unpredictable relative to growth and
stability and often significantly overgrow creating a dentofacial deformity [5, 6].
Sternoclavicular grafts tend to have a better growth potential similar to normal TM
growth and better stability than a rib graft [10]. With either graft system, there is a
possibility that the grafts will not grow, overgrow, resorb, or fracture during the
initial healing phase.

112

L. M. Wolford

Another option for early intervention is the use of distraction osteogenesis [13–
19]. This technique has shown mixed results in the literature with the problem that
it requires multiple operations to place and remove the distractors, and it can lead to
difficulty in controlling the vector of distraction. Lengthening of the ramus under
the pressure of the pterygo-masseteric sling may be difficult to accomplish and may
significantly overload the already hypoplastic TMJ causing further degenerative
changes and risk of ankylosis. Orthognathic surgery is usually necessary following
completion of growth to maximize the functional and esthetic results.
Predictability of results and limiting correction of the jaw and TMJ-related
deformities to one major operation can best be achieved by waiting until growth is
relatively complete, provided that the patient is functionally and psychologically
stable. Females usually have the majority of their facial growth (98%) complete by
the age of 15 years, and males by the age of 17–18 years [47]. Since asymmetric
growth is a component of HFM and some required orthognathic surgical procedures
may have further adverse effects on subsequent facial growth, performing orthognathic surgery during the growing years may result in the need for additional surgery
at a later time to correct asymmetry, antero-posterior discrepancy, and malocclusion
that may develop during the completion of growth.
There are definite indications for early surgery such as requirement for growth
center transplant (i.e., rib or sternoclavicular grafts) or distraction, to correct masticatory dysfunction, airway obstruction, sleep apnea, and psychological factors.
Wolford et al. have previously published on maxillary and mandibular orthognathic
surgery and the effects on growth, with age consideration guidelines for surgical
intervention [48–50], as well as age consideration and surgical treatment protocols
for the common TMJ pathological conditions [51]. HFM patients have one side of
the mandible with a normal-growing condyle that rarely requires TMJ reconstruction; thus the recommendation to wait until growth of that condyle is complete to
achieve predictable treatment outcomes with one surgical intervention for correction of the TMJ, skeletal, occlusal, and airway issues.
Early treatment with a patient-fitted TMJ TJP can also be considered during
growth as it is more stable and predictable than CCG or SCG, but without growth
potential. Over-correction with the TJP may be indicated by over-advancing and
creating an ipsilateral posterior open bite. This may require additional surgery after
cessation of normal growth. This could require changing out the mandibular component for a longer component verses additional orthognathic surgery.

Outcome Studies
Relative to the HFM patient, there are important studies relative to the various surgical technique outcomes, and of particular interest are comparison studies evaluating
the outcomes between ABG and TJP for TMJ reconstruction.

6

Surgical Management of Hemifacial Microsomia with Temporomandibular Joint…

113

 omparative Studies: Autogenous Bone Grafts Versus
C
Alloplastic TMJ Reconstruction
There have been a few comparison studies of autogenous tissues versus total joint
prostheses.
Henry and Wolford [52] in 1993 reported a study of 107 patients in whom autogenous tissue grafts or Techmedica TJP were placed to reconstruct the TMJs severely
damaged by failed Vitek Inc. Proplast/Teflon TMJ devices. A 4-year follow-up subjective and objective evaluation of pain, occlusal stability, and jaw function reported
the percentages of successful outcomes for each autogenous tissue graft (costochondral, 12%; sternoclavicular, 21%; dermal, 8%; temporal fascia, 13%; temporal fascia with mandibular sagittal split osteotomies, 31%; auricular cartilage, 25%). The
Techmedica TMJ TJP had an 86% success. Although this was a different TMJ
pathology than HFM, it showed superiority of TMJ TJP over autogenous tissues.
Freitas et al. [53] in 2002 compared outcomes for costochondral grafts, sternoclavicular grafts, and total joint prostheses. They evaluated 12 patients with 24 operated joints. Six patients received costochondral grafts or sternoclavicular grafts, and
six patients received TMJ Concepts total joint prostheses. The follow-up ranged
from 48 to 58 months. The total joint prostheses provided statistically significant
better objective and subjective outcomes, decreased the operating room time, and
produced significantly better skeletal and occlusal stability particularly when the
maxilla and mandible were advanced.
Wolford et al. [54] in 2010 evaluated 13 patients with TMJ ankylosis with the age
range of 5–15 years. Four patients received CCGs, six SCGs, and three TJPs with a
follow-up of 2–13 years. Seven of the 13 patients had fat grafts packed around the
reconstructed TMJs. Of the four CCGs, three grafts demonstrated excessive overgrowth. None of these CCGs had fat placed around them, and all four re-ankylosed.
Four patients received SCGs and had fat grafts packed around the articulating area
of the grafts. There was no re-ankylosis in this group, and they had good jaw function, although decreased translation ability. Two of the SCGs did not receive fat
grafts and both re-ankylosed. With the SCGs, bony remolding occurred under
increased loading to the joints with mandibular advancement resulting in occlusal
changes. Three patients received TJPs with fat packed around the prostheses. There
was no re-ankylosis nor mandibular relapse. The TJP incisal opening presurgery
ranged from 2 to 29 mm, and post-surgery ranged from 35 to 52 mm, demonstrating
good outcomes. The use of fat grafts packed around the articulation area of the
SCGs and around the TJP prevented re-ankylosis of the TMJs.
Saeed et al. [55] in 2002 evaluated 49 patients with 66 CCGs and 50 patients
with 68 TJPs using the Christensen system (TMJ, Inc. Golden, CO, USA) with
metal-on-metal articulation. The mean follow-up ranged from 43 to 49 months, and
the mean age was 38 years. The authors reported complications in 27 patients with
CCG and 34 patients that received the TJP. However, the authors reported 26 of 49
CCG patients (53%) required reoperation, whereas only 6 of 50 TJP patients (12%)

114

L. M. Wolford

required reoperation. The TJP provided better subjective and objective outcomes.
The authors recommended TJP in cases of ankylosis, multiply operated joints, and
previously failed alloplastic implants.
Key Points
These comparative studies demonstrate the following:
1. TJPs provide better outcomes relative to pain, function, stability, and
esthetics compared to autogenous bone grafts.
2. With the use of TJP, concomitant TMJ and orthognathic surgery can be
performed at the same operation with highly predictable outcomes relative
to skeletal and occlusal stability, function, esthetics, and decrease in pain.
3. TJPs work better in poorly vascularized tissues compared to free autogenous grafts.
4. Packing fat grafts around the articular area of the autogenous grafts or TJP
decreases the risk of heterotopic bone formation and ankylosis, increases
function, and decreases pain.

TMJ Concepts Outcome Studies
There have been more than 150 papers published in reference to the use of the TMJ
Concepts TJP. The efficacy of TMJ Concepts TJP has been well documented in the
literature by numerous studies including those by Wolford et al. [52–54, 56, 57] and
Mercuri et al. [58–60]
Coleta et al. [61] in 2008 evaluated 47 female patients for surgical stability after
bilateral TMJ reconstruction using TMJ Concepts TJP, TMJ fat grafts, and counterclockwise rotation of the maxillo-mandibular complex with the mandible advancing
an average of 18.4 mm. At an average follow-up of 40.6 months, the surgical results
remained very stable (no relapse).
Pinto et al. [62] in 2008 evaluated the same 47 female patients for pain and dysfunctional outcomes. Significant improvements (37–52%) were observed for TMJ
pain, headaches, jaw function, diet, and disability. Jaw opening increased 14%.
These two studies showed that patients with end-stage TMJ pathology could be
treated in one operation with TMJ Concepts TJP, fat grafts, and correction of an
associated dentofacial deformity with good stability and improvement in pain and
TMJ function.
Although the life expectancy of the TMJ Concepts TJP is unknown, Wolford
et al. [63] published a 21-year follow-up study of 56 patients who had received the
Techmedica TJP between 1989 and 1993. There were statistically significant
improvements for incisal opening, jaw function, TMJ pain, and diet, with 85.7% of
the patients reporting significant improvement in their quality of life. There were no
reports of device removal due to material wear or failure.

6

Surgical Management of Hemifacial Microsomia with Temporomandibular Joint…

115

 MJ Total Joint Prosthesis in Treating Hemifacial
T
Microsomia Patients
Wolford et al. [64] in 2012 introduced the use of TMJ Concepts total joint prosthesis
for the treatment of HFM. They evaluated six HFM patients treated with this surgical
protocol. The average age at surgery was 23.5 years (range from 14 years to 39 years),
and the average follow-up was 6 years and 2 months (range from 1 year to 11.4 years).
For all subjective parameters including facial pain, headaches, TMJ pain, jaw function, diet, and disability, all patients improved or remained the same. Incisal opening
improved from 36.3 to 39.2 mm. The mean surgical changes showed the forward
horizontal movement of anterior nasal spine (ANS) was 1.3 mm, upper incisor tip
(U1T) advanced 7.4 mm, lower incisor tip (L1T) 8.9 mm, point B 14.8 mm, pogonion (Pog) 18.6 mm, and menton (Me) 17.5 mm. The occlusal plane angle (OPA)
decreased by a mean −12.3°. Post-surgical stability analysis demonstrated point A,
PNS, and U1T moved approximately 1 mm posteriorly at long-term follow-up. All
mandibular anatomical points remained very stable as did the OPA with virtually no
change at 6 years post-surgery. Two patients (33%) had concomitant contralateral
disc displacement repaired with the Mitek anchor technique with good outcomes.
Polley et al. [65] in 2019 reported on a multicenter study of ten HFM patients
treated with reconstruction of the ipsilateral side with TMJ Concepts total joint
prosthesis, contralateral mandibular ramus osteotomy, and Le Fort I osteotomy. The
cases were reported to have good outcomes with improved incisal opening, stable
occlusion, and improved facial balance. However, no cephalometric evaluation for
surgical change and stability or subjective evaluation relative to pain, diet, disability, or quality of life was reported.

Case Presentations
Case #1 This 10-year-old female had right sided-HFM, Kaban Type III, with
absent right TMJ (Figs. 6.5a–d and 6.6a). She was treated at 10 years old with a
right TMJ and mandibular reconstruction with a SCG and a left ramus inverted “L”
osteotomy and genioplasty to advance the mandible in a counterclockwise rotation
creating posterior open bites, significantly greater on the right side to level the mandible horizontally (Fig. 6.6b). Post-surgery, the occlusion was leveled orthodontically. She grew symmetrically post-surgery with active growth of the SCG equal to
the contralateral side through the age of 18 years (Figs. 6.7 and 6.8a). At 18 years
old, routine double-jaw orthognathic surgery was performed to correct the residual
dentofacial deformity to maximize the functional and esthetic result (Fig. 6.8b). The
patient is seen 2 years post-orthognathic surgery (Fig. 6.9a–d). Maximal incisal
opening was 38 mm, excursive movement to the right 5 mm, to the left 3 mm, no
pain issues, and a stable Class I occlusion. Although this case had a great result relative to growth of the SCG and nice functional and esthetic result, some cases with
SCG grafts have compromised outcomes relative to deficient growth of the graft.

Summary
Many options have been proposed for surgical correction of Kaban Type IIB and III
HFM patients. For many years the most popular technique to reconstruct the
deformed or absent TMJ was ABG including CCG and SCG, but results are not
predictable and stable when the maxilla and mandible require surgical repositioning, particularly advancement and vertical lengthening of the ipsilateral ramus.
Distraction osteogenesis has also become popular to lengthen the hypoplastic mandible and works best with an existing ipsilateral TMJ. The distraction vectors may
be difficult to control, and most cases will require secondary orthognathic surgery
to optimize the functional and esthetic outcomes. The literature shows that ABGs
are not reliable in providing predictable treatment outcomes relative to stability of
skeletal and occlusal relationships, particularly if performed concomitant with
orthognathic surgery, as significant relapse can be expected related to graft remodeling, flexibility, warping, fracture, extended healing time, loading, and biological

6

Surgical Management of Hemifacial Microsomia with Temporomandibular Joint…

127

responses. In addition, there can be significant donor and recipient site
complications.
The TMJ Concepts patient-fitted TJP in conjunction with orthognathic surgery
for TMJ and jaw reconstruction is a valid option for patients with HFM. Research
has clearly demonstrated that TMJ and orthognathic surgery can be safely and predictably performed at the same operation to surgically correct the facial deformities
associated with HFM [64, 65] but does necessitate the correct diagnosis and treatment plan as well as requires the surgeon to have expertise in both TMJ and orthognathic surgery. The application of computer-assisted surgical simulation with virtual
surgical planning (VSP) for cases requiring TMJ reconstruction with patient-fitted
TJP and orthognathic surgery has significantly improved treatment quality by
decreasing the preoperative workup time and increasing the accuracy of surgical
preparation and subsequent surgery [25, 26].
Corrective surgical procedures for HFM can be performed in childhood if indicated for functional, psychological, or airway issues such as growth center transplants (CCG, SCG) or distraction. Patient-fitted TJP can also be considered as there
is less chance of complications compared to AGB. Any of these procedures done in
childhood will require additional surgery at a later time for optimal functional and
esthetic outcomes. In order to do one-stage surgery for the TMJ reconstruction and
orthognathic surgery phase, it would be best to delay until 15 years old for females
and 17–18 for males when at the end of pubertal growth. Using TMJ TJP in conjunction with orthognathic surgery provides the patient with a better, more predictable, and functional result compared to multiple-staged ABG reconstructions done
early. No other surgical technique is able to provide the amount of mandibular
advancement, ramus lengthening, and stability as the patient-fitted TMJ TJP to correct the severely deformed HFM patient.

Conclusion
TMJ Concepts TJPs are superior to ABGs for TMJ reconstruction in the HFM
patient population for the following reasons: (1) no bone harvest required
eliminating donor site morbidity; (2) osseointegration of the TMJ Concepts
fossa and mandibular components provides long-term stability; (3) posterior
stop on the fossa component stabilizes the joint, jaw position, and occlusion;
(4) concomitant orthognathic surgery can be performed at the same time as
the TMJ is reconstructed with predictable outcomes even with large skeletal
changes and advancements; (5) fat grafts packed around the articulating area
of the prostheses improve outcomes relative to decreased pain, improved jaw
function, and decreased requirement for repeat surgery; (6) highly predictable
outcomes relative to skeletal and occlusal stability, TMJ and occlusal function, esthetics, and improvement in the airway; and (7) a 20-year follow-up
study on TMJ Concepts TJP demonstrated improvements in pain, jaw function, diet, incisal opening, and quality of life, with no removal of devices
secondary to failure or wearing out.

Definitive Reconstruction of Associated
Maxillomandibular Deformities
in Craniofacial Microsomia
Fabio G. Ritto, Paul W. Orjuela, Kevin S. Smith, and Paul S. Tiwana

Introduction
Craniofacial microsomia (CFM) has a wide range of clinical presentations, and the
treatment will be determined by a number of factors such as the patients’ complaints, severity of the disease, and existing comorbidities. This chapter will discuss
the definitive treatment for the CFM patient, and therefore it will address patients
that have reached skeletal maturity or skeletal stability, where any residual growth
that may occur will not compromise the surgical result.

Growing and Skeletal Maturity
Skeletal maturity is usually reached around 14–16 years old in girls and 15–17 years
in boys [1]. Different studies have been performed to evaluate the potential growth
of the affected mandibular side in a CFM patient. Most of the studies have shown
that the asymmetry present at the early age is carried throughout the adolescence
[2–5]. This means that the ramus is stable horizontally and vertically, even in the
most dramatic type III cases. In 2020 Meazzini et al. [6] published a long-term
study with 20 type III patients, 10 of which were submitted costochondral graft
(CCG) reconstruction and 10 were not submitted to any surgical procedure. The
authors concluded that restoring the height of the ramus with a CCG leads to an
immediate restitution of facial symmetry, but in the long term, there is a return to the
asymmetrical pattern. In the control group, the asymmetry was stable during years
F. G. Ritto · P. W. Orjuela · K. S. Smith· P. S. Tiwana (*)
Department of Oral & Maxillofacial Surgery, The University of Oklahoma Health Sciences
Center, Oklahoma City, OK, USA
e-mail: Fabio-Ritto@ouhsc.edu; Wilmer-Orjuela@ouhsc.edu; Kevin-Smith@oushc.edu;
Paul-Tiwana@ouhsc.edu
© Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2022
D. M. Yates, M. R. Markiewicz (eds.), Craniofacial Microsomia and Treacher
Collins Syndrome, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-84733-3_7

133

134

F. G. Ritto et al.

with no increase of the facial deformity. Therefore, it can be concluded that definitively treating the patient after skeletal maturity seems to be a reasonable treatment
option, since it reduces the number of necessary procedures and eliminates growth
as a stability factor.
Another philosophy states that the asymmetry is progressive, especially on the
most severe type IIB and III cases, and that operating the mandible during mixed
dentition would be more appropriate to correct the facial asymmetry [7, 8]. The
surgery generates an open bite on the affected side that needs to be managed with an
acrylic splint, so that the maxilla won’t grow asymmetrically to compensate the
open bite, which would generate a vertical asymmetry. The splint needs to be progressively trimmed to adjust to the maxillomandibular growth. The elongation of
the mixed dentition mandible is achieved either by costochondral graft (CCG)
reconstruction of the TMJ, which has several potential complications, or by distraction osteogenesis. Meazzini et al. [4] demonstrated that even though aesthetic and
psychological advantages of early mandibular distraction osteogenesis are well
accepted, early surgery should only be applied after careful patient selection and
honest clarification of the long-term recurrence by a predetermined guided craniofacial growth pattern.
When patients are operated early on in life, the chances of them needing orthognathic surgery after reaching skeletal stability are relatively high. Therefore, it may
be advantageous to follow these patients and defer the definitive treatment for the
maxillomandibular deformities until after skeletal maturation.
For this reason, the authors’ preferred approach in the treatment of CFM patient
is to wait for skeletal maturity; personal experience and scientific data have demonstrated that this approach delivers the most favorable outcomes [9, 10].

Clinical Presentation
The malocclusion commonly seen in CFM is proportional to the degree of skeletal
asymmetry. These patients are five times more likely to have missing teeth than the
general populations. Usually the hypoplastic side will display crowding, crossbite,
and inclination of incisors toward the affected side [11]. The craniofacial surgeon
and orthodontist will have to establish clear communication in order to properly
time dental extractions and dentoalveolar decompensation prior to surgery. Once
the patient is orthodontically ready for surgery, the pre-operative workup will consist of a clinical examination, composite photos, imaging, and dental records. With
the use of all acquired information, a surgical plan is designed as mentioned above;
the surgical splints and guides are fabricated according to the specific plan.
The findings in the craniofacial microsomia patients are broad, depending on the
severity, and may include angle class II anterior open bite; transverse cant in the
occlusal plane and skeletal structures; hypoplasia or absence of mandibular condyle, ramus, and body on the affected side and decreased posterior facial height;
diminished horizontal projection; retruded and deviated chin; hypoplastic maxilla,

7

Definitive Reconstruction of Associated Maxillomandibular Deformities…

135

zygomatico-orbital complex, and temporal bone; hypoeruption and/or partial anodontia; and decreased airway volume and sleep apnea [12, 13]. The discrepancies
created by the upward cant in the maxilla, gonial angles, and pyriform apertures are
better appreciated in the coronal plane; planning the leveling of the discrepancies in
this plane is a proper starting point [14].
The most important factor to be evaluated before determining the definitive treatment of the associated maxillofacial deformities is the health and stability of the
temporomandibular joint. Notice that the shape of the TMJ components is not of
paramount concern, since they will almost invariably have some degree of
deformation.
As a general rule, healthy joints provide adequate function without eliciting pain.
When this concept is applied to the temporomandibular joints, a stable and reproducible occlusion must be present, along with adequate range of motion and absence
of joint pain. It is important however to differentiate articular disorders from muscular disorders, since the latter not necessarily interfere with the surgical stability. It
is outside the scope of this chapter to discuss the diagnosis of temporomandibular
disorders.
Adequate function for CFM patients can be considered when a mouth opening
between 35 and 45 mm is present and protrusion and lateral movements between 5
and 10 mm can be achieved. Deviations during opening are normal in these patients,
since there is usually a size discrepancy between the right and left joints. Active
joint disease will usually present with pain, occlusal changes, cortical defects, subchondral cysts, and osteophytes. A thick cortical bone usually denotes a stable
condyle.
Another important aspect on the clinical evaluation is the soft tissue. The skeletal
asymmetry will be exacerbated due to soft tissue deficiency, which will range from
thinner muscles to atrophy of all soft tissues that surround the facial bones (muscle,
fascia, subcutaneous tissue, skin, and mucosa). In severe cases some muscles may
be absent. Obtaining perfect skeletal symmetry after orthognathic surgery should be
the goal, and Padwa et al. in 1997 [15] found that a four-degree asymmetry on the
occlusal cant is the threshold for recognition by 90% of trained and untrained individuals and, therefore, a four-degree range seems to be a clear and reasonable goal
to pursue. However, because of the soft tissue impairment, it is almost impossible to
achieve perfect facial symmetry with skeletal surgery alone. Applying fillers to the
soft tissue is a good alternative to improve facial balance after the skeletal surgery
has been performed.

Treatment Plan
The concept of natural head position is extremely valuable on these patients, since
it is difficult to find reliable anatomical landmarks to orient the head position. Gross
head inclinations have to be adjusted during clinical evaluation and planning, but
some degree of head tilting usually remains after surgery. Goldenhar patients often

136

F. G. Ritto et al.

present with some degree of cervical spine involvement, which makes head positioning and planning even more difficult.
Virtual surgical planning (VSP) has a very important role in obtaining bone symmetry. Mounting models on a semi-adjustable articulator was a real challenge in this
group of patients, because their external auditory canal is usually absent. The first
thing to do in the virtual platform is to orient the CT volume according to the
patient’s natural head position, and different options have been described for that
purpose [16–18]. There are different sequences that can be used when performing
VSP, but the maxillary position is usually used as a reference to correct the occlusal
plane cant, pitch, and yaw, and the mandible will follow the maxillary position.
After having the skeletal face reconstructed on the virtual platform, with the
scanned dental arches superimposing the CT teeth, the first thing to do is set the
final occlusion, driving the lower arch to match with the upper. To facilitate visualization, hide the mandible and focus on the maxillary position, but move both jaws
while performing any movement. Start the planning by correcting the cant according to the facial evaluation, either by maxillary impaction or down grafting. After
that align the upper arch midline with the facial midline, and adjust the yaw as
necessary to obtain horizontal symmetry. Remember that moving the maxillomandibular complex to correct the yaw will influence both the buccal corridors and the
outline of the face over the mandibular angles. Perform any vertical and anteroposterior corrections deemed necessary on the maxilla, and adjust the occlusal plane on
the sagittal view. After the maxilla is in a good position, un-hide the mandible proximal segments and chin position. Further adjustments on the yaw, occlusal plane, and
chin position might be accomplished to obtain the best possible facial balance.
Three-dimensional planning is extremely important, since the correction of one
dimension will either positively or negatively affect the other two dimensions. For
instance, when the mandible is rotated vertically to correct the occlusal cant, the
distal segment on the non-affected side will push the proximal segment exacerbating the facial fullness. On the other hand, when a sagittal split osteotomy is used to
rotate the mandible horizontally, correcting the lower midline, the ramus on the
affected side will be pushed laterally by the distal segment, while the ramus on the
contralateral side will move medially, improving the facial balance at the ramus
level (Fig. 7.1).
Once the final plan is reached, the splints can be constructed virtually according
to the surgeon’s preference in terms of surgical sequence – mandible or maxilla first.
Since the TMJs are usually not stable, and it may be difficult to obtain records on
centric relation, it seems more reasonable to start surgery on the mandible and then
cut the maxilla. Customized guides such as cutting and positioning guides are
extremely effective for transferring the VSP to the surgical scenario, but they require
more complex softwares for the regular VSP ones and add extra costs that are usually not necessary for the conventional orthognathic cases, but are precious for the
CFM patients.
Aligning the occlusal plane correctly in all three planes will not generate a symmetric face in the CFM patient. The mandible is small along the ramus, body, and
symphysis, and further procedures are necessary to correct the facial balance. The

CT is the best image to obtain measurements, compare right and left sides, and plan

Treatment
After the patient reaches skeletal maturity, treatment is more predictable and resembles a regular orthognathic case. Orthodontic treatment should be established to
remove dental compensations and allow for a complete skeletal correction of the
deformity. These patients usually present with class II and anterior open bite malocclusion, maxillomandibular cant due to decreased facial height of the affected side,
midline shifted to the affected side, and small symphysis, body, and ramus on the
affected side. During the orthodontic treatment, compensations have to be eliminated and arches coordinated, which will further increase the malocclusion. It is
important to avoid extrusive movements in an attempt to close the open bite because
of two reasons: first, these movements are unstable and tend to relapse and reopen
the bite, and second the extruded teeth hinder the surgeon from fully correcting the
anterior open bite skeletally. If however the open bite is slightly increased during
orthodontic treatment, any dental relapse that occurs after removing braces will be
extrusive, increasing the long-term stability. Orthognathic surgery has been shown
to be an effective and stable technique to treat the CM patients [19].
The first decision that needs to be made from a surgical standpoint is if the
affected temporomandibular joint is reliable. If the TMJ needs to be reconstructed,
we believe the best option for the skeletal mature patient is total joint replacement
with a customized prosthetic device, which will be addressed elsewhere in this
book. If TMJ is reliable, which is the case of most type I and IIa patients, the definitive treatment for the maxillomandibular deformities will consist of orthognathic
surgery. Most types IIb and III will need temporomandibular joint reconstruction,
and the current most reliable option for that is a total joint replacement (Fig. 7.2).
There is still space for CCG or sternoclavicular grafts (SCG) in the growing patient,
but due to the morbidity involved on the harvesting site and the lower predictability
when compared to temporomandibular prosthesis, there seems to be very limited
indications to perform a TJR with a costochondral graft in a non-growing patient.
There may be a roll for CCG or SCG in countries with limited or no access to temporomandibular prosthesis or in patients with proven allergy to one of the prosthesis
components, but those would be extreme exceptions.
The four techniques that need to be mastered to adequately treat the maxillomandibular deformities in craniofacial microsomia patient include Le Fort I maxillary
osteotomy, sagittal split mandibular osteotomy, inverted L mandibular osteotomy,
and genioplasty. Additional procedures such as iliac bone harvesting, bone augmentation with autogenous or alloplastic materials, and dermal fillers are also
advantageous.

A Le Fort I osteotomy will be necessary to correct the maxillary position, usually
by a combination of down grafting on the affected side, impaction on the contralateral side, and horizontal shifting to correct both midline yaw positions. The vertical
movement is determined by the amount of teeth exposure – with the lip in repose
and during smile – and by the desired occlusal plane rotation. Bone grafts are usually necessary to increase stability on the down-grafted side.
The mandible may be approached either by bilateral sagittal split osteotomies
(BSSO) or by a combination of sagittal split osteotomy on the contralateral side and

two of the three most common indications, including distorted anatomy and large
advancement. The advantage of the inverted L is that it improves the mandibular
angle outline and offers less risk to the inferior alveolar nerve. Disadvantages

Monasterio et al. (1997) [21] described a technique to perform maxillomandibular distraction osteogenesis (DO) for the hemifacial non-growing patient. The surgery involves performing a Le Fort I osteotomy preserving both the nasal septum
connection to the maxilla and the pterygomaxillary junction on the non-affected
side. An osteotomy is also performed on the affected mandibular ramus, and the
distractor is installed. No procedure is accomplished on the contralateral ramus.
After 5 days the patient is placed on maxillomandibular fixation, and the distractor
is activated at a rate of 1 mm per day. The overall effect is rotation of the whole
maxillomandibular complex. The authors concluded that simultaneous maxillary
and mandibular distraction is the procedure of choice in patients with hemifacial
microsomia over 14 years of age.

Modifications to this technique include performing a complete Le Fort I and
fixating the non-affected side with titanium plate or wire. The exact position of the
fixation device may vary according to the desired center of rotation. For instance,
fixating close to the piriform rim will result in less down grafting of the maxilla and
preservation of pre-operative teeth exposure, as opposed to fixating the zygomaticomaxillary buttress, which will result in greater facial elongation. Advantages of performing bimaxillary DO include good stability when correcting large vertical

7

Definitive Reconstruction of Associated Maxillomandibular Deformities…

145

defects, no need for graft, and the fact that the correction can be continuously evaluated during the treatment [22].
The main problems with DO are that the surgical precision is lower than orthognathic surgery, and it does not allow to freely move the maxillomandibular complex
three dimensionally. There is no control of the horizontal maxillary movement and
no control of the occlusal plane rotation on the sagittal plane, the mandibular
advancement is limited by the amount of ramus elongation, and the maxilla cannot
be positioned superiorly; therefore teeth/gingiva exposure is always increased on
the affected side and maintained or increased on the contralateral side. Also, the
chin is not addressed by the DO, and future genioplasty is usually necessary. Liu
et al. 2017 [23] performed a study and concluded that maxillomandibular DO with
subsequent orthognathic surgery might be the best approach to achieve the most
favorable results.
No matter how good the correction of the cant, pitch and yaw is, some asymmetry will still remain due to intrinsic mandibular deficiency on the affected side.
Ramus, body, and mandibular symphysis are hypoplastic and will demand attention
after the maxillomandibular complex has been corrected at the occlusal plane level.
A genioplasty is required to correct the symphysis, and different augmentation procedures are usually necessary over the body and ramus region.
Ideally, during the pre-surgical orthodontic treatment, the midline of the lower
teeth and chin will be aligned. Therefore, when the occlusal plane is adequately
positioned, the midlines of the upper teeth, lower teeth, and symphysis will be
aligned with the facial midline. The symphysis however is also hypoplastic on the
affected side, and a genioplasty is required to rotate the chin vertically and/or horizontally. The amount of rotation can be easily calculated on the pre-operative CT
scan, but transferring this three-dimensional movement to surgery can become very
challenging depending on the complexity of the movement. Surgical guides are very
helpful to adequately position the chin in these complex three-dimensional movements. This technique is also valuable to correct any anteroposterior deficiency that
remains after the orthognathic surgery, improving the facial profile. Sometimes it
may be advantageous to perform the genioplasty as a second procedure after the
edema from the orthognathic surgery has resolved.
The hypoplastic mandibular body and ramus usually demand some augmentation procedure to obtain skeletal symmetry. This may be accomplished with autogenous or allogenic bone graft and alloplastic material. The advantage of the
autogenous graft is that it is readily available and infection rate is very low. However
it requires a second surgical site, and the resorption rate is unpredictable. Allogenic
bone will spare the second surgical site but has a higher infection rate and can also
resorb. Alloplastic materials such as porous polyethylene are excellent options since
they dispense a second surgical site, can be easily adapted to reconstruct different
mandibular regions, and do not resorb. Infection is the main concern with these
implants, and they are preferably inserted from extra-oral wounds with gloves that
haven’t touched the mouth.

146

F. G. Ritto et al.

Conclusion
Craniofacial microsomia patients require different levels of treatment according to
the severity of the disease. The maxillomandibular reconstruction is essential to correct function and balance of the middle and lower facial thirds. Different techniques
can be applied to obtain these goals, according to the clinical examination, including Le Fort I, BSSO, inverted L osteotomy, and genioplasty. Virtual surgical planning plays a major role in obtaining the best results and must be used in these
patients. Finally, any remaining asymmetry after the maxillomandibular complex is
adequately positioned can be addressed with bone and soft tissue augmentation
procedures.

Presentation and Diagnosis
Patients with craniofacial microsomia (CFM) typically display reduced growth and
development of half of the face owing to abnormal development of the first and
second branchial arches. CFM is also none as craniofacial microsomia (CFM). But
for the purpose of this chapter, we will refer to the entity as CFM. This malformation sequence is usually unilateral but occasionally may involve both sides [1, 2]. A
systematic review and meta-analysis carried out to determine the influence of gender and laterality on the incidence of CFM showed no significant difference between
male and female rates. Also, the frequency of laterality was nearly equal; there was
no clear evidence to prove any association between the laterality of CFM and gender [2, 3].
Patients with this condition have a striking appearance caused by progressive
failure of the affected side to grow, which gives the involved side of the face a
reduced dimension in all planes. In addition, aplasia or hypoplasia of the external
ear (microtia) is common, and the ear canal is often missing. Delayed dental eruption and hypodontia on the affected side have also been reported [4]. From the
orthodontist perspective, the best imaging tool is multidetector computed tomography (MDCT) or cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). The primary radiographic finding is a reduction in the size of the bones on the affected side; additional
findings are summarized on Table 8.1. The differential diagnosis involves ruling out

The vast heterogeneity and phenotype require a classification system to assist the
clinician to develop adequate therapeutic guidance [5]. One of the most widely used
systems for preoperative assessment, due to its simplicity and inclusion of the anatomy and function of the TMJ in addition to its inherently therapeutic approach, was
developed by Pruzansky [6] and expanded by Kaban et al. [7]. The classification
categorizes CFM patients into four groups based on the size and function of the
temporomandibular joint (TMJ): types I, IIA, IIB, and III. This classification system
will be used in this chapter to discuss orthodontics’ main concern, treatment strategies, and prognosis. The most common clinical issues related to the orthodontic
intervention are summarized on Table 8.2.
A common problem in children with mandibular hypoplasia is upper airway
obstruction. A retrospective review of 62 patients with CFM revealed a prevalence
of 11.2%; this is double the incidence of OSA in the general pediatric population
[8]. A systematic review of the literature on children with craniofacial microsomia
showed a prevalence of OSA ranging from 7% to 67% [9]. These results are based
on subjective measurements, such as questionnaires (i.e., the Pediatric Sleep
Questionnaire, [10]), and on the retrospective evaluation of medical charts or are
based on polysomnography performed in a small proportion of the group of patients
studied.
Children with craniofacial conditions are at known risk for a variety of psychosocial problems, including low self-esteem, learning and speech problems, depression, anxiety, and negative social reactions from peers [11, 12]. In light of these
risks, the American Cleft Palate-Craniofacial Association recommends periodic
assessment of the psychosocial needs of children with craniofacial conditions and

Comprehensive Orthodontic Management
Preceding to the beginning of orthodontic treatment, a diagnosis of the patient’s oral
health condition must be made. The diagnosis gives rise to a treatment plan that
addresses the patient’s chief complaint: medical and dental history and dental,
facial, skeletal, functional, and/or psychosocial problems. The treatment plan should
be periodically reassessed throughout treatment with progress records taken as
deemed appropriate by the clinician. This reassessment should take into consideration various limiting factors and establish short- and/or long-term objectives.
Overall, the orthodontic treatment plan includes the following strategies: (1)
modifying the occlusion with a functional appliance and providing support for the
mandibular muscles to function with a more symmetrically positioned mandible in
anticipation of completing surgery on the abnormal side of the mandible; (2) early
surgical intervention to correct the abnormal side, extending the mandible by distraction osteogenesis, or replacing the missing condyle with tissue that includes
growth sites or growth center tissues such as a costochondral graft; (3) wait much
later and not intervening in a young subject, hence decreasing the episodes of surgical intervention (see Chap. 7 on “Definitive Management”). A summary of treatment option based upon dentofacial development is presented on Table 8.3.
The usual protocol is a phase 1 orthodontic treatment to alleviate dental issues
with a possible growth modification followed by a second phase of treatment when
skeletal maturity is complete. This approach allows that this phase of treatment is
final in which results of surgery can be better predicted. The severity of the bony
hypoplasia will dictate the type of surgery used. In cases of Type I and II A, conventional orthognathic surgery can achieve great results. In cases of increased

 ttempt of Modification of Dentofacial Growth Using
A
Orthopedic Treatment Approach
Reports from as early as the 1980s indicated that mild forms of CFM can be treated
successfully by proper orthopedic and orthodontic intervention, fostering mandibular growth and reducing further need to orthognathic surgery [14–16]. However,
those reports usually present mild and some moderately involved growing individuals (Type I, Type IIA) [18]. The treatment approach involves a nonsurgical orthopedic treatment with functional appliance (phase I) completed through fixed
orthodontic treatment (phase II). A slight chin deviation, maximum mouth opening
at a normal range, and both condyles showing proper transitory movements are
required for a favorable scenario. For maintaining the results, long-term retention
may be necessary. This involves fixed retainers and nighttime wearing of a functional appliance.
As described by [17], the functional appliances are made up in various combinations from three basic functional components. These components produce basal and
dentoalveolar changes by acting on the following:
1. Eruption (bite planes)
2. Linguofacial muscle balance (shields or screens)
3. Mandibular repositioning (construction or working bite)
To benefit patients with CFM, the functional appliance must be designed to reposition the mandible downward, forward, and shifted to the unaffected side, producing a posterior open bite. The acrylic is progressively removed from the occlusal
surface of the maxillary posterior teeth to allow overeruption for the purpose of
leveling the occlusal plane. This approach must focus on:
1. Correcting the mandibular deviation and maxillary cant occlusion
2. Controlling the vertical growth pattern to prevent excessive mandibular clockwise rotation
3. Monitoring proper permanent dentition development
4. Achieving an aesthetical, functional, and stable occlusion
The use of the asymmetrical functional orthopedic appliance in growing patients
with more severe CFM presentation (Type IIB and Type III) is limited due to the
severity of the neuromuscular and soft tissue deficiency. Meazzini MC et al. [18]
suggested that orthopedic treatment has little possibility of changing abnormality of

154

A. Da Silveira and P. M. de Moura

early embryonic development such as CFM pattern. The authors pointed out that
there is a peculiar type of mandibular asymmetry, often labeled in the literature as
CFM, that might be an incorrect diagnosis; those case might be successfully treated
with functional appliances.
Preoperative and postoperative treatment with a functional appliance has been
recommended to improve muscle function and to stimulate growth of the soft and
hard tissues (Vargervik K, Ousterhout DK, Farias M 1986; [16, 19]). Recently, in a
pilot study, to solve mandibular canting and deviation, a hybrid treatment combining distraction osteogenesis of the mandibular ramus with a mandible-guided functional appliance was applied in early reconstructive therapy for CFM which was
proposed by Wang Jie et al. [20]. The functional appliance was designed to augment
autologous bone growth, navigate maxillary, and mandibular repositioning and stabilize the occlusal relationship during the entire distraction and consolidation period.

 ong-Term Stability of Orthodontic Treatment Adjunctive
L
to Surgical Interventions
Although various studies on long-term results were published in the last three
decades, they usually report data on preadolescent children and are focused on surgical technique, and few information can be gathered in relation to the orthodontic
intervention [21–26].
In order to analyze the dentofacial changes observed longitudinally, a 12-year-­
old girl, Type IIB CFM, undergone DO with an external device, was followed for
10 years by means of six Björk-type titanium implants placed bilaterally in the
mandible. Marked lengthening was achieved during the active phase of mandibular
distraction. The ratio between the ramus heights of the affected and normal sides
improved significantly in the affected side’s favor as the mandible was lengthened;
however this ratio returned to its initial value after 10 years. The dental occlusion
remained stable despite the changes in the occlusal plane canting and mandibular
symmetry in the follow-up period. The authors concluded that although there was
some growth at the affected side during the 10-year follow-up period, it was not
enough to catch up with the growth of the condyle at the normal side. Therefore, the
asymmetry relapsed because of the expected growth pattern in this growing craniofacial microsomia patient [25].

Background
Incidence of Outer Ear, Middle Ear, and Inner Ear Anomalies
Treacher-Collins Syndrome
The majority of malformations of the external and middle ear in patients with TCS
are symmetric. Approximately 89% of patients have symmetric microtia of which
28% are classified as type I and 67% type II by the Marx classification (Table 9.1).
All patients have abnormalities of the external auditory canals which is most commonly symmetric. Seventy-eight percent of patients have bilateral atresia, and 22%
have bilateral stenosis. The middle ear cavity is hypoplastic and dysmorphic in nearly
all patients. The ossicular chain is classified as dysplastic in 44% and absent in 56%
of cases [2]. The cochlea is usually normal, but dysplasia of the lateral semicircular
canal and vestibule may occur [3]. All patients were noted to have poorly pneumatized mastoids, and 22% of patients have an aberrant facial nerve course with facial
nerve dysfunction, which has only been described as occurring unilaterally [2, 4].
Hemifacial Microsomia
Malformations of the external and middle ear with HFMS are predominantly asymmetric and with equal incidence in the right and left ears [5]. The incidence of
anotia/microtia is reported between 66% and 100%, preauricular tags between 34%
and 67%, and 60% of patients have ear canal atresia [6, 7]. The incidence of middle
ear abnormalities is approximately 10%, and anatomic anomalies of the inner ear
are not usually observed [5].

I ncidence of Conductive Hearing Loss, Sensorineural Hearing
Loss, and Mixed Hearing Loss
Treacher-Collins Syndrome
Conductive hearing loss (CHL) resulting from anatomic abnormalities of the external and middle ear structures accounts for the majority of hearing loss in patients
with TCS, found in approximately 75% of patients. Some patients may also have

sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) with approximately 10% of patients presenting
with mixed hearing loss (MHL). Sensorineural hearing loss alone is uncommon
occurring in approximately 1% of patients and is unilateral in 73% of patients [4].
Conductive hearing loss is generally symmetric with hearing differing by less than
10 dB [2].
Nearly all patients have bilateral hearing loss with an average hearing loss of
64.3 ± 8.5 dB. Of tested ears, approximately 17% have moderate CHL, 67% have
moderately severe CHL, and approximately 17% have severe CHL. As anatomic
abnormalities are generally symmetric, hearing between the two ears generally differs by less than 10 dB [2].
Hemifacial Microsomia
Overall, between 60% and 85% of patients with HFMS have hearing loss [6].
Conductive hearing loss is present in 40–60% of ears, sensorineural hearing loss in
20–30% of ears, and mixed hearing loss in 10% of ears. Normal hearing was present
in 30% of ears, mild hearing loss was present in 30–40% of ears, moderate hearing
loss was present in 20–50% of ears, and profound hearing loss in 10% of ears [5].

Evaluation and Workup
History and Examination
The majority of these children are either identified prenatally via ultrasound or on
the immediate postpartum examination. Family history of craniofacial anomalies
should be sought. Referral to genetics and the craniofacial team should be made
immediately. Airway compromise should be assessed frequently. A complete head
and neck examination should be performed to assess the status of the outer and
middle ear anatomy, including patency of the ear canals and appearance of the tympanic membrane and ossicular chain. Cranial nerve examination should report the
status of the facial nerve, as well as the oculomotor nerves, and gag reflex (sensory
limb via cranial nerve IX, motor limb via cranial nerve X). Ophthalmologic exam
should note any abnormalities.

Audiologic Assessment
Infants born in hospital facilities typically receive some type of universal newborn
hearing screening (either OAE or AABR); however infants identified with anatomical malformations of the outer ear should be referred directly to a pediatric audiologist for a diagnostic evaluation according to the JCIH 2019 Position Statement [8].
The diagnostic audiological evaluation should include evoked auditory brainstem

170

E. C. Cumpston et al.

responses (ABR), evoked otoacoustic emissions (OAEs – either distortion product
DPOAEs or transient evoked OAEs (TEOAEs), and high-frequency tympanometry
when possible.
A patient with unilateral microtia or atresia needs to have the contralateral ear
fully evaluated to verify hearing status because that is typically the better hearing
ear. A screen only in the better ear can overlook a mild loss, high-frequency hearing
loss, or reverse sloping loss. The ear with atresia cannot be able to be assessed with
all measures because there is not an ear canal opening in which to place the testing
probe, but it is possible to test via bone conduction to evaluate inner ear status. In
the case of bilateral atresia, bone conduction ABR testing is recommended though
it is difficult to obtain ear-specific data in this situation. Behavioral audiometry
should be attempted once the baby is about 6–9 months old to start to obtain baseline behavioral hearing threshold data in patients with both unilateral and bilateral
microtia/atresia. The patients with unilateral atresia need the opposite ear monitored
every 4–6 months for any changes in hearing and to monitor middle ear function so
prompt referral for medical intervention can be made if needed. Patients with either
unilateral or bilateral atresia should also be referred as soon as possible to the local
early intervention team for further evaluation and help with development of their
communication and language skills [8]. The patient should also be referred to a
craniofacial team if that has not already been done.

Additional Testing
Genetic evaluation and possible testing should be considered early on. Imaging of
the temporal bones with CT can be done at a later date, as it does not change the
initial management of these children. If planning otologic surgery (atresiaplasty,
canalplasty), a high-resolution CT scan of the temporal bones should be performed
to assess the location of the facial nerve, ventilation of the middle ear and mastoid,
and the presence/absence of the ossicular chain.

Treatment
Conventional Hearing Aids
Due to the predominance of external ear malformations in these patients, conventional hearing aids have limited application. Even in patients who undergo reconstructive surgery, functional and audiologic outcomes are often disappointing with
conventional hearing aids [9].

9

Management of Hearing Loss in Patients with Treacher-Collins Syndrome…

171

Bone Conduction Amplification Options
Bone conduction amplification should be considered as early as possible even in
cases of unilateral atresia in order to provide good speech sound awareness to both
ears which is needed for timely development of communication. Ideally amplification should be fit within the first month of life and no later than 6 months of age [8].
Most patients should be fit with bone conduction devices. In a study by Rosa et al.,
the pure tone average (PTA) in free field by bone conduction was 26.8 ± 4.1 dB with
an estimated gain of 32.8 ± 8.3 dB [2].
Historically hearing aid companies modified behind-the-ear (BTE) hearings to
connect with a cable to a bone conduction oscillator which was then fit on a headband or softband (Fig. 9.1). These hearing aids are no longer being manufactured by
most US hearing aid companies because there are now alternative options from
implant manufacturers to use their speech processor on softbands. Cochlear
Americas has the Baha and Oticon Medical which makes the Ponto, both of which
are easily fit on infants and young children using softbands.
Both companies offer surgical options once the patients are at least 5 years of age
(see further explanation below). However, some families are undecided about what
surgical interventions to choose and can opt for a SoundArc (Fig. 9.2) in lieu of the
softband if they use a Baha.

Another option is the MED-El ADHEAR (Fig. 9.3) which is a speech processor

Implanted Devices
In patients with TCS and HFMS, bone-anchored hearing devices are a very effective
method of hearing implantation. The audiologic results of implanted conduction
devices have been shown to have a PTA in free field 18.3 ± 1.3 dB with an estimated
gain of 38 ± 5.5 dB. Advantages of bone-anchored hearing devices over conventional hearing aids are improved amplification and sound quality, improved bone
conduction, as well as aesthetic appearance [2]. The FDA has approved several
implantable bone conduction devices for children, and these include the Cochlear
Baha and Osia, as well as the MED EL Bone Bridge. The Baha system has been
approved in children since 1999. Two versions are in current use: an abutment system (Fig. 9.4) and an implantable magnetic system (Fig. 9.5). Both involve implanting a titanium pedestal into the mastoid or parietal bone, under a general anesthetic.
Either a transcutaneous abutment (Baha Connect) or an implanted magnet (Baha
Attract) is attached to the implanted pedestal. The child may begin to wear the hearing aid within a few weeks of the surgery.
The MED EL Bone Bridge (Fig. 9.6) and the Cochlear Osia (Fig. 9.7) are FDA
approved over the age of 12 years. These both require implanting the hearing aid
under the periosteum of the mastoid, and the microphone/receiver is attached via
external magnet on the skin surface.
The use of middle ear implants has also been described in patients with TCS;
however, further studies are needed to confirm audiologic outcomes as well as long-­
term follow-up to evaluate possible long-term adverse effects [10, 11]. These are not
FDA approved for use in the United States.
Because severe to profound SNHL in patients with TCS and HFMS is rare and
SNHL in these patients is most often unilateral, cochlear implantation in these

Atresia Surgery
Ear canal reconstruction surgery is rarely indicated in TCS/HFMS due to the numerous associated abnormalities, including aberrant facial nerve location, dysmorphic
ossicular chain, and hypo-pneumatization of the middle ear and mastoid. This surgery includes the creation of an ear canal and tympanic membrane through a postauricular incision. A split-thickness skin graft is used to line the newly formed ear

Chapter 10

Microtia Reconstruction in Patients
with Craniofacial Microsomia
Tania Kraai, Katherine Vandenberg, Sheryl Lewin, and Rosemary Seelaus

Introduction
The options for microtia reconstruction have vastly improved due to the innovation
of dedicated surgeons and anaplastologists who have devoted their careers to this
particularly challenging condition [1–6]. The goal of this chapter is to describe current protocols for reconstruction based on their work and the expertise of the authors
with a focus on the three most common techniques: autologous cartilage, porous
implant, and prosthetic ear reconstruction. All three of these techniques can achieve
optimal results; however, expertise for a particular technique will influence the
results. These techniques should only be undertaken by those who are dedicated to
learning and caring for patients with complex auricular anomalies. The focus will
be on timing, pearls to achieving an excellent result, and the pros and cons of different approaches to auricular reconstruction.
During the preoperative auricular reconstruction consultation, the surgeon should
characterize the auricle and analyze the facial profile, noting the presence of asymmetry, hypoplastic tissue, consistency of the postauricular skin, presence of a canal,
and the location of the hairline. Numerous classifications have been proposed to

characterize the auricle [4, 7–13]. We find it most helpful to grade based on the
increasing severity of the anomaly (see Fig. 10.1).
The protocol described in this chapter will focus more on severe congenital
auricular deformities, i.e., grades II–IV. Grade I microtia is highly variable, and
reconstruction in these cases needs to be tailored to each anomaly; there are various
methods described to address these less severe anomalies [12, 14]. Each grade may
be associated with a low-lying hairline, which is one of the more challenging characteristics associated with microtia. Table 10.1 lists several surgical techniques
described in the literature that address a low hairline, which should be considered
prior to making reconstructive recommendations.
The age, availability of sufficient costal cartilage, potential need for an implanted
hearing device, and associated syndromes and comorbidities are also relevant during the presurgical consultation. Since the dominant vascular supply to the auricle
and surrounding tissues may vary in patients with craniofacial microsomia, the vessels should be considered preoperatively by palpation or Doppler [44, 45]. The surgical approach should be modified based on relevant patient factors and their goals.
Careful consideration of all options to address microtia is necessary, including the
option to not reconstruct the ear as not all patients desire or benefit from reconstruction. The advantages and disadvantages of some of the most common microtia
reconstruction techniques are summarized in Table 10.2.

Autologous Costal Cartilage Auricular Reconstruction
Numerous published approaches and entire books are dedicated to autologous cartilage microtia reconstruction [4, 11, 38, 46]. This chapter will provide a protocol
with a focus on two-stage reconstruction as popularized by Drs. Nagata and Firmin
while incorporating considerations from other techniques.

 irst-Stage Auricular Reconstruction Using Autologous
F
Costal Cartilage
The first stage includes excision of the vestigial cartilage, transposition of the remnant lobule, harvesting and constructing a three-dimensional (3D) framework from
autologous costal cartilage, and correct placement of the cartilaginous framework
within the temporal pocket. Placement should be dictated by the contralateral auricle in unilateral cases. In severe forms of microtia, the external auditory canal may
be displaced inferiorly and anteriorly making positioning of the reconstructed ear
more challenging. Transposing or even closing the canal may be necessary for optimal positioning, but this carries the risk of recurrent external auditory canal infection or cholesteatoma. Careful consideration should be given in these cases with

appropriate expertise. Even in the most skilled hands, this procedure can take an
entire day to complete, and most experienced teams involve two surgeons. For
example, one surgeon may harvest cartilage, while the second surgeon removes
vestigial cartilage, elevates a skin flap, carves, and sets the framework. The steps
with surgical pearls (*) are as follows:
Preoperative Steps
1. Position the patient for a long procedure.
* Pad or suspend pressure points including the heels, scapula, and hips.
2. Shave, braid, or tie hair away from the surgical area.
* Minimal hair removal is preferred by our patient population.
3. Determine and mark the location for the reconstructed ear.
* The angle of the ear should be 15–20 degrees back for bilateral cases and
should match the contralateral ear for unilateral cases.
* Measure the following contralateral ear landmarks: lateral orbital rim to
helical root, nasal ala to tragus and oral commissure to anterior lobule insertion
prior to taping the endotracheal tube.
* The Frankfort horizontal line and zygomatic root should cross just above
the planned tragus.
* The angle of the nasal dorsum can serve as a reference.
* Create a positioning template using the contralateral ear position with cutouts for the ear, lateral brow, commissure of the eye, nasal ala, and oral commissure using radiographic film, and sterilize per institutional guideline. The
positioning template and contralateral anteroposterior measurements are used to
verify the correct location, size, and angulation of the ear [17, 38].
* The outer edge of the planned ear position may be tattooed on the skin at the
beginning of the case using methylene blue and a 25-gauge needle.
* The top of the planned microtia reconstruction should be even with the
contralateral ear and usually at the level of the lateral eyebrow unless the opposite ear is low set. The sideburn to helical root distance is usually 1.5 cm.
* In more severe forms of hemifacial microsomia, the position may need to
be slightly more anterior and slightly smaller than the contralateral ear, but the
sideburn measurement should be respected [11, 18].
4. Create and sterilize a carving template based on the cartilage to be reconstructed
(see Fig. 10.2).
* Measure the height and width of the contralateral ear. For bilateral microtia,
the patient may choose the size; generally, a smaller size is preferable.
* The contralateral ear can be used to create the carving template using radiographic film. Dr. Nagata uses sized preprinted templates [4].
* 3D templates have also been described using various methods and materials
and may improve patient satisfaction while decreasing surgical time [47, 48].
5. Plan costal cartilage harvest incision.

184

T. Kraai et al.

a deep conchal bowl

* Identify ribs 6–9 on the ipsilateral side to the microtia ear. Contralateral
costal cartilage can be used, but for the carving technique in this chapter, the
ipsilateral cartilage is described.
* Mark a 4-cm oblique or horizontal chest incision near the inferior border of
the seventh rib. Oblique incisions improve access, while horizontal incisions
correspond with relaxed skin tension lines.
* The incision may need to be extended in obese patients but may be as small
as 2 cm in non-obese patients [46].
6. Prepare and drape the patient with the opposite ear in the operative field for ease
in confirming accurate placement.
* Be mindful of fire risks with some sterilizing solutions particularly if hair is
exposed.
* Most patients with microtia have aural atresia (76%). However, if an ear
canal is present, then prepare the ear canal with 5% betadine [49].
* In patients with an ear canal, antibiotic otic drops for 1 week prior to surgery has been described [3].

1. Plan and mark the lobule transposition incision. The incision and subcutaneous
vascular pedicle sites are marked based on microtia classification and location of
the remnant auricle (see Fig. 10.3). For grade IV reconstruction, see Figs. 10.4
and 10.5.

* In some patients with grade IIa (conchal type) microtia, the incision does
not need to extend around into the postauricular sulcus if the ear is not significantly over projected, e.g., Fig. 10.6.
* The vascular pedicle should be at the normal location of the external auditory canal, which is just below the root of the zygomatic arch, and can be confirmed using the carving template. The pedicle improves the blood supply to the
skin flap, deepens the conchal bowl, and tethers the skin down to create a depression that mimics the external auditory canal and accentuates the tragus, e.g.,
Fig. 10.7 [50].
* In lobular-type microtia, ample skin from the posterior lobule and mastoid
should be elevated to line a deep conchal bowl.
* If possible, the anterior surface of the tragal cartilage should be covered
with the skin contiguous with the cheek to avoid a more visible scar.

* If there is a significantly low-lying hairline (>15%) (usually grade III or
IV), then a temporoparietal fascial (TPF) flap and skin graft may be necessary to
cover the framework where the hair-bearing skin must be excised (see TPF harvest description in stage 2). A separate fascial flap will be necessary for stage
2 in these cases.
2. Remove the vestigial auricular cartilage; leave the tragus and antitragus if
present.
* Straight tenotomy scissors, 15-blade, q-tip, and cottle, are helpful for skin
elevation.
* If present, removing the vestigial conchal bowl cartilage improves the depth
of the neo-conchal bowl.
3. Create a subcutaneous temporal pocket, which should be elevated at least 2 cm
past the marked framework position while maintaining a vascular pedicle.
* Elevate a uniform flap to allow the skin to drape evenly over the framework.
If the skin flap is too thin, then the risk of skin necrosis, cartilage atrophy, and
exposure of the cartilage framework increases. If the skin flap is too thick, the
auricular contours will be less pronounced.
* Maintain the subdermal plexus by elevating just over fascia. The mastoid
fascia, which contains the posterior auricular muscles, is continuous with the

10

Microtia Reconstruction in Patients with Craniofacial Microsomia

189

TPF cranially and the superficial cervical fascia caudally [51]. The subcutaneous
layer thins over the mastoid tip, and care should be taken to maintain a sufficiently thick subcutaneous flap to avoid a skin thickness mismatch with the lobular transposition flap. Maintaining intact fascia also protects venous outflow
from the TPF.
Costal Cartilage Harvest
1. Consider options for decreasing postoperative pain using an intercostal block,
paravertebral regional block, or pain pump.
2. Make the preplanned incision down through the subcutaneous tissue, and create
a suprafascial pocket overlying costal cartilages 6–9.
3. Elevate the rectus and external oblique muscle from the perichondrium to
widely expose ribs 6–9.
* Muscle transection may be minimized by lateralizing these muscle groups.
4. Divide the anterior perichondrium of the sixth and seventh ribs with care to
avoid injuring the underlying cartilage. The rib anatomy is variable, but these
ribs usually have a synchondrosis.
* Use a flat paddle Bovie tip on a low setting or a 15-blade scalpel.
* Elevate the perichondrium superiorly and inferiorly with a freer or
osteotome.
5. Once the costochondral joint is exposed, divide at the bony cartilaginous junction using a molt or malleable to protect the pleura, leaving a small beveled rim
of cartilage on the bone.
6. Elevate the costal cartilage off the posterior perichondrium from lateral to
medial. Divide the medial attachment at the sternochondral joint.
* If possible, maintain the synchondrosis for stability of the base framework.
* Finger dissection under the rib can aid in elevation.
7. Harvest the eighth and possibly the ninth rib.
* Free the medial attachments, and elevate each rib laterally with care not to
overbend and fracture the rib, leaving the perichondrium on the harvested
rib [3].
* Conchal-type microtia reconstruction may not require the ninth costal cartilage, but enough cartilage should be harvested to bank for the second-stage
projection graft if a second stage is required.
8. Place the harvested costal cartilage in antibiotic saline solution (e.g., gentamicin 50 mg/500 mL).
9. Check for a pleural tear and repair if present.
10. Close the sixth and seventh rib perichondrial sleeve leaving a small opening for
replacing the cartilage off-cuts.
11. Close the chest incision after carving the framework so that cartilage off-cuts
can be replaced prior to closure.
