Fig. 10.8 Creating the cartilage framework. (a) The base framework is carved from the sixth and
seventh rib synchondrosis. The scapha and triangular fossa are deepened. The conchal bowl is
removed except for a small projection for attachment of helical crus. (b) The helical rim is attached
first at the projection piece. A step-off is carved on the undersurface at the root where the helix
transitions onto the base framework. The antihelix, antitragus, and tragus are carved as needed
from different off-cuts of cartilage and secured to the base framework. (c) The conchal floor graft
and sometimes a projection block (for single stage) are secured under the base framework and
helical crus to create a deep conchal bowl. (d) The three-layered costal cartilage graft

Creating the Cartilage Framework (See Fig. 10.8)
Microtia reconstruction surgery requires meticulous attention to detail, and carving
the framework requires spatial expertise in ear anatomy to create an optimal 3D
structure. Care should be taken when handling cartilage and should be treated as a
living sculpture. For lobular-type microtia (grade III) and anotia (grade IV), the full
cartilage framework will need to be created as described below. For conchal-type
microtia (grade II), the tragus and sometimes the antitragus do not need to be reconstructed if they are well-formed, e.g., Fig. 10.9. Older patients may have calcified
costal cartilage, and a drill may be necessary to create portions of the framework.
Use a 5.0 double-armed steel suture (or 40 gauge) for efficient attachment of cartilage components. Permanent clear suture (e.g., 4.0 or 5.0 Nylon) may also be used
if steel suture is not available.
Base Framework
1. The ipsilateral sixth and seventh costal cartilages are flipped over so that the
inner surface of the costal cartilage in situ becomes the lateral surface of the ear
framework, taking advantage of the natural curve (see Fig. 10.10).
* The surgeon carving the framework should sit on the same side as the
microtia to help avoid mistakenly carving the wrong side.
* The synchondrosis may need suture reinforcement if the attachment is
loose. If the location of the synchondrosis has a notch or does not fit the template
correctly, then the sixth and seventh rib should be separated and reattached.
* Use a 15-blade, gouge, or biopsy punch for carving [46].

Helix, Antihelix, Antitragus, Intertragal Notch, and Tragus (Fig. 10.10b)
2. Divide the eighth rib to create the helical rim, which is generally ~3 mm wide.
* Thin the cartilage until it will bend without breaking. If possible, leave the
perichondrium intact on the outer edge.
3. Attach the helical rim to the base framework.
* A small incision in the cartilage allows the steel suture to recess into the
cartilage as it is tightened, which helps prevent suture extrusion. Suture extrusion thins the skin and can lead to cartilage atrophy or exposure.
* Begin by attaching the helical rim cartilage to the base framework at the
projection where the helical crus crosses the conchal bowl.

192

T. Kraai et al.

* The helical rim wraps around the base framework to the level of the antitragus. If the eighth costal cartilage graft is short (<10 cm), then a second piece may
need to be added to prevent an unnatural notch at the transition between the bottom of the helix and lobule.
4. Carve the antihelix from one of the following pieces: an off-cut from the sixth,
seventh, or eighth rib (after creating the base framework and helix, respectively),
or the ninth rib.
* The inferior crus is usually thinner than the more broad superior crus.
* The antihelix is often more projected than the helix in the mid portion of the
ear on the frontal view and should mirror the contralateral ear.
* The antitragus can be created from an extension of the antihelix, but there
should be a change in the angle at the transition from the antihelix to the
antitragus.
5. Carve out the tragal attachment from an off-cut of the sixth or seventh rib.
* Some surgeons carve the tragus, antitragus, and intertragal notch from a
single piece of cartilage [3].
6. Attach a thin piece of cartilage (conchal floor graft) under the base framework
and helical crus to create a deep conchal bowl leaving a space for the vascular
pedicle.
7. A projection block may also be added under the framework to improve projection if considering a single-stage reconstruction [42].
8. Close the chest incision after replacing the remaining off-cuts into the sixth and
seventh rib perichondrial sleeves.
* Placing off-cuts into the perichondrial sleeve allows for regeneration of
more structurally sound costal cartilage and prevents a chest wall deformity [39].
* If a second stage is required for projection of the framework, then bank a
piece of cartilage in the subcutaneous fat to be used as a projection block for the
next stage.
Cartilage Graft Placement, Dressing, and Postoperative Care
9. Ensure hemostasis and insert a drain into the temporal pocket.
10. Place a permanent tacking suture on the deep side of the framework at the level
of the anterior triangular fossa, and pass the same suture through the deep fascia
at the correct level prior to placing the framework into the temporal pocket
while access is optimal. This suture will secure the framework and prevent
migration.
* Take care to avoid injuring the superficial temporal artery (STA).
11. Place the cartilage framework by rotating it counterclockwise into place around
the vascular pedicle.
* Use the positioning template, preoperative measurements, and direct comparison to the contralateral ear to confirm the correct position and angle.

10

Microtia Reconstruction in Patients with Craniofacial Microsomia

193

* Check the capillary refill along the helical rim when the framework is in
place and suction is activated. If the skin does not drape easily over the framework or blanches significantly, the pocket size should be enlarged.
12. Once the correct position is confirmed, tie the tacking suture.
13. Transpose the lobule and mastoid flaps into the correct position, and close
the skin.
* Excise redundant skin with care to avoid devascularization of the skin flap.
* Small z-plasties at the transverse closure across the antihelix and helix
may help hide the incision.
* Placing a deep permanent suture between the tragus and helical root once
the framework is in place helps maintain the shape of the cartilage framework.
* If a TPF is necessary to cover the cartilage framework due to a severely
low-lying hairline (common in grade IV), then the cartilage framework is
placed, and the TPF flap is folded over the top of the framework, sutured in
place, and covered with a skin graft.
* Close the incisions with 6.0 permanent or 5.0 fast-absorbing sutures.
14. Dressing and postoperative care.
* Cover the reconstructed ear with antibiotic ointment, and suture a bolster
in place for 5–7 days using Xeroform sterile non-adherent petrolatum gauze
secured with 3.0 Prolene sutures or similar material.
* Place a mastoid dressing with care to ensure the dressing is not too tight
using fluffs and Kling gauze.
Negative pressure without a bolster has also been described [41].
* Remove sutures on postoperative day 10.

 econd-Stage Auricular Reconstruction Using Autologous
S
Costal Cartilage
The second stage is often necessary to achieve adequate projection in order to match
the contralateral ear. In this stage a cartilage graft is placed in the postauricular sulcus to elevate the framework. The cartilage projection graft is then covered with
fascia and a skin graft. This stage is generally performed 6 months after the first
stage. Some patients do not require a second stage as shown by Drs. Kasrai and
Fisher [42]. See Fig. 10.11 for an example of a single-stage bilateral
reconstruction.
Preoperative Steps
1. Measure and record the superior, middle, and inferior projection distances of the
contralateral and reconstructed ear.
* Minor adjustments in the position and angle of the ear can be made if
needed once the ear is elevated.

* The skin graft may need to be as long 10 cm and as wide as 4 cm.

5. Position and prepare the patient as previously described.
Banked Costal Cartilage and Skin Graft Harvest
1. Harvest banked costal cartilage from stage 1.
* Further costal cartilage may need to be harvested if insufficient cartilage
was harvested during the first stage.
* Some surgeons use a custom-designed polyethylene wedge [66].
2. Harvest the skin graft for postauricular coverage.
I ncisions for Ear Elevation and TPF Flap Harvest to Cover
the Postauricular Cartilage Graft and Helical Rim
3. Make the initial postauricular incision into the dermis, and elevate an ultra-­
delicate split-thickness skin graft anteriorly over the unwanted hair follicles on
the helical rim.
4. Excise the subcutaneous tissue containing the unwanted hair follicles under
the UDSTSG.
5. Complete the postauricular incision down to the TPF superiorly and mastoid
fascia inferiorly.
* Making a small TPF access incision into the scalp helps with visualization
for TPF elevation and avoids a larger scalp incision. This is also where a dog ear
generally forms once the postauricular scalp is elevated and advanced.
6. TPF flap elevation.
* Elevate a suprafascial flap posterior to the ear (3–4 cm) and superior
(9–10 cm) to the helical rim. This will allow the scalp to advance forward for
closure and provide access for harvesting the TPF. The plane is just under the
subcutaneous fat where dermal fibrous attachments are carefully divided to
elevate the flap.
* An extended Colorado® microdissection monopolar cautery, long retractor, and Andrews suction are useful for elevating the skin flap off the fascia.
* The flap width (generally 6–7 cm) should allow for coverage of the cartilage projection graft, helical rim, and extend down to the level of the lobule for
grade III (lobular-type) microtia. The TPF helps reduce helical rim cartilage
atrophy by improving blood supply to the cartilage.
* Once the skin has been adequately elevated over the TPF, incise the anterior edge of the planned flap at least 2 cm anterior to the dominant STA branch
above the level of the inferior temporal septum (ITS), which is approximated by
the hairline. Below the ITS, the loose areolar tissue becomes a fibrofatty layer
that is more difficult to dissect; this also helps avoid the temporal branch of the
facial nerve [67]. The anterior branch of the STA is generally divided to improve
mobility of the flap.

200

T. Kraai et al.

Fig. 10.15 Cartilage
projection block

* Incise the posterior edge of the planned TPF flap followed by the superior edge.
* Elevate the deep side of the TPF in the loose areolar tissue plane superficial
to the periosteum and deep temporal fascia in a cranial to caudal direction using
a Kittner, blunt right angle forceps, and scissors.
* Some advocate including the loose areolar fascial tissue in the harvested
TPF flap to improve vascular supply and allow the skin to slide over the cartilage [33].
* Keep the flap hydrated and in its anatomical position until it is ready to be
sutured in place.
7. Carve the projection block using the template (see Fig. 10.15).
* The height of the projection block should be based on the superior, middle,
and inferior measurements from the contralateral ear minus the height of the
reconstructed framework (usually 6–8 mm). Cartilage may need to be stacked
to achieve the correct height and secured using a 5.0 steel or a permanent suture.
8. Elevate under the cartilage framework over the underlying fascia, and place the
projection graft to achieve symmetry with the contralateral ear.
* Secure the projection graft to the framework and the underlying soft tissue
with a permanent suture to prevent migration.
9. Place a 10 French channel suction under the elevated scalp to prevent hematoma.
10. Fold the TPF over the helical rim and postauricular sulcus, and secure the flap
to the cartilage with fine suture such as 5.0 Monocryl.
11. Advance and secure the postauricular scalp flap with deep tacking sutures.
* Avoid advancing the superior hair-bearing scalp into the superior auricular
sulcus, which will be lined with a skin graft.
* Excise and close the dog-ear deformity at the TPF access incision.
12. Place the harvested skin graft, and suture in place with a 6.0 permanent or
absorbable suture.
13. Place a bolster over the skin graft sutured in place to the cartilage framework
and postauricular scalp, and place a dressing as described in stage 1.
14. Remove bolster on postoperative day 5–7 and sutures on postoperative day 10.

Postoperative swelling improves over 3–6 weeks after each stage. Patients are
asked to avoid activities that could injure the reconstructed ear for 3 months after

and after stage 1 and stage 2 autologous cartilage auricular reconstruction.

Porous Implant Ear Reconstruction (PIER)
Porous Implant Ear Reconstruction (PIER), first described in 1982 by Dr. Alexander
Berghaus, has become an accepted alternative to autologous costal cartilage ear
reconstruction for the treatment of microtia [5, 35, 68–71]. Much like the rib cartilage technique, reconstructions using porous polyethylene have a steep learning
curve and are technically challenging. Far fewer surgeons use the PIER technique
as compared to rib cartilage, which is likely due in part to less exposure to this technique during training [36].
Surgery may be performed as young as 3 years old and is ideally completed
before a child enters kindergarten. There is a psychological advantage to patients
who get early reconstruction (3–6 years) [72]. The author’s youngest age for surgery
was increased to 4 years old in October 2015, after the release of a consensus statement on the use of anesthetic and sedative drugs in infants and toddlers that recommended waiting until 4 years of age before performing elective surgery longer than
3 hours.

202

T. Kraai et al.

Certain anatomic conditions predict a more difficult ear reconstruction (e.g.,
hemifacial microsomia, presence of a surgical canal, an inferiorly positioned native
canal, anteriorly displaced microtia remnant). This section will discuss the author’s
protocol for single-stage total ear reconstruction using porous polyethylene
implants. The description below will focus on the most typical anatomy encountered, grade III microtia with aural atresia.

Preoperative Surgical Planning
1. The patient is positioned 180° from anesthesia with appropriate padding.
* A shoulder roll is placed at the beginning of surgery to aid with visualization during TPF flap harvest and then removed once the flap dissection is
completed.
* Extremities are moved every 2 hours to avoid pressure ulcers.
* The anesthesiologist is informed not to use any paralytics so stimulation of
the frontal branch of the facial nerve will be evident during the flap dissection.
2. The hairline is shaved 2 cm around the microtic ear.
3. Create a positioning template of the unaffected ear on clear film.
* The positioning template should include the ear, hairline, sideburn, eyebrow, eyelid, and the position of the midline at the radix.
4. Determine and mark the appropriate size and position of the ear.
* When operating on young children, surgeons must be aware of the growth
patterns of the ear over time in order to estimate the adult size of the unaffected
ear [73].
* In symmetric patients, the position template is reversed, and the position of
the ear is marked. The author uses a 3D-printed mirror image model of the unaffected ear to confirm the position.
* For patients with hemifacial microsomia, the implant should be placed
closer to the midline than the opposite ear depending on the degree of asymmetry.
* If the orbit on the side of the microtia is smaller and more inferior, the eyelid and eyebrow on the positioning template must be adjusted to account for the
bony asymmetry.
* Inclination of the ear is referenced against the angle of the nasal dorsum.
* Although some utilize precise measurements to determine ear position, the
author relies heavily on past experience, and therefore implant position is ultimately a subjective one determined during surgery.
* Care must be taken to keep a boundary of hairless skin around the reconstructed ear symmetric to the unaffected side.
* There will almost always be some area of hair-bearing scalp superiorly that
must be resected and discarded.

5. Mark out the TPF flap and its blood supply (see Fig. 10.17).
* Starting at the level of the microtic remnant, the STA, which is usually
located just anterior or sometimes underneath the remnant, is palpated and
marked. If the latter occurs, extreme care must be taken when excising the cartilaginous remnant to avoid injuring the vascular pedicle.
* The surgeon should note the position of the postauricular artery (to avoid
injury) and the anterior branch of the occipital artery (to preserve in the event a
salvage reconstruction is required).
* Mark the boundary of the TPF flap.
* If the anterior branch is very close to the lateral eyebrow (<1 cm), an alternate flap is designed utilizing the posterior branch of the STA and the anterior
branch of the occipital artery to avoid injury to the frontal branch of the
facial nerve.
* In cases where the anterior branch courses too close to the facial nerve,
there may be small branches that take off more inferiorly that can be safely
incorporated into the flap to augment the blood supply.
6. Mark an inferiorly based lobule flap leaving a 1.5-cm pedicle.
7. Mark an anteriorly based auricular skin flap incorporating all of the hairless skin
around the microtia remnant.
* The auricular skin is used either as an anteriorly based flap or a full-­thickness
skin graft depending on the patient’s anatomy.
8. Prepare and drape the patient.
* The non-sterile positioning template is trimmed and placed between two
sterile Tegaderms onto the operative field.

204

T. Kraai et al.

Implant Preparation
There are two main implant manufacturers [Medpor (Stryker), Su-Por (Poriferous
LLC)] that make two-piece porous polyethylene implants consisting of a helical rim
and an antihelical base that are soldered together to create the ear. The two-piece
implant is the most prevalent option at this time and therefore will be described
below. However, the author currently uses one-piece implants of her own design
based on a 3D scan of the patient’s opposite ear (see Fig. 10.18).
9. Carve the antihelical base to create a more realistic shape based on the patient’s
unaffected ear.
* Thin and shape the inferior crura, and create a more realistic curvature to
the conchal bowl.
* Remove the tragus and intertragal incisura as they are preferably reconstructed with cartilage from the microtia remnant.
10. Solder the inferior helical rim to the antihelical base along all aspects including
the superior and inferior crura using a high-temperature fine-tip battery-­powered
cautery.
* The positioning template of the unaffected ear, projected to adult size
based on the child’s age, is used to guide the length and shape of the helical rim.
* If there is no canal, the rim is brought into the notch of the antihelical base
to form the helical crus.
* A smoke evacuator is used during the soldering process to the reduce fume
inhalation.

11. Strengthen the two-piece implant.
* Extra pieces of polyethylene are soldered between the open spaces of the
rim and the base at all sites except the triangular fossa. One of these pieces is
used to create a more broad and subtle shape of the superior crura.
* This step is required to minimize the risk of implant fracture.
12. The base of the implant is altered to create symmetric projection and angulation
of the implant.
* The implant is kept in saline until ready for use.
* It is important to ensure there are no sharp edges on the implant, especially
when carving detail into the thin inferior crura.

Dissection of Microtia Remnant and Auricular Skin
13. Incise the lobule transposition flap.
* The lobule of the microtia is usually too anterior and too superior. The dissection should allow for a posterior and inferior rotation that will match the
opposite earlobe.
* In the case of a lobule remnant that is much lower than the unaffected earlobe, the lobule may be rotated posteriorly on a superior pedicle to achieve
better symmetry if the anatomy is appropriate.
14. Raise the anteriorly based auricular flap between the subcutaneous tissue and
the superficial TPF to include all hairless skin around the microtic ear (see
Fig. 10.19).
Fig. 10.19 Lobule
transposition and anteriorly

T. Kraai et al.

* Colorado-tip cautery is used for precise dissection.
* The flap is defatted to remove all of the subcutaneous tissue. The skin flap
is left attached until the implant and fascia are in place, at which point it is laid
onto the anterior surface of the reconstructed ear. If the skin orientation is compromised by the limitations of the anterior attachment, the skin is removed and
used as a full-thickness skin graft.
15. The vestigial cartilage remnant is then dissected free of the surrounding soft
tissues, removed, and kept in saline until ready for use in the tragal
reconstruction.
* All vascular structures near the remnant are noted and protected during
cartilage excision. When the cartilage is in close proximity to a vessel, only the
portion above the plane of the surrounding fascia is removed.

Fascial Flap Dissection (See Fig. 10.20)
The TPF flap is the most critical aspect of PIER surgery [33, 74]. In 2006, the author
developed a technique to harvest the TPF flap with no scars in the scalp using a
lighted retractor through a periauricular incision. However, until one is completely
comfortable with this flap dissection, a zig-zag or horizontal scalp incision will
allow for better visualization.
16. Dissect the superficial surface of the TPF.
* The blood supply to the flap is within the fascia proximally and becomes
more superficial distally. In some patients, the distal vessels must be pulled
down from the subcutaneous tissue. In order to avoid injuring these small vessels, the author uses the tip of a Yankauer suction to push on the subcutaneous
fat upward in order to create enough tension to visualize the plane just above
the vessel.
Fig. 10.20 TPF flap

10

Microtia Reconstruction in Patients with Craniofacial Microsomia

207

* Bovie dissection with a fine Colorado tip (3-inch length with 1-cm
45-degree tip) is used at the lowest effective cautery settings (cutting 12, coagulation 10) to avoid injuring the hair follicles. In older patients, these settings
must be raised.
* Surgicel may be used for minor bleeding to preserve the flap vascularity.
17. Dissect the deep surface of the TPF.
* Start near the pedicle of the STA.
* The correct depth of dissection, which is below the subgaleal fascia, is
identified using tenotomy scissors.
* Dissection should continue just above the characteristic whitish-blue color
of the deep temporal fascia along the anterior, superior, and then posterior
borders.
* Take care to coagulate both the anterior and posterior branches where they
cross the flap perimeter to avoid bleeding from these larger vessels
postoperatively.
* Blunt dissection with cherry dissector sponges is used to dissect the deep
surface of the superficial TPF along with its underlying subgaleal fascia.
Including the subgaleal fascia creates a bilaminar flap that aids with skin mobility over the implant, improving durability. This is especially critical in young
children since their tissue is so thin.
* Stimulation of the frontal nerve should be noted when dissecting close to
the eyebrow. If excessive movement is seen, the anterior branch of the STA
should be cut more proximally. Alternatively, the posterior branch of the STA
and the anterior branch of the occipital artery may be used to supply the flap.
* In older patients, the surgeon may prefer to leave the subgaleal fascia
behind in order to get a thinner flap.
* The deep surface of the flap becomes more adherent inferiorly, so it may
be more effective to switch to tenotomies for the last 2–3 cm of dissection.
* The inferior border of the flap should stop at the superior margin of the
final implant position.
* If the flap seems too small to completely cover the implant, extra length
can be gained by releasing along the STA pedicle inferiorly. If this vessel is not
easily seen in the field of view, the flap is transilluminated from below.
18. Irrigate copiously and ensure hemostasis of the scalp and the flap.
* No drain is used for the scalp unless the patient was noted to bleed more
than a typical amount during the flap harvest.
* The TPF flap should always be placed under the scalp until ready for use.

Covering the Implant with the Fascial Flap (See Fig. 10.21)
19. Secure the porous implant to the deep fascia.
* The implant is placed into the proper position and inclination as determined by the template and visual assessment of symmetry.

T. Kraai et al.

Fig. 10.21 TPF flap
folded over the 3D implant

* 3–0 PDS sutures are used to hold the implant in place, taking care not to
injure any vessel within the fascia.
* A 10 French round channel drain is placed through the posterior hairline
and laid against the back surface of the implant.
20. Wrap the TPF flap around the implant and apply suction.
* If necessary, a 5–0 Monocryl is sutured around the periphery to achieve
satisfactory adherence of the flap to the implant.
* Care must be taken that 100% of the implant is covered by the flap. The
flap should be generous enough in size to conform to all the interstices of the
implant without tenting over any concavities, especially the helical rim.
* If the flap is still too small after all options for dissection have been completed, the implant will need to be altered by carving down the inferior aspect
and/or removing some of the base so that it projects less.
* If a patient has a particularly large ear, an extra centimeter of flap should
be designed at the beginning of the surgery.

21. Use auricular skin on the front of the ear whenever possible to have the best
color match.
* All of the non-hair-bearing skin around the microtia is used as either a flap
or a full-thickness skin graft.
22. Harvest full-thickness skin graft from behind the unaffected ear.

* Approximately 6 cm × 2 cm of the skin may be taken and used in conjunction with the skin from the microtia side to cover the majority of the front of
the ear.
* In order to avoid altering the projection of the unaffected ear, a postauricular scalp flap is advanced anteriorly and sutured near the postauricular sulcus.
This will move the postauricular hairline about 1 cm anteriorly but will still
leave enough of a skin perimeter around the back of the ear to look appropriate.

be covered with abdominal skin graft.
23. If there is not enough hairless auricular skin to use on the front of the ear, harvest full-thickness skin graft from the upper inner arm.
* This occurs most commonly in patients with bilateral microtia, a low hairline, significant hemifacial microsomia, prior atresia repair, or prior failed
microtia surgery.
* An ellipse of 10–12 cm length by 3 cm wide may be taken from the arm
without undue tension on the closure.
* The arm scar has a tendency to widen and should be managed with silicone
tape. If possible, avoid using arm skin in patients prone to thickened scars or
keloids.
24. Harvest full-thickness skin graft from the lower lateral abdomen avoiding the
central hair-bearing area to cover the posterior aspect of the ear
reconstruction.

T. Kraai et al.

25. Place the final scar between the anterior skin grafts and the posterior skin graft
along the apex of the helical rim so the scar will be less conspicuous.
* All grafts are sutured in place with interrupted 5–0 and 6–0 chromic suture.

Tragal Reconstruction
26. Carve the remnant cartilage into a neo-tragus using the template to match the
shape of the tragus on the unaffected ear.
27. An anteriorly based cheek flap is raised just under the subcutaneous fat in order
to advance the skin posteriorly to cover the tragus. The flap is folded over both
above and below the cartilage and secured to the deeper tissues to hold the
position.
* It is best to incorporate some auricular skin with the cheek skin to ensure
full coverage of the cartilage graft.
* It can be challenging to reconstruct the tragus in a symmetric position
because it is essentially suspended in front of the canal.

Dressing and Postoperative Care
28. Cover all skin grafts with antibiotic ointment.
29. Pack Vaseline gauze into the bowl, the helical rim, and the postauricular sulcus.
30. Place a non-adherent dressing around the ear against the scalp and face.
31. A two-component silicone-based ear impression material (Azoft, Oticon
Germany) is placed over the entire ear (see Fig. 10.23).

* 3–0 Prolene is used to secure the Azoft mold to the scalp.
* Attention must be given to avoid placing sutures at areas of the ear where
the flap could be injured.
32. Remove the drain.
33. Wrap the head and ears with gauze using Hypafix tape around the face.
* 3–0 Prolene is sutured at the top of the scalp to keep the gauze from

* Cover with a Velcro headband and a protective ear cup (Romo-Guard).
34. The dressing is removed 5–8 days after surgery.
35. Daily cleaning and application of ointments are initiated.

color of skin grafts can continue to change over a year. Postoperative results of a

that in both patients, the PIER ear is intentionally larger than the unaffected side,
which has not yet reached adult size.

Prosthetic Ear Reconstruction of the Pinna
External prosthetic reconstruction of the pinna using artificial materials, e.g., medical grade silicone, is a well-demonstrated treatment option for the patient with congenital microtia [75, 76]. Historically, proponents of surgical versus prosthetic ear
reconstruction may have viewed these as competing treatment options; however, the
well-informed and experienced practitioner recognizes the value of a patient-­
centered approach in presenting these complementary treatments [29, 46, 71, 77].

Fig. 10.24 Preoperative and 6 months postoperative PIER patient (two-piece Su-Por implant)

212

T. Kraai et al.

Fig. 10.25 Preoperative and 3.5 months postoperative PIER patient (3D Lewin ear implant
by Su-Por)

The patient is best served when treatment potential is presented in a comprehensive
and collaborative manner – the purpose of this chapter.
The function of facial prosthetics is to improve an individual’s quality of life
[78]. Aside from restored facial and auricular symmetry, the prosthetically reconstructed ear enables the individual to wear devices designed to fit in, on, or around
the external ear such as eyeglasses (sun, safety, reading, or other corrective lenses).
One example specific to healthcare providers is the ability to use a stethoscope in a
customary manner.
When considering prosthetic ear reconstruction, the patient can elect either a
surgical or non-surgical approach. The consulting practitioner must have a sound
understanding of the fundamentals of prosthetic rehabilitation and associated
options such that they can appropriately and accurately educate the patient and family and subsequently that the patient fully understands their commitment to a respective treatment choice. This section will review the fundamentals of facial prosthetic
rehabilitation; explain non-surgical and surgical treatment approaches, and address
aspects of prosthetic rehabilitation related to function, psychological considerations, quality of life, and lifetime maintenance.

Consultation and Education
Patient education is critical to achieving successful outcomes. Appropriate education about prosthetic reconstruction helps establish the patient’s and family’s expectations from the beginning. All too often patients are introduced to unachievable
expectations, which lead to disappointment and possibly even depression. When
patient expectations are managed carefully from the start, they possess the greatest
potential for treatment success and full rehabilitation [79].

Microtia Reconstruction in Patients with Craniofacial Microsomia

Facial Prosthetic Rehabilitation: The Basics
An ear prosthesis, or epithesis, is an external removable device made of alloplastic
materials – typically a medical-grade silicone elastomer (see Fig. 10.26). Prostheses
are designed to be removed daily for cleaning and skin hygiene and to maintain a
healthy tissue bed. Facial prostheses are typically made by a skilled anaplastologist
(or other prosthetic specialists), who manages the patient’s treatment from consultation through device design, fitting, delivery, and lifetime maintenance. Ideally, the
anaplastologist is part of a multidisciplinary team of specialized practitioners dedicated to the comprehensive surgical, reconstructive, and rehabilitative care of the
patient with microtia and/or craniofacial microsomia. Silicone prosthetic devices
are relatively short-lived, lasting on average 18–36 months. Reasons for replacement of prostheses are discoloration, material degradation, fungal growth in the silicone leading to adverse skin reactions, and changes in the tissue bed contour as a
result of developmental growth or surgery. The type of retention used to secure the
prosthesis also influences the lifespan [80, 81].

The Process of Prosthesis Fabrication
Prosthetic devices are fashioned based on the patient’s existing anatomy or borrowed from a donor form. A digital database of anatomic forms may also be utilized, particularly for patients with bilateral microtia [82].
Patient Records
1. A full series of clinical photographs are recorded for the pre-treatment record at
the initial clinic visit (see Fig. 10.27).
* Position the head in the Frankfurt horizontal position for reference consistency [83].
* Clinical and technical standards for patient photography and other data
acquisition methodologies should be maintained for reliable treatment records
and planning [84].
2. A 3D form of the patient’s existing anatomy is created for treatment planning
and design fabrication. This can be achieved by conventional means of a direct
impression (or moulage) of the patient in clinic or by digital means with 3D
surface scanning, photography (photogrammetry), or CT/cone-beam CT (CBCT)
radiographic imaging [85, 86].
* Patient positioning and technical props are carefully considered when capturing digital data to ensure that facial anatomy is adequately captured, to accurately mimic the patient’s position during daily activity and function with a
donned prosthetic device, and to not obscure relevant anatomical information.
Figure 10.28 demonstrates that the chin prop contributes to image integrity by
stabilizing the head position but may compromise usefulness of the virtual model
for facial analysis purposes. In this instance, the chin prop did not compromise
effective design of the prosthetic ear.
Design
The restored anatomical deficiency is designed by the anaplastologist with feedback
from the patient, family, and treating practitioners. Conventionally, this is done in
wax or clay; however, digital techniques using 3D modeling software and computer-­
aided design/manufacturing (CAD/CAM) methods have become routine and are
quickly becoming the standard of care (see Fig. 10.29).
* Design should address the functional needs and goals of the patient.
* and allow for anything the patient might wear in, on, or around the restored prosthetic pinna, i.e., eyeglasses, earrings, earbuds, headphones, hearing device,
stethoscope, etc.

considered when designing the size, shape, and projection. With marked facial
asymmetry, “visual symmetry” is often achieved with parts unidentical in size,
shape, and projection. Exact mirrored anatomical replicas often look unnatural,
oversized, and malpositioned when viewed in situ in the patient with facial
asymmetry.

Casting
Once approved, the final prosthetic form is cast in silicone from a mold.
Conventionally, the wax prototype is literally “cast in stone,” i.e., dental stone or
gypsum using a “lost-wax” technique common in dentistry. Contemporary digital
methods are working toward direct printing of silicone prosthetic devices, though
precise methodologies are still in development [87, 88].
* The patient and family must fully understand and appreciate that once a wax prototype is approved, no further changes can be made in shape, size, or fit. Patients
and families who do not fully appreciate this are often disappointed when changes
cannot be made to shape or size when the technical process has passed the design
prototype stage. Digital methods may offer greater flexibility in making design
changes.

218

T. Kraai et al.

Color Matching
Color matching of silicone to the skin is an essential step requiring an artistic eye
grounded in scientific knowledge of color science and materials. A convincing color
match to the skin is critical to a successful prosthetic outcome (see Fig. 10.30). A
poor color match to the surrounding skin results in a more conspicuous prosthetic
restoration. Skin color matching can be done subjectively “by eye” or with the aid
of a skin color measurement device like a colorimeter or spectrophotometer.
Artistically trained anaplastologists often rely on subjective “by eye” color matching techniques [89].
* A combination of both subjective and objective methods offers the greatest potential for managing prosthetic outcomes and maintenance while saving time through
a repeatable and predictable process, providing greater reassurance to the patient
and clinician [89, 90].
Fitting, Finishing, and Delivery
The prosthesis is generally processed by heat curing methods in a laboratory, which
requires several hours. Faster processing is possible with appropriate selection of
silicone; however, this can compromise the final outcome and ultimate mechanical
properties of the cured silicone, which can lend to a shorter prosthetic lifespan. The
prosthesis must then be carefully trimmed and fitted to the patient.

match of silicone to surrounding skin. Color was matched using a combined technique of using
spectrophotometery and computerized color formulation to establish the “base” color and “by eye”
technique for remaining colors and their respective distribution in the mold

* It is essential that during trimming the retentive complex is not altered, disturbed,
or compromised. Care should be taken to avoid scratches to the titanium surface
of magnets (which protects the magnet from corrosion) or separation of the silicone from the acrylic retentive substructure for bar-clip retention systems.
* Secure seating of the retentive components and fit against the skin along aesthetic
margins must be ensured with the prosthesis in situ.
* Silicone should be relieved in areas of excessive pressure. Pressure sores easily
develop if excess silicone is present in bulky areas of the prosthesis. Keep in mind
that the prosthesis may be worn daily for up to 18 hours per day.
* Comfort and fit should be assessed on the patient with the prosthetic ear in situ,
during dynamic behaviors such as chewing, speaking, yawning, with extended
neck and head movements, and with donning and doffing of “ear accessories,” i.e.,
headphones, sunglasses, and stethoscope, e.g., Fig. 10.31.
* Additional coloring on the exterior of the prosthesis may be necessary if the
“intrinsic” color match seems inadequate. This should be primarily driven by the
patient’s interests and feedback rather than the clinician; the skilled practitioner
will always find “something to fix,” which is not always in the patient’s best
interest.
* Patients should be instructed to “ramp” up the amount of time wearing the prosthesis daily, in the same manner that one might break in a new pair of leather
shoes. This will provide time for silicone-skin adaptation in areas previously left
uncovered.

* Re-educating the patient on daily care and maintenance of the prosthesis and
managing the skin-fitting surface (including the periabutment tissue) are
essential.
* Providing time for the patient to practice placement and removal of the prosthesis
(in the clinic with supervision) helps ensure smooth adaptability.
* The “delivery” visit is a critical moment when the patient will leave donning their
newly fitted prosthetic device. This can be a substantial adjustment for the patient
and family alike. A positive, supportive environment should be provided to enable
this unveiling and the patient’s renewed becoming [91].

Non-surgical Prosthetic Options
For biological, psychological, or social reasons, not all patients are good surgical
candidates. Developmental age, personal preference, and inability to commit due to
time, cost, or travel constraints are a few potential considerations. If a patient elects
not to pursue surgery for any reason, a prosthetic solution may be available. This has
provided a good option for some children who are undecided about whether surgical
reconstruction is the right choice [92].
When surgery is not involved, a prosthetic device can be worn with the use of
adhesives, by engaging portions of existing anatomy or by mechanism of external
retention, like eyeglasses. While these alternative options are possible and may
seem simple as they do not require surgery, they are not always ideal and have variable reliability for comfort and retention. Among the non-surgical options, the use
of adhesives has provided the most historically reliable solution [78].
Regardless of the type of retention, a prosthetic device should be removed daily
to allow for cleaning and aeration of the tissue bed. When using adhesives, the prosthesis must be carefully relieved of all adhesive upon doffing before cleaning with
soap and water. Adhesive is applied anew each time the prosthesis is donned. The
length of time a prosthesis will stay in place varies among patients and with the type
of adhesive. Environmental factors such as humidity can impact the wear time and
retentiveness of adhesives, particularly for water-based products.
* The patient must demonstrate good manual dexterity to manage the daily tasks of
adhesive application and removal.
* The optimal tissue bed for adhesive use is the skin that is flat, tight, immobile, and
non-hair-bearing.
* An adhesive-retained prosthesis is typically designed over and around the existing
anatomy and tissue tags or remnants. Because of this, fabricating an exact mirrored replica of the contralateral ear is not always possible.
* A low hairline can interfere with adhesive retention, and accumulation of adhesive
in the hair can become a nuisance for the patient. This has been identified as a
contributing factor in patients’ subsequent decision to pursue surgery either to
place implants for prosthetic retention or for auricular reconstruction.

10

Microtia Reconstruction in Patients with Craniofacial Microsomia

221

* Prosthetic adhesives are available in variable bond strengths; both water-based
and acetate- or silicone-based adhesives are available. The type of adhesive an
individual patient uses should be determined by the anaplastologist and the
patient, and typically is identified through a trial-and-error period following delivery. Some adhesives require a solvent for removal.
* Adverse skin responses should be carefully monitored through multiple follow-up
visits post-delivery.
* Prostheses should be replaced on a regular basis to minimize fungal or bacterial
colonization in the silicone and development of a skin infection.
* Skin products, e.g., Skin Prep, can be applied to aid in retention and to protect the
skin from adverse reactions. Adhesive is generally applied to the silicone-fitting
surface of the prosthesis and not the patient’s skin.
* An adhesive-retained prosthesis can be provided as an interim prosthetic solution,
while the patient considers more definitive surgery, either surgical ear reconstruction or the placement of implants to retain a prosthetic ear [29].

Surgery for the Prosthetic Patient
Surgery can complement prosthetic treatment to ensure optimal outcomes but must
be carefully coordinated with the anaplastologist and in keeping with the patient’s
goals [29, 77].
Pre-prosthetic Surgery
Surgery to optimize the tissue bed is often required to ensure the best prosthetic
outcome. Contouring the soft tissues is necessary to accommodate a prosthesis and
may be necessary to remove an extruding implant or cartilaginous framework, manage infection, remove skin tags or remnant cartilage, or for scar revision. The tissue
bed must be well healed before the prosthesis can be definitively fitted. Soft tissue
contouring can be performed before or after placing surgical implants. This decision
is based on the patient’s needs and the tissue to be addressed, e.g., some patients use
their existing microtia to assist with wearing glasses. Compared to autologous or
alloplastic surgical ear reconstruction, surgical placement of implants to retain a
prosthetic ear is less complex. However, it requires diligence by the surgeon to
ensure good implant stability with precise technical execution [32].
* Create a flat, immobile, and hairless tissue bed that accommodates the prosthesis.
Surgical modification of the hairline can also contribute to greater ease with retention and prosthetic management over the patient’s lifetime.
* Flaccid, mobile tissue tags without cartilaginous or bony structural support generally should be removed, though patient-specific conditions should be first discussed with the anaplastologist.

222

T. Kraai et al.

* Periodically, incorporation of existing anatomy into the prosthetic restoration is
possible and should be discussed with the anaplastologist and patient. It may also
be necessary to move tissue to achieve natural proportions and position. Surgical
repositioning of the tragus, for example, may improve the final prosthetic result.
* The patient and family should be well educated on what needs to be removed
and why.
* If there are psychological concerns related to the removal of the patient’s existing
and natural anatomy, then consultation with a psychologist is recommended. The
anaplastologist can explore design options to work around these issues. Patients
born with congenital microtia have described emotional and mental attachment to
their “special ear,” so any plans to remove any part of the ear should be carefully
presented and managed.
Implant Placement and Osseointegration
Osseointegration was introduced by P.I. Branemark in the late 1970s. It describes
the situation whereby bone grows in close proximity to commercially pure titanium.
By means of osteogenesis, bone can anchor a screw in the skull and thus allows for
rehabilitation with “bone-anchored” devices for hearing and prostheses [93].
Osseointegrated implants were first used to retain a bone conduction hearing device
and a prosthetic ear via percutaneous abutments in 1977 and 1979, respectively [94,
95]. Implant-retained prostheses represent the most reliable retention method for
patients seeking facial prosthetic treatment and are considered the gold standard
[78, 96].
Placement of implants to retain a facial prosthesis requires collaboration between
the surgeon and anaplastologist. The anaplastologist must be consulted before
implants are placed so that accurate positioning of the implants can be preplanned.
Implants are placed into available bone in the vicinity of the prosthetic reconstruction and allowed to “osseointegrate.” The amount of time allowed for osseointegration can vary substantially based upon patient-specific conditions and comorbidities
ranging from 3 to 12 months. Shorter healing times have been described in the literature for bone-anchored hearing devices in healthy adults [97, 98].
For pediatric patients with microtia or adults with compromised bone quality, the
implant is frequently placed as a two-staged surgical procedure. The titanium
implant is placed first and allowed to osseointegrate for a minimum of 3 months.
The second stage attaches the abutment/bar-clip or magnet retention system to the
implant. Patients with congenital conditions such as hemifacial microsomia,
Treacher-Collins syndrome, or Goldenhar syndrome may present with anomalous
anatomy in the craniofacial skeleton. Therefore, bone volume and quality should be
carefully evaluated to ensure availability of adequate bone. A single-staged surgical
procedure may be considered in healthy adults with good temporal cortical bone
[32, 95].
Connection of the percutaneous abutments (the “second stage”) puts a load on
the implant in the bone, and therefore timing of this connection should be carefully

10

Microtia Reconstruction in Patients with Craniofacial Microsomia

223

considered [99, 100]. When an extensive healing period is expected for osseointegration, often a temporary prosthesis can be fabricated to assist the patient during
this time.
Preoperative Planning
Precise implant positioning must be guided by the anaplastologist so that the optimal aesthetic result can be achieved. Virtual surgical planning (VSP) can be performed to specifically indicate implant positions, and soft tissue or bone-fitting
guides can be fabricated by 3D printing to clearly indicate the recommended positions for implant placement (Figs. 10.32 and 10.33). Alternate implant positions and
“sleeper implants” should be included in the VSP to provide options for the surgeon
if the bone quality at primary implant sites is suboptimal. VSP is possible when
relevant patient data is captured by scanning methodologies that enable the creation
of a patient-specific virtual 3D model.
* Surgeons interested in patient-specific 3D-printed guides or models should first
investigate recommendations related to data acquisition of patient information.
Scanning protocols specific to 3D printing are commonly required [101, 102].
* Accuracy and integrity of data capture are often dictated by the intended clinical
application. It is best to consult with the anaplastologist (engineer or other technicians) who may provide 3D-printed model(s) or guides for planned surgical
procedures.
* Bone-fitting guides designed with CBCT data have demonstrated less reliability
in exact seating compared to bone-fitting guides designed from medical CT data.
Material choice for fabrication often contributes to this, as acrylic guides may
“slip” more easily over the bone surface and/or periosteum compared to, for
instance, 3D-printed guides fabricated in metal, i.e., stainless steel by selective
laser sintering (SLS) technology.
* If medical grade CT is used, imaging the area of interest using a bone algorithm
and a slice distance of <1 mm is recommended [103, 104]. No cushions or straps
should be used that may compress, distort, or contort the ears (both the treatment
side and the non-treatment side). This provides a greater value in using the data
not only for surgical planning but for prosthetic design and fabrication as well.
* Request that the imaging protocol includes the entire pinnae bilaterally in both the
anterior-posterior and superior-inferior directions. When planning for the placement of implants into bone, it is easy to forget about the importance of capturing
accurate soft tissue anatomy.
* If CBCT imaging is utilized, a field of view sufficient to capture as much of the
full head as possible is recommended (23cmD × 17cmH “V17” for iCAT FLX,
Henry Schein, USA) [102].
* Communicate clearly to the anaplastologist (or other VSP technicians) timelines
related to surgery to ensure that necessary imaging, guide design, and 3D printing
of guides can be completed with sufficient time to allow for test-fitting, cleaning,
and sterilization of guides before surgery, typically a minimum of 2–3 weeks.

Implant Placement (First Stage)
Two implants are required for bar-clip retention for the ear. For the right side, the
implants are placed at the 8:00 and 10:30 o’clock positions relative to the external
auditory meatus (EAM) (Fig. 10.34) or expected location of the EAM for patients
with aural atresia and 1:30 and 4:00 o’clock for the left side. The implants are
placed approximately 20 mm from the native EAM or expected EAM. The implants

226

T. Kraai et al.

should be placed 12–15 mm apart measured from outer perimeter to outer perimeter. This is not always possible, especially with implant manufacturers introducing
implant designs with larger diameters. While greater implant circumference may
provide greater surface area for osseointegration, it also contributes to design challenges for the anaplastologist. For magnet retention, three triangulated implants are
recommended. Additional “sleeper” implants may be necessary in the pediatric
population or for patients with known compromised bone. Implants should be parallel to one another and perpendicular to the bone and skin surface to facilitate design
of retentive structures for the prosthesis, assist with patient home hygiene, and provide greater ease for placing and removing the prosthesis. Often a “perpendiculator”
appliance is available in the surgical set to assist in visualizing the correct angle.
1. Mark the implant sites using the prepared surgical guide (Fig. 10.35).
* Soft tissue-fitting guides and implant positions must be determined prior
to the injection of local anesthetic. Local anesthetic may prevent full seating of
soft tissue guides and distort the perceived position of planned implant locations.
* Implant positions are first marked on the soft tissue and then transferred
down to the bone using methylene blue and a 25-gauge needle.
* The anaplastologist can often be available in the OR to assist with accurate
surgical guide positioning so that VSP can be efficiently and accurately
executed.
2. A “C”-shaped incision is typically made 10–15 mm posterior to the position of
the implants and carried down through the periosteum.
3. Elevate and reflect a flap in the sub-periosteal plane.
4. Verify implant positions.
* If bone-fitting guides are used, seating of the guide onto the bone surface
should demonstrate reliable positioning by engaging unique landmarks on the
bone surface.
a

b

c

Fig. 10.35 (a) Placement of soft tissue-fitting guide, (b) marked implant positions, and (c) position verified with bone-fitting guide

10

Microtia Reconstruction in Patients with Craniofacial Microsomia

227

5. Use the guide drill at 2000 rpm to drill pilot holes using continuous irrigation.
* The inferiorly positioned implant should be placed first. This allows greater
flexibility to identify alternate sites superiorly should the initial planned site
prove unusable.
* Irrigation is essential to prevent injury to the bone from excessive heat;
osteocyte death can occur at 42 °C [107].
* Move the guide drill up and down and with the slight widening motion to
allow irrigation to reach the tip of the guide drill [107].
* Drill perpendicular to the bone surface using the 3-mm stop on the guide
drill first; then if sufficient bone remains with probing, proceed to 4 mm depth
with the guide drill.
* If less than 4 mm of bone depth is achieved, the shorter 3 mm implant
should be used.
* Drilling to the full depth of planned implant length with the guide drill is
important for reliable full seating of the implant.
6. Use the widening drill to widen the pilot hole to enable subsequent placement
of the implant also at 2000 rpms with continuous irrigation (Fig. 10.36).
* Use the appropriate length widening drill to match the depth of the drilled
pilot hole.
* Continue with the widening drill to create a slight countersink (0.5 mm)
around the circumference of the hole.
* Do not overwiden when using the widening drill. Movement of the drill
should be limited to strict up and down movement with no lateral movement.
There are no “rescue implants” for craniofacial applications, so overwidening
the hole intended for implant placement can mean complete loss of “bone real
estate” in that area.
7. The implant is picked up directly from its ampule using the implant inserter in
the drill hand piece.
* Implants are made of commercially pure titanium, and the surface of the
implant should never be touched by anything other than the bone into which it
a

b

Fig. 10.36 (a) Widened pilot hole with countersink and (b) two implants in place

228

T. Kraai et al.

is placed. Contamination of the implant surface can compromise
osseointegration.
* Surgical implant kits are designed to enable careful handling of implant-­
containing vessels, and surgical teams should be well trained in the handling of
implant components and instrumentation.
8. Carefully position the implant perpendicularly into the widened hole; the
implant should be inserted by two full rotations before irrigation begins.
Irrigation continues until the implant is fully seated; the drill will stop when the
implant reaches the set torque.
* Implants are placed with a torque setting appropriate to the softness or
hardness of the bone. The recommended setting for hard, compact bone is
40–50 NcM. For soft or compromised bone, recommended torque setting is
20–30 NcM.
9. Carefully remove the implant inserter from the top of the implant, avoiding any
levering motion that may loosen the implant.
10. If a two-staged approach is elected, cover screws are placed into the implants,
and the surgical site is closed including the periosteum.
Abutment Placement Surgery (Second Stage)
The second stage of surgery involves the connection of skin-penetrating abutments
and reduction of the subcutaneous tissue in the area of the planned prosthesis such
that the overlying skin can be sutured directly to the periosteum lending to flat,
immobile, periabutment tissue. Mobile tissue around the abutment is believed to
contribute to soft tissue responses that can be difficult to manage [108]. The second-­
stage surgery is also the recommended time for the removal of residual microtia
remnant:
1. An incision is designed to remove any unwanted soft tissue and access the
implants for abutment placement (Fig. 10.37).
2. Cover screws are removed, and either healing abutments or standard definitive
abutments are connected to the implants.
3. Abutments are placed using a uni-grip or external hex screwdriver and then
torqued to 25 NcM using a torque wrench or drill hand-piece.
4. Subcutaneous tissue is removed to allow for direct adhesion of the skin to the
bone surface.
* Removal of subcutaneous tissue may require extending and ramping the
soft tissue reduction outward from the area directly around the implant/abutment
complex to minimize “stair-stepping” or an abrupt drop-off of the subcutaneous tissue.
5. Abutments are brought through the skin using a biopsy punch or cruciform
incision.
* Suture (or tack) the incision made for removal of the remnant ear once the
implant sites have been visualized, so that the skin incision for the abutment is
made in the correct position over the implant.

b

Fig. 10.37 (a) Incision for remnant removal and access to implants for abutment placement using
a torque wrench and (b) closed incision with appropriate soft tissue reduction showing abutments
wrapped with Xeroform dressing

* Xeroform gauze is wrapped around the full circumference of each abutment
and should remain for 10–14 days to assist in the skin healing flat and tight
against the bone surface.
* If definitive standard abutments are connected during second-stage surgery,
then the exact length should be determined in consultation with the anaplastologist who likely has a design plan in mind using specific abutments.
* In the absence of a plan, definitive abutment length should be selected such
that the external abutment surface is exposed above the skin surface 1–2 mm at
a minimum (3–4 mm is preferred by this author) to facilitate home hygiene protocols and minimize the potential for skin overgrowth. Abutment lengths vary
and generally range from 3.5 mm to 7.5 mm for facial prosthetic applications.
Custom abutments can also be designed in special circumstances [109].
* Healing abutments may be preferred to allow healing of the surgical site
before definitive abutment length is determined.
Combined Prosthetic Ear and Hearing Device Implant Placement
Congenital microtia is commonly associated with aural atresia and hearing loss,
which can be rehabilitated using an implant-retained bone-anchored hearing device
(Fig. 10.38). In this situation, careful consideration should be made regarding the
placement of implants. The implant to retain the hearing device should be well out
of the field of any planned surgical or prosthetic ear reconstruction, so as to not
interfere with necessary surgical procedures, flaps, or vascular supply. Additionally,
the planned ear reconstruction should not come into contact with the hearing processor as this can cause unwanted and audio feedback. Hearing concerns are at
times addressed earlier than external ear reconstruction, particularly for children
with bilateral microtia and aural atresia. For this reason, placement of an implant to
address hearing loss should take into account the patient’s potential interest in future
external ear reconstruction.

Lifetime Maintenance
The “delivery” visit in many ways may seem like the “finish line” with the completion of what for many patients has been a very long journey. It may very well represent the end of one journey, but it is also a new “starting point.” The patient having
received their finished and fitted prosthesis will then embark on a lifetime of prosthetic maintenance. For this reason alone, surgical reconstructive options should be
considered as a “best first” option. Prosthetic restorations are always a possibility to
complement surgical reconstruction or as a “backup plan” when surgical outcomes
do not meet the defined treatment goals.
* For ongoing prosthetic maintenance, patients should have reliable access to skilled
and experienced anaplastology services.
* Annual visits recommended for lifetime maintenance with at least two to three
visits in the first year.

Conclusion
Microtia reconstruction is challenging and ideally involves an interdisciplinary
team. Explaining the advantages and disadvantages of reconstruction are key to
informed decision-making and consent. Every effort should be made to explain the

10

Microtia Reconstruction in Patients with Craniofacial Microsomia

231

different options to avoid surgical regret due to uninformed decisions or unrealistic
expectations. One major challenge is obtaining assent in this frequently young population. A single-stage reconstructive surgery is possible, more commonly with
porous polyethylene reconstruction. This technique is also advantageous in that it
can be performed at an earlier age, avoids harvesting costal cartilage, and addresses
the frequently low hairline. Autologous cartilage reconstruction has evolved dramatically over decades and avoids the use of alloplastic material, which has a higher
rate of infection, and the skin quality overlying the framework may be less variable.
Prosthetic reconstruction is also a good option, particularly for those preferring a
simpler surgical procedure (for implant-retained) or those wanting to avoid surgery
all together (for adhesive-retained). Prosthetic reconstruction is also an option for
patients who have less than optimal autologous or alloplastic reconstruction. The
disadvantages and surgical outcomes are heavily dependent on experience. The psychological impact of a poor reconstruction can be long-standing, and the need for
revision surgery should be avoided in all manners possible as the results are less
favorable. Long-term complications such as autologous cartilage atrophy or alloplastic implant exposure decades after repair are not well understood. For prosthetic
reconstruction there is an ongoing need for replacements due to damage or fading
and potential skin problems surrounding implants. Ultimately, specialists devoted to
caring for patients with this unique condition should tailor the technique to the goals
and unique characteristics of each patient.

drawings demonstrating the approach to different grades of microtia for autologous auricular
reconstruction.

Chapter 11

Correction of the Soft Tissue Deformities
Associated with Craniofacial Microsomia:
Facial Reanimation and Soft Tissue
Grafting Techniques
Farooq Shahzad

Manuscript
Craniofacial microsomia is a spectrum of deformities that occur due to abnormal
development of structures derived from the first and second branchial arches
(Table 11.1). The involved territory is represented by Tessier # 6, 7, and 8 facial
clefts [1]. There is bilateral involvement in approximately 15 to 24% of cases which
is usually asymmetric [2, 3]. The SAT and OMENS classification systems include
soft tissue deficiencies in their scheme (Table 11.2). The SAT system is modeled
after the TNM classification of tumors [4]. The OMENS system is more comprehensive, with a later modification including extra-craniofacial involvement with a
plus (+) [3, 5].
The first step in management is an assessment of all structural and functional
abnormalities so that a plan and timeline for reconstruction can be made. Involvement
of multiple structures implies that several reconstructive procedures will be needed.
These operations need to be properly sequenced for optimal long-term aesthetic and
functional outcomes (Fig. 11.1).

Soft Tissue Reconstruction
The soft tissue involvement in craniofacial microsomia is highly variable. There can
be deficiency of all types of soft tissue components including the skin, subcutaneous
tissue, muscles of mastication, and parotid gland. Ear abnormalities comprise a
spectrum of severity from accessory tragi to microtia or anotia. Middle ear

hypoplasia may also occur, leading to conductive hearing loss. The eye may be
involved, resulting in microphthalmia or anophthalmia. Eyelid abnormalities can
include lateral canthal displacement, colobomas, and missing lashes. Transverse
facial clefting from the oral commissure may occur leading to macrostomia of variable degrees. Hypoplasia of muscles of mastication may contribute to occlusal
abnormalities and chin point deviation toward the hypoplastic side. Hypoplasia of
the palatal muscles may also occur leading to palatal deviation and velopharyngeal
dysfunction. The degree of soft tissue deficiency has been shown to be positively
correlated with the degree of mandible, orbit and facial nerve abnormalities, and the
presence of macrostomia [2].
Management of facial asymmetry has traditionally consisted of correction of
skeletal abnormalities followed by volume augmentation with soft tissue flaps [6].
This results in creation of a stable skeletal base allowing a more precise assessment
of soft tissue deficiency for accurate volume correction. The advent of structural fat
grafting has changed this paradigm. Fat grafting does not provide as much volume
in a single operation as a soft tissue flap but is a much less invasive operation. Fat
injections can be started at an earlier age and even combined with other reconstructive procedures. Alloplastic implants are a useful method for targeted and precise
volume correction with the least donor site morbidity. A comparison of these techniques is outlined in Table 11.3.

Flaps
Soft tissue flaps provide a large volume of autologous tissue. They are a good choice
in severe deformities where a considerable amount of soft tissue may be needed for
volume correction. Volume restoration can be performed in a single operation. Bone
can also be incorporated in the flap for simultaneously mandible or midface reconstruction. The main disadvantage of flaps is donor site morbidity like scarring, pain,
contour deformity, and possible functional deficits. Flaps sag with time due to gravity, and therefore secondary operations are typically needed for flap resuspension
and soft tissue contouring [7]. Both pedicled flaps and free flaps can be used, based
on soft tissue requirements.

Free Flaps
Free tissue transfer provides an almost unlimited supply of soft tissue for volume
repletion. It also allows greater flexibility of flap inset, allowing customized flap
design. Any type of fasciocutaneous or adipofacial flap can be used, depending on
volume requirements and available donor sites. Pure muscle flaps are not generally
used as they atrophy unpredictably over time. Soft tissue flaps almost always require
a revision procedure for resuspension, contouring, or volume redistribution. The
most common complications of free flaps are hematoma, wound dehiscence, infections, and flap loss [8].
The most commonly reported flap for craniofacial microsomia reconstruction is
the parascapular flap and its variant, the inframammary extended circumflex scapular (IMECS) flap [9, 10]. Other reported flaps are the gracilis, rectus abdominis,
anterolateral thigh, latissimus dorsi, omentum, deep inferior epigastric perforator
(DIEP), superficial inferior epigastric artery (SIEA), superficial circumflex iliac
(SCIA), and groin flaps. The most commonly used recipient vessels are the superficial temporal vessels, followed by the facial vessels.
Each flap has its own advantages and drawbacks. The scapular/parascapular flap
is popular because it provides a large amount of soft tissue with low donor site morbidity. If a very large flap is required, tissue expansion of the donor site be performed for primary donor site closure [8]. The inframammary extended circumflex
scapular (IMECS) flap is a variant of the parascapular flap in which the incision is
slightly more anteriorly placed and curves to the inframammary fold [10]. This

242

F. Shahzad

allows harvest in an oblique position obviating a position change and allowing
simultaneous face recipient site and flap dissection. A larger volume of tissue can be
harvested with a more aesthetically placed scar. A chimeric flap based on the subscapular system can be harvested comprising bone (lateral scapular border) and soft
tissue (scapular/parascapular flaps) for simultaneous soft tissue and skeletal reconstruction [11, 12].
The latissimus dorsi flap is a good choice when a very large volume of tissue is
required [13, 14]. The thoracodorsal artery perforator flap spares muscle and minimized donor site morbidity [15]. Chimeric flaps based on the thoracodorsal vessels
can be designed for simultaneous soft tissue and bone reconstruction. The soft tissue latissimus flap is used for soft tissue augmentation, and the serratus/costochondral flap is used for ramus and condyle reconstruction [16].
Groin-based flaps like the SCIA and SIEA flaps provide a moderate amount of
soft tissue with low donor site morbidity [17]. The scar is in a relatively hidden location. The deep circumflex iliac artery osteocutaneous flap can be used for simultaneous ramus reconstruction and volume augmentation. The rectus abdominis
myocutaneous flap provides a large volume of tissue [18]. The deep inferior epigastric artery perforator flap decreases donor site morbidity and increases volume predictability by eliminating the issue of post-operative muscle atrophy [19]. The
anterolateral thigh flap and superior gluteal artery-based flaps can also be utilized in
the appropriate candidate [20, 21]. The omentum flap provides a large volume of
pliable tissue that allows freedom of inset into different areas of volume deficiency
of the face [22]. A major disadvantage of the flap is that it requires a laparotomy.
Surgical technique:
• The patient is marked preoperatively in the upright position. The areas of volume
deficiency are marked in a topographic fashion with areas of thicker and thinner
tissue needs identified.
• Intubation is performed orotracheally. The endotracheal tube is secured to the
premolar teeth with silk suture or wire.
• A template of the defect is made, marking the areas of thicker and thinner soft
tissue needs.
• Local anesthetic containing epinephrine is injected widely in the face. A preauricular incision is made. If exposure is not sufficient, the incision can be extended
retro-auricularly or into the neck (modified Blair incision). The incision should
not compromise future ear reconstruction, if planned.
• The cheek skin flap is elevated in a plane just above the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS). Dissection is carried out about a centimeter beyond the
area of deficiency.
• The recipient vessels are dissected out and prepared. The superficial temporal
vessels are most commonly used. If future ear reconstruction is anticipated, these
vessels are preserved as they will be needed for supplying the temporoparietal
fascia flap. Alternatively, the neck vessels (facial, superior thyroid, lingual,
occipital) can be used.

11

Correction of the Soft Tissue Deformities Associated with Craniofacial…

243

• The template is placed on the donor site. The flap pedicle position with respect
to the recipient vessels in the face/neck is considered while positioning the
template on the donor site. The template is centered on the main axis of the
flap, with the area of the thickest tissue needs on this central axis. Flap skin
paddle depends on the ability to close donor site and size of soft tissue
required. If larger flap is needed than the skin paddle, it is harvested in SQ
plane so that donor skin can be closed. The position of the template can also
be adjusted later once the location of the perforators and main pedicle are
visualized.
• The harvested flap is temporarily secured to the face. Microvascular anastomoses
are performed.
• Flap inset is then performed meticulously. The flap is usually completely buried.
If overlying skin is deficient and closure may cause pedicle compression, a skin
paddle is left in the preauricular area, and the remainder of the flap is de-­
epithelialized. The flap is secured to the periosteum of the zygoma and inferior
orbital rim. If needed, fixation to the piriform aperture can be performed via an
intraoral incision. A lateral upper eyelid incision can be useful for fixation of the
flap high on the lateral orbital rim [23]. Facial extensions of the flap can be used
to augment areas around the lips, chin nose, and eyes. If there is depression of the
alar base or ear, these structures can be released, and the flap placed under to
build up their base support. The edges of the flap are beveled to create a smooth
contour. The distal parts of the flap are suspended to the overlying skin via transdermal sutures tied to petrolatum gauze bolsters. Quilting sutures are performed
from the flap to parotid fascia. Patient is sat up after inset for assessment, and any
necessary fine-tuning is performed.
• Patients are placed on prophylaxis dose low-molecular-weight heparin while
they are in the hospital and on aspirin for 1 week. Flap monitoring is performed
via implantable Doppler, every hour for the first 2 days, then every 2 hours for
the next 2 days, and then every 4 hours. Patients are discharged after 3 to 5 days.
Transcutaneous bolsters are removed in 1 week. A case example is illustrated in
Fig. 11.2.
Microsurgical considerations:
1. Blood vessels should be handled with extreme care in children. The vessels are
small and tend to spasm when injured or handled roughly.
2. The superficial temporal artery vessels may be small in patients with craniofacial
microsomia [21, 24]. More proximal dissection of these vessels in the substance
of the parotid gland will yield vessels of larger size [25]. Alternatively, the facial
vessels can be dissected in the area of the sub-mandibular gland. Neck vessels
may also be used.
3. Neck vessels may be diminutive or displaced from their normal position, e.g.,
the facial vessels have been reported be absent or malpositioned in children with
craniofacial microsomia [26].

Additional procedures are required in the majority of patients for flap resuspension
and/or fat contouring. Revisions are performed after 6 to 12 months. If there are
minor contour problems, liposuction is performed for areas of volume excess, and

fat grafting is performed for areas of volume deficiency. However, in most patients,
direct flap contouring is needed. The preauricular incision is opened up, and a skin
flap is developed in the subcutaneous plane. The flap is re-elevated and suspended.
Soft tissue is excised in areas of excess [27]. Usually there is tissue excess in the

in the upper face which needs fat augmentation.
Pedicled Flaps
Regional pedicled flaps have the advantage of obviating the need for microsurgery. They
are, however, limited by available soft tissue and their arc of rotation. Various flaps have
been described. With the ubiquitous and routine use of free tissue transfer, the use of
pedicled flaps for management of craniofacial microsomia has become very infrequent.
However, they are useful in situations where microsurgery facilities are not available.
The submental flap can be used for volume replacement of the lower and midface
[28]. The main drawback of this flap is a scar in the neck. The temporoparietal fascia
flap in itself does not have a sufficient bulk to correct the typical volume deficits in
craniofacial microsomia. Temporoparietal fascia flap can be combined with dermis-­
fat grafts to increase bulk [29].
Composite soft tissue and bone flaps have also been used for simultaneous correction of bone and soft tissue deficits. A chimeric flap based on the thoracodorsal
pedicle has been described. The serratus/costochondral segment is used for ramus/
condyle reconstruction, and the de-epithelialized skin paddle of the latissimus segment is used for soft tissue augmentation [16]. A composite temporoparietal fascia
and parietal bone flap has also been described for simultaneous mandibular reconstruction and soft tissue augmentation [30].

Grafts
Structural Fat Grafting
Structural fat grafting has become the most popular technique for volume replacement in patients with facial contour abnormalities like craniofacial microsomia and
Romberg’s disease. Its major advantage is that it is a short, minimally invasive
