F. Shahzad

outpatient procedure without the donor site morbidity of a free flap. By obviating
the need for extensive facial dissection, facial suspensory ligaments and dermal
attachments are preserved. Volume correction can be targeted to areas of deficiency.
Fat grafting can be undertaken at any age, and procedures can be staged through
childhood at times convenient for the patient. Fat grafting can also be performed at
the time of other reconstructive procedures that these patients may need, thus
decreasing the total number of operations. The major disadvantage of fat grafting is
that fat take is unpredictable. Approximately 50 to 60% of the injected fat survives
[31]. Therefore several sessions of grafting are typically needed for optimal volume
correction. A systematic review showed that the mean number of fat grafting sessions in patients with craniofacial microsomia is 2.7 with a range of one to six sessions [9]. Operations are spaced at a minimum of 1 year apart. Enrichment of fat
grafts with adipose-derived stromal cells may increase fat graft take [32].
Fat grafting can be performed prior to school age so that better facial symmetry
is achieved prior to child’s interaction with their peers [33]. Fat grafting improves
the quality of the overlying skin due to regenerative effects of adipose-derived stem
cells. One point that should be kept in mind is that the injected fat retains the characteristics of the donor site. Therefore, as the patient gains weight, the transplanted
fat hypertrophies more than the native facial fat [34]. Fat grafting is a safe procedure, with a recent systematic review reporting an overall complication rate of less
than 5% [31]. The most commonly reported complications are infections, hematomas, and contour irregularities.
Technique:
• The areas of volume deficiency are marked preoperatively with the patient
upright. Topographic markings are made according to the amount of volume
deficiency.
• The donor sites are assessed. Most common donor sites are the lower abdomen
and flanks. In young kids or thin individuals, the medial thighs or buttocks are
used. Topographic markings are performed that identify harvest areas.
• Tumescent solution containing normal saline, lidocaine, and epinephrine is
injected at the donor sites. The maximum amount of lidocaine that can be administered via tumescent solution is 35 mg/kg.
• Hand suction of fat is performed using a 3-mm (2.5-mm) blunt cannula connected to a 30-mL Luer-Lok syringe. Pulling back on the plunger generated
negative pressure for suction. It is important to harvest from the wide area so as
not to create a donor site contour deformity (Fig. 11.3).
• The suction cannula is taken off the syringe and replaced with a cap. The fat-­
filled syringe is placed vertically on a stand for 10 minutes. With gravity, injected
fluid and blood separate at the bottom. This layer is removed by opening the
plug. The fat is then placed in Telfa gauze, which absorbs the oil. This purified
fat is loaded into 1 mL syringes.
• Access incisions of 2 mm are made depending on areas to be injected. Common
locations are the oral commissure and the preauricular side burn.

Dermal Fat Grafting
The efficacy, safety, and versatility of structural fat grafting have relegated dermal
fat grafting to a secondary role in facial volume augmentation. However, it is useful
for targeted correction of contour abnormalities and mild volume augmentation
[36]. Its drawbacks are unpredictable graft resorption and donor site scar.
When used for volume correction of the hemiface, the procedure is similar to a
vascularized flap but without the microsurgical component. The areas of deficiency
are marked, a template of the defect is made, and access to the face is obtained via
a preauricular incision. The groin is the most common donor site, although any
available site can be used. De-epithelialization is performed in situ, and the graft is
harvested with a thin layer of fat. Inset is performed very precisely suturing to the
underlying periosteum and deep fascia.
A useful application for dermal fat grafts is lip volume augmentation. Mobile
areas such as lips have poor long-term retention of fat grafts [37]. Dermal fat grafting has been used successfully for correction of vermillion deficiencies [38].
Whether dermal fat grafting is more effective than fat injections in these areas is not
known. However, it may allow more precise placement of fat.

F. Shahzad

Alloplastic Implants
Alloplasts allow precise correction of contour abnormality by augmenting the skeleton in localized areas of deficiency without any donor site morbidity. Furthermore,
the result is predictable as there is no resorption as is seen with fat, bone, and cartilage grafts. Areas that are commonly corrected with implants are the malar areas
[7], mandibular angle [39], chin [40], and temple [41] (Fig. 11.4). The implants are
typically placed in the subperiosteal plane and secured to the facial skeleton with
screws. Access can be obtained by standard extraoral or intraoral incisions. These
procedures are performed after completion of skeletal growth.
Implant materials that have been used include silicone [7], porous polyethylene
(PPE) [39, 42], ceramics [40], polyetheretherketone (PEEK) [43], expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) [41], and hydroxyapatite [44]. Each material has its benefits and drawbacks. The most common complications of alloplasts are infection,
displacement, and extrusion.
Porous polyethylene (PPE) is a popular choice for skeletal augmentation. PPE
has a porous structure which allows fibrovascular ingrowth allowing tissue incorporation, thus preventing implant migration and providing resistance to infections.
PPE comes in different shapes and sizes, which can then be trimmed with a scalpel
to the desired configuration. The implants can be screwed in place. Their ease of
use, versatility, and good safety profile have made PPE one of the most popular
choices for facial skeletal augmentation [45].
Hydroxyapatite cement can be used for augmenting localized areas of skeletal
deficiency. The power is mixed with liquid to form a putty that can be placed over
the bone at the area of deficiency and molded to the desired shape. Hardening occurs
over a few minutes. Hydroxyapatite is osteoconductive, allowing ingrowth of bone

Fig. 11.4 Common areas of facial contour correction with alloplastic implants

11

Correction of the Soft Tissue Deformities Associated with Craniofacial…

249

and thus tissue integration. It is useful for augmenting localized areas of skeletal
deficiency like the paranasal areas, malar area, mandibular angle, and forehead [44].
The most accurate method of skeletal contour correction is by custom-made
implants created by virtual surgical planning [43]. A three-dimensional computer
tomographic scan of the face is obtained which is used for computer-aided design
(CAD) and computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) of custom implants [46]. The
implant is thus of ideal size, shape, and volume for correcting the deformity. The
biggest limitation to CAD-CAM at this time is high cost. As 3D printing and
computer-­assisted technology become cheaper and more widely available, custom
implants will likely become the technique of choice for skeletal augmentation.

Facial Reanimation
Facial nerve palsies are present in 10–45% of patients with craniofacial microsomia
[3, 47]. There is a wide spectrum of facial nerve involvement ranging from mild
weakness to complete paralysis and involving a single branch to the entire facial
nerve. The etiology is thought to be abnormal development of the temporal bone
which houses the facial canal through which the facial nerve runs [47]. Multiple
facial nerve abnormalities have been described, including anomalous course through
the middle ear, posterior displacement, bifurcation, and complete absence [48].
Hypoplasia or absence of facial musculature may also occur [48, 49]. A meta-­
analysis by Kline et al. showed that partial nerve involvement (63%) is more common than paralysis of all branches of the facial nerve (37%) [48]. Of the partial
involvement, paralysis of lower divisions is twice as common as that of the upper
divisions. There has been shown to be a positive correlation between the degree of
the facial nerve involvement and ear abnormalities [2]. The association with mandibular abnormalities is not as strong as that with the ear [48].
Facial asymmetry usually becomes evident soon after birth when the child cries.
It is important to distinguish between traumatic and developmental facial palsies
(Fig. 11.5) [50]. Traumatic facial palsy typically improves over time, while developmental does not. Evidence of birth trauma includes prolonged labor, use of forceps, bruising/marks over the mastoid, and hemotympanum. Facial asymmetry or
dysmorphic features may indicate developmental facial palsy associated with craniofacial microsomia or a syndrome (Mobius, CHARGE, etc.).
Electrophysiologic studies can help determine the cause of facial palsy if the
clinical picture is not clear. Electroneurography (ENoG) measures the compound
muscle action potential of facial muscles. This test consists of transcutaneous stimulation of the facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen and then recording the action
potentials at various facial nerve branch locations [51]. Since it takes up to
48–72 hours for Wallerian degeneration to occur, ENoG is normal in traumatic
facial palsy if performed during this time. In traumatic palsy, it can be repeated
every 3–5 days to assess the degree of nerve degeneration which predicts prognosis
for recovery. The study is not useful after 3 weeks, since by that time Wallerian

Hearing evaluation should be performed in all babies with facial nerve palsy and
craniofacial microsomia, since ear abnormalities and hearing loss are associated
with craniofacial microsomia. Auditory brainstem response (ABR) is used for
screening of hearing loss. A computed tomographic scan of the temporal bones can
assess for abnormalities of the facial canal and middle and inner ear.
Clinical assessment of facial nerve function is performed by facial nerve grading
scales. The most commonly used instrument is the House-Brackmann scale
(Table 11.4) [53]. Its popularity lies in the fact that it is simple and easy to use. Its
major criticism is that it is very subjective and does not detect subtle changes after
treatment [54]. The Sunnybrook scale is a more objective system that assigns points
to different facial regions (Table 11.5). Assessments are made for resting symmetry,
movement, and synkinesis. This scale has good inter- and intraobserver reliability
and is more sensitive in measuring changes. These scales are not accurate in bilateral facial paralysis as there is no normal side for comparison.
The timing for surgical management should take into account functional and
psychological development of the child. Periocular operations are usually not
needed in infancy as adequate corneal protection can be achieved with non-surgical
methods. We perform facial reanimation surgery at around 5 years of age, as younger

Facial rehabilitation procedures can be static or dynamic. Static procedures
improve facial symmetry at rest, while dynamic procedures recreate the function of
the paralyzed muscles. Dynamic procedures are of two types: (1) reinnervation of

252

F. Shahzad

native facial muscle via direct neurotization and (2) substitution of paretic muscles
via regional or free muscle flaps. Direct muscle neurotization can augment the function of paretic muscles in incomplete facial palsy. A needle EMG can help determine viability of facial muscles. If EMG shows viable muscles (fibrillations, positive
sharp waves), direct muscle neurotization can be performed. If after waiting for a
suitable period of time (9–12 months), muscle reanimation does not occur or is
insufficient, muscle substitution is performed to which this nerve is coapted. If the
initial EMG shows electro silence, muscle substitution is performed.
For the purposes of facial paralysis management, the face can be divided into
three: the upper face (periorbital region), midface (lip elevation), and lower face (lip
depression).

Upper Face
Paralysis of the orbicularis oculi results in lagophthalmos (upper lid) and ectropion
(lower lid). Incomplete eye closure causes corneal dryness which can lead to ulceration and eventual blindness. Corneal protection is therefore the top priority in management of facial paralysis. Epiphora occurs because of lid ectropion resulting in
eversion of the lacrimal punctum, dysfunction of lacrimal pump due to orbicularis
paralysis, and reflex increase in tear production because of corneal dryness.
All patients with facial paralysis should be evaluated by an ophthalmologist. The
width of the palpebral fissures is compared between both eyes. The position of the
upper and lower eyelids is assessed at rest and with blink. The marginal reflex distance (MRD 1, distance of corneal eye reflex to upper lid margin; MRD 2, distance
of corneal eye reflex to lower lid margin) is measured and compared to the non-­
paralyzed eye. Bell’s phenomenon (oculogyric reflex) is reflex vertical rotation of
the globe on eye closure. Patients with absent Bell’s reflex are at risk for exposure
keratopathy, especially when they are in the supine position.
Patients are immediately started on a corneal protection regimen consisting of
lubricating eye drops every 2–3 hours during daytime and corneal ointment at night.
Eye patching and lid taping can be done at night. Tarsorrhaphy are rarely performed
in children. They are short-term temporizing measures in patients who present with
corneal ulceration, and there is concern about non-compliance with eyelid protection regimen. In infants, occlusion of the visual axis, even for a short period of time,
leads to deprivation amblyopia which can result in permanent deterioration of vision.
Brow
Brow asymmetry typically does not manifest till adulthood. Brow asymmetry in
young patients can be corrected with botulinum toxin injection to paralyze the normal side. Brow lift can be performed via endoscopic or direct excision techniques
(Fig. 11.6).

11

Correction of the Soft Tissue Deformities Associated with Craniofacial…

253

Endoscopic Brow Lift
Endoscopic brow lift has the advantage of having small concealed scars in the hairline. It is useful if a small amount of elevation is needed.
Direct Brow Lift
Direct excision allows correction to a large degree with longer-lasting results.
Excision can be performed just above the brow hairline (supraciliary lift), at the
midbrow (midbrow lift), or at the hairline (coronal lift). We prefer the supraciliary
lift for its predictability. The patient is marked preoperatively in the sitting position.
The incision is made at the upper edge of the brow hairline. The amount of desired
elevation at midbrow and at fixed points medially and laterally is marked. In the
operating room, the marked ellipse of the skin is removed leaving the frontalis
intact, thus preserving the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves. The brow is then
fixed into position by tacking its deep surface to the frontalis at four to five spots.
The skin is then closed in layers. The scar usually heals very well as there is minimal stress on the incision due to absent frontalis muscle action.
Upper Eyelid
Lagophthalmos occurs due to paralysis of the orbicularis oculi and unopposed
action of the levator palpebrae superioris and Muller’s muscle. Passive techniques
to correct lagophthalmos consist of active or passive counteraction of the upper lid
elevators. Eye opening then entails an active effort of levator contraction.
Lid Loading
Upper eyelid loading by placement of weights counteracts the effect of the lid elevators, allowing the lid to close passively with gravity (Fig. 11.6). Gold is inert and
malleable and has high density allowing a small volume of implant to be placed.
Problems with gold weights are visibility, migration, capsule formation, infection,
extrusion, entropion, and gold allergy. The long-term extrusion rate is approximately 10% [55].
Weights are most commonly placed in the pretarsal location. The appropriate
weight is selected by taping the weight on the upper lid which results in adequate
eye closure with minimal ptosis. Most commonly used weights are in the range of
0.6–1.4 g. An incision is made in the eyelid crease at the peak of the upper lid. The
skin and orbicularis are elevated off the anterior surface of the tarsus, creating a
pocket centered over the medial corneal limbus and staying at least 2 mm above the
lid margin. The weight is secured in place with 60 silk sutures’ partial thickness
through the tarsus and then through the positioning holes of the weight. The

254

F. Shahzad

superior hole is aligned with the superior tarsal border. The orbicularis and skin are
closed in layers.
The weight can also be placed in the post-septal location. The orbital septum is
opened, postseptal fat is retracted, and the implant is fixed to the levator aponeurosis
just superior to the upper tarsal border. Another technique is to recess the levator off
the tarsal plate and place the implant between the upper border of the tarsus and
lower edge of the levator aponeurosis. The postseptal location decreases the risk of
visibility, astigmatism, extrusion, and entropion. However, sizing is more difficult.
and typically a heavier weight is required (0.2 g heavier on average), since this is a
mechanically less favorable position [56]. This is also a useful technique in revision
procedures for complications of pretarsal weights.
Platinum is denser than gold, and therefore platinum weights have a thinner profile. Platinum weights have shown to have a lower rate of extrusion [57]. Platinum
chain implants contour better to the shape of the tarsus than platinum weights. This
results in better cosmesis and less chance of corneal astigmatism. Multiple fixation
holes also allow more points of fixation, thus potentially decreasing the risk of
implant migration. Platinum segment chains are even more versatile as the individual segments can be added or removed if adjustments are needed [58].
Autologous conchal cartilage has also been used for lid loading [59]. It obviates
the complications associated with synthetic materials. It is a less precise technique,
and therefore correction may not be complete. However, it is a useful technique if
gold or platinum weights are not available.
Palpebral Springs
Palpebral springs actively close the upper lid [60]. The central coil of the spring is
fixed to the lateral orbital rim, the superior arm to the superior orbital rim, and the
inferior arm to the tarsus (Fig. 11.6). Springs produce a brisker blink. However, they
have a higher rate of extrusions than upper lid weights and need more frequent
adjustments. They are also technically challenging procedures and thus have a steep
learning curve. Their best indication is for motivated patients who desire a more
dynamic blink and understand the need for revision procedures. Patients who do not
have satisfactory corneal protection with eyelid weights (especially in supine position) may also be candidates for conversion to palpebral springs [61].
Levator Lengthening
Levator lengthening consists of recession of the levator aponeurosis and interposition of graft material (fascia or cartilage) between the tarsus and levator aponeurosis
[62]. This lengthens and weakens the levator, thus decreasing the lagophthalmos.
However, correction is usually not complete, and residual lagophthalmos remains.
It is a useful technique in patients who have complications of eyelid weights or
springs.

Lower Eyelid
The lower lid is typically not affected in children because of good eyelid tone and
cheek position. Ectropion starts laterally and then spreads medially over time. The
normal position of the lower lid is at the level of the lower limbus of the cornea.
Malposition of the lower lid leads to inadequate globe protection and inefficient tear
film maintenance. The projection of the globe is a very important consideration in
lower lid surgery; eyelid elevation procedures are more difficult in patients with
proptotic eyes (negative vector). Treatment of the midface paralysis, via static or
dynamic procedures, supports the lower lid and increases the effectiveness and longevity of lower lid elevation [63].
Lateral Canthopexy
Fixation of the lateral canthus is useful in correcting a small amount of scleral show.
It is useful in younger patients with mild ectropion. However, it does not address the
medial eyelid. Canthopexy can be performed via an anterior or posterior (transorbital) approach [64]. The transorbital canthopexy procedure can correct a more significant degree of lid laxity.
Lateral Canthoplasty
The lateral canthal strip procedure causes lid elevation and tightening (Fig. 11.6). It
is very useful in older individuals with long-standing paralysis and horizontal lid
laxity. A lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis are performed. The skin and
mucosa are removed from the lateral edge of the tarsus. This lateral strip of tarsus
is then sutured to the periosteum just inside the lateral orbital wall, thus creating a
superoposterior vector of fixation of the lower lid. A slight overcorrection is
achieved by fixing the canthal position a little higher. A sharp lateral canthal angle
is created by approximating the grey lines. Orbicularis and skin are closed in layers.
This procedure does not address medial lid, and therefore there may be recurrent
eyelid droop over time. Furthermore, it may worsen the position of the medial
canthus.
Lower Lid Cartilage Graft
A conchal cartilage graft can be placed between the lower border of the tarsus and
the inferior orbital rim to better support the lower lid. A lateral tarsal strip procedure
is also performed. The drawbacks of this technique are a visible bulge in the lower
lid and risk of visual field restriction in downgaze.

257

Tendon Sling
Elevation of the entire lid can be effectively performed by a lower lid sling
(Fig. 11.6). The palmaris longus tendon or a strip of fascia lata is used. The palmaris
tendon is harvested from the non-dominant forearm. A subciliary tunnel is created
from lateral to medial canthus, protecting the lacrimal system with a probe. The
tendon graft is anchored at the medial canthal tendon. It is then tensioned in a superoposterior vector and fixed at the desired position at lateral orbital rim with a suture
anchor, opposing the lid to the globe and producing a slight overcorrection of lid
position.
Blink
Restoration of spontaneous blink is one of the most challenging undertakings in
facial reanimation. Although it is difficult to obtain complete eye closure with
dynamic techniques, a combination of dynamic with static techniques can result in
full eye closure with excellent functional and aesthetic outcomes [65]. The addition
of dynamic procedures has been shown to confer better corneal protection compared with static procedures alone [66].
The only way to achieve spontaneous blink is via cross-face nerve grafting from
contralateral facial nerve branches responsible for eye closure. The best results are
obtained via direct muscle neurotization of the orbicularis oculi [67]. Younger age
at neurotization may result in better outcomes [67]. A needle EMG can be used to
see if any viable muscles (fibrillations, positive sharp waves) are present. If there is
evidence of muscle activity (incomplete facial palsy), cross-face nerve graft with
direct muscle neurotization is performed. If there is insufficient return of orbicularis
function after waiting for 9–12 months, muscle substitution with free muscle transfer is performed to which the cross-face nerve grafts are connected. If there is no
muscle activity on the initial EMG (complete facial palsy), a stage cross-face nerve
graft is performed following 9–12 months later by muscle substitution (Fig. 11.6).
Gracilis and platysma free muscle flaps can be used for muscle substitution [68].
Terzis has also described cross-face nerve graft neurotized to pedicled frontalis
muscle [67].
The pectoralis minor muscle can be used for both lip elevation and blink restoration, as described by Terzis [69]. The multiple slips more closely mimic the muscles
of facial expression. The uppermost slips have separate innervation (lateral pectoral
nerve) from the remainder of the muscle (medial pectoral nerve) and thus can be
neurotized separately to cross-face nerve grafts, thus providing independent blink
function. This is however a technically challenging operation due to inconsistent
neurovascular anatomy of the pectoralis minor muscle.
The pedicled temporalis muscle can be transferred for eye sphincter closure.
This is a one-stage operation that obviates the need for microsurgery. However, the

258

F. Shahzad

patient has to bite down to activate the muscle. Chewing produced eye movements,
and aesthetically the eyes have a slit-like appearance. This is a good operation in
elderly patients in whom nerve regeneration is not as robust and a multistage technique is not desired.

Midface
The majority of work in facial reanimation has focused on upper lip animation.
Smile has been categorized into three patterns: the Mona Lisa smile (corners of
mouth pulled up to show upper teeth), canine smile (levator labii superioris activated to show canines), and full denture smile (upper lip elevators and lower lip
depressors simultaneously activated to show all the teeth) [70]. In children, static
procedures are rarely performed as every attempt is made to perform dynamic smile
reconstruction (Fig. 11.7). Children demonstrate better outcomes with dynamic procedures due to superior nerve regeneration and cortical plasticity.
Two-Stage Free Muscle Flap with Cross-Face Nerve Grafting
Spontaneous smile that is synchronous with the other side can be obtained by muscle substitution by a free muscle flap with neural input provided by contralateral
facial buccal branches via cross-face nerve grafts (Fig. 11.7). Muscle flaps that have
been used and described include gracilis, pectoralis minor, and latissimus dorsi [69,
71, 72]. The gracilis has emerged as the muscle of choice for the majority of surgeons due to its consistent neurovascular anatomy, ability to trim the muscle, low
donor site morbidity, and location in the lower extremity permitting a two-team
approach.
In the first stage, facial nerve dissection is performed on the normal side via a
preauricular incision. The branches for lip elevation are stimulated, and the appropriate branch is chosen. If eye sphincter or lower lip animation is also planned, the
appropriate facial nerve branches are stimulated and identified. Sural nerve grafts
are then coapted to these nerve branches in an epineural manner. The nerve grafts
are then tunneled to the contralateral side: the graft for lip elevation across the
upper lip, lip depression across the lower lip, and periocular area across the
forehead.
Regeneration of axons across the nerve graft is clinically documented by an
advancing Tinel sign. When axonal growth across the graft is judged to be complete,
a process that takes 6 to 12 months, the second stage is performed.
The nasolabial fold, oral commissure, and vector of smile are marked preoperatively. A two-team approach is used, one for facial preparation and the other for
muscle flap harvest. A preauricular incision is made on the paralyzed side, and the

Post-operatively, patients are referred for therapy, although this is difficult in
children. Movement of the muscle is seen around 3 months. Revisions may be
needed for debulking a thick flap or reinsetting a malpositioned flap. If eventual
smile excursion is suboptimal, additional procedures like a mini-temporalis transfer
can be performed for smile augmentation [73].
One-Stage Free Muscle Flap with Masseteric Nerve Transfer
An effective one-stage reconstruction can be achieved by free muscle flap to which
the masseteric motor branch of the trigeminal nerve is coapted. The masseteric nerve
provides more powerful neural input than a cross-face nerve graft. The masseteric
nerve is located deep in the masseter at the area of the sigmoid notch, approximately
3 cm anterior to the tragus and 1 cm inferior to the zygomatic arch (Fig. 11.7) [74].
The fibers of the masseter are spread, and the nerve is located with the aid of a nerve
stimulator. The descending branch is dissected for approximately 2 cm, transected,
and then brought up for end-to-end coaptation to the motor nerve of the muscle flap.
The procedure is useful if a single-stage operation is desired or if contralateral facial
nerve donors are not available (bilateral facial palsy). Patients practice smiling by
biting down. The age of surgery is thus an important consideration as patients need
to able to participate in post-operative therapy. Studies have shown that in a significant proportion of patients, the smile eventually becomes spontaneous [75].
Dual innervation of a free muscle flap by both a cross-face nerve graft and masseteric nerve transfer has recently become popular [76]. The masseteric nerve provides more power as there are a larger number of axons, while the cross-face graft
provides spontaneity. The goal is to enable faster muscle recovery with a spontaneous smile that is stronger and thus more symmetric with the contralateral side. A
case example is illustrated in Fig. 11.8.
Temporalis Transfer
Local muscle transfers are infrequently performed in children as outcomes with free
tissue transfer are superior. Their advantage is that they are a single-stage procedure
that does not require microsurgical expertise. They may be useful if contralateral

Lower Face
Isolated lip depressor paresis is one of the most common phenotypes of facial
paralysis in craniofacial microsomia. Paralysis of lip depressors precludes a
full-denture smile and causes asymmetry on lip animation. Techniques that
attempt to create lower lip symmetry are of two types: procedures that paralyze
the contralateral normal lip and those that animate the paralyzed ipsilateral
lower lip.
Contralateral Lip Paralysis
Lip symmetry can be achieved by paralyzing the depressors of the normal lip.
Paralysis can be obtained by botulinum toxin injection into the depressor complex.
Fifteen units are injected in the depressor muscles, staying 1 cm below the vermillion border to avoid the orbicularis. The injections need to be repeated every 4 to
6 months. If patients are happy with the aesthetic and functional outcome and desire
permanent paralysis, depressor myomectomy or marginal mandibular neurectomy
can be performed [78, 79]. These procedures are technically simple with minimal
additionally donor site morbidity. However, they result in lip closure weakening
which may impair oral continence. Furthermore, they are permanent and preclude
future dynamic procedures.
Ipsilateral Lip Depression
Fascial Slings
A “semi-dynamic” method of reconstruction was described by Watanabe et al.
(Fig. 11.9) [80]. A fascia lata graft is placed along the length of the paralyzed lip,
extending a bit to the normal side. A second fascia graft is placed from the midpoint
of the lip graft to the lower mandibular border. This maintains the distance of the
lower lip from the mandibular border, thus maintaining a symmetric lip position on
animation. This technique is also useful for upgrading an unsatisfactory result of a
dynamic lower lip animation procedure.

263

Digastric Muscle Transfer
The digastric muscle may be absent in up to 40% of patients with craniofacial
microsomia and up to 55% patients with marginal mandibular nerve palsy [81].
Imaging, such as ultrasound, can be useful to evaluate for the presence of muscle.
The anterior belly of digastric is supplied by the facial artery and the mylohyoid
branch of the trigeminal nerve. After division of the posterior belly, the anterior
belly and intermediate tendon are transferred to the lower lip via a subcutaneous
tunnel (Fig. 11.9). The neurovascular bundle, which lies posterior to the muscle, is
carefully preserved. The tendon is longitudinally split into four strips and sutured to
the lower lip orbicularis, via an incision just posterior to the junction of wet and dry
vermillion. The mandibular origin of the muscle may be transected and reinset to
create a vector of pull that matches the contralateral side. This operation restrains
the lower lip down, thus resulting in more symmetric lip animation [82]. Active lip
depression that is synchronous with the contralateral side can be obtained by coapting a cross-face nerve graft to the motor nerve of the transferred digastric muscle.
Cross-Face Nerve Grafting
Synchronous lower lip movements can be achieved with cross-face nerve grafting
from the contralateral marginal mandibular nerve branches. If there is partial facial
nerve palsy, as indicated by clinical examination and needle EMG, direct depressor
muscle neurotization of the cross-face nerve graft may be performed. If after 9 to
12 months, restoration of lip depression is unsatisfactory, muscle substitution can be
performed to which the cross-face nerve graft is coapted. If there is complete depressor palsy with no evidence of muscle viability on EMG, a two-stage procedure of
cross-face nerve grafting followed by muscle substitution is performed.
The muscles most commonly used for lower lip depressor substitution are the
anterior belly of digastric and the platysma. The platysma may be absent in craniofacial microsomia, and therefore imaging should be performed to conform its presence [83]. The platysma is supplied by the facial artery and cervical branch of the
facial nerve. The lateral 2/3 of the muscle can be harvested carefully protecting its
neurovascular pedicle, tunneled to the lower lip, and sutured to lower lip via several
slips. The cross-face nerve graft is neurotized to the cervical branch of the facial
nerve. If the digastric and platysma are absent or not available, a free muscle flap,
e.g., gracilis, can be coapted to the cross-face nerve graft (Fig. 11.9).
Mini-hypoglossal Nerve Transfer
The mini-hypoglossal nerve transfer to the facial nerve was described by Terzis
as a “baby sitter” operation to maintain viability of the facial muscles while
waiting for a cross-face nerve graft to regenerate [84]. In incomplete lower lip

Michael Miloro, Alexis Olsson, and Michael R. Markiewicz

Introduction
Craniofacial microsomia (CFM), also known as hemifacial microsomia, described
by Gorlin and Pindborg in 1964, has been called oculoauriculovertebral syndrome
due to the affected areas of clinical involvement [1, 2] (Figs. 12.1 and 12.2). This
entity has been referred to as one of the first and second branchial arch syndromes
due to involvement of the derivatives of these branchial arches. The first, or mandibular, branchial arch gives rise to the muscles of mastication; stylohyoid, anterior
belly of the digastric, tensor tympani, and tensor veli palatini muscles; and the malleus, incus, and Meckel’s cartilage, as well as the third division of the trigeminal
nerve (V3). The second, or hyoid, branchial arch provides the muscles of facial
expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of the digastric muscle, as
well as the stapes, styloid cartilage, lesser cornu of the hyoid bone, and Reichert’s
cartilage, and the facial (VII) nerve. From an epidemiologic standpoint, CFM occurs
in 1:5000 live births (range: 1:3500–1:5600) making it the second most common
facial anomaly after cleft lip and palate [3].

Etiology and Pathogenesis
While the precise etiology is unknown, involvement of any mechanism that may
interfere with the development of the first and second branchial arches during the
first 4–6 weeks gestation is considered a possible causative factor in the pathogenesis of CFM, resulting in unilateral hypoplasia or underdevelopment of the facial
skeleton and associated soft tissues. CFM occurs in 1:3000–1:5000 live births.
There is a sporadic inheritance pattern, although reports of successive generation
genetic inheritance exist as well [4]. A male predilection exists (male-female = 3:2),
and the right side is more commonly involved than the left side (ratio 3:2) [5]. Risk
factors for CFM include low socioeconomic status and delayed recognition of pregnancy (> 9 weeks) [4, 5]. Since the exact etiology of CFM is not known, various
theories have been proposed. In 1973, Poswillo proposed that CFM was vascular in
origin (sheep study) resulting from a focal in utero expanding hematoma of the
stapedial artery that supplies first and second branchial arch development on, or
about, day 33 of gestation. Another support for this theory includes an increase in
CFM that has been shown to occur in children of mothers who used vasoactive
medications (pseudoephedrine), especially with smoking (1–10 cigarettes/day), in
the first trimester and had a 4.2 times higher risk [4, 6]. The exact size of the hematoma or magnitude of vasoconstriction and resultant tissue involvement may explain
the variable clinical presentation of CFM. Other theories involve neural crest cell
deficiencies with presumed failure of migration to the first and second branchial
arches and decreased levels of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) that promote the growth of Meckel’s cartilage [3]. Animal studies have shown that the introduction of retinoic acid during early pregnancy results in neural crest cell death,
with offspring that are phenotypically very similar to CFM. The etiology is most
likely multifactorial and heterogeneous and includes maternal conditions such as
diabetes mellitus, maternal teratogens such as thalidomide and retinoic acid, intrauterine fetal compression, and over-ripeness ovopathy among other factors
(Table 12.1) [3]. Even though most cases are sporadic in nature, chromosomal
defects including an autosomal dominant pattern (involving chromosome 14) and
autosomal recessive pattern with reduced penetrance are possible. Twin studies
have shown concordance for both monozygotic and dizygotic twins. Specific chromosomal alterations include chromosome 5p deletion, 7q duplication, 22q11.2
Table 12.1 Pathogenic factors (Chap. 1)

deletion, and trisomy 7, 8, and 9 mosaicism [3]. For a thorough discussion on this
topic, please refer to Chap. 1.

Clinical Findings
There is a variable and complex phenotypic expression of the unilateral clinical
findings involving the mandible, craniofacial hard and soft tissues, orbits, external
and middle ear, and nerves. Mandibular hypoplasia results in maxillary growth
restriction with facial asymmetry and an occlusal cant. There may be a “scissors-­
bite” or complete crossbite of the occlusion. There is orbital asymmetry and dystopia, as well as ear deformities. Goldenhar syndrome, or oculoauriculovertebral
dysplasia, is a more severe variant of CFM comprising approximately 10% of the
total [4]. Goldenhar syndrome presents with hemifacial hypoplasia, epibulbar or
conjunctival lipodermoids, accessory auricular appendages, and vertebral anomalies including fusions, hemivertebrae, and scoliosis. The facial skeletal defects seen
in CFM include variable forms of bony hypoplasia of the zygoma, zygomatic arch,
orbit, frontal bone, pterygoid process of the sphenoid bone, mastoid and tympanic
processes of the temporal bone, ear ossicles and bony external auditory canal, as
well as maxillary involvement, with cleft palate seen in 10% of CFM cases.
Regarding the mandible, involvement may be the earliest skeletal manifestation of
CFM and, again, may have variable degrees of severity ranging from a small or flattened condyle to complete agenesis of the condyle, ascending ramus, and glenoid
fossa [7]. There is impaired vertical and horizontal mandibular growth that inhibits
ipsilateral vertical maxillary and midface growth resulting in an occlusal cant and
ipsilateral mandibular deviation upon mouth opening. In the mandible, there is no
correlation between the magnitude of the bony hypoplasia and the degree of associated muscular atrophy. The dentition may have dental crowding and crossbites, and
the anterior teeth may be inclined toward the affected side [8]. There may be
hypodontia in 25% of individuals, particularly in the mandible, and delayed tooth
development and enamel hypoplasia on the affected side. Also, there may be mandibular midline and chin deviation toward the affected side. Mandibular protrusion
may deviate toward the affected side, and ipsilateral lateral excursive movements of
the mandible may be limited [9]. In addition, there are variable facial soft tissue
defects with decreased mass of subcutaneous tissues involving the eyes, parotid
gland, and muscles of mastication and muscles of facial expression. As opposed to
the mandible, the degree of facial soft tissue hypoplasia is usually correlated with
the degree of facial bony involvement. There may be macrostomia (asymmetric
toward the involved side), and soft tissue tags, or appendages. Ear deformities are
notable in CFM, and the ipsilateral ear may be low-set with microtia of the lobule,
or occasionally complete anotia, as well as underdevelopment of the ear ossicles
and external auditory meatus. A detailed review of the correction of the Associated
Ear Deformities in the Craniofacial Microsomia Patient can be found in Chap. 10.
There may be associated hearing loss and chronic otitis media in some affected

12 An Overview of Treatment and Recommendations for the Craniofacial Microsomia… 273

individuals. Neurologic issues may include facial nerve palsy in 22–45% of cases,
with the marginal mandibular branch being most often affected. A review of management of hearing Loss in patients with Treacher Collins syndrome and hemifacial
microsomia can be found in Chap. 9. There may also be palatal deviation toward the
affected side. Nerve issues correlate with ear deformity severity and not skeletal
severity. Finally, extracranial issues are present in up to 55% of cases and include
cardiac anomalies (atrial or ventricular septal defects), renal agenesis, and vertebral
fusions (L3-L4-S1) which are not only seen in Goldenhar syndrome but may be
present in over 10% of CFM cases as well [5]. A full review of extracranial manifestations of microsomia is provided in Chap. 4. There are certainly also psychosocial issues in these patients due to their appearance including denial, decreased
self-confidence, and social withdrawal [10]. There may be breathing difficulties,
sleep disorders, and speech impairment due to the presence of a cleft palate with
velopharyngeal insufficiency and unilateral hearing loss. For a thorough discussion
on the initial evaluation of the craniofacial microsomia patient, refer to Chap. 2.

Diagnosis and Classification Systems
Patient assessment and diagnosis is best managed in a multidisciplinary team setting (including an orthodontist, pediatric dentist, craniofacial surgeon (oral and
maxillofacial surgery, otolaryngology, or plastic surgery), prosthodontist, speech
therapist, audiologist, psychologist, and geneticist) with an appropriate history,
clinical examination, radiographs (panoramic, 3D CT scan, MRI, lateral cephalography, chest radiograph, abdominal ultrasound, others), hearing and speech evaluation, laryngoscopic exam, and focused neurologic, cardiac, renal, and psychological
evaluations. A multitude of anatomical and surgical classification systems have
been proposed over the years including those by Gorlin, Poswillo, Prusansky,
Kaban, Lauritzen, David, Vento, and Epker. Some have focused more on the mandibular and temporomandibular joint (TMJ) deformities (Pruzansky, Kaban), while
others have included the spectrum of anomalies (Vento, Mulliken). The SAT system
includes Skeletal, Auricular, and soft Tissue deformities. The OMENS system
includes Orbital, Mandibular, Ear, Nerve, and Soft tissue deformities, while the
OMENS+ classification also includes extracranial anomalies. These classification
systems were reviewed extensively in previous chapters (Table 12.2). The Pruzansky
and Kaban classifications include Types I, IIA, IIB, and III with progressive hypoplasia of the mandible and articular structures. In Type I, the condyle is present and
normal in shape but small in size. Type IIA has a condyle that is small and abnormal
in shape but with normal TMJ function. The differentiating factor between Types
IIA and IIB is the abnormal function in IIB with significant medial displacement of
the small and abnormally shaped condyle with minimal or no condyle-fossa articulation resulting in abnormal TMJ function. In Type III, there is complete absence of
the condyle and ramus of the mandible [4, 7]. This particular classification scheme
therefore guides the treatments that may be indicated for mandibular reconstruction.

The differential diagnosis of CFM may include idiopathic unilateral mandibular
hypoplasia, Parry-Romberg syndrome, and other branchial arch disorders such as
Treacher Collins syndrome, Nager syndrome, and Pierre-Robin Sequence [11].
Variants of craniofacial microsomia are listed in Table 12.3.

Overall Management
It is important to understand that treatment of CFM requires a multidisciplinary
approach that is sequenced appropriately based upon the age of the patient. Of
course, airway issues, if present, are paramount, and are of primary concern, as are
issues associated with feeding difficulties and failure to thrive. Obstructive sleep
apnea signs and symptoms warrant evaluation with polysomnography [5, 6]. For a
thorough review of this topic, see Chap. 3. During the first year of life, excision of

ear tags, macrostomia reconstruction, and cleft palate repair may be considered [12].
Within the first 2 years of life, severe plagiocephaly, if present, may be addressed
[4]. At years 4–5 of life, neurologic dysfunction of the facial nerve may be corrected
with microneurosurgical reconstruction or facial reanimation procedures. Next, in
the 5–8 years of age range, with costochondral development, ear reconstruction may
be considered using cartilage, as well as TMJ and ramus reconstruction with rib
grafting for CFM Types IIB and III. Of course distraction osteogenesis may be an
option for CFM Types I, IIA, and possibly IIB and III using transport distraction
techniques in an attempt to create a new condyle [4]. At this time, consideration can
be given for simultaneous correction of severe orbital dystopia. After age 12, other
treatment options may include skeletal augmentation using autogenous (bone grafts)
or alloplastic (e.g., porous polyethylene) materials and implants, and soft tissue augmentation using local, regional, or distant pedicled, non-vascularized, or vascularized tissue flaps [7, 13]. Upon growth cessation, maxillary, mandibular, and genial
orthognathic surgical procedures are performed if indicated. Also, consideration
may be given toward TMJ and glenoid fossa reconstruction with autogenous or alloplastic total joint replacement as described in previous chapters in this text. The use
of 3D imaging allows a comprehensive assessment of the complexity geometry of
the skeletal deformities and allows precision and accuracy in the diagnosis and virtual surgical planning (VSP) for each individual case [14].

Maxillofacial Treatment
Mandibular management is the keystone for facial reconstruction in CFM, and
treatment protocols vary based upon age and stage of dental development. Variations
of these treatment protocols have been described in this book. The specific surgical
techniques, methods, and materials vary with the severity of the individual

276

M. Miloro et al.

deformity and experience and preferences of the team but typically involve orthodontic intervention, orthognathic surgical procedures, distraction osteogenesis
(DO), and TMJ reconstruction with costochondral grafting, vascularized flaps (e.g.,
fibula), or alloplastic joint replacement. Various treatment options are discussed in
detail in Chaps. 5, 6, and 7. In general, in the primary dentition stage, consideration
for mandibular surgery exists only for Type III cases with TMJ reconstruction. This
allows the creation of an ipsilateral open bite with vertical elongation of the ramus
and the use of an occlusal splint (functional appliance therapy) that is reduced
sequentially to allow the mandibular occlusal plane to remain corrected while
allowing the maxilla to grow normally without interference by the mandibular dentition [9]. In the mixed dentition stage, orthodontic activator appliances may be used
effectively in Type I, and some IIA, deformities to improve function and possibly
prevent continued asymmetric development of the hard and soft tissues. Types IIB
and III are managed with ramus and condyle reconstruction as described with rib
grafting and open bite creation with the expectation for continued maxillary/midface growth without mandibular restriction (Figs. 12.3, 12.4, and 12.5). Also, distraction osteogenesis is another option for management for Types IIA and IIB
(Fig. 12.6), and DO in Type III cases is controversial since there is no condyle to
physically distract, and this may not achieve the desired outcome and require additional surgery [15, 16] (Figs. 12.7, 12.8, 12.9, 12.10, 12.11, 12.12, and 12.13). In the
event that the patient is evaluated first in the permanent dentition stage of dental

open bite also require the use of interocclusal splints for maxillary growth; however,
another option is bimaxillary DO, or simultaneous maxillary-mandibular DO. In
bimaxillary DO, a unilateral mandibular osteotomy is created with application of a
DO device, while simultaneously a LeFort I osteotomy is performed, and maxillomandibular fixation (MMF) is used during the distraction period such that both the
mandible and the maxilla are distracted simultaneously when activating the mandibular distraction device. This avoids the need to create an open bite on the involved
side and unpredictable maxillary growth and poor occlusal control. Of course, the
decision regarding treatment depends upon the recommendations of the multidisciplinary team, as well as the education, training, and skills of the surgeon. The outcomes and success of treatment are based upon many factors but include the
magnitude, severity (e.g., degree of occlusal cant), and complexity of the individual
case. It should be noted that despite the use of VSP, complete symmetrical correction of hard and soft tissue asymmetries may not be possible, and acceptable results
may be preferred over ideal, or perfect results, and secondary or revision surgical
procedures are not uncommon in complex facial asymmetry cases [17].
The associated soft tissue deformities and nerve abnormalities are significant to
the patient with hemifacial microsomia and cannot be overlooked. They play a critical role in the quality of the life of the patient. Chap. 11 reviews in detail the correction of the soft tissue deformities associated with craniofacial microsomia and
discussed facial reanimation and soft tissue grafting techniques. Briefly, soft tissue
volume correction can be achieved with soft tissue flaps, fat grafting, and alloplastic
implants. Various static and dynamic procedures can be implemented for the restoration of facial function and aesthetics with the ultimate goal is rehabilitation of
spontaneous movement of facial musculature.

Conclusions
It must be recognized that there is no consensus on diagnosis or management of
CFM and, therefore, evidence-based decisions are difficult based upon the existing
low-level evidence [18]. There is certainly controversy about the preferred treatment for condyle and ramus reconstruction using either distraction osteogenesis
(DO), rib grafts, vascularized fibula flaps, or alloplastic TMJ prostheses for the
CFM Type III (and, even IIB) patient, and this certainly depends upon the severity
of the complex maxillofacial issues and the age at the time of intervention [7]. Of
course a team approach is the best, and an individualized sequenced treatment plan

282

M. Miloro et al.

approach may be the most ideal. Despite these limitations, some progress has been
made in an attempt to develop guidelines for CFM assessment and treatment by the
Facial Asymmetry Collaborative for Interdisciplinary Assessment and Learning
(FACIAL) group established in 2009 to support CFM research and collaboration, as
well as the International Consortium for Health Outcome Metrics CFM Group to
evaluate patient-centered health-related quality of life outcomes of the various
forms of treatment for this complex condition [4].

Introduction to Treacher Collins Syndrome
Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis, Treacher Collins-­
Franceschetti syndrome, Franceschetti-Zwahlen-Klein syndrome) (OMIM 154500)
is a rare disorder of craniofacial development (1:50,000 live births), and 60% of
cases arise as de novo mutations [1, 2]. The syndrome is named after nineteenth-­
century British surgeon and ophthalmologist Edward Treacher Collins, who first
described the essential traits of the condition in 1900, particularly the outer notching
of the eyelids and malar bone defects [3]. Genetically, it is of variable genotype and
penetrance, and in terms of severity, it has a wide phenotypic variation from
extremely mild to severe malformations. It is a disorder of development of the first
and second branchial arches in the embryo. Defects of bone and tissues derived from
these arches include malar and zygomatic hypoplasia, maxillary and mandibular
defects including micrognathia and retrognathia, cleft palate, and ear defects

13 Etiology and Anatomical Variation in Treacher Collins Syndrome

287

including auditory canal stenosis or atresia, microtia or anotia, and incomplete or
missing middle ear ossicles. External characteristics include not only the aforementioned outer ear defects (microtia or anotia) but also downward slanting of the eyes
due to the incomplete orbital rims, sunken cheeks for lack of zygomatic arches, and
retruded chin due to the micrognathia and retrognathia [1, 2]. Figure 13.1 shows the
characteristic facial features of a severe manifestation of Treacher Collins syndrome.
The inheritance pattern of Treacher Collins syndrome is autosomal dominant [1, 2].

Part I: Etiology of Treacher Collins Syndrome
TCOF1: The Master Gene of Treacher Collins Syndrome
The gene responsible for the majority of cases of Treacher Collins syndrome is
TCOF1. Through studies of families with Treacher Collins syndrome, their pedigrees, and candidate gene analysis, Dixon and colleagues [1, 2] pinpointed the true
chromosomal location of the gene. After eliminating other putative chromosomal
sites for the gene [1], Dixon and colleagues further narrowed the candidate region
to a region on the long arm of chromosome 5, at locus 5q31–34 [2]. The locus was
eventually more precisely pinpointed to 5q32–33.1 [4].
To understand the potential function of the gene TCOF1, Dixon and colleagues [5] isolated the mouse homologue of TCOF1, designated as tcof1. Tcof1, on
mouse chromosome 18, was found to encode a low-complexity protein 133 kDa in
size and rich in the amino acids serine and alanine; this protein was found to have
61.5% identity with human and other species’ homologues [5]. This protein is conserved among species especially in regions of amino acid repeats and signals for
nucleolar localization [5]. The nucleolus, located within the cell’s nucleus, is where

Fig. 13.1 The classic
facial features of Treacher
Collins syndrome,
including microtia,
downward slanting eyes,
sunken cheeks, and
micrognathia. Note
tracheostomy tube. (Photo
of author at age 2, from
author’s personal archive)

288

F. J. Smith

ribosomes (the protein machinery of translation of messenger RNA into proteins)
are made, so the localization of the tcof1 protein product to the nucleolus suggested
to Dixon et al. [5] that this protein would be involved in ribosome biogenesis and
nucleolar-cytoplasmic transport. Tcof1 was shown to be expressed in a wide variety
of mouse embryonic and adult tissues and regions, with peak expression in the
embryonic neural folds immediately prior to fusion [5], and also in the developing
branchial or pharyngeal arches at critical morphogenetic stages, all derived from the
progenitor cell population known as the neural crest. Craniofacial tissues and structures are derived from cranial neural crest cells. Wise et al. [6] confirmed that human
TCOF1 encodes a nucleolar phosphoprotein (Treacle), and mutations within TCOF1
(as seen in the families they studied) cause defects in this nucleolar trafficking and
ribosomal biogenetic protein that is critical to craniofacial development. A study of
the mutational spectrum of TCOF1 in Treacher Collins syndrome by Edwards
et al. [7] revealed a premature termination codon which leads to formation of a
truncated Treacle protein; this malformed protein cannot carry out its ribosomal
biogenetic and nucleolar trafficking functions; TCOF1 mutations appear to be
family-­specific. Edwards and colleagues [7] concluded that Treacher Collins syndrome results from haploinsufficiency of TCOF1 and, in turn, a defective Treacle
protein. Marsh and colleagues [8] confirmed the requirement for Treacle to localize
specifically to the nucleolus, via induced mutations that caused the defective Treacle
to localize to random locations in the cell; these mutations deleted putative nucleolar localization signals in the gene. These findings supported the hypothesis that part
of Treacle’s function is shuttling between the nucleolus and cytoplasm [8].
Jones et al. [9] found that Treacle protein contains kinase phosphorylation sites in
its sequence, which might be critical to its function; they found kinase activity in
embryonic branchial arches 1 and 2 coinciding with expression of Treacle at its
peak in these arches. Hot spots for mutations in TCOF1 were found to be clustered
in five exons (exons 10, 15, 16, 23, and 24), which are responsible for 50% of all
pathogenic mutations [10]. In these hot spots, mutations in exons 10, 15, and 16
occur in a region of repetitive sequences that are normally phosphorylated by casein
kinase II, and mutations in exons 23 and 24 occur in the nucleolar localization signal sequence [10] that demonstrate critical functions in Treacle involving nucleolar
localization, shuttling, and kinase activity.
The function of Treacle was finally pinpointed in the mid to late 2000s. Treacle
was found to have a critical function in transcription of ribosomal DNA (rDNA) by
binding with upstream binding factor (UBF), in the process of ribosome biogenesis
in the nucleolus [11]; Treacle and UBF were found to be co-localized in the nucleolus. Treacle and UBF interact together with rDNA chromatin during rDNA transcription; this was shown to be a critical interaction when Treacle expression was
downregulated by the use of specific targeted short interfering RNA, preventing
transcription of rDNA and cell growth [11]. Gonzales et al. [12] observed that
Treacle, through its interaction with UBF and RNA polymerase I, controls transcription of the ribosomal DNA gene and methylates the pre-rRNA.
Further, since Treacle is most actively expressed in the embryonic neural crest
and later on in the branchial arches (specifically arches 1 and 2), Dixon et al. [13]

13 Etiology and Anatomical Variation in Treacher Collins Syndrome

289

discovered in the mouse model they created for tcof1/Treacher Collins syndrome
via germline mutations that these mutations (and the resulting defective Treacle
protein) lead to deficiency in formation and proliferation and, at the same time,
mass apoptosis (death) of neural crest cells—those embryonic migratory progenitor
cells that give rise to craniofacial bones, tissues, and structures—and result in craniofacial hypoplasia characteristic of Treacher Collins syndrome. This demonstrated the critical function of Treacle as a spatiotemporal regulator of mature
ribosome biogenesis, and deficiency of Treacle results in disrupted neural crest cell
formation and proliferation via mass apoptosis in the neural crest in response to
deficient ribosome production [13]. However, these defects can be experimentally
reversed, as Jones and colleagues [14] discovered through their targeted inhibition
of p53 (a molecule involved in apoptosis) in neural crest cells, resulting in reduced
neuroapoptosis (neural crest-specific mass apoptosis) and rescue of craniofacial
defects in mouse embryos, a potential therapeutic avenue. Another role for Treacle
is to protect the neuroepithelium and its daughter neural crest cells from reactive
oxygen species (ROS), the oxygen radicals that cause metabolic oxidative stress
that can be toxic to these cells and cause the neuroapoptosis leading to the craniofacial hypoplasia of Treacher Collins syndrome [15].

 OLR1C and POLR1D Cause Rare Forms of Treacher
P
Collins Syndrome
While mutations in TCOF1 and defects in its protein product Treacle are responsible for most cases of Treacher Collins syndrome, there are two other genes more
recently implicated in rarer forms of the syndrome including an autosomal recessive
inherited form of TCS. These two additional genes, POLR1C and POLR1D, encode
subunits of RNA polymerases I and III, which transcribe rRNA [16, 17]. Mutations
in POLR1C cause an autosomal recessive form of Treacher Collins syndrome, while
mutations in POLR1D can be either autosomal recessive or dominant [16–18]. In
their zebrafish model for Treacher Collins syndrome, Watt and colleagues [17]
observed that Polr1c and Polr1d are expressed spatiotemporally and dynamically at
first ubiquitously throughout the embryo in the earliest stages, then more prevalently around the eyes and at the midbrain/hindbrain border, and especially in the
craniofacial pharyngeal arches. Mutations in these two genes lead to craniofacial
cartilage hypoplasia and cranioskeletal defects characteristic of Treacher Collins
syndrome. On a mechanistic basis, these mutations cause a loss of function of the
RNA polymerase I and III subunits, leading to a deficiency of mature ribosome
production [17]. This in turn causes neuroepithelial cell death (neuroapoptosis)
dependent on Tp53 and in turn a deficiency of migratory neural crest cells. Research
on TCOF1 and POLR1C and POLR1D demonstrates that Treacher Collins syndrome is both a ribosomopathy (disorder of ribosome production) and a neurocristopathy (deficiency of neural crest cells). Watt et al. [17] also found that the
Tp53-dependent neuroapoptosis can be genetically inhibited, and this could be a

290

F. J. Smith

potential avenue for prevention of Treacher Collins syndrome, as much as the
research by Jones and colleagues [14] on Tcof1 p53-dependent neuroapoptosis in
mice shows that p53 can be inhibited leading to rescue of Treacher Collins syndrome anomalies. The research by Watt et al. [17] on mutations in POLR1C and
POLR1D demonstrates the necessity for, and function of, these RNA polymerase I
and III subunits in transcription of rRNA, mature ribosome biogenesis, proliferation
of neural crest cells, and craniofacial development.

Part II: Anatomical Variation in Treacher Collins Syndrome
Treacher Collins Syndrome Is a Neurocristopathy
Craniofacial development begins in the neuroepithelium, the early embryonic tissue
that gives rise to the neural crest. The neural crest forms when the neural plate
invaginates to form parallel neural folds, which in turn close dorsally to form a tube
(the neural tube) [19]. In the neural crest, neural crest cell formation is induced by
signals from surrounding tissues, including Wnt signaling across the ectoderm-­
neural plate border, fibroblast growth factor (Fgf) signaling from the paraxial mesoderm surrounding the neural tube, and bone morphogenetic proteins (BMP) within
the neural crest itself. During this process, neural crest cells are encouraged to begin
migrating in a dorsoventral path away from the neural crest [19]. Induction of the
neural crest is illustrated in Fig. 13.2.
Neural crest cells migrate along defined pathways leading from specific regions
of the neural crest in the forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain, and along the hindbrain
there are rhombomeres r1 through r7 [20]. These pathways lead to particular destination regions including the anterior portions of the embryonic head as well as
branchial arches (numbered 1–4). The craniofacial region of particular interest
regarding Treacher Collins syndrome encompasses the region formed from arches 1
and 2 [20]. Neural crest cell migration along these defined pathways to particular
destination regions is illustrated in Fig. 13.3.
The skull and its associated tissues originate from two progenitor populations—
the paraxial mesoderm from somites and somitomeres and the neural crest. The
frontal, nasal, zygomatic, lacrimal, ethmoid, sphenoid, anterior (squamous) temporal bones, maxilla, mandible, and hyoid originate from neural crest-derived cartilage, while the parietal, occipital, and posterior (petrosal) temporal bones originate
from the paraxial mesoderm [21, 22]. The first arch neural crest-derived bones are
the maxilla, mandible, zygoma, and the lower portion of the squamous temporal
bone and, in the middle ear, the malleus and incus. Derived from the second arch are
the hyoid and, in the middle ear, the stapes [21, 22]. Figure 13.4 illustrates the origins of skull bones from the paraxial mesoderm and neural crest.
However, as reviewed earlier, in Treacher Collins syndrome, faulty Treacle and
RNA polymerase activity lead to metabolic oxidative stress, and this results in

 natomy of Treacher Collins Syndrome: Craniofacial
A
Malformations and Airway Obstruction
The anatomical abnormalities present in Treacher Collins syndrome are the result
of hypoplasia of neural crest-derived branchial arch 1 and 2 cartilages which in turn
cause hypoplastic cranioskeletal defects. These include hypoplasia or absence of
the middle ear ossicles and stenosis or atresia of the auditory canals, as well as cleft
palate, malar and maxillary hypoplasia, incomplete formation of the zygomatic
arches and orbits, and mandibular defects including micrognathia (small mandible)
and retrognathia (retruded mandible) and temporomandibular joint (TMJ) defects
[1, 2]. Figure 13.5 illustrates the cranioskeletal defects of Treacher Collins
syndrome.

These cranioskeletal defects influence the development of overlying tissues and
structures, previously illustrated in Fig. 13.1. The incomplete or absent zygomatic
arches coupled with the open lower orbital rims give rise to a downward slanting of
the eyes, colobomata of the eyelids, and a triangular appearance to the maxillary
and malar region of the face (sunken cheeks). The mandibular micrognathia and
retrognathia present themselves in a visible lack of a chin as well as an anterior open
bite and lips widely parted at rest. The outer ear defects are either microtia (small
outer ears) or anotia (total absence of outer ears), either with a visible stenotic ear
canal opening or absent ear canal opening. These external defects vary with the
severity of presentation of Treacher Collins syndrome.
Internal defects include a cleft palate (and even when repaired, short palate and
velopharyngeal insufficiency) which can impair speech, as well as a stenosis or
atresia of the auditory canals and incomplete or absent ossicles (malleus, incus, and
stapes), which can cause conductive hearing loss or deafness. The nasal cavity and
airway can be abnormally small, and in some severe cases, there is choanal atresia
(blockage of the inferior openings of the nasal cavity, or choanae). The oral cavity
is also abnormally small, with limited jaw opening and overcrowding of teeth due
to the mandibular hypoplasia. The mandibular micrognathia and retrognathia also
cause oropharyngeal airway obstruction, via glossoptosis (blockage of the oropharyngeal airway by the tongue forced posteriorly by mandibular hypoplasia). The jaw
deformities, small mouth, cleft palate, and constricted throat create difficulties for
mastication and swallowing, speech, and breathing.

294

F. J. Smith

Upper airway obstruction is the most serious, and potentially fatal, complication of Treacher Collins syndrome. Complications resulting from the upper airway obstruction include choking, impaired respiration, difficult intubation and
airway placement, and sleep-disordered breathing and can lead to early death
perinatally, postnatally, and any other time throughout life. Polysomnography
(PSG), or sleep study, is a valuable diagnostic tool for sleep-disordered breathing including obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), which occurs with a higher prevalence in Treacher Collins syndrome [23]. Three-dimensional oronasopharyngeal
imaging by computed tomography (CT) scanning for analysis of airway morphology and volume has also been used for studies on the oronasopharyngeal
airway obstruction in Treacher Collins syndrome [24–26]. The studies by
Ma et al. [24, 25] and Ribeiro et al. [26] have found reduced nasal, oral, and
pharyngeal airway volume, which they have connected to skeletal dysmorphology in those regions including micrognathia, retrognathia, and skeletal hypoplasia in the nasal, oral, and pharyngeal regions. Figure 13.6 illustrates the upper

Chapter 14

Initial Evaluation of a Patient
with Treacher Collins Syndrome
Paulo Zupelari Goncalves, Sean Peter Edwards, and Sharon Aronovich

Background
Treacher Collins syndrome-1 (TCS1) is a rare congenital craniofacial syndrome
characterized by anomalies of structures arising from the first and second branchial
arches. It is reported to have a birth incidence of 1 in 50,000 [1]. It was initially
reported by a British ophthalmologist, Edward Treacher Collins, who described
essential components of the syndrome. Later, Franceschetti and Klein coined the
term mandibulofacial dysostosis (MFD1) to describe the same constellation of
facial features and further characterized the disorder [2, 3]. It can arise as a de novo
mutation or may be inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. It is caused by a
heterozygous mutation in TCOF1 on chromosome 5q32 which encodes the treacle
gene (a nuclear phosphoprotein), which leads to neuroepithelial cell apoptosis and
interferes with normal spatial and temporal regulation of ribosome biogenesis. This
results in an insufficient number of neural crest cells and generalized craniofacial
hypoplasia, dysplasia, or aplasia [4].
TCS exhibits genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity, with several other less common subtypes recognized such as TCS2 via mutation of POLR1D on chromosome
13q12, TCS3 via POLR1C on chromosome 6q21 and TCS4 via POLR1B on chromosome 2q14 [5].

Clinical Features
The clinical features of TCS result from a hypoplasia of the orbits, midface, mandible, and ears. More specifically, orbitomalar/zygomatic arch hypoplasia is present
in all patients with TCS. This results in a more inferior position of the lateral canthus and thereby the hallmark down-slanting of the palpebral fissures. Coloboma, a
structural defect of the eyelid or the eye that appear as a cleft in the lid margin or the
iris, while not present in every case, is highly specific for TCS. Lacrimal system
anomalies are also common with atresia of the lacrimal puncta and canaliculi being
typical. The mandible is also a prominent feature of the phenotype with a characteristic micrognathia that features marked antegonial notching and a steep mandibular
plane. The TMJ may also be hypoplastic and/or dysplastic. The ears are typically
bilaterally involved with microtia/anotia, atresia of the auditory canal, anomalous
middle ear ossicles leading to a bilateral conductive hearing loss. Also common are
preauricular skin tags and preauricular hair displacement. Less common features
include cleft palate, maxillary hypoplasia, and an over-projected nasal dorsum
(higher nasal root) [6]. Intelligence is usually normal in affected individuals.
Aside from craniofacial malformations, cardiac malformations such as patent
ductus arteriosus and septal cardiac defects have also been reported in 12% of
patients with TCS1. Anomalies of the kidneys, limbs, and calvarium (i.e., microcephaly) or brain are rare but have been reported [7].
These anatomical aberrations lead to a myriad of functional concerns, which
must be considered during the initial evaluation of a newborn with suspected
TCS. The micrognathia may result in airway obstruction and feeding and swallowing problems. The orbitomalar hypoplasia combined with colobomas of the eyelids
may result in exposure keratopathy and visual disturbances. The auricular and
ossicular anomalies typically lead to a bilateral conductive hearing loss which jeopardizes normal speech and language development. As the child grows, these functional concerns will need to be monitored and interventions timed and planned so as
to minimize morbidity and treatment burden and maximize benefit. Long-term
dependence on tracheostomies and gastrostomies are not infrequent and often the
focus of these interventions. Speech and language development must be monitored
along with hearing. Jaw function should be observed as well for the impact of malocclusions and limitations in mouth opening. Neuropsychological monitoring is
essential to support psychological and mental development and identify any cognitive delays or deficits [8].

Prenatal Screening
Prenatal diagnosis of TCS may be accomplished during a second trimester ultrasound. Primary sonographic features identified include micrognathia and microtia
[9]. Methods to identify micrognathia on prenatal 2D ultrasound include the

14 Initial Evaluation of a Patient with Treacher Collins Syndrome

299

mandible/maxilla ratio with values below 0.785 considered pathognomonic, the jaw
index which incorporates the anterio-posterior and bigonial mandibular measurements to quantify a mandibular diameter/biparietal diameter x 100 [10] and the
fronto-naso-mental angle [11]. These measures do little however to distinguish TCS
from Robin sequence. The presence of additional features such as microtias and
down-slanting palpebral fissures can help secure a diagnosis. As a result, 3D or 4D
sonographic imaging or prenatal magnetic resonance imaging is more likely to aid in
the identification of characteristic facial features [12]. Chorionic villus sampling may
also be used to help with the diagnosis in at-risk families or suspected fetuses [13].
Specific aspects of the evaluation to prioritize in a patient with TCS can be divided
into different time points in a child’s development. These include the neonatal period
and infancy, childhood, adolescence, and adulthood. Note that the treatment during
these periods is not separated, and they merge one in another (Fig. 14.1) [6].

TCS in the Neonate and Infant
Airway
Recognition of micrognathia and airway obstruction are primary concerns in a newborn with TCS. Airway obstruction may be identified with labored breathing, cyanosis, frank apneas, stridor, desaturations, feeding difficulties, and hemodynamic
alterations. Mild cases may be managed with positional changes or a nasopharyngeal airway placement, while severe cases may require emergent intubation or tracheostomy [8, 14]. If time permits, a polysomnogram (PSG) in a dedicated pediatric
sleep laboratory can aid in the diagnosis of pediatric obstructive sleep apnea, while
also identifying the presence of hypoventilation and central apnea. In addition to
micrognathia, choanal atresia, adenotonsillar hypertrophy, glossoptosis, tracheomalacia, and laryngomalacia may contribute to airway obstruction [15].
