Choanal atresia, seen with a frequency of 14 to 28% in TCS, is stenosis or complete obstruction (atresia) at the nasal choana in the posterior nasal cavity. The
obstructive tissue may be membranous and/or bony. This condition prevents the
passage of air into the nasopharynx. Choanal atresia or stenosis may be unilateral or
bilateral, with the former being more common as an isolated finding, whereas bilateral cases are more likely to be associated with a specific syndrome (i.e., CHARGE
syndrome) and multiple other congenital anomalies [16]. A flexible nasoendoscopy,
done awake or under intravenous sedation, should be considered to evaluate all sites
of potential obstruction. A maxillofacial CT scan may help characterize the severity
of choanal atresia and micrognathia and guide surgical treatment with computer-­
assisted planning or surgical navigation.

Feeding
Feeding difficulties, while often seen in the presence of airway obstruction, are
compounded by the presence of a cleft palate. Infants are obligate nasal breathers,
and the presence of choanal atresia may further hinder feeding. A bedside swallowing evaluation by an experienced member of the cleft and craniofacial team should
be performed and should include an assessment of general tone, ability to latch,
suck-swallow reflex, and oro-motor coordination. If a cleft palate is present, use of
specialized bottles should be trialed under the guidance of a cleft palate feeding
specialist. Caloric intake and weight changes should be monitored closely. Enteral
feeding or a gastrostomy tube may be considered on an individual basis.

Ocular and Eyelid Anomalies
Eyelid abnormalities are often readily recognizable features of TCS. Patients may
present with an eyelid coloboma, hypoplastic or missing eyelid appendages, downward slanting palpebral fissures, ectropion, excessive scleral show, and lagophthalmos. Exposure keratopathy may lead to corneal scarring, ulceration, and even
blindness in severe cases and should be recognized and managed early. Ophthalmic
ointments can be used in mild cases or as a temporizing measure in more severe
instances. Early tarsorrhaphy may be considered in severe cases in consultation
with a pediatric ophthalmologist or oculoplastic surgeon. Ophthalmological evaluation should be performed on a regular basis to assess vision and examine the cornea.

Hearing
Adequate hearing is a prerequisite for proper speech and language development and
mandates early consultation and intervention. Most patients with TCS have at least
a moderate conductive hearing loss, 58 dB loss on average, which correlates with

14 Initial Evaluation of a Patient with Treacher Collins Syndrome

301

the severity of external auditory canal and middle ear aberrations. The external
auditory canal is often stenotic and may be atretic. Anomalies in the ossicular chain
are common. The ossicles may be hypoplastic or ankylosed to the medial or lateral
wall of the tympanic recess [17]. A pediatric otolaryngologist and audiologist must
be part of the multidisciplinary team involved in the initial evaluation and provision
of removable (i.e., removable bone conduction hearing aids (BAHA) headbands or
softbands) and later implantable (i.e., permanent BAHA) hearing aids. Stenotic
auditory canals need to be monitored for the development of cholesteatomas [6, 8,
18–20]. Patients with TCS should have serial audiological evaluations.

Speech
When cleft palate is present, special attention is given to determine the ideal timing
for palatoplasty [6, 19, 21]. While there is data demonstrating that palatoplasty after
12 or 18 months of age increases the incidence of compensatory misarticulations,
there are various factors that may delay timing of palate repair. Presence and severity of OSA, medical comorbidities, weight gain, cognitive development, and prelinguistic screening by a speech language pathologist may help guide the surgeon
regarding timing of palatoplasty. Palatoplasty may worsen existing OSA or contribute to recurrent airway obstructions. Thus, a definite plan to manage and monitor
the airway should be in place. Regular speech therapy appointments with a speech
language pathologist on the cleft team are anticipated.

Genetics Counseling
Genetic consultation is typically sought to confirm the diagnosis of Treacher Collins
syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis-1). Various genetic mutations have been
identified that present with features of mandibulofacial dysostosis. These autosomal
dominant types of mandibulofacial dysostosis include Guion-Almeida (MFDGA),
Bauru, X-linked type Toriello, and Hedera-Toriello-Petty. Patients with CHARGE
syndrome also present with auricular anomalies, choanal atresia, and hearing loss.
While patients with oto-facial syndrome and those with a HOX2A gene mutations
may present with deafness, microtia, and cleft palate.
Nager syndrome (NS) should be distinguished from Treacher Collins syndrome
given the similarities in presentation. Nager syndrome usually presents more severe
auricular deformation and limb defects that typically involve the anterior elements
of the upper limbs and manifest as small or absent thumbs, triphalangeal thumbs,
radial hypoplasia or aplasia, and radioulnar synostosis. Phocomelia of the upper
limbs and, occasionally, lower limb defects have also been reported [22]. Regarding
the affected genes, TCS is related to mutations of TCOF1, POL1B, POLR1C, and
POLR1D genes, while NS is related to haploinsufficiency of SF3B4 gene
(Table 14.1) [23].

The genetic counseling for a TCS patient and family consists in providing information related to the natural inheritance of the pathology and implications of the
syndrome. It is advisable that individuals presenting at least two of the main phenotypic characteristics of the syndrome should undergo confirmative genetic testing
[4–6, 23].

TCS in Childhood to Adulthood
As a child with TCS grows, general considerations include ongoing monitoring for
vision and corneal protection, hearing assessments with audiology, speech, signs
and symptoms of sleep disordered breathing, dental and jaw development, and psychosocial concerns. Among others, an orthodontist is typically involved in the care
throughout childhood. Sleep disordered breathing should be monitored regularly
and can be elicited verbally or assessed with screening instruments such as the PSQ
(pediatric sleep questionnaire) [24].

Facial Skeletal Assessment
The maxillofacial assessment should include an evaluation of facial profile, symmetry, and proportions, as well as specific characterization of peri-ocular, zygomatic, nasal, auricular, and dental or occlusal abnormalities. Initial and follow-up
facial and intra-oral photographs help document and track changes over time.
Craniofacial features of TCS remain stable (non-progressive) over time, as demonstrated by similar facial proportions and extent of convexity between children and
adults [25].
Two-dimensional cephalometric and panoramic radiographs help quantify the
extent of maxillomandibular retrognathism relative to the neurocranium, airway
narrowing, occlusion, and dental development. Furthermore, maxillomandibular
growth and development can be followed with serial lateral cephalometric imaging.
Three-dimensional imaging with computed tomography provides further detail to
accurately characterize the severity of mandibular, temporal, and orbitomalar hypoplasia and dysmorphology.

Midface, Maxillary, and Oral Findings
Most patients with TCS have a prominent nasal dorsum with obtuse nasofrontal
angle and a convex facial profile secondary to retro-micrognathia and normal nasomaxillary projection. Some patients present with a transversely hypoplastic maxilla,
narrow palate, and increased buccal corridors on smile. In patients with a history of

14 Initial Evaluation of a Patient with Treacher Collins Syndrome

305

a cleft palate, maxillary hypoplasia may be present in all three planes of space. An
anterior open bite with angle class 2 malocclusion is seen with increased frequency
in TCS. The latter can be attributed to a hyperdivergent mandibular growth pattern
and likely compensatory posterior vertical maxillary excess.
A standard occlusal and dental evaluation should be accomplished and include
an assessment of oral hygiene, missing and impacted teeth, caries, and periodontal
disease [26]. Dental anomalies such as tooth agenesis (33%), enamel opacities
(20%), and ectopic eruption of the maxillary first molars (13%) are present in 60%
of the individuals [7]. Patient with TCS requires care by a pediatric or general dentist, and age-appropriate orthodontic treatment and monitoring, and combined surgical orthodontics for future phases of care.

Mandible
The hyperdivergent facial form of patients with TCS is due to short posterior facial
third, a steep mandibular and occlusal plane angle. Deep antegonial notching and a
short chin throat length are characteristic features that result. These clinical findings
have been confirmed with 2D cephalometric analyses of patients with TCS at various ages. These demonstrate a more acute skull base angle (B-S-N), an obtuse joint
angle (S-Ar-Go), severely shortened ramus height (Ar-Go), a reduced mandibular
corpus length (Go-Pg), increased lower anterior face height (ANS-Me), a very steep
cranio-mandibular angle, a steep mandibular plane angle, and a retruded lower lip
and chin [27].
In severe cases, the mandibular condyle and glenoid fossa of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) may be severely hypoplastic and dysplasic, or absent. TMJ and
myofascial dysfunction and ankylosis have all been reported. The latter may be
iatrogenic as a complication of prior grafts or distraction osteogenesis surgery [28].
The masseter and temporalis muscles may be hypoplastic [29]. Clinical assessment
should include a query about diet consistency tolerated, tenderness to palpation over
the lateral TMJ capsule and muscle of mastication, TMJ noises with movement,
maximal mouth opening, and protrusive and lateral excursive movements. The Jaw
Functional Limitation Scale (JLFS) is a validated questionnaire that helps assess
jaw function in patients with TMJ disorders and may be a helpful tool for any patient
with syndromic TMJ abnormalities [30].

Zygoma and Orbit
Orbitomalar hypoplasia is a hallmark of TCS and involves both vertical and horizontal deficiencies, as well as asymmetries. Patients may also exhibit relative medial
protrusion of the orbital walls, diminished length and projection of the lateral orbital
rim, and greater than normal globe protrusion. Compared to controls, patients with

306

P. Z. Goncalves et al.

TCS have shorter zygomatic arch length, and smaller interzygomatic distances, as
measured on axial CT scans [31]. Zygomatic dysmorphology and volume deficiency have been classified into three types, with type I being minor (all normal
components with hypoplasia), type 2 being moderate (some normal components),
and type 3 being severe (no normal components and inferior-lateral orbital cleft) [29].

Ocular
Hypoplasia and clefting of the lower eyelids, along with downward slanting of the
palpebral fissures, are hallmarks of TCS. Depending on the severity of the lower lid
retraction, and underlying bony support, definitive soft tissue reconstruction is usually better delayed until the bony orbitomalar reconstruction is completed.

Auricular
Microtia is a common feature of TCS, with the conchal type (grade 2 with external
auditory stenosis) and lobular type (grade 3 with external auditory canal atresia)
predominating. A smaller proportion of patients may have mild microtia (grade 1)
with low-set ears. Rarely, anotia (grade 4) is seen. The severity of external auricular
anomalies seems to correlate with the severity of ossicular anomalies and conductive hearing loss. Preauricular skin tags may also be present and are typically
removed in infancy.
In addition to the soft tissue hypoplasia of peri-orbital and auricular structures,
soft tissue hypoplasia or atrophy may be present in other parts of the face. A relative
macrostomia is not unusual. A tightness of the soft tissue envelope, including the
suprahyoid muscle attachments, may complicate surgical access and may limit the
extent of bony advancement during orthognathic surgery.

Staging and Classifications
The OMENS classification has been previously described for Oculo-Auriculo-­
Vertebral Spectrum [32]. While not specific to TCS, it helps address some of the
major findings of this syndrome when the zygomatic and peri-ocular findings are
included. OMENS assigns a three-point grading scale to characterize hypoplasia,
dysplasia, or aplasia or functional deficits involving the O – orbit; M, mandible; E,
ears; N, nerve; and S, soft tissue.
Hayashi et al. described a grading system for patients with TCS that assigns a
score for each of eight features of the syndrome, with increasing severity being
given a higher number. The total cumulative score is then used to assign one of three

14 Initial Evaluation of a Patient with Treacher Collins Syndrome

307

grades. Features assessed included the malar bones, lower eyelids, mandible, ear,
cleft palate, nasal root, other deformities, and mutation of TCOF1 [33].

Psychosocial Considerations
The identification and management of psychosocial disorders in patients with craniofacial differences is of critical importance. Low self-esteem, relationship difficulties, nonacceptance of his/her features, bullying, and prejudice are commonly
reported by individuals with TCS [34].
A neuropsychologist or a psychologist familiar with craniofacial differences
should be part of the craniofacial team to assess cognitive, emotional, and social
development as well as assess family dynamics and available support. Diagnosable
mental health disorders should be identified and managed. Psychological counseling and additional resources such as peer support groups can be offered to help build
resilience and healthy coping skills and improve self-esteem and quality of life
[6, 8, 35].

Patient Involvement in Decision-Making
Once a patient is mature enough, their active participation should be encouraged in
treatment decisions. Time should be taken to help a patient understand their condition and the goals of various nonsurgical and surgical treatment options.
Modifications to the treatment plan should be considered, once health conditions
allow, based on the patient preference [33].

Conclusion
The initial assessment of a patient with TCS is critical to optimizing outcomes for
affected individuals. Such a comprehensive assessment will confirm a diagnosis
and evaluate the functional consequences of the anatomical features of the syndrome. From this point, a staged reconstruction can then be effectively planned
prioritizing those impairments with the greatest impact on the health of the patient.
Planning at this level of complexity is best accomplished in an interdisciplinary
fashion with a team that comprises a pediatric otolaryngologist, ophthalmologist,
geneticist, audiologist, a speech pathologist, cranio-maxillofacial surgeon, orthodontist, social worker, neuropsychologist, pediatric dentist, and care coordinator.
Coordinating efficient and comprehensive care, while prioritizing patient and family needs, as well as quality of life, should be the guiding principles for all
providers.

Chapter 15

A Look at Breathing, Feeding, and Speech
Problems in Patients with Treacher Collins
Syndrome
Karin De La Fuente and Kevin E. Bright

The role of the speech pathologist in caring for patients diagnosed with Treacher
Collins syndrome (TCS) is multifaceted and dynamic and requires interaction with
multiple disciplines.
Collaboration with a strong interdisciplinary team helps to determine the services needed and clarify the treatment focus by integrating the expertise of all of the
team members.
Treatment optimally starts during the prenatal period if the anatomic abnormalities are observed with prenatal ultrasound evaluation. Prenatal counseling can help
the child’s parents prepare for the birth of their child with special needs by familiarizing them with the sequence of evaluations and treatments which may be required
and introducing them to members of the multidisciplinary team.
The earliest challenges which these children typically encounter are breathing
and eating.

Breathing
At birth, breathing difficulties may be caused by mandibular hypoplasia and resultant hypopharyngeal obstruction. Temporomandibular joint anomalies, cleft palate,
glossoptosis, and significant micrognathia combine to narrow the airway and can
potentially result in acute respiratory distress.

Airway management may be necessary in the delivery suite, the newborn nursery, or the neonatal intensive care unit. If severe retrognathia is noted on prenatal
ultrasound, a referral and prenatal evaluation by the craniofacial team is helpful in
determining possible need for an EXIT procedure. The inferior facial angle is critical in measuring mandibular retrognathia and the need for a possible EXIT procedure prenatally. A decreased inferior facial angle (IFA) is a reliable predictor of
retrognathia as measured on US. It is measured by taking the intersection of two
lines: (1) a line perpendicular to the vertical part of the forehead, drawn at the level
of the synostosis of the nasal and frontal bones, and (2) a line from the tip of the
mentum and the anterior border of the more protrusive lip. An IFA of >2 standard
deviations from normal (65.5°) corresponds with an angle of <50 degrees and is a
reliable indicator for retrognathia (Figs. 15.1a–c and 15.2) [1]. Of neonates presenting with micrognathia, 54% require immediate airway support from simple positioning to tracheotomy [2, 3] (Figs. 15.1a–c and 15.2). If it is determined EXIT
procedure is not needed, immediate helpful interventions may include prone positioning, placement of a nasal trumpet, or an oral airway with use of supplemental
oxygen therapy. Should these interventions fail to provide relief, a tongue stitch or
intubation may be required.
Securing an airway in these children is frequently challenging. Providers attempting to intubate these children should be familiar with the challenges associated with
their unusual anatomy. When the child is stable from a respiratory perspective, the
intubation attempt should be carefully planned. Different facilities have different

Treacher Collins syndrome airways are especially challenging secondary to limited ability to open the mouth, crowding of the posterior oropharynx by the tongue,
and a very anterior glottis. Some of these children may be successfully intubated
using standard direct laryngoscopy with a McIntosh or Miller laryngoscope.
Frequently a stylet in the endotracheal tube is helpful. When the glottis cannot be
adequately visualized in a standard fashion, alternative techniques should be available. In some circumstances, a laryngeal mask airway (LMA) may fit and be a satisfactory way to ventilate the patient.
A Storz Parson’s slotted neonatal/pediatric laryngoscope will frequently allow
visualization of the very anteriorly located glottis and allow for intubation
(Fig. 15.3). Visualization may also be accomplished in many cases using a rigid
pediatric ventilating bronchoscope to place an endotracheal tube changing bougie
and then sliding the tube over the bougie to intubate (Fig. 15.4). Glide scopes have
become increasingly popular for managing difficult pediatric airways and frequently
have a role in intubating these patients. There is a role particularly in older patients

for flexible fiberoptic trans-nasal intubation of these patients (Fig. 15.5). Oral intubation of these children has also been accomplished in a retrograde fashion by placing a percutaneous guidewire through the skin of the neck into the trachea, bringing
it out of the mouth or nose, and sliding the endotracheal tube over the wire to
intubate.
Multiple attempts at oral intubation may cause significant swelling and further
compromise the airway causing prolonged hypoxia and neurologic complications.
Selecting the most skilled provider available to perform the intubation is generally
advisable.
In children with the most severely abnormal airways, it is important to be prepared to perform an urgent tracheostomy at the time of the attempted oral or nasal
intubation. The tracheostomy instrumentation should be completely set up and the
surgeon fully prepared to surgically intervene.
For TCS children with less critically compromised airways who are failing to
thrive, a discussion of early surgical interventions could include a lip tongue adhesion, tracheostomy, or early distraction osteogenesis with mandibular advancement.

316

K. D. L. Fuente and K. E. Bright

The timing of any palate repair should also take into account the absence or presence of any ongoing airway obstruction.
A lip/tongue adhesion is a short-term intervention which can allow the mandible
time to grow. It can be well tolerated; however it is of limited use in this population
generally due to the degree of retrognathia. It will typically need to be taken down
when the lower front teeth erupt.
A tracheostomy has been and remains the most dependable way to treat moderate to severe hypopharyngeal obstruction. It is not however without significant morbidity and risks. Children with tracheostomies require significantly greater resources.
These includes prolonged hospitalization, parental training, possible need for ongoing skilled nursing, and expensive durable medical supplies. The mortality associated with a tracheostomy is said to be 1% for each year that the tracheostomy
remains in place. The mortality and morbidity associated with a tracheostomy are
multifactorial. It is associated with plugging, inadvertent decannulation, drowning,
and infections. An additional disadvantage to tracheostomy in infants and young
children is the adverse effect which the procedure may have on the development of
speech and language.
Children with chronic hypopharyngeal obstruction frequently fail to thrive not
only as a result of increased work of breathing and hypoxia but also because they
have difficulty eating and breathing concurrently. Once they receive a tracheostomy,
the patient frequently will be able to tolerate oral intake without difficulty. As a
result, the tracheostomy procedure may help these children avoid placement of a
gastrostomy tube. This can be greatly beneficial developmentally because it helps
prevent the oral aversion that is frequently seen in children who are fed with a gastrostomy tube. Most TCS patients who require a tracheostomy are ultimately
decannulated!
Maxillary and mandibular advancement when appropriate are also used to
resolve upper airway obstruction and can help to avoid the need for a tracheostomy
in some skeletally mature patients. This option will be discussed thoroughly in later
chapters.

Tracheostomy Considerations for the SLP
Airway Assessment
The speech language pathologist needs to be familiar with the management of
infants, children, and occasionally teens or young adult TCS patients with a tracheostomy. The issues which need to be addressed vary by age and the indication for
the tracheostomy. This will be part of the evaluation process and the baseline for
further assessments.

15 A Look at Breathing, Feeding, and Speech Problems in Patients with Treacher…

317

Communication with the neonatologist, pulmonologist, intensivist, otolaryngologist, nurse, and respiratory therapist may all be helpful in developing an appropriate SLP treatment plan.
Factors to consider in assessment:
1. Information about oxygenation, mode of ventilation, and tolerance.
2. Visual inspection of structures and missing anatomic components.
3. Tracheostomy type.
(a) Cuffed, cuffless, inflated or deflated, oxygen support.
4. TCS patients with tracheostomy tubes may not want to have their tracheostomy
removed because it provides them a sense of security.
5. Instruction on how to care for the tracheostomy may be provided by the surgeon,
the nurse, and/or the speech language pathologist.

Treatment
The role of the speech language pathologist is to complete a dynamic assessment of
airway tolerance and to coordinate the follow-up and support the pulmonologist’s
recommendations.
1. Decannulation can be considered or recommended when:
(a) The upper airway is patent.
(b) Oral and tracheal secretions are minimal.
(c) Capping/plugging or use of a speaking valve is well tolerated.
(d) The risk of aspiration has been assessed.
(e) The patient can tolerate cuff deflation (if applicable).
(f) The upper airway is being used for respiration, cough, throat clearing,
and speech.
If the patient can manage their secretions, swallows safely, tolerates capping of
the tube or prolonged use of a Passy Muir Valve, and does not need the tracheostomy to remain in place for pending surgical procedures, then decannulation may be
considered and will likely be tolerated.
When patients do not meet the criteria for decannulation, the speech therapist’s
primary role is to assist them with communication and eating.
The structural abnormalities associated with TCS can contribute to sleep apnea.
Breathing anomalies may not be evident at birth, but over time failure to thrive may
become more evident due to increased work of breathing with hypoxia and/or
hypercapnia. In these patients, a pediatric polysomnogram can determine the severity of the obstructive sleep apnea and determine whether supplemental oxygenation,
nasal CPAP, oral pharyngeal surgery, or tracheostomy is necessary.

318

K. D. L. Fuente and K. E. Bright

Feeding
Respiratory complications may affect oral feeding at birth. Coordination of breathing and swallowing is primordial, and when affected, alternate modes of nutrition
must be considered.
These babies present with flat or missing cheekbones, low-set ears with microtia
and/or atresia, and micrognathia. They may also present with a cleft palate.
These abnormalities affect normal function:
1. Decreased intra-oral pressure (suck).
2. Increased risk of aspiration.
3. Difficulty coordinating breathing and swallowing.

Feeding Assessment
The evaluation starts with a thorough review of the case history, complications at
birth, and initial craniofacial assessment by the physician. Initial assessment will
focus on coordination of breathing and swallowing with careful observation of
breathing with stress and movement, followed by an assessment of nutritive and
nonnutritive sucking.
In some instances, delayed feeding problems may arise due to prematurity, long-­
term hospitalization, and an impaired sensory system.
If the breathing and swallowing are not coordinated, then an alternative mode of
nutrition may become necessary. This problem may be short or long term. If oral
feeding appears to be safe, determining a feeding method that will deliver adequate
nutrition safely and in a timely basis is the next step.
Examination begins with a visual inspection of oral structures, primitive reflexes,
sensory responses to touch, and movement. Non-nutritive sucking provides an
impression of intraoral pressure and coordination and assesses fatigue and tolerance.
This portion of the assessment includes direct observation, monitoring of respiratory status, tolerance, positioning, and response to pacing. These observations
provide a basis upon which recommendations can be made. After the initial assessment and formulation of a treatment plan, intermittent monitoring may be warranted.
When there are signs or symptoms of possible aspiration including rapid changes in
breathing with movement, etc., SLP evaluation may be deferred until the child is stable.
If there are overt signs or symptoms of possible aspiration, a modified barium swallow
may be indicated to ensure that the feeding method chosen does not result in aspiration.
When a complete oral assessment has been completed and if the child is not meeting nutritional goals from breast or bottle, alternative feeding strategies will need to
be considered. A feeding system which decreases the need for negative intraoral pressure particularly in those TCS children with cleft palates may need to be provided.
There are a wide array of feeders available that may allow the child to meet their
nutritional needs. These vary in availability and cost. Feeding success is determined

15 A Look at Breathing, Feeding, and Speech Problems in Patients with Treacher…

319

by trial and error. (Dr. Brown’s Specialty Feeding System, SpecialNeeds Feeder by
Medela®, Haberman Feeder, and Pigeon feeder with one-way valve are commonly
used commercially available options.)
Posture, time to complete feeding, and patient/parent tolerance will need to be
monitored simultaneously.
Most mothers will want to breastfeed or use their breast milk. Lactation consultants can be a valuable resource. Counseling and support for pumping and providing
breast milk via bottle can be extremely beneficial.
Not all TCS children will tolerate oral feeds even with specialty feeders. In some
instances, oral feeding may need to be augmented alternatively to reduce nutritional
and/or respiratory compromise. When the nutritional requirements cannot be met
with oral feeds, temporary feeding with a nasogastric tube, gavage feeds, or placement of a gastrostomy tube may need to be considered. As mentioned previously,
children who undergo a tracheostomy will frequently be able to tolerate oral feedings shortly after surgery. Strong consideration should be given in any TCS child
who requires tracheostomy tube placement to postponing gastrostomy tube placement until after a post-tracheostomy swallow evaluation has been completed.

Cultural Competence
The speech language pathologist and the craniofacial team as a whole need to be
familiar with different cultural beliefs about craniofacial anomalies and breastfeeding and be able to determine the family’s level of trust in the medical profession.
A culturally competent professional will be open minded and provide education
accordingly.
The mother’s need to be able to feed her child is incredibly important, and their
input is important during the decision-making process.

Treatment Goals for the SLP
1. In the NICU, establishing a safe oral mode of nutrition while maintaining a safe
airway and assisting with nutritional needs.
2. Reassessing, teaching, supporting, and communicating with key team members.
3. Change of nipples, modification of posture, reevaluation under fluoroscopy, and
reeducation.
4. Troubleshooting different textures and identifying foods that cannot be part of
the diet due to mastication difficulties.
5. Transition from alternative mode of nutrition to oral feeding.
Not all TCS patients will have feeding problems, but for those that do, the speech
language pathologist’s skills and timely interventions will prove invaluable.

320

K. D. L. Fuente and K. E. Bright

Speech
The structural abnormalities associated with Treacher Collins syndrome have multiple effects on the development of speech and language. These patients have abnormal intraoral relationships. Their tongues are disproportionately large in relation to
their oral cavity. They frequently have cleft palates. Their mandibles do not move
normally. They typically have significant hearing loss associated with microtia and
atresia. All these factors contribute to speech and language anomalies.

Speech Assessment
An interdisciplinary evaluation that provides information on hearing, musculoskeletal changes, maxillofacial abnormalities, and past and future surgeries is part of a
thorough speech assessment. Information from the parents, teachers, caregivers,
and from the patient help complete the evaluation.
The evaluation progresses as the patient ages, and their speech needs will evolve
as they mature. A good sound inventory and speech intelligibility at both word and
conversational level should be documented. Assessment of resonance and how it
affects overall intelligibility is particularly valuable and should when possible be
standardized and ideally recorded to determine responses to therapy and surgical
interventions. When a cleft palate is present and timeline for closure is determined,
the SLP will tailor the therapy to coordinate with the surgery.
Stimulability for correction, when possible, should be assessed. Identification of
obligatory errors and compensatory errors with comparison to norms is part of the
comprehensive evaluation.
Determination of whether direct therapy can improve articulation, resonance, or
both and the design of a treatment plan may be dependent upon endoscopic evaluation of the nasopharyngeal and hypopharyngeal anatomic structures and their relationships. The timing of future maxillofacial surgeries and associated recovery
periods should be considered when creating a speech and language treatment plan.
Successful assessment of communicative competence with language comprehension and expression, combined with appropriate SLP therapy, in conjunction
with surgical repair of anatomic defects, can diminish the risk of social isolation and
ensure that appropriate supports are in place.

Treatments
Integration of testing results, patient prognosis, and current and future patient’s
goals will allow design of a therapy plan that will have a major impact on communicative effectiveness. Some TCS patients have communication challenges that are

15 A Look at Breathing, Feeding, and Speech Problems in Patients with Treacher…

321

so severe that they may need to develop nonverbal communication skills as well.
Many of these patients will learn to sign.
Hearing loss can contribute significantly to their communication challenges.
Most TCS patients will require amplification and/or otologic surgery to treat their
hearing loss and allow them to communicate verbally. The SLP works closely with
the audiologist and otolaryngologist tailoring the therapy plan based on the patient’s
ability to hear.
Co-articulation probing, modification of sound production, and dynamic changes
to treatment throughout the surgical and reconstructive journey are necessary parts
of successful treatment planning.
Open communication between parents, teachers, audiologists, and SLPs is
needed to maximize progress.
Fine-tuning of the treatment plan involves addressing those sounds (determined
through analysis) that will maximize speech intelligibility. Focusing on these will
provide the most rapid improvement (pick the low-hanging fruit first).
Treatment is dynamic as surgeries can modify resonance and/or assist with
articulation.
Tonsillectomy with or without adenoidectomy, palatoplasty, and jaw surgeries all
may improve the impaired resonance in this population. Treatment plans may need
to be modified before, during, and after these surgeries are completed. These procedures all alter the oral and nasal pharyngeal spaces which will affect breathing,
sleep, resonance, and articulation.

 he Role of the Speech Language Pathologist in the Medical
T
Setting vs. the School Setting
Medical Setting
The primary focus is on establishing breathing and swallowing coordination while
maintaining nutrition and preventing aspiration. Collaboration with the medical
team, provision of education to the primary caregiver, and conducting dynamic
assessments are the main responsibilities of the medical speech language pathologist. These interactions can be direct or indirect depending upon the unique needs of
the individual.
Typical involvements would include:
1. Initial consultation.
2. Re-evaluation.
3. Parental training/instruction.
4. Frequent feeding sessions and establishing postural modifications.
5. Determination of the optimal nipple/feeder.
6. Providing supportive and informative education to the primary caregiver.

322

K. D. L. Fuente and K. E. Bright

School Setting
The school speech language pathologist will typically:
1. Assess speech and language skills.
2. Follow up on hearing evaluation recommendations.
3. Develop a customized educational plan including therapy to help the student
with TCS maximize their educational opportunities (TCS patients have normal
intelligence!).
Prioritizing therapy and focus in the TCS patient requires knowledge and education. These patients will undergo multiple surgeries, which will affect resonance
and articulation. Treatment modifications coordinated with the surgical team will
help streamline services and allow the patient to improve to the best of their ability.
Evaluation for an alternative mode of communication may be necessary when
speech intelligibility is severely affected. The selected system may be temporary or
permanent but will need to be dynamically assessed as the patient develops language and their communication needs change.
The focus is to help the patient be understood by others outside of his immediate
environment.
There are social factors that the school speech language pathologist can address.
Children with TCS often live their lives with significant facial disfigurement. Their
appearance puts them at high risk of bullying and victimization.
The school speech language pathologist can provide education about TCS to key
staff prior to enrollment. Role playing to provide more tools for social communication may improve social competence and independence.
Referral to a counselor or psychologist can be initiated by any member of the
team to help the patient manage social challenges and provide the tools needed to
overcome them.
Velopharyngeal insufficiency (VPI) is a challenge in the school setting.
Articulation may be intact, but VPI may dramatically diminish intelligibility.
Evaluation methods and treatment modalities have improved in recent years. An
endoscopic nasal examination can determine which surgical intervention is most
appropriate and clarify the therapy goals for the SLP. Complete velopharyngeal
competence is not always surgically or therapeutically attainable.

Speech Therapy Focuses for VPI
1. Placement.
2. Articulation.
3. Precision of strong consonants.
4. Using coarticulation to reduce velopharyngeal insufficiency.
5. A strong plan that fosters repetition and follow-up.

15 A Look at Breathing, Feeding, and Speech Problems in Patients with Treacher…

323

The mandibular deformities associated with TCS result in difficulty in opening
and closing the jaw. This further affects their intelligibility. The school speech language pathologist can focus on strengthening voice projection and articulation precision to facilitate speech intelligibility.
The role of the speech language pathologist in caring for the Treacher Collins
patient is multi-faceted, dynamic, and collaborative. The multidisciplinary craniofacial team approach to the evaluation, treatment, management, and education of TCS
patients is considered the standard of care.

Associated Systemic Health Conditions
Associated with Treacher Collins
Syndrome
Pat Ricalde and Imran Ahson

Treacher Collins syndrome (TCS) is a well-known condition that was named after
Edward Treacher Collins, an English surgeon and ophthalmologist, who described
its essential traits in 1900 [1]. There have been many publications since that time
further analyzing and characterizing the features of the syndrome, discussing its
etiology, genetic abnormalities, embryologic changes in the first and second branchial arches, as well as reports describing a myriad of treatment options. There is
limited information, however, on the systemic manifestations associated with the
syndrome. Since there is a wide spectrum of phenotypes, these manifestations may
affect patients differently. A patient’s craniofacial malformations should not be
addressed in isolation. Rather, patients with Treacher Collins syndrome should be
assessed with a holistic approach, taking into consideration how their syndrome
may affect all body systems. The focus of this chapter is to review the literature and
outline a review of systems that is appropriate to engage with patients with TCS. This
list is by no means exhaustive, as the literature is heavily influenced by the unique
craniofacial characteristics of this syndrome; we aim to redirect the focus to a
patient-centric approach to management.

Nutrition
Patients with Treacher Collins syndrome can have difficulty feeding due to their craniofacial differences. Feeding difficulties may occur shortly after birth due to an associated cleft palate or micrognathia. There have been case reports describing infants
with failure to thrive, need for nasogastric tube feeding, and even gastrostomy tube
feeding. Typically, people with this syndrome have normal feeding reflexes and an
appropriate swallowing mechanism. If they have a cleft palate, they cannot create
negative pressure to allow transfer of milk from a breast or from a normal bottle into
their mouth. Specialized bottle and nipples have been developed to allow for a
mechanical form of milk expression, to allow for the infant tongue or alveolar ridges
to compress the nipple to transfer milk. Or, they will allow the caregiver to compress
the bottle or nipple to mechanically express milk into the infant’s mouth. This can also
be very important in infants with TCS who have mandibular retrognathia or glossoptosis, which can substantially increase their work of breathing. The increased work of
breathing will make it more difficult to maintain an appropriate suck/swallow pattern
while simultaneously maintaining their oxygen saturation. Often the amount of work
to breathe may burn more calories than the feeding will provide, and the infant will
not gain weight adequately. Increasing calories to their formula or breast milk may
help, but it is most important to decrease the work of breathing by making the feeding
process more efficient. Often feeding therapy by a certified speech and language therapist can help overcome difficulties to avoid surgical intervention. It is also important
to assess for narrowing or obstruction of the nasal airways (choanal stenosis or atresia) [2]. This, too, will increase work of breathing as infants are obligate nasal breathers. Flexible endoscopy can help to evaluate for laryngomalacia as well, which may
not be directly related to TCS but will certainly complicate feeding issues.
Difficulty feeding can also lead to abnormalities of bone mineral density and
nutritional deficits. Specialized formula can be provided to offset these deficits but
requires early nutritional intervention [3]. Patients with Treacher Collins syndrome
should be followed closely to make sure they are feeding and gaining weight appropriately, and any deviation from normal should prompt early nutrition and/or gastroenterological evaluation. Feeding issues in infancy can be very stressful for
caregivers and must be discussed and managed with calm, nurturing providers of
care. Not all treatment options will be accepted by families in the same way.
Consideration of the home environment, social support networks, and religious and
cultural beliefs must all be made before finalizing the infant’s feeding plan.

Head and Neck
People with Treacher Collins syndrome have a characteristic facial appearance, and
the craniofacial manifestations of this syndrome will be more closely outlined elsewhere. However, the characteristic craniofacial appearance can create symptoms that
affect the entirety of the child’s development, and must therefore be addressed

16 Associated Systemic Health Conditions Associated with Treacher Collins Syndrome

327

promptly, oftentimes before surgical intervention. For example, it may become evident during a review of systems that the patient has many ocular complaints, due to
dry eyes, chronic tearing, chronic rubbing or eye redness, squinting, poor focusing or
trouble following objects, or sensitive eyes. These may be the result of canthal dystopia, orbital lipodermoids, limbal dermoids, microphthalmos, anophthalmos, cataracts, lacrimal duct atresia, pupillary ectopia, uveal colobomas, paucity of eyelashes,
or visual impairment [4]. Many symptoms may also be a result of surgical interventions to try and manage these conditions. Surgical scarring around the eyelids or
complications from periorbital surgery can lead to entropion or ectropion, or abnormal lacrimal drainage systems [5]. The characteristic downward slanting palpebral
fissures and adnexal hypoplasia/aplasia often leave a patient with Treacher Collins
syndrome with a strong stigma of a person with facial differences, so both functional
and aesthetic differences need to be considered during the review of systems.
Vision can be affected early in life, with many patients having amblyopia, anisometropia, refractive errors, strabismus, and visual loss [6]. Visual loss can lead to
problems with learning as well as delays in all areas of development. In adults, it
can lead to difficulty with daily activities, such as reading mail, watching television,
paying bills, or walking up and down stairs. It can also affect psychosocial development and family relations and will require early therapy services.
All neonates with Treacher Collins syndrome need a formal otolaryngology and
auditory assessment due to the common otologic manifestations. Patients typically
present with external ear abnormalities including absent, small, or malformed ears,
external auditory canal stenosis or atresia, as well as middle ear malformations.
Otoscopy may be difficult or impossible. Up to 50% of patients will have associated
conductive hearing loss. Children with hearing loss often can interact socially on
equal terms with children without hearing impairment [7]. The child’s ability to
develop social skills will depend on their age, degree of hearing loss, time of diagnosis, treatment, and personality of the child and family dynamics. Hearing loss
needs to be addressed early and aggressively because it can lead to speech delays,
language delays, and social delays. Often children benefit from preferential classroom seating, and treatment, usually in the form of hearing aids. Early amplification
is an important intervention, with band hearing aids for younger children and later
bone-anchored hearing aids. Final rehabilitation usually involves fitting a BAHA
with or without pinna epithesis and close audiology follow-up.
As mentioned above, nasal issues such as choanal stenosis/atresia can cause
nasal breathing and feeding issues, which can affect nutrition, weight gain, and
respiratory issues. These symptoms can occur throughout the patient’s life and
should be monitored closely by their craniofacial team.

Neurologic
Patients with Treacher Collins syndrome have normal intelligence. There can be
various indirect effects on the neurologic system, however, as evidenced by secondary losses to cranial nerve function regarding visual deterioration and hearing loss.

328

P. Ricalde and I. Ahson

It has also been reported that patients with TCS can have difficulty with balance and
coordination requiring physiotherapy [8]. This is not from any direct effect on the
vestibular system but may have some association with hearing loss. In general, hearing loss has been shown to be negatively associated with other neurologic systems
as well. Hearing loss (whether bilateral or unilateral) may also be related to dementia in older adults [9]. Although intelligence is not affected in Treacher Collins syndrome, developmental delays are strongly associated with visual impairment and
with hearing loss, both of which are common in this condition. Expectant management of cognition, especially in the developmental years, is much more effective
than retroactive management.

Respiratory
When reviewing the respiratory system, one needs to focus questions based on
patient age. Patients with Treacher Collins syndrome often have micrognathia or
glossoptosis that will leave a neonate in distress immediately after birth. They may
have periods of time when they are doing quite well but then may also deteriorate
and have severe obstructive sleep apnea. Left untreated, chronic upper airway
obstruction can lead to cor pulmonale and other apnea-associated conditions.
Because they have decreased airflow through the upper airway, this can occur at any
time, with varying degrees of severity. It is always important to ask about snoring
but also to do sleep apnea-targeted screener questionnaires based on the patient’s
age [10]. There are many screeners available that have been evaluated for correlation with OSA in children. These can be used easily in the office setting, to help
guide the clinician regarding proper timing for reevaluation with a polysomnogram.
See below for one such example, the Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire (Fig. 16.1).
Taking into account the patient’s age is important when evaluating for sleep
apnea, as each age group will present differently. Neonates typically present with
failure to thrive, whereas young children may present with small stature, hyperactivity, or bedwetting (in a previously potty-trained child). Other symptoms that are
important to ask about include behavioral changes, poor attention, daytime drowsiness, or hyperactivity. Older children may describe shortness of breath and tachypnea or may report choking at night and difficulty staying asleep [10]. Older children
may also present with the classic adult signs and symptoms of obstructive sleep
apnea including difficulty concentrating, daytime somnolence, falling asleep easily
doing quiet activities, and mood swings. Speaking with a child’s teacher may also
be helpful in diagnosing nonspecific symptoms, such as disruptive behavior in class.
Chronic sleep deprivation in adults can lead to a myriad of other symptoms including sadness, decreased libido, irritability, etc.
The gold standard for evaluation of sleep is overnight polysomnography at a
sleep laboratory or appropriately qualified facility. Recordings usually include four
channel electroencephalogram (EEG), right and left electrooculogram (EOG), and
submental electromyogram (EMG). Ribcage and abdominal wall movements are
measured using respiratory inductance plethysmography. Pulse oximetry, EKG, and

Obstructive sleep apnea is very common in patients with Treacher Collins, varying in prevalence from 46 to 100% [11]. Severity of apnea is independent from the

from further follow up.

Cardiovascular
There have been isolated reports of patients with Treacher Collins syndrome having
cardiac malformations, although this is rare. In normal development, some neural
crest cells migrate to form aspects of the aortopulmonary and conotruncal complex,
as well as being involved in the formation of the semilunar valves. Ablation of these
cells in experimental models has led to truncus arteriosus, transposition of the great
vessels, double outlet right ventricle, tetralogy of Fallot, and the absence of various
combinations of aortic arch arteries [12]. Theoretically, TCS could lead to any of
these malformations. Isolated case reports in the literature include tetralogy of
Fallot, transposition of the great vessels, and sinus of Valsalva aneurysm [13, 14].
Presenting symptoms in these isolated case reports included (in the case of tetralogy
of Fallot and transposition of the great vessels) bluish coloration of the skin, poor
weight gain, and shortness of breath during feeding. These two cases were found
shortly after birth. Of note is that some of these abovementioned conditions are
disorders of the connective tissue of the heart and its vessels, leading to issues later
in life rather than in the patient’s early years. In one case, a man suffered a sinus of
Valsalva aneurysm; the only presenting symptom was shortness of breath at 48 years
old. The aneurysm was found on clinical follow-up after vague symptoms including
chest pain and coughing [14].
Congenital heart defects can be broadly divided into two types: cyanotic heart
defects and acyanotic heart defects. These can be classically differentiated by the
potential to turn blue or not based on shunting of the heart from the right side to the
left side (cyanotic) versus left side to the right side (acyanotic) [15]. This classification is shown below in Fig. 16.2.
Cyanotic heart disease is usually diagnosed early in the child’s life, due to bluish
discoloration of the patient’s skin and more immediate and obvious symptoms.
These include episodes of syncope, squatting as a compensatory mechanism, and

fatigability. Digital clubbing may be a late presentation as well. Acyanotic heart
disease does not include the bluish tinge to the skin but can cause the patient to be
easily fatigued. These patients are usually diagnosed by heart murmur and can have
respiratory symptoms such as coughing due to congestive heart failure. Long term,
all patients with congenital heart defects can have growth retardation [16]. Close
clinical follow-up with a cardiologist is recommended for any of these symptoms.
Another consideration are cardiovascular consequences of long-standing
obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Patients with TCS are at higher risk of relapse of
OSA even after treatment. Therefore, if symptoms warrant it, a workup should commence to include repeat polysomnogram if needed.

Gastrointestinal
The altered craniofacial complex can lead to issues with oral feedings, failure to
thrive, and nutritional deficits that can lead to distention, constipation, diarrhea, and
belly pain. Children tend to be poor historians with lower GI symptoms, so patients’
parents should be asked about feeding patterns and changes in mood. There should
be a high index of suspicion for gastroesophageal reflux and regurgitation, which is
common in patients with Treacher Collins syndrome. Classic symptoms such as
sore throat and postnasal drip are most diagnostic but are often hard to elicit [17].
Vague symptoms such as excessive crying or colic, sleep disturbance, night coughing, or bad taste in the mouth should warrant referral to a GI specialist. Also, unexplained chronic rhinitis or sinusitis may be present. For those patients who are fed
via gastrostomy tube, symptoms such as nausea and vomiting, constipation or diarrhea, and/or bloating or distention need to be monitored. These symptoms may be
associated with an incorrect volume of tube feeds being delivered or could be due to
reflux [18, 19].
In the same manner that neural crest cells may contribute to cardiac development, animal models have shown the role of the TCOF1 gene in ganglionic cell
migration of the foregut. This can lead to colonic aganglionosis in mice, although
the same results in humans have not been seen. Giabacini et al. reported a case of
chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction in a child with Treacher Collins syndrome
[20]. These issues of the ganglionic cells failing to migrate can lead to a decrease in
gastric motility. Although rare, intestinal motility issues such as these can lead to
constipation or bloating and should be investigated.

Genitourinary
Cryptorchidism is the most common trait found in patients with TCS, although other
rare conditions such as micropenis and anovaginal fistula have been reported [13].
Apart from a general evaluation of the genitourinary area, symptoms such as blood

332

P. Ricalde and I. Ahson

in the urine, painful urination, testicular pain, or an asymmetric or nonpalpable testis
should be referred to a pediatric urologist immediately. Referral to a pediatric urologist is of paramount importance before the first year of life to manage the potential
complications of cryptorchidism. These include infertility or subfertility, testicular
cancer, testicular torsion, and inguinal hernia. Even after a surgical intervention
(orchiopexy), the testis can still ascend and be susceptible to potential sequelae.
Parents and children should be taught to examine and monitor this area themselves
and report any suspicious findings, especially masses. Children with cryptorchidism
are much more susceptible to testicular cancer, despite intervention [21].
Treatment can be hormonal, surgical, or both. Surgery is usually dependent on
whether the testes are palpable and should occur between 6 months and 2 years of
age. Delays in treatment can lead to lower surgical success, increased rates of testicular cancer, and probable impairment of spermatogenesis [22].

Dental
It is important to ask about masticatory dysfunction, tooth or jaw pain, and speech
articulation disorders, as these issues may all be a consequence of the oral manifestations of Treacher Collins syndrome. Due to many variables, high levels of plaque
and low effectiveness of tooth brushing have been described in patients with
TCS. Many patients will also have Pierre Robin sequence, which includes micrognathia, a tongue that is displaced farther back in the mouth than normal (glossoptosis), and cleft palate. Even in patients where the palate fuses, it may remain high
arched which can result in dental crowding and jaw malformation. These patients
often present with jaw and dental abnormalities, such as teeth that are hypoplastic
and/or misaligned (malocclusion) [23]. Tooth agenesis occurs in 60% of patients
(most commonly lower second premolars) as well as occasional clouding or discoloration of the enamel of teeth (enamel opacity) and ectopic eruption of maxillary
molars [24]. In addition, these patients may have decreased salivary flow, mouth
breathing, and orthodontic crowding. These all can exacerbate oral disease such as
gingivitis, periodontitis, and carious lesion formation. Salivary flow is known to
increase caries index, and half of all TCS patients have some form of salivary gland
dysplasia or aplasia. Despite decreased salivary flow, there are typically minimal
complaints of salivary dryness [25]. Despite these predisposing conditions, patients
with routine dental care can have normal oral health without high caries levels.

Psychiatric
Living with a craniofacial difference can be very challenging for children and
adults and can lead to a number of psychiatric issues. Even in comparison to other
children with craniofacial disorders, adults with TCS report higher levels of

16 Associated Systemic Health Conditions Associated with Treacher Collins Syndrome

333

depression and lower levels of overall quality of life, well-being, and physical
health-related quality of life [26]. To be clear, these children aren’t born with
depression or stress; it is their experiences with other people that lead to feelings
of isolation and difficulty with socialization. TCS patients often report feeling
isolated due to their facial appearance, which can lead to a lack of socialization
and stress during social settings [27]. These outcomes can be expectantly managed, with excellent results shown with early and frequent pediatric psychiatric
intervention. It is important for surgeons to be keenly aware of these issues and to
be mindful when recommending procedures for “aesthetic” reasons, especially
around the eyes and cheekbones, since these procedures often leave the patient
with multiple interventions with little gain. The stigma of a facial difference in
TCS is rarely corrected with surgery but rather with thought-provoking conversation and acceptance. It is more important to develop self-confidence and selfesteem during childhood, rather than subject these children to numerous ill-proven
and minimally effective treatments and interventions trying to make them “look
normal.”

Conclusion
Although primarily a craniofacial syndrome, patients with Treacher Collins syndrome can have systemic involvement. Also, like many challenging craniofacial
syndromes, patients with TCS are at risk for being lulled toward surgical “corrections” that will “normalize” their appearance. This thought process from well-­
meaning clinicians will usually lead to multiple failed or repeated interventions
with little true gain for the patient and increased financial and psychological exhaustion. It is important as surgeons to consider holistic management with true multidisciplinary treatment for these patients.

Orbital Features
The periorbital soft tissue dysmorphism seen in patients with Treacher Collins syndrome is greatly influenced by the skeletal malformation affecting the zygoma and
the orbit. The normal cross-sectional anatomy of the orbit and lower eyelid is shown
in Fig. 17.1. While a discussion regarding the midfacial bony deficiencies is discussed elsewhere in this text, a brief overview is worth highlighting given its impact
on the overlying soft tissues. Tessier noted that the bilateral periorbital deformity
seen in patients with Treacher Collins syndrome was a manifestation of clefts 6, 7,

and 8 (Fig. 17.2) [1, 2]. The tissues affected in TCS arise early in embryonic development within the first and second branchial arches.
In combination, the clefts isolate the zygoma and produce malar deficiency.
However, the degree of involvement resulting from the clefts is variable. For example, clinical forms of Treacher Collins syndrome have been described as complete,
incomplete, abortive, unilateral, or atypical by Franceschetti and Klein [3]. The
complete form presents with all features of the syndrome, whereas the incomplete
form produces less severe malformations. The abortive form is largely confined to
soft tissue abnormalities of the eyelid. Furthermore, the location of the deficiency
on the zygoma can be medial, lateral, or a combination, presumably reflecting varying expression of the clefts.
The number 6 cleft accounts for the medial malar hypoplasia and extends toward
the mandibular angle. The number 8 cleft affects the lateral orbital wall with deficiency at the zygomaticofrontal suture. Given the deficiency of the lateral orbital
wall, the lateral canthal attachment can be attenuated or absent, creating the
downward-­slanting palpebral fissure. The zygomatic deficiency causes the orbit to
become shallow with inferolateral rotation, thereby creating an elliptical orbital
shape [4]. The hypoplastic orbito-zygomatic complex also creates a perception of
enophthalmos due to the normal nasal and frontonasal development and size
(Fig. 17.3) [5].
The contribution of these underlying bony periorbital anomalies to clinical findings has been confirmed radiographically with computed tomographic (CT) data
[6]. The average orbital width, as measured between medial and lateral walls, is
normal. However, when utilizing the lateral orbital rim as a reference, lateral orbital

Orbital volume and shape are also affected [7]. Significant central orbital and lateral
orbital depth deficiency are present, whereas medial orbital depth is unchanged.
The lateral orbital depth deficiency correlates with the clinical findings of inferolateral orbital-zygomatic hypoplasia. The central orbital deficiency and normal medial
orbit depth can be considered distinctive of the syndrome. Moreover, orbital volumes are decreased in Treacher Collins patients compared to unaffected patients.
However, orbital volume in syndromic patients typically normalizes with age, suggesting a catch-up phenomenon may occur with the orbit in these patients [7].
While there is limited data regarding the evolution of the deformity over time, a
small case series also demonstrated relative stability with facial growth over
time [8].

Ophthalmic Features
A review of the literature demonstrates a paucity of data regarding the ophthalmologic manifestations of Treacher Collins syndrome. The main findings will be discussed, although a comprehensive overview is beyond the scope of this text. Hertle
and colleagues presented a case series of 24 patients with Treacher Collins syndrome [9]. All patients had an ophthalmologic abnormality that included refractive
errors (58%), vision loss (37%), strabismus (esotropia, exotropia, cranial nerve

17 Ophthalmologic Findings and Reconstruction of Soft Tissue Orbital Deformities…

341

palsy; 37%), and amblyopia (33%), all of which commonly require treatment. They
found that vision loss was likely due to amblyopia. While vision improved with
treatment, normal visual acuity was not obtained at follow-up and remained unequal
(anisometropia) between the eyes in the majority of patients. Amblyopia may have
multiple etiologies, including refractive error, keratopathy from poor ocular surface
protection due to eyelid anomalies, and deprivation amblyopia from congenital
cataracts and upper eyelid ptosis to name a few. Oblique astigmatism is common in
affected patients due to the downward-slanting palpebral fissure, as the slanting of
the fissure affects corneal curvature [10, 11].
Congenital cataracts, uveal colobomas, microphthalmos, and anophthalmos have
also been documented in Treacher Collins syndrome [9]. Other case reports have
reported rare findings including microcornea, retinal detachment, corneal scleralization, and uveal, lens, and retinal dysmorphology [12, 13]. Corneal scarring,
exposure keratopathy, ulceration, and ultimately blindness may occur as a result of
inadequate globe protection from the lower eyelid colobomata [14]. Assessment for
an intact Bell’s phenomenon is also important for the integrity of the corneal surface.

Eyelid and Adnexal Features
Initial case reports of Treacher Collins syndrome focused on the ocular and periorbital findings. Indeed, one of the early descriptions of Treacher Collins syndrome
was in 1889 by Scottish ophthalmologist Dr. George Andreas Berry, who discussed
the congenital lower eyelid colobomas [15]. The periorbital findings were later
expanded in Edward Treacher Collins’ 1900 case report of two patients [16]. In fact,
three of the four necessary features for a diagnosis Treacher Collins syndrome, as
asserted by Axelsson in 1963, relate to periorbital findings: antimongoloid palpebral
fissures, lower eyelid abnormality (coloboma, deficient lashes), malar hypoplasia,
and mandibular hypoplasia [17]. Many still consider the complex soft tissue periorbital features to be characteristic of the syndrome (Fig. 17.4).
The number 6 soft tissue cleft produces the lower eyelid coloboma beginning at
the junction of the middle and lateral third of the eyelid; it also contributes to the
antimongoloid slant [1, 2]. Studies demonstrate that clefting early in embryogenesis
produces larger colobomas and results in greater abnormalities of the developing
eye and ocular surface. On the other hand, colobomas occurring later tend to be
smaller and are associated with less functional malformations of the underlying
globe [18]. Eyelid true colobomas describe congenital, full-thickness defects, and
pseudocolobomas refer to hypoplastic subcutaneous tissue and muscle with loss of
the posterior lamella. Pseudocolobomas may be the more commonly encountered
deformity in Treacher Collins syndrome (Fig. 17.5) [19]. Multiple large series demonstrate that lower eyelid colobomas are found in greater than 50% of cases [20,
21]. The hypoplastic soft tissues associated with pseudocolobomas may result in
thin lower eyelid skin and deficient orbicularis oculi muscle, the latter which exacerbates eyelid laxity and predisposes to ectropion [14].

The overlying soft tissues in the area of the number 8 cleft at the lateral orbital
rim and zygoma are respectively dysmorphic. The orbicularis oculi continuity is
disrupted in this region with loss of lateral canthal fixation, lateral canthal dystopia,
and eyelid laxity and retraction. In combination with the inferolateral extension of
the number 6 cleft, the phenotype presents as a downward-slanting palpebral fissure, producing the distinctive antimongoloid slant. The palpebral fissure morphology has been shown to be the most consistent finding in patients with Treacher
Collins syndrome [9, 18, 20]. Lateral canthal dysmorphology and its effects were
further elucidated by Bachelor and Kaplan, who noted absent lateral canthal tendon
in two patients [22]. It produced lower eyelid retraction with rounding and medialization of the lateral canthus that was more pronounced with forced eyelid closure.
Other findings include a shorter horizontal palpebral fissure length at rest with a
decrease on closure (termed the “fissure narrowing sign”) [10]. The lower eyelid
may also be vertically deficient due to tethering of the orbital septum to the inferior
orbital rim.

17 Ophthalmologic Findings and Reconstruction of Soft Tissue Orbital Deformities…

Other soft tissue findings associated with Treacher Collins syndrome include
dacryostenosis, blepharoptosis, ectropion and entropion, ciliary abnormalities, and
epibulbar dermoids [9, 10, 23]. Lacrimal system dysfunction produces epiphora.
Lacrimal anatomy is demonstrated in Fig. 17.6. Bartley identified a high prevalence
of inferior punctal and inferior canalicular atresia (Fig. 17.7) in a case series with
70% of patients experiencing epiphora [24]. Complete absence of the inferior lacrimal puncta has also been documented [10]. Congenital blepharoptosis is occasionally seen, and severity ranges from mild to severe, depending on the deficiency of
levator palpebrae muscle function. This phenotype may be the result of a variant of
Treacher Collins syndrome [10, 25]. Ptosis may also result in amblyopia from visual
axis distortion. Ectropion is associated with abnormalities of the eyelid support
structures (tarsus and lateral canthal tendon) and anterior lamellar vertical deficiency (Fig. 17.8). Varying degrees of scleral show are observed and can produce

corneal and conjunctival irritation as well as epiphora due to poor protection of the
ocular surface. Entropion is thought to be the result of congenital aberrancy in the
attachment of the lower eyelid retractors or posterior lamellar hypoplasia causing
corneal irritation from inward turning of the lashes (trichiasis). Other ciliary abnormalities are noted commonly. The hallmark ciliary finding in Treacher Collins syndrome is the deficiency or absence of lashes on the medial third of lower eyelid and
is considered to be pathognomonic of the condition (Fig. 17.9). Distichiasis (accessory lashes at the posterior tarsal meibomian orifices) and trichiasis have been also
presented in the literature.
Epibulbar dermoids refer to benign masses on the surface of the eye and contain
keratinized epithelium, hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and sweat glands.
Lipodermoids contain adipose as well but are covered by normal conjunctiva. They
are usually located at the superotemporal recess and may extend posteriorly into the
orbit to involve extraocular muscles, lacrimal gland, or other orbital structures
(Fig. 17.10a). Limbal dermoids are found at the scleral-corneal junction or on the
cornea (Fig. 17.10b). The mass encompasses the entire wall thickness. Their size may
obstruct vision entirely if excessively large, but more commonly, they may result in a
degree of corneal distortion and exposure keratopathy and corneal scarring with moderate-sized masses. As a consequence, astigmatic amblyopia can occur, with deprivational amblyopia occurring for significant lesions.

Treatment
Management Overview
Patients and their families are evaluated in multidisciplinary clinics including craniomaxillofacial surgeons, plastic surgeons, ophthalmologists, oculoplastic surgeons, otolaryngologists, anesthesiologists, dentists, orthodontists, pediatricians,
speech therapists, and geneticists. Guidelines have been described to provide a
protocol-driven approach to Treacher Collins syndrome. Comprehensive treatment
protocols have been established by multiple institutions [26]. The ophthalmologic
and periorbital soft tissue treatments will be discussed; a treatment protocol is
shown in Fig. 17.11. These patients are often referred to plastic surgeons, craniofacial surgeons, ophthalmologists, or oculoplastic surgeons for treatment.
General treatment goals strive to produce excellent aesthetic and functional
results that are long-lasting while minimizing operations and revisions. Treatment
for these patients often begins in the neonatal period due to the urgent concern of
ocular surface protection and amblyopia risk. Upper face and periorbital reconstruction is the focus through the childhood years (2 through 12) [27]. Ophthalmic treatment begins as early as possible with the goal being to obtain and preserve binocular
vision. Periorbital soft tissue management, namely, eyelid reconstruction, can occur
early in infancy (first year of life) or deferred until later in childhood (5–7 years),
depending on the severity [28, 29]. The treatment of the other adnexal abnormalities
outlined above are often dictated by parental concerns or as symptoms arise.
Overall, periorbital soft tissue and ophthalmologic treatment in Treacher Collins syndrome produces variable results. The multiple strategies and surgical techniques for soft
tissue management achieve the functional goal of ocular surface protection and vision.
Unfortunately, the cosmetic results are one of the main shortcomings in treating affected
patients. Residual deformities persist, and multiple revisionary procedures are the rule
rather than the exception [29]. Despite being least satisfied with the reconstructed eyelid
appearance, most patients are satisfied with their vision [30]. Careful patient and family
counseling in this regard is crucial to establishing reasonable expectations.
