Ophthalmologic Rehabilitation
Preservation of vision is a primary concern in affected patients, as amblyopia is a
common cause of vision loss. Assessment by a pediatric ophthalmologist is prudent.
To prevent corneal scarring, ulceration, and vision loss, the initial management in
the neonatal period involves lubrication and occasionally moisture chambers if necessary. Should exposure keratitis occur, treatment with topical antibiotics and lubricants can provide rapid improvement. Temporary suture tarsorrhaphy can be
performed if conservative measures fail. It is important to be cognizant of iatrogenic
causes of deprivational amblyopia that may occur from frequent lubricant application, dressings, tarsorrhaphies, or reconstructive procedures.
Early thorough optometric and ophthalmologic examination in infancy is imperative and will allow prompt, aggressive treatment of refractive errors, amblyopia,
and strabismus in an effort to prevent vision loss. Additionally, with the exception
of rare cases, the impact on vision observed in Treacher Collins syndrome is predominantly the result of anterior segment, rather than retinal, abnormalities.
Manifestly, a good prognosis for vision loss is possible if corrected early [31].

17 Ophthalmologic Findings and Reconstruction of Soft Tissue Orbital Deformities…

347

Early surgical treatment is considered if the ocular surface is compromised, risking corneal ulceration or scarring, or deprivation amblyopia as manifested by congenital cataracts or severe ptosis. Treatment may include temporary tarsorrhaphy,
ptosis repair, or cataract surgery. Nonsurgical treatment for amblyopia and strabismus is initiated early and includes eyeglasses, prisms, cycloplegic agents (e.g., atropine drops), and occlusion therapy. Strabismus surgery is undertaken early at
12–24 months and after amblyopia and refractive error correction. During strabismus surgery, a fornix rather than limbal incision is preferred by many as it facilitates
assessment of all extraocular muscles. A higher index of suspicion for anomalous
muscle anatomy (aberrant insertions, hypoplastic muscles, or missing muscles)
must be maintained during the procedure.
Ophthalmic outcome is dependent on timely recognition and treatment, as well
as patient compliance. In this regard, a few other considerations are worth mentioning. Hertle’s group noted that, of the patients that did not achieve equal visual acuity, all had documented poor treatment compliance [9]. They also commented that,
for parents, facial profile/cosmetic, airway, and auricular concerns may supersede
visual dysfunction, which can consequently limit compliance to vision treatment.
Another practical issue that may interfere with treatment includes difficulty with
eyewear due to auricular malformations and hearing aids. Finally, given that most
patients with Treacher Collins syndrome suffer from conductive hearing loss in
addition to amblyopia, there is a risk of cognitive deprivation [32]. As a result, it is
clear that patients should be provided with prompt diagnosis and treatment, frequent
counseling and follow-up, and support and resources under the guidance of a multidisciplinary care team.

Eyelid Reconstruction
Eyelid reconstruction and protection of the ocular surface is the primary focus of
periorbital soft tissue rehabilitation in patients with Treacher Collins syndrome.
One of the main components of the reconstructive efforts is lower eyelid coloboma
repair. General principles for eyelid reconstruction are maintained for coloboma
and pseudocoloboma repair. It is critical to ensure that the bilamellar structure of the
lower eyelid is reconstituted, addressing important structures of the anterior lamella
(skin and orbicularis oculi muscle) and posterior lamella (tarsus and conjunctiva),
as shown in Fig. 17.1b. Skin can be provided from flaps or skin grafts. Local
advancement or rotation flaps are utilized from the periorbital area owing to their
similar tissue characteristics and quality. They can be limited by their tendency to
“pin cushion” at the scar margins and create contour abnormalities, which exacerbates the operated appearance [29]. Skin grafts are full-thickness grafts to minimize
secondary contracture and may be harvested from upper eyelid, preauricular, postauricular, and clavicular areas. They are generally reserved as a salvage option following multiple revisions or as an aspect of complication management (e.g.,
ectropion) due to their patchy appearance [29]. Posterior lamellar eyelid support can

348

A. Francis et al.

be provided from upper tarsus, septal or auricular cartilage, or acellular dermal
matrices. Lining can be replaced by buccal or nasal mucosa or amniotic membrane
allograft. Additionally, septal composite chondromucosal grafts, hard palate mucosal grafts, and upper eyelid tarsoconjunctival grafts can be utilized to reconstruct the
posterior lamella. Care must be taken to preserve the integrity eyelid muscle function including the orbicularis oculi, levator aponeurosis, Mueller’s muscle, and
lower eyelid retractors.
Timing of eyelid reconstruction is largely dictated by the defect size, extent of
globe exposure, and effect on visual function. Small and moderate-sized defects
without corneal complications can be observed until school age when more eyelid
tissue is available for reconstruction. Early intervention focuses on eyelid reconstruction when the patient is of appropriate age for general anesthesia and can be
combined with other procedures such as cleft palate repair. The result may need to
be revised at a later age when the orbital framework is reconstructed. Delayed
reconstruction permits correction of the hard and soft tissues concurrently. It allows
the orbital skeleton and periorbital soft tissues to reach their mature, adult size,
which occurs at 8–10 years of age [33]. A staged approach can be employed wherein
coloboma repair is performed after zygomatic skeletal and/or soft tissue reconstruction [34]. Eyelid reconstruction and correction of canthal malposition is more accurate following reconstruction of the lateral orbital wall and malar hypoplasia to
support the soft tissue repair [14]. More predictable and durable results are presumably achievable with this approach, though a need for revision is not infrequent.
Still, many prefer early eyelid reconstruction to provide globe protection and mitigate the stigmata associated with the syndrome.
In the presence of a lateral lower eyelid coloboma, defect size is characterized as
small, moderate, or large and directs the reconstructive approach. The size may be
overestimated due to the opposing pull of the orbicularis at the edges of the coloboma. Additionally, lateral canthal malposition distorts the eyelid architecture and
should be repositioned prior to repairing the defect. In all cases, there may be tethering of the soft tissues to the underlying skeletal framework, necessitating release of
the skin, orbicularis oculi, and occasionally the orbital septum to relax the eyelid.
Small defects (less than one third of the eyelid) are amenable to primary closure
after excision of the coloboma margins. The vertical scar that results can be prone
to cicatricial ectropion. Z-plasty techniques minimize this risk by reorienting the
central limb along relaxed skin tension lines [35].
Moderate defects (one third to one half of the lower eyelid margin) can be
repaired with local flaps but require inclusion of a lateral canthotomy to release the
eyelid margin. The Tenzel semicircular flap is commonly utilized for this purpose
(Fig. 17.12). It is designed in the lateral orbital area and dissected deep to the orbicularis oculi in this region. After lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis, the
tissue is advanced and repaired in a full-thickness fashion. It is crucial to secure flap
to the lateral rim periosteum to avoid eyelid retraction. Another viable option for
moderate to large colobomas are musculocutaneous Tripier transposition flaps
(Fig. 17.13). These may be uni- or bipedicled and utilize Z-plasty principles to also
reestablish lower eyelid vertical height. Tarsoconjunctival reconstruction is required.

Lateral Canthal Repositioning
Repair of the eyelid defect is one component of correcting the periorbital soft tissue
deformity associated with Treacher Collins syndrome. The downward-slanting palpebral fissure, a result of the lateral orbital wall and zygomatic hypoplasia as well as lateral canthal dysmorphology, must be reconstructed with lateral canthoplasty techniques
to restore a more aesthetic appearance. Lateral canthal reconstruction can be performed
at the same time as coloboma repair or later during orbito-zygomatic reconstruction.
In some cases, the lateral canthus can be simply repositioned. The lateral canthal
tendon can be elevated with a cuff of periosteum from the lateral orbital wall [40].
A more common procedure is the tarsal strip canthoplasty (Fig. 17.17). Lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis is performed, and the desired eyelid position is
determined. In general, lower eyelid position should be 1–2 millimeters above the
inferior limbus. A portion of eyelid margin including lashes, conjunctiva, and skin

Ptosis and Other Periorbital Treatments
The management of blepharoptosis is dependent on the extent of levator function
from downward to upward gaze while stabilizing the brow. Timing is dependent on
the severity and the resultant risk of deprivational amblyopia as well as the ability
to obtain reliable exam findings. Early correction is favored when significant visual
obstruction is identified, whereas asymptomatic patients may be deferred until
school age [41]. Patients with mild ptosis and good levator function can be treated
with the Fasanella-Servat procedure (tarsoconjunctival mullerectomy). Levator
resection and advancement is indicated for moderate ptosis with fair levator excursion. The levator should be advanced 4 millimeters for every millimeter of ptosis
and should be centered over the mid-pupil. Severe ptosis with poor or absent levator
function requires frontalis suspension with autologous fascia (fascia lata or deep
temporal donors) or synthetic materials (Gore-Tex, Prolene suture, silicone). This
procedure synchronizes upper eyelid elevation to the frontalis muscle via the brow.
It provides static (related to the degree of material tightening) and dynamic (integration with brow elevation) components to the procedure. Multiple techniques have
been described for this purpose; the Crawford double triangle is shown in Fig. 17.18.

Congenital ectropion and entropion are treated in a fashion similar to acquired
cases. Initial management is conservative with lubrication. Hyaluronic acid filler,
injected below the anterior lamella, expands the soft tissues of the lower eyelid and
can also be considered as a temporizing measure [42]. Surgical intervention is indicated for corneal scarring, exposure keratitis, infection, or for cosmesis. With
respect to ectropion, lateral tarsal strip canthoplasty provides tarsoligamentous
tightening, and the anterior lamellar soft tissue deficiency can be addressed with
skin grafts, flaps, or midface suspension techniques. Some cases may require scar or
adhesion release. On the other hand, entropion does not improve over time and
requires surgery. It can be treated with excision of excess pretarsal skin and orbicularis which also relieves the associated trichiasis. Another option consists of reattachment of the lower eyelid retractors to the tarsus through a subciliary incision.
Lower eyelid lamellar scarring in either case may result in ectropion. If posterior
lamellar deficiency is observed, spacer grafts—most commonly hard palate mucosa,
allografts, or upper free tarsal grafts—are options to restore the vertical dimensions
of the lower eyelid.
Ciliary treatment is required when conjunctival or corneal irritation occurs. If
confined to the conjunctiva, primary management consists of lubricating ointment
or drops; surgical treatment is recommended for persistent conjunctival irritation.
Due to the risk of vision loss, corneal irritation is managed more aggressively with
a lower threshold for surgery. Less-invasive treatments for trichiasis and distichiasis
include cryotherapy and electroepilation of lash follicles at the posterior tarsal margin. These procedures are prone to recurrence and may also cause pigmentary
changes and eyelid distortion [19]. Though there are other surgical options for distichiasis, a more successful treatment consists of excision of the affected strip of
eyelid margin (Fig. 17.19). Since the pathology involves the meibomian gland

orifices, cryotherapy of the underlying tarsus is recommended to destroy any residual lash follicles.
Epiphora in patients with Treacher Collins syndrome can result from lacrimal
system abnormalities proximally in the lower eyelid (punctal or canalicular atresia)
or distally (nasolacrimal duct stenosis or atresia). Traditionally, conservative management with massage and topical antibiotics to prevent dacryocystitis are attempted
first and have a high rate of success up to 12 months of age. If epiphora persists and
the nasolacrimal collecting system is present, then probing and irrigation with stenting can be performed under general anesthesia. Stents are removed in an ambulatory
setting or with general anesthesia after 3–6 months depending on the complexity of
the obstruction. Dacryocystorhinostomy may be performed if stenting fails to
resolve the epiphora.
For proximal lower lacrimal drainage lesions, epiphora may not be seen. Such an
observation is the result of demand compensation of a typically normal superior
lacrimal puncta and canalicular system, despite the inferior canaliculus being the
major outflow source in unaffected patients. As a consequence, many patients do
not require treatment for proximal inferior punctal and canalicular atresia. If epiphora is present despite a patent superior outflow system, one treatment option is the
creation of a pseudo-punctum on the lower eyelid margin that connects to any patent
component of the inferior canaliculus via an open approach to the lacrimal sac.
Another procedure is the creation of a new canalicular system from the eyelid margin to the lacrimal sac directly with a hypodermic needle. Following silicone stenting of this new passage, a neopunctum is created in the sac. More severe cases or
extensive atresia of the canaliculus, nasolacrimal duct, or of the entire nasolacrimal
system may require conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy or canaliculodacryocystorhinostomy with Jones tube insertion.
Epibulbar dermoids are addressed when causing distorting adjacent structures,
astigmatism, cosmetic concern, or visual disturbance. Lipodermoid excision, except
for large masses, is largely a cosmetic undertaking. Timing for most tumors is
around 6 months of age when anesthetic risk is diminished, though early surgery is
needed if vision is affected or if mass effect is noted. Given that the lesion usually
extends posteriorly into the orbit and complete resection can damage critical structures in the area (lacrimal gland, lateral rectus muscle, lateral horn of the levator
muscle), debulking is often the procedure of choice. The conjunctival surface is
preserved, and the visible portion of the lipodermoid up to the level of the fornix is
conservatively excised. Since complete excision is not possible in most cases, lipodermoid regrowth may occur as the child ages. Limbal dermoid excision can be
more challenging. Superficial keratectomy can be attempted for small, superficial
tumors but can result in scarring, corneal vascularization, and pseudopterygium formation [43]. For thicker limbal dermoids, anterior lamellar keratoplasty is required
wherein corneal defect is reconstructed with a corneoscleral allograft or amniotic
membrane grafts [44, 45]. Most lesions are full thickness, and complete resection is
unlikely. While appearance is often improved and vision remains stable, residual
corneal stigmata persist.

359

Conclusion
In conclusion, periorbital soft tissue anomalies associated with Treacher Collins
syndrome play a critical role in the classification of this craniofacial disorder.
Though ophthalmic manifestations and treatment studies are few, early evaluation
of ocular surface and visual function are essential in providing the best functional
visual outcome. Coordination with multidisciplinary teams to create an individualized plan for each patient can help assist in reconstructive staging, minimize additional surgeries, and optimize the aesthetic and functional outcome.

Correction of Orbital Zygomatic
Deformities in the Treacher Collins Patient
Douglas P. Sinn and Danielle Gill

Introduction
Treacher Collins syndrome (TCS) is a relatively rare congenital disorder, but once
manifested, it may stigmatize affected individuals with multiple craniofacial features, most notably in the midface region. Zygomatic hypoplasia or, in some cases,
zygomatic aplasia and deficiency of the lateral aspect of the orbit are some of the
key anomalies. In most cases, these anomalies present bilaterally but not always
symmetrically [1]. Surgical reconstruction is deemed necessary in order to achieve
the desired cosmetic outcome.
There have been many attempts to come up with both safe and efficient surgical
solutions for these individuals, but because of the phenotypic variation of TCS, no
gold standard has been established. All surgical techniques provide adequate reestablishment of midfacial and orbital contours but come with varying limitations.
Precise anatomical evaluation, timing of surgery, and anticipating the need for
future surgeries must be efficiently assessed in order to secure a successful outcome.
This chapter aims to outline the anatomical deformities associated with TCS,
classifications associated with these abnormalities, timing associated with intervention, as well as, identifying potential treatment options.

Anatomy
The most significant factors having an impact on the severity of the disease and
patients’ appearance are associated with the underlying skeletal deformities. To
understand how to correct these deformities, it is important to recognize what the
distinctive anatomy is for a TCS patient.
The hallmark characteristics of the TCS patient show a degree of hypoplasia of
the zygomatic bones, retrusion of the malar region, shortening of the lateral and
inferior orbital walls, and narrowing of the facial skeleton in the upper one-third.
Flattening or even indentations below the orbits are also very common traits [1–3].
Patients with documented TCS also present with an abnormal shape of the anterior
cranial vault due to diminished intercoronal (bitemporal) distance as well as
decreased cephalic length [4–6] (Fig. 18.1).
The inferior lateral angle of the orbit is deficient, and the superolateral part of the
orbit is displaced caudally. These characteristics give the TCS patient the classic
egg-shaped appearance [7]. Other orbital anomalies include moderate protrusion of
the eyeballs, orbital hypoplasia, lipodermoids, and limbal dermoids. Colobomata of
the lower eyelids and iris, ectropion, absence of eyelashes in the medial aspect of
the lid, lacrimal system dysfunction or frank aplasia with resultant epiphora, strabismus, amblyopia, congenital cataracts, refractive errors, and/or vision loss have also
been reported [3, 5, 7–9].

The lid and adnexal abnormalities (canthal dystopia, dacryostenosis, blepharoptosis, lateral lower lid true coloboma, and pseudocolobomas) are found in 96% of
TCS patients. Downward slanting of the palpebral fissures have been noted in 89%
of cases of TCS, notching of the lower eyelids in 69% of cases, and absence of lid
lashes medial to the defect in 69% of cases [7].

Classifications of the Orbitozygomatic Regions
The orbitozygomatic region in a TCS patient can vary in morphology. This can
make reconstruction of this region extremely complex. Grouping these patients by
their morphological similarities gives the surgeon a comprehensive idea of the
underlying anatomy and helps to better determine possible treatment options that
may have been successful for these patients [1, 10].
Chang et al. previously published data discussing a classification system based
on the orbitozygomatic complex. The type I deformity is represented by a small
zygomatic body with all articulations with the exception of the arch [1] (Fig. 18.2a).
The type II deformity has a diminished malar structure and a notable defect
along the lateral orbital wall (zygomaticosphenoid suture). The inferolateral orbital
rim is preserved, but the arch is incomplete and shows no evidence of the temporal
aspect of the zygomatic process (Fig. 18.2b) [1].
Lastly, the type III deformity shows minimal volume with only remnants of the
malar apparatus at the zygomaticofrontal or maxillary region. The absence of all

a

b

c

Fig. 18.2 Treacher Collins syndrome classification. (a) Small zygomatic body with all articulations except for the arch. (b) Diminished malar structure and absence along the lateral orbital wall.
Inferolateral orbital rim intact, arch is incomplete. (c) Remnants of malar structure at the zygomaticofrontal or maxillary region

366

ZMC articulations, and the near aplasia of the zygoma, accounts for the classic
malar flattening and lid and lateral canthal malposition that is seen in a typical TCS
patient. The type III zygoma is the most frequent deformity in the TCS patient
(Fig. 18.2c) [1].
Nikkhah and colleagues [10] based their classification system on 3D CT images
(Table 18.1). Type 1 defects are mild and are characterized by a hypoplastic or dysplastic orbitozygomatic complex. Most TCS patients that fall within this category
can be treated by fat transfer only [10].
Type 2 defects usually have a bony discontinuity of the zygomatic arch with a
dysplastic or absent lateral orbital wall. These types of defects require surgery to
address the hard tissue defect. These types of defects may warrant a malar osteotomy, alloplast onlay, autograft onlay techniques, or simultaneous osteotomy with an
onlay technique [10].
Types 3 and 4 are the most severe defects, and both types require bony or alloplastic augmentation [10]. Type 3 defects have a hypoplastic zygomatic body and a
dysplastic orbital wall. The zygomatic temporal process is completely absent in
these patients. Type 4 presents with a complete absence of the entire orbitozygomatic complex [10].

Timing of Reconstruction
Once a patient has been diagnosed with TCS, determining when to surgically intervene is important to the overall success of the reconstruction. By 7 years of age,
hypoplasia of the lateral wall of the orbit is associated with dislocation of the external canthus and antimongolian positioning of the eyelid fissure. This may be corrected preferably on or after the patient turns 7 years old, bearing in mind the
cranio-orbitozygomatic bony maturation is close to completion by the age of 7 [4,
6, 11]. At this age, adult-sized cheekbones may be constructed and implanted with
little concern about how growth will alter the result. Other surgeons have recommended various methods and timing for the correction of zygomatic and orbital
deformities associated with TCS [6, 12, 13].
Surgical correction before the age of 5 years old is not indicated unless severe
corneal exposure problems have occurred [6, 14]. Neonatal tarsorrhaphy can be
performed to prevent corneal scarring, ulceration, or blindness [1]. Other periorbital

corrections should be delayed. This is because the extent of the lower lid skin deficit
can be better assessed after skeletal correction.
Given the cosmetic anomalies that TCS can cause, surgeons must also think
about the psychosocial concerns of the patients when considering intervention.
Weighing the potential for scarring and revision surgery with earlier intervention
versus evaluating the mental stability of a patient must be taken seriously. This can
often be very a difficult decision when planning for surgical intervention [15].

Treatment Options
Correcting the orbitozygomatic region in a TCS patient can be achieved via an array
of surgical interventions. Minimally invasive to invasive techniques have been
described to correct or camouflage deficiencies brought about from TCS. Fat grafting and injectables have been used to augment soft tissue. Hard tissue onlays with
either autologous bone grafts or alloplastic materials have been used to augment the
underlining bony structure of the orbitozygomatic complex [4, 15].
Some authors advocate for the use of vascularized bone graft transpositions from
the cranial vault, citing more predictability of the reconstructed area, while other
employ the zygomatic osteotomy and protrusion of the orbital margins with simultaneous support of the osteotomized fragments with bone grafts or hydroxyapatite [4].
As a secondary procedure, McCarthy and Hopper [16] have proposed distraction
of the zygomatic bone with an onlay graft procedure for reconstruction of these
defects [4, 17].
Once the bony augmentation is complete, in order to achieve normal protrusion
of the cheeks, temporal region, and lower eyelids, soft-tissue grafts are sometimes
transferred under the skin [4].
Each procedure can be used alone, or in conjunction with one another in order to
reconstruct these defects and achieve the desired cosmetic outcome. Surgical intervention for these patients is still debated in the literature, and all will be discussed
in detail below.

Fat Grafting
Patients that have mild deformities associated with TCS can take advantage of fat
transfer. The technique has the benefit of being repeatable as well as the ability to be
implemented before skeletal maturity as it does not interfere with bony growth. This
is particularly advantageous in the growing child who has psychosocial concerns
[1, 18].
Fat transfer also plays a role in more severe defects but must be used in combination with hard tissue augmentation. Protocol for the reconstruction of the

368

D. P. Sinn and D. Gill

orbitozygomatic area in these complex patients must include the following steps in
this order: fat grafting, bone reconstruction, and final revisions [18].
Fat grafting, per Konofaos et al. [18], is performed two to three consecutive times
every 6 months, after the age of 6 months. Bone reconstruction, using calvarial bone
grafts, is then performed 6 months after the last fat transfer procedure. At the revision stage, fat grafting can also be used to augment the orbitozygomatic area [18].
The fat transfer procedure is completed under general anesthesia and typically
harvested from the abdomen or the flank. Fat can also be harvested from the thigh
or breast regions [19]. The aspirated fat is centrifuged for 3 minutes at 3000 rpm.
After the supernatant is removed, fat is transferred into 1 mL syringes and injected
immediately into the orbitozygomatic region [18, 20]. The adipose tissue should be
evenly distributed subcutaneously in a fan-shaped manner [19]. In the lower eyelids,
1–4 mL is placed, and in the malar area, 5–7 mL of fat is infused [18].
Fat transfer is increasing in popularity due to minimal donor site morbidity as
well as its minimally invasive nature. In regard to future orbitozygomatic reconstruction, the idea of fat transplantation, possibly with the use of stem cells, may
play an increasingly important role. This may reduce the need for larger reconstructive surgical procedures, significantly reducing associated overall morbidity [19].

Autologous Bone Grafts
The most common recommendation for zygomatic reconstruction in the TCS
patient is the traditional autologous bone graft. Autologous bone grafting is a well-­
known and reliable procedure associated with less than a 1% complication rate in
the literature [21]. Resorption is the main limitation of the bone graft, especially in
TCS patients requiring large bone volume.
Its noted that, quite often, this procedure has to be repeated due to the significant
resorption of the nonvascularized bone [5]. Because the bone graft is not subjected
to any functional load as it would be in most mandibular or maxillary osteotomies,
the grafted zygomatic region is thought to be less resistant to resorption. While the
literature shows a decreased rate of resorption when split or full-thickness calvarial
bone grafts are used in reconstruction versus the previously reported use of costochondral grafts, resorption is still a concern [1, 3]. Fan and colleagues [22] have also
found a correlation between the age of the patient at time of grafting and degree of
resorption. They note that as age increases, the likelihood of bony resorption
decreases. There seems to be a correlation with a lower rate of resorption when it is
performed after age 12 or at the end of craniofacial growth [22–25].
In an effort to combat excessive resorption, some surgeons recommend prior or
early age fat transfer before orbitozygomatic reconstruction to improve the bone
graft revascularization [18, 22].
The Posnick and colleagues technique for reconstruction utilizes full-thickness
calvarial bone grafts that have been contoured three-dimensionally to form a new
zygomatic complex [6]. These are then inset and stabilized with microplate and

18

Correction of Orbital Zygomatic Deformities in the Treacher Collins Patient

369

Fig. 18.3 Schematic of a cranial autologous harvest and inset

screw fixation (Fig. 18.3) [6, 14, 26]. Exposure for the reconstruction is provided by
a coronal (scalp) incision without periorbital incisions. Orbital floor defects are then
reconstructed, and cranial vault graft donor sites are repaired with fixed split-­
thickness autogenous cranial bone or bone substitutes (i.e., calcium phosphate
cements). Lateral canthopexies are completed through the coronal (scalp) incision
and secured to each new lateral orbital rim [6].
Preoperative and postoperative CT scanning should be obtained to evaluate the
increases in lateral orbital wall length, lateral orbital (rim) distance (width), interzygomatic arch distance (width), and zygomatic arch length for patients [6, 14].
Computer-assisted surgery (CAS) results in better skeletal volumetric analysis
that may improve the autologous graft procedure [25].
A presurgical simulation can be performed with a 3D computed tomography
(CT) scan. Using this data can allow for the surgeon to obtain optimal shape and
volume of the needed bone, cutting guides for the harvest of the bicortical calvaria
avoiding critical neurovascular structures, as well as drilling guides and the customized plates for the frontozygomatic fixation [14, 27].
CAS allows for the calvarial harvest and orbitozygomatic reconstruction to be
perfectly adapted to each patient’s morphology. This provides for the manufacture
of custom positioning and cutting guides, avoiding dangerous areas and limiting
imprecise graft/bone interface contact, palpable edges, persistent asymmetry, and
the need for repeat bone grafting [14].

Alloplastic Custom Implants
The alloplastic custom implant is an attractive option permitting anatomical reconstruction. Medpore, silicone, or polyether ether ketone (PEEK) can be used
(Fig. 18.4) [10, 28]. It is a simple surgery without autologous harvest that would
involve donor-site comorbidity [24]. In addition, an implant allows reconstruction
that conforms to the mechanical properties of the implantation site and does not
suffer from resorption. The downside is that this procedure could produce complications such as chronic inflammation, infection, displacement, or extrusion of the
implant [1, 3, 24, 28]. This could require additional surgical procedures in the
future, including removal of the implant.
The surgical procedure involves intraoperative access via an upper buccal sulcus
incision followed by subperiosteal malar tissue dissection to the periorbita. Further
dissection is performed to the lateral orbital rim, with the masseter freed from its
anomalous lateral periorbital attachment. The implant is then inserted into the dissected pocket. The position of the implant is then verified clinically and secured
with plates and screws. During placement, one must continually assess pupillary
diameter and globe hardness [29]. The surgeon should be aware that there is an

372

D. P. Sinn and D. Gill

increased risk of globe compression with implant placement with orbitozygomatic
defects. This is especially true in cases where there is a complete absence of the
zygoma, and the periorbital soft-tissue boundaries are unaccounted for during the
procedure [28].

Zygomatic Osteotomy
The malar osteotomy is another surgical intervention that has been utilized to reconstruct the orbitozygomatic region. It is a simple technique with low patient morbidity and very effective at treating midfacial width. The technique has some limitations
in its ability to increase anterior projection of the zygoma [31]. In addition, the
vertical height of the zygoma is usually reduced in TCS because of a decrease of
bone stock. For those reasons, most surgeons prefer to perform the zygomatic osteotomy in combination with an onlay technique for reconstruction of the orbitozygomatic complex in the TCS patient [10].
The Mommaerts zygomatic osteotomy is a favorite given it does not change
orbital volume or widen the orbit [10, 30]. It involves accessing the zygoma by either
a LeFort I-type osteotomy approach or by way of a horizontal incision of 1.5 cm
length in the upper buccal sulcus [30]. The medial anterior surface of the zygoma is
dissected subperiosteally up to the infraorbital rim. The dissection stops cephalad to
the semi-horizontal groove palpable below the orbital rim. Laterally, the periosteum
is tunneled up to the junction between the frontal and temporal processes. The posterior aspect of the zygomatic crest is also degloved for approximately 2 cm. A vertical osteotomy, through both the anterior and posterior walls of the maxillary sinus.
The osteotomy cut stops about 4 mm below the infraorbital rim. An oblique horizontal bone cut is made under raspatory protection, proceeding antero-medially from the
junction of the zygomatic arch and body, transecting the sinus walls beneath the
orbital floor, and joining the vertical osteotomy at its superior end. The bone cuts are
completed with small chisels. A greenstick fracture occurs at the temporo-zygomatic
suture. A hydroxyapatite (HA) block or bone grafting material is then carved to a
trapezoid of desired width and wedged into the vertical osteotomy space. As a result
of this outward rotation, more anterior fullness is created [30, 31].

Vascularized Flaps
To many surgeons, the microvascular soft-tissue approach is effectively considered
a salvage effort for persistent suboptimal outcomes instead of a primary reconstructive procedure, but vascularized flaps can provide a long-lasting or even permanent
outcome as a primary procedure. Pedicled flaps may be of a little use in facial contouring due to pedicle length and restriction in flap size, but vascularized free flaps,

18

Correction of Orbital Zygomatic Deformities in the Treacher Collins Patient

373

depending on their donor sites, can provide an appropriate bulk that the patient
desires without the restriction of the pedicle.
Parascapular Flaps
The parascapular flap is a thin, fasciocutaneous flap with the vascular supply based
on the circumflex scapular vessels [32]. The versatility of the parascapular flap
allows for detailed contouring of the tissue to address the specific deficiencies in
each patient [2]. Good esthetic results can be achieved with minimal complications
and minor revisions.
Saadeh and colleagues state that a two-team approach is best but not required
to complete the procedure. Procedure begins with simultaneous ipsilateral parascapular flap harvest and facial pocket dissection [2, 33, 34]. A preauricular facelift incision is used for access, allowing for both adequate exposure and a discreet
scar, regardless of the soft-tissue requirements. Facial dissection is then carried
out in the subcutaneous facelift plane, continuing 1 cm beyond preoperative
markings [2].
Once the parascapular flap is harvested, the microvascular anastomoses are completed [2]. Absorbable buried sutures were used to secure the flap to the periosteum
near the anastomoses. Absorbable sutures are then used to suspend the flap from the
infraorbital rim, lateral orbital rim, and zygoma. The flap should then be secured
with tie-over bolster sutures of preplaced 4–0 nylon. The final flap contour and in-­
setting should be confirmed with the patient being upright [2].
Groin Flaps
The use of groin flaps has also been described in the orbital reconstruction of TCS
patients. They are advantageous because they require less preoperative planning and
have a relatively short operation time [29]. Other hallmarks of the procedure include
acceptable donor site morbidity, ability to conceal scars, and primary closure of the
donor site, and functional impairment is less likely except for limitation of ambulation during immediate postoperative periods [29, 35, 36].
Heo and colleagues [29] describe the procedure as the following: On each side of
the groin, a flap with approximately 13 × 6 cm-sized skin paddle is designed. Flaps
are elevated with superficial circumflex iliac artery and vein. Bilateral preauricular
incisions were made, and dissection was done above the superficial musculo-­
aponeurotic system (SMAS) plane. Recipient vascular pedicles used were the
superficial temporal artery and vein. De-epithelialization of both flaps is then completed. Donor vascular pedicles are then disconnected on each flap. Microanastomosis
is then completed, one flap at a time. This is completed in an end-to-end fashion.
Lastly, the de-epithelialized flaps are slid into each defect zone, and the wound is
closed in a layered fashion. Negative-pressure closed-suction drain in each side
should be placed and sutured before complete closure [29].

374

D. P. Sinn and D. Gill

Distraction Osteogenesis
Distraction osteogenesis is typically used in secondary cases where there is suboptimal malar projection of a previously reconstructed zygomatic complex. When
compared with serial bone grafting, distraction osteogenesis has the benefits of
slowly stretching the associated soft-tissue envelope and avoiding the need for
repeat bone graft harvest [16].
The disadvantages of this technique are that the vector of distraction may be
compromised by the placement of the previous bone grafts. This may lead to a nonunion of the zygomatic arch. Additionally, all steps are taken to maintain the periosteal blood supply to the distracted segment, but there is also the risk of
devascularization of the bone-grafted segment during the procedure [16].

Tissue Engineering
Tissue engineering of the zygomatic maxillary complex segment may be an additional option to reconstruct the craniofacial skeleton [1, 4, 37, 38]. This could be a
critical breakthrough for TCS patients with severe defects of the orbitozygomatic
region. Lengthy operations, multiple revision surgeries, and additional donor site
morbidity could all be potentially eliminated with advancements in tissue engineering. The ability to provide an exact replica of a missing bone, with normal growth
potential, and be resistant to infection is an exciting possibility for TCS patients [38].

Orbital Soft-Tissue Reconstruction
There are several surgical techniques dedicated to the improvement of the soft-­
tissue deficiencies associated with the eyelid and adnexal regions. Most surgeons
prefer staging the surgical correction of the coloboma after zygoma and orbital
reconstruction. This is to better assess the extent of lid skin deficit after the skeletal
correction [1, 3, 6, 7].
The surgical technique and timing of intervention depend upon the size of the
defect and the presence of corneal exposure. Defects are graded as small (less than
25% of the length of lid margin), moderate (25 to 50% defect), and severe (more
than 50%) [39].
Depending on the deformity, orbicularis transposition, skin grafting, Z-plasty,
and/or canthopexy can be performed [1, 3, 40] (Fig. 18.5). Not all of these procedures have produced the most esthetically pleasing soft-tissue eyelid results [4, 17].
The transposition of pedicled upper eyelid skin muscle flaps to deficient regions of
the lower eyelid typically causes adnexal scarring [3, 6]. The scarring can then be
severe and may detract from any positive advantages of the procedure [6, 39].

18

Correction of Orbital Zygomatic Deformities in the Treacher Collins Patient

375

Fig. 18.5 Coloboma correction surgery. Upper eyelid rotational flap followed by results of the flap
rotation with lateral canthopexy

Mustarde’s cheek rotation flap is particularly useful for reconstruction involving
larger, vertical defects of the lower lid. Lower eyelid defects involving the entire
lower eyelid may be reconstructed using a Mustarde’s cheek rotation flap. A large
skin muscle flap is rotated from the cheek to repair large lower eyelid defects while
the posterior lamella can undergo reconstruction with tarsoconjunctival, nasal cartilage, or mucous membrane grafts [39].
Full-thickness skin grafts to reconstruct the lower eyelids are another frequently
mentioned procedure. This procedure can leave a “patchy” look and should be
reserved only for patients with unresolved corneal exposure [6].
With meticulous planning and execution, the transfer of soft-tissue flaps (groin
flap) from other body regions, with microvascular reanastomosis, offers an alternative for augmentation of the adnexal, temporal, and cheek soft tissues [33, 34, 41].

Conclusion
Treacher Collins syndrome is a congenital disorder known for significant deficiencies in the midfacial region. Surgical reconstruction is planned based on the morphology and severity of the defects. There are many surgical options available to
TCS patients for the correction of midfacial and orbital anomalies. Surgical intervention should not occur before the age of 7; however, psychosocial concerns may
warrant earlier intervention. Although there is no gold standard for the reconstruction of these patients, all surgical techniques may provide adequate reestablishment
of midfacial and orbital contours. To determine which surgical intervention is best,
precise anatomical evaluation, timing of surgery, psychological state, and potential
for future surgeries must be adequately assessed.

Background
Maxillomandibular differences in patients with Treacher Collins syndrome remain
challenging for patients and surgeons alike. While mandibular deficiency is a hallmark of the condition (“mandibulofacial dysostosis”), there is a spectrum of presenting phenotypes that are managed by a similarly broad range of interventions,
from minimal medical management of mildly hypoplastic skeletal structures to
complex, staged interventions for management of severe dysplasias. The
phenotypic hallmark of severe maxillomandibular discrepancy is characterized by

clockwise rotation of a hypoplastic maxillomandibular complex, with concomitant
orbitozygomatic hypoplasia (Figs. 19.1a-d) [1–11]. This rotational deformity presents as a long anterior face height, short posterior face height, prominent nasal dorsum, anterior open bite, and a retruded mandible with steep mandibular plane angle
with associated microgenia. Hypoplasia (or aplasia) of the zygomatic bones, often
with associated soft tissue clefting, contributes to mandibular dysmorphology due
to a developmentally deficient glenoid fossa. The primary skeletal differences are
frequently accompanied by hypoplasia of the associated lateral facial soft tissues,
including the muscles of mastication and facial expression. Dental anomalies are
not infrequent within the population of patients with TCS [11].
The anatomic differences associated with maxillomandibular skeletal dysmorphology are frequently translated to pathologic airway obstruction [12–15]. Airway
obstruction in patients with TCS is a complex phenomenon but is primarily related

381

to occlusion of the oropharyngeal airway by a hypoplastic skeletal framework,
although abnormalities of the entire upper airway can exist [14–15]. Management
in infancy is predicated on establishing appropriate upper airway physiology, feeding, hearing, preservation of vision through corneal protection, and management of
facial/palatal clefts (if present). The complexity of management of these various
components necessitates multidisciplinary care to establish a treatment plan and
continually follow progress over time, as surgical interventions can be numerous
and extend over the course of many years [2].
Maxillomandibular disharmony plays a critical role in the pathophysiology of
TCS. Unlike other congenital craniofacial differences, however, TCS is not generally progressive [11]. The magnitude of the skeletal discrepancy at birth is relatively
stable over time. This feature distinguishes TCS from other congenital and developmental conditions involving the maxillomandibular complex, such as craniofacial
microsomia, Goldenhar syndrome, and oculo-auriculo-vertebral syndrome. Airway
challenges are multifactorial and may include nasal obstruction related to choanal
atresia/stenosis, glossoptosis related to micrognathia, and lower airway anomalies
such as tracheomalacia. Infants with mild degrees of facial dysplasia may only
require noninvasive maneuvers such as special positioning and monitoring of oxygen saturation. In patients with severe presenting phenotypes, airway embarrassment is not infrequent, and tracheostomy placement at birth or infancy is
well-described. Interventions in the growing child vary from center to center but
share the common goal of establishing an advanced jaw position to facilitate airway
expansion.
One critical component of management of the skeletal difference in TCS is recognition of the condition as non-progressive. Roberts and colleagues, in 1975, characterized the morphologic features of TCS using lateral cephalometry [10]. They
reported small sella-nasion-B point angles (consistent with marked retrognathia)
but relatively normal sella-nasion-A point angles (suggestive of relatively normal
maxillary angular position). Facial heights were correspondingly suggestive of a
lower facial deficiency with upper facial heights notably normal and total facial
heights longer than normal. Sella-nasion to mandibular plane and sella-nasion to
palatal plane angles were obtuse, consistent with clockwise rotation of the maxillomandibular complex. These cephalometric parameters were clinically evident as
a convex facial profile defined by decreased horizontal length and increased anterior
vertical length with associated mandibular deficiency characterized by a truncated
ramus height and shortened body length. Remarkably, this constellation of facial
differences was age-independent; the characteristic deficiency was relatively
unchanged from infancy through skeletal maturity. These preliminary observations
were confirmed by a number of other investigators, who documented stability of the
mandibular position over time, suggestive of constant growth without “catch-up”
potential [7–9, 11]
The clinical observations regarding the lack of accelerated growth normalizing
mandibular morphology led many surgeons to consider early mandibular advancement, most recently through the use of distraction osteogenesis. While there is some
evidence that early distraction osteogenesis improves airway dynamics to the extent

382

S. M. Susarla et al.

that decannulation is possible in tracheostomy-dependent children, early distraction
has also been reported to have potentially detrimental effects on jaw growth, may be
prone to relapse, and damage the temporomandibular joints. In this context, some
surgeons advocate delaying skeletal reconstruction until maturity, if feasible
[3–5, 11].
The magnitude of the mandibular deficiency in TCS has been well-described.
The Pruzansky classification of the mandibular deformity in craniofacial microsomia, subsequently modified by Kaban, has been applied to the mandibular difference in TCS [16–17]. Under this paradigm, the severity of the mandibular dysostosis
is related to two components: the glenoid fossa and the ramus-condyle unit. In the
most mild cases (Type I, Fig. 19.1d), the degree of hypoplasia is minimal – all of
the skeletal components are present but may be hypoplastic. These patients may
have normal TMJ function. Moderate cases (Type II) have more significant hypoplasia of the individual components and are subdivided according to the stability of
the TMJs. In Type IIA differences, the condylar apparatus (glenoid fossa + condylar head) may be dysplastic but has stable joint function. In contrast, Type IIB cases
have severe condylar hypoplasia, resulting in unstable TMJ function without a reliable centric relation; this pattern of dysmorphology is relatively infrequent in
TCS. The most severe mandibular deficiency (Type III, Fig. 19.1b) results in a
ramus-condyle unit and glenoid morphology that is hypoplastic to the extent that
no articulation between the mandible and skull base is possible. The adjunctive tissues of the temporomandibular joints – the articular disc, capsule, and glenoid
fossa – are not present. The ramus-condyle unit is vertically short, and the sagittal
position of the mandible is significantly retruded, with associated clockwise rotation. This degree of dysmorphology is frequently associated with complex airway
challenges, frequently necessitating tracheostomy placement at birth or in early
infancy.

Paradigms for Skeletal Reconstruction
Timing of skeletal reconstruction of the maxillomandibular deficiency in TCS is
largely predicated on the degree of dysmorphology. In patients with mild deficiency, surgical intervention may not be required or may be limited to orthognathic
interventions at skeletal maturity. Patients with severe deficiency may benefit from
early interventions but frequently require multiple operations to achieve appropriate skeletal positioning. Surgical intervention in growing children is largely predicated on management of severe facial dysplasia and the associated airway
compromise.
In this regard, the goals of craniofacial reconstruction in the growing child with
TCS are threefold: improve airway physiology by expansion of the skeletal scaffold
for the oropharynx and hypopharynx, establish appropriate maxillomandibular relationships and occlusion, and create balanced facial aesthetics. Bimaxillary orthognathic surgery in skeletally mature children with stable temporomandibular joints

19

Management of the Mandibular Deformity in Growing Patients with Treacher…

383

undergoing smaller rotational movements has been effective in some reports but
may not be applicable to many patients with TCS. In contrast, isolated mandibular
surgery in growing children with severe deformities, via distraction osteogenesis or
skeletal reconstruction with autologous bone grafting and rigid fixation, had initially showed promise, but recent data have demonstrated significant relapse rates as
well as incomplete or inadequate resolution of airway obstruction, necessitating
multiple interventions with limited potential for success [18–24]. These specific
challenges are heightened in the context of data demonstrating a paucity of improvement in the frequency and severity of airway obstruction in TCS with growth, consistent with the non-progressive nature of the deformity and lack of identifiable
catch-up growth.
Contextually, early treatment for the tracheostomy-dependent child remains
challenging. Interventions should construct appropriate skeletal morphology and
improve airway dynamics, while also establishing an appropriate facial balance.
Isolated mandibular interventions (e.g., distraction lengthening, genioglossus
advancement) have limited utility in this regard, as they do not effectively address
the clockwise rotation deformity that is uniformly present in patients with severe
disease. Counterclockwise rotational movements of the maxillomandibular complex remain controversial in orthognathic surgery, precisely because of concerns
regarding stability over time [25–30]. Prevailing explanations for the instability are
related to the muscle pull from the suprahyoid system, as well as proximal segment
changes. Confounding the picture is the available evidence suggesting that stability
of the rotational movement is predicated on TMJ stability, which many patients with
TCS lack a priori [27–29].
Analysis of airway volumes in patients with TCS has clearly demonstrated that the
degree of clockwise maxillomandibular rotation and associated hypoplasia contribute
to obstruction [14–15]. As such, counterclockwise movements are needed to counteract this primary deficiency. The apex example of conventional surgery for counterclockwise rotation was Tessier and Tulasne’s “procedure integral,” which incorporated
a LeFort II osteotomy with mandibular advancement for composite subcranial rotation [31]. While a valid theoretical approach, this technique failed to gain widespread
acceptance, due to high rates of relapse of the maxillary and mandibular plane rotations, the need for extensive bone grafting, and high degree of soft tissue resistance
from the deficient lateral facial soft tissues and suprahyoid musculature.

 anagement of Severe Clockwise Rotation
M
in the Growing Child
A more recent modification of this technique has sought to overcome these specific
challenges, utilizing distraction osteogenesis to perform subcranial advancement
with associated counterclockwise rotation [32]. Counterclockwise craniofacial distraction osteogenesis (C3DO) is an emerging technique that holds promise for management of tracheostomy dependent children with TCS (Fig. 19.2). The C3DO

procedure involves concomitant maxillomandibular rotation via distraction, utilizing a LeFort II osteotomy with bilateral inverted-L mandibular osteotomies.
Following completion of the osteotomies, the maxillomandibular complex is rotated
in a counterclockwise direction, affording expansion of the oropharynx and hypopharynx, establishing appropriate palatal and mandibular planes, and creating balanced facial proportions.
Preliminary results from this technique have demonstrated successful decannulation in the majority of patients undergoing this procedure, including those with prior
failed mandibular distraction. The success attributed to this intervention is believed
to be related to the large degree of movement possible with coordinated maxillomandibular distraction. Among the preliminary cohort undergoing this procedure,

In this regard, our treatment protocol for the growing child with TCS characterized by severe Pruzansky-Kaban type III maxillomandibular deficiency (Figs. 19.3a-­
f) and tracheostomy-dependent airway is as follows [32–33]. In the first stage,
appropriate ramus-condyle morphology is established, using autologous rib grafts.
Once adequate healing has occurred and stable joint anatomy is established, as evidenced by a reproducible range of mandibular movement and a stable occlusion,
counterclockwise craniofacial distraction osteogenesis is performed. After the
appropriate maxillomandibular position is established, as evidenced by correction
of the palatal and mandibular plane discrepancies, improvement of the anterior and
posterior facial height ratios, improved occlusion, and, most importantly, optimized
upper airway anatomy, orbitozygomatic reconstruction with calvarial autograft is
completed. While effective for management of severe airway obstruction, the end-­
distraction morphology is prone to 20–30% skeletal relapse, manifested as recurrent
anterior open bite (Figs. 19.3e-f). This relapse does not appear to affect airway
dynamics but will likely necessitate definitive orthognathic surgery at skeletal maturity for management of the end-stage facial and occlusal dysmorphology [32].

 anagement of Mild to Moderate Dysplasia in the Growing
M
and Skeletally Mature Child
In patients with mild to moderate dysmorphology (e.g., minimal clockwise rotation)
who do not have severe airway disease, reconstruction of mandibular rami and the
orbitozygomatic complex can be completed in the mixed dentition (Figs. 19.4a-b).
Definitive correction at skeletal maturity can be reliably accomplished with conventional orthognathic surgery in the form of mandibular ramus osteotomies with autologous bone grafting, midface advancement at the LeFort I level, and advancement
genioplasty (Figs. 19.4c-f and 19.5a-h).

Conclusion
Management of the growing child with Treacher Collins syndrome remains challenging. The characteristic facial deficiency is related to clockwise rotation of the
maxillomandibular complex, with variable degrees of severity based upon the mandibular ramus-condyle unit morphology. The non-progressive nature of the deformity necessitates careful planning for reconstruction, starting in infancy. Successful
treatment is predicated upon establishing a physiologic upper airway, improving
facial proportions and occlusion, and balancing facial aesthetics. In growing children with mild to moderate mandibular dysplasia, orbitozygomatic reconstruction
and ramus-condyle unit reconstruction in the mixed dentition may be considered,
followed by bimaxillary orthognathic surgery at skeletal maturity. For patients with
severe, tracheostomy-dependent disease related to excessive clockwise facial rotation, subcranial counterclockwise rotation via synchronous maxillomandibular distraction has emerged as a promising technique.

TMJ Total Joint Prosthesis in Treacher

Adam Wandell, Daniel Perez, and Aaron Liddell

Introduction
Total joint replacement utilizing endoprostheses has become the standard of care for
diseased diarthrodial joints, providing predictable outcomes with long-term function
and stability. In the 1890s, the German surgeon Thermistocles Gluck championed
total joint replacement utilizing ivory as a replacement for osseous bone substrate.
Through the mid-1900s, Sir John Charnley led the development, implementation,
and refinement of operative techniques of total hip arthroplasty. These modifications
were spurred by advancements in aseptic technique and material science [1].
Improvement in material biocompatibility and decreased surgical time produced predictable outcomes, improving function and patient satisfaction while, at the same
time, reducing the occurrence and severity of complications [2]. Many of the advancements in orthopedic total joint replacement have carried over into craniomaxillofacial
(CMF) surgery. Both Dr. Louis G. Mercuri and Dr. Larry Wolford have contributed a
tremendous amount of research and clinical work in total joint replacement surgery.
Although not without growing pains (including catastrophic failures in material biocompatibility), contemporary alloplastic total joint replacement of the TMJ has borne
out to be safe and predictable and provides long-term stability that is difficult to
reproduce with autograft or conventional osteotomies. Advancements in CT imaging
and the implementation of virtual surgical planning platforms have enhanced the
predictability of the most complex cases. These advances make it possible to replace
temporomandibular joints (TMJ) in patients who suffer from a myriad of craniofacial
deformities, including congenital, developmental, and post-traumatic. The aim of

this chapter is to describe a combined or staged approach utilizing orthognathic surgery and TMJ TJR in patients with TCS and CFM.

Background
Treacher Collins syndrome (TCS) is a condition that, with variable expressivity,
results in a variety of growth aberrancies of the craniofacial skeleton. Notably,
patients with TCS have symmetrical abnormalities within the first and second branchial arches. In addition to a myriad of soft tissue abnormalities, facial skeletal
growth abnormalities often affect the cranio-orbital-zygomatic complex (including
hypoplastic growth with/without clefting) and can be as proximal as the glenoid
fossa of the temporal bone (Fig. 20.1a, b). Often, hypoplastic growth tendencies of
the maxilla and mandible result in “clockwise” rotation of the maxillomandibular
complex [3]. These changes are frequently exaggerated by dysmorphologic or
aplastic growth patterns of the mandibular condyles, resulting in apertognathia and
significant deprojection of the skeletal chin point [4]. The aforementioned findings
result in significant masticatory impairment, cosmetic deformities, malocclusion,
and in some cases severe breathing disorders.

a

b

Fig. 20.1 (a) 16-year-old patient with TCS. (b) 17-year-old patient with HFM

20

TMJ Total Joint Prosthesis in Treacher Collins Syndrome and Hemifacial…

395

Craniofacial microsomia (CFM) is part of the oculoauriculovertebral spectrum
(OAVS) and like TCS involves growth disruption of the first and second branchial
arches. Like patients with TCS, growth and developmental abnormalities can involve
the craniozygomatic region in addition to the maxillomandibular complex and auricular soft tissues. In this population, there is significant variability in phenotypic
expressivity. Consequently, cases can be very minor, with minimal facial asymmetry,
or severe, involving complex clefting patterns of the lateral facial skeleton. Because
of the typically unilateral expression, significant facial asymmetries are frequently
noted, which progress until facial skeletal maturity is attained [4]. A full description
of the multitude of classification systems and associated deformities in CFM are
beyond the scope of this chapter; suffice it to say most involve varying degrees of
hypoplasia of the ramus-condyle unit and glenoid fossa. This atypical formation of
the ramus-condyle and glenoid fossa results in significant unilateral hypoplasia and
in marked asymmetrical growth tendencies into both the maxilla and mandible.
In both TCS and HFM, the reconstruction of the ramus-condyle unit and the correction of the significant facial asymmetry and malocclusion present the biggest
challenge. It is difficult to be predictable and consistent with your surgical results,
and the timing of reconstruction is a subject of controversy among clinicians [5, 6].

Reconstruction Considerations
A variety of surgical approaches have historically been used to reconstruct the craniofacial abnormalities associated with TCS and CFM. Additionally, the timing and
techniques for addressing these patients continue to evolve. Improvements in rigid
internal fixation techniques and material science evolution have, in many instances,
changed classical paradigms. Surgical treatments should be tailored to the severity
of the skeletal deformity. There is no doubt that conventional mandibular orthognathic surgery osteotomies (inverted L and sagittal split ramus osteotomies) can frequently be employed to achieve functional, stable, and esthetic outcomes when
defects are mild. However, with increased mandibular/skull base dysmorphology, or
when the demands of mandibular movement exceed the parameters of stability that
conventional osteotomies afford, practitioners have historically been left with distraction osteogenesis, microvascular surgery, or autografts. Although excellent outcomes can and have been achieved with each of these modalities, the interventions
are exceedingly technique sensitive and often require multiple procedures to address
relapse or persistent asymmetry.
As three-dimensional imaging capabilities have improved and virtual planning
software has evolved, the ability to manage the maxillomandibular growth aberrancies in TCS and HFM patients has been dramatically enhanced. Specifically, the
ability to utilize patient-fitted customized TMJ prostheses enables surgeons to
reconstruct an aplastic or dysmorphological glenoid fossae as well as malformed or
hypoplastic abnormalities associated with the ramus-condyle unit of the mandible
(Fig. 20.2) [7–12]. Virtual surgical planning, in this context, enables these

396

A. Wandell et al.

Fig. 20.2 Example of virtual surgical planning of a patient with HFM who will receive a right
TJR, left BSSO, and LeFort 1

procedures to be completed in a single stage procedure with stable and predictable
long-­term outcomes, minimizing the morbidity associated with staged surgical
treatment modalities.
In the most complex cases, especially when function is severely limited, consideration should be given to a staged approach, usually reconstructing the articulation
first, followed immediately by aggressive physical therapy. Malocclusions can be
addressed with conventional orthognathic surgery osteotomies after improved function has been achieved.

Timing of the Surgery
When utilizing total joint replacement combined with orthognathic surgery techniques, interventions should be completed at the cessation of anticipated skeletofacial growth. This is not always possible, particularly when the quality of life for the
patient supersedes conventional reconstruction paradigms. In some severe cases,
TMJ TJR may be performed in very young patients with the understanding that a
revision or replacement is likely to be required in the future [13]. In TCS and CFM,
the degree of malformation present at birth is presumed to be relatively stable and
not progressive, outside of changes that are noted secondary to hypoplastic growth
tendencies. Based on these observations, early intervention (outside of intervention
based on airway concerns), including conventional osteotomies and distraction

20

TMJ Total Joint Prosthesis in Treacher Collins Syndrome and Hemifacial…

397

osteogenesis, will frequently require secondary revision. Accordingly, whenever
possible, definitive interventions should be completed when facial growth is presumed to be complete [5, 14, 15]. In females, this entails waiting on surgical intervention until the age of 15–16 years, whereas in males, definitive surgical
interventions would be held until 17–18 years (Fig. 20.1) [4, 5, 15].

Orthodontic Considerations and Virtual Surgical Planning
Early orthodontic intervention (so-called “phase 1” therapy) in patients with CFM
and TCS should be avoided whenever it is feasible, outside of correcting transverse
deficiencies in the maxilla. Transverse issues can be corrected prior to skeletal maturation using conventional expansion mechanics. Subsequently, traditional decompensation techniques should be started as patients are nearing skeletal maturity and
are completed in the standard fashion of presurgical orthodontics, with aims of leveling, aligning, and uprighting the teeth over the basal skeletal bone. When orthodontic
decompensation has been completed, virtual surgical planning can be initiated.
Over the last decade, virtual surgical planning has widely replaced conventional
model surgery and can be used to plan both standard orthognathic surgery and
orthognathic surgery combined with TMJ replacement [8, 16, 17]. Virtual 3D model
renderings are used to design the TMJ prostheses in addition to intermediate and
final positioning splints.
Virtual surgical planning begins with a non-contrast CT scan of the patient’s
craniofacial skeleton, utilizing 1 mm or smaller cuts and zero gantry tilt. The
DICOM files from the CT scan along with dental models (or intraoral scans of the
patient’s dentition) are rendered using software tools that allow the surgeon to visualize the impact of adjustments to the patient’s vertical and anterior/posterior maxillomandibular positions. The software makes it possible to simulate translational
adjustments of yaw, pitch, and cant in order to achieve optimal skeletal positioning.
As in conventional model surgery, decisions regarding the surgical movements of
the maxilla and mandible should be made based on clinical evaluation, dental models (or scans), and patient goals. Soft tissue surgeries should be delayed after the
final bony reconstruction has healed, allowing for a more predictable cosmetic result.
After the desired positions of the maxilla and mandible have been optimized
utilizing computer simulation software, a digital file is created that enables fabrication of a stereolithographic model that is used to fabricate the custom TMJ prostheses (Fig. 20.3). Once the joint(s) have been designed, the data is then used to
facilitate production of intermediate and final splints, based on the newly designed
rotation point of the neo-condyle and fossa. It is important to keep the occlusion in
a holding pattern with no changes in the bite once the fabrication of the device has
been initiated. Two to three weeks prior to the planned surgery, a new set of models
or scanned occlusion should be uploaded and compared with the original plan to
assure that the splints will fit. It is at this time that the splints should be printed.

A. Wandell et al.

model with joint prosthesis

Surgical Protocol
This section describes the steps used in our surgical protocol.

Preparation
The surgery for completing TMJ TJR with concomitant orthognathic surgery begins
with standard naso-endotracheal intubation, using a nasal RAE tube. In many
instances, patients with CFM and TCS have reduced mandibular range of motion
and, consequently, require nasal fiberoptic intubation. Airway management, in these
cases, can be difficult; therefore, careful selection of an anesthesia provider that is
comfortable/competent in nasal fiberoptic technique is critical. On occasion, where
airway anatomy is significantly abnormal or where multiple attempts at nasal intubation have been made without success, a standard tracheostomy can be used to
safely procure a stable airway. Following nasal intubation, the endotracheal tube is
sutured to the nasal septum above the columella with a 2-0 or 3-0 silk suture. The
patient’s head is placed in a supine position, with the neck in a neutral to slightly
flexed position (Fig. 20.4a). The patient’s head is wrapped using a standard surgical
towel, and the endotracheal tube is secured to the head wrap with standard 2″ silk
tape. It is important to assure that there are no pressure spots where the tube is
secured. Local anesthetic is then infiltrated into the preauricular region and via
auriculotemporal nerve block. Subsequently, the face, neck, mouth, ears, and nose
are scrubbed with a betadine solution, and the face is isolated and draped with sterile towels (Fig. 20.4b). To assure that the ear canals have been adequately prepared,
a cotton-tip applicator is used to clean the external auditory area with betadine solution. A cotton ear plug is then fashioned and soaked in mineral oil or betadine solution and gently packed into the external auditory canal. The mouth and nose are

20

TMJ Total Joint Prosthesis in Treacher Collins Syndrome and Hemifacial…

399

covered using an Ioban wrap to prohibit contamination of the TMJ surgical field
with oral/nasal microbial flora.

Surgical Approaches for the TMJ Prosthesis
Multiple approaches to the temporomandibular joint have been described, a full
elaboration of which is beyond the scope of this paper [18–20]. Our standard
approach utilizes an endaural incision, which we have found enables rapid, predictable access to the TMJ capsule minimizing the risk of damaging cranial nerve VII,
the superficial temporal artery, and the cartilaginous external auditory canal
(Fig. 20.5a). That being said, one of the challenges in TCS and HFM patients is that
frequently the external auricular anatomy is either abnormal or missing entirely.
Therefore, standard anatomic landmarks that are conventionally used in the dissection are frequently not present, which may include osseous structures such as the
zygomatic process of the temporal bone and the lateral glenoid fossa. Accordingly,
intraoperative nerve monitoring may be required during the surgical approach to

assisted intraoperative navigation can be considered to assure that site preparation
for the glenoid fossa component occurs in the appropriate position along the caudal
aspect of the temporal bone [21, 22] (Fig. 20.5b).
We utilize a submandibular incision in order to introduce and fixate the ramus
component (Fig. 20.6). This incision provides access to the inferior-lateral area
of the ramus. The submandibular incision is placed 2 cm inferior to the lower
border of the mandible and is generally 2 cm in length. Dissection is carried to
the level of the platysma. The platysma is then sharply divided, monitoring the
nerve activity of the marginal mandibular nerve. In the subplatysmal plane, dissection is carried superiorly on the superficial layer of the deep cervical fascia to
the inferior border of the mandible. Frequently, the facial artery and vein can be
left intact; however, if needed, these vessels can be ligated and separated. At the
mandible, the pterygomasseteric sling is divided along the inferior border of the
mandible, and dissection is carried in a subperiosteal plane to connect to the
superior dissection cavity. Any contouring of the lateral ramus can then be completed, as per the virtual surgical plan to facilitate passive adaptation of the ramus
component.

Site Preparation for Prosthesis Insertion
In cases when the mandibular condyle is present, a condylectomy is performed
according to the virtual surgical plan. Cutting guides, which can be fabricated during the surgical planning, can be used to assure that the condyle resection mimics
the virtual plan. Once the condylectomy has been completed, the joint space is
prepared to facilitate placement of the prosthesis. Because of the vertical elongation
of the ramus that frequently occurs with prosthesis placement in the TCS and CFM
population, adequate space is usually procured for placement of the fossa and ramus

components of the prosthesis. If vertical lengthening of the ramus is not significant,
a minimum 20 mm space is needed for passive fit of the prosthetic components,
measuring from the superior aspect of the cut ramus to the base of skull (Fig. 20.7).
During site preparation at the skull base, careful attention should be given to the
superior aspect of the parotid gland during this phase of site preparation. This gland
is a reproducible landmark that suggests proximity to the superior branches of the
facial nerve [23].
Through the endaural access, a coronoidectomy can be also performed. We have
found that by using a piezoelectric saw, the risk of damaging underlying vasculature
during the coronoidectomy is minimized. The aims of coronoidectomy are to detach
the temporalis muscle which facilitates a larger and more passive advancement of the
mandible. Bone from the condylectomy and coronoidectomy may be saved and used
to graft bone defects that may be present following fixation of the maxillary osteotomy.
At this point, it should be noted that many TCS and CFM patients require significant counterclockwise rotation of the maxillomandibular complex. When this is the
case, significant effort may be required to fully mobilize the mandible to attain passive
fit of the intermediate splint. Aggressive intraoperative “stretching” of the mandible
can be quite cumbersome and requires patience and persistence. Frequently, the vertical elongation of the mandibular ramus can result in a significant increase in the distance from the foramen ovale to the lingula. Patients must be informed that paresthesia
to the inferior alveolar nerve is a significant risk during this procedure due to the nature
of the counterclockwise rotation necessary to optimize function and esthetics [24].

Mobilization of the Uninvolved Side Where Indicated
In TCS patients, the above noted protocol is followed for both sides, in anticipation
of bilateral TJR. However, in patients with CFM, frequently the uninvolved side has
developed normally and is amenable to conventional sagittal ramus osteotomy to
enable occlusal plane leveling and counterclockwise rotation of the maxillomandibular complex. This osteotomy, when indicated, can be completed using a

402

a

A. Wandell et al.

b

Fig. 20.8 (a) Fixated sagittal split osteotomy (b) Patient in IMF in intermediate splint

transmucosal intraoral incision, as described by Obwegeser, with modifications as
described by DalPont and Hunsuck [25–27] (Fig. 20.8a). It is important that instruments used for the intraoral aspect of the procedure be placed on a separate table
and not be mixed with or contaminate instruments that were used to access the
TMJ. Prior to entering the oral cavity, the TMJ access site(s) are covered with a
large Tegaderm, and the face is draped with new surgical towels, such that only the
oral cavity is exposed. The Ioban which was placed over the mouth and nose at the
beginning of the procedure is divided in order to gain access to the oral cavity.
Subsequently, a unilateral sagittal split osteotomy is performed, the proximal and
distal segments are separated, and then the patient is placed into intermaxillary fixation utilizing the intermediate splint (Fig. 20.8b). Once the mandible has been passively rotated into the intermediate splint, the mandible is wired to the maxilla and
the proximal segment is seated into centric relation. The segments are fixated, as per
the surgeons’ preference. Following fixation of the mandible, the surgeons re-scrub
and change gowns and gloves, and the mouth and nasal complex are sealed off with
Ioban, such that sterility can be maintained for placement of the TMJ prosthesis.

Placing and Fixating the Prostheses
Once the oral and nasal cavities have been covered, the surgeon places the fossa
component of the prosthesis into the patient’s glenoid fossa, when present, or onto
the base of the temporal bone when there is significant glenoid dysmorphology. The
component is fixated with four screws whose length is predetermined according to
the virtual surgical plan. The condylar component is then placed through the submandibular incision (Fig. 20.9). Careful attention must be paid to assure that the
prosthetic condylar head is in the most posterior-superior aspect of the fossa prosthesis. The mandibular component is then secured to the lateral ramus using eight
screws of predetermined length. We have found that placement of the first screw
with a posterior-superior offset relative to the screw hole facilitates positioning the
joint into centric relation.
