Preventing Heterotopic Bone Formation
One of the concerns in orthopedic reconstruction relates to the development of heterotopic bone at the site of surgery. This phenomenon has been reported in the
context of TMJ TJR and can be difficult to manage [28]. Accordingly, our protocol
prefers to obliterate any dead space surrounding the fossa-condyle interface with
free fat graft. A variety of techniques and harvest sites have been described [28, 29].
We have found that a simple technique involves either a suprapubic or periumbilical
harvest of free fat. The technique is very simple and involves a curvilinear incision
adjacent to the umbilicus or a linear incision in the suprapubic region. The incision
is carried through the skin into the subcutaneous fat. Sharp dissection is completed
with curved mayo scissors in this plane, leaving a layer of fat superficially at the
fat-dermis junction. An additional dissection plane is created deep to this plane, in
the subcutaneous fat, and approximately 5–10 cc free fat is harvested. Hemostasis
is verified, and the wound is irrigated and closed. The fat is then immediately transferred to the periprosthetic region and packed via the preauricular incision around
the prosthesis, both medially and laterally (Fig. 20.10). The endaural incision is then
closed in layers. Following closure of the endaural incision, the submandibular site

is irrigated and closed. Attempts should be made at re-suspending the pterygomasseteric sling over the ramus of the mandible. On occasion, a bicortical hole may be
drilled through the caudal aspect of the mandibular ramus, and the masseter may
then be sutured to the mandible through this hole using 2-0 Vicryl. Layered closure
of the remaining tissue planes can then be completed.

Moving the Maxilla into Final Position
Once the joints have been placed and the extraoral wounds have been closed, the
maxilla may then be repositioned. This repositioning is completed based on the final
splint that was fabricated during the virtual planning. Once the extraoral wounds
have been closed, there is no longer a risk of instrument contamination. The maxilla
is typically repositioned at the LeFort 1 level, using conventional orthognathic surgical techniques (Fig. 20.11). A septoplasty may also be performed at this time.
Once the maxilla has been adequately mobilized, the maxilla is wired to the mandible using the “final” splint, which may be wired in place if done in the context of
segmental maxillary osteotomies, and the mandible is autorotated to position the
maxilla relative to the uncut midface. A K-wire, which is placed at the nasofrontal
junction, can be used as a fixed vertical reference point for repositioning of the vertical location of the central incisor. Once vertical positioning has been established,
the maxilla is fixated in place, and bone grafting to facilitate bone to bone contact is
completed. Tissue closure is then initiated with careful attention to complete an alar
cinch suture and V-Y advancement of the upper lip [30].
Occasionally, the decision is made to complete the maxillary osteotomy in a
delayed fashion. This decision is made based on the ability to rapidly restore passive
mandibular range of motion in cases where preoperative range of motion is significantly restricted, and early aggressive physical therapy is required. We have found
that heavy fulcruming off a recently osteotomized/fixated maxilla causes maxillary

is advised, and the maxillary osteotomy is completed in a delayed fashion once

have found that patients tolerate the intermediate malocclusion well, for the short
period required to optimize mandibular function.

Complications
Like conventional orthognathic surgery, there are a variety of known risks associated with total joint replacement. In this section, these risks are discussed, in addition to techniques that we have used to mitigate (or at least minimize) these risks in
the preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative periods.

Nerve Injury
Injuries to cranial nerve V are a well-known risk associated with any orthognathic
surgical procedure [31]. In addition to cranial nerve V trauma, patients who undergo
TJR surgery are at increased risk of damage to cranial nerve VII, particularly in
cases where external anatomic landmarks are not present, as described above.
Accordingly, the surgical approaches are designed to avoid encountering and injuring these nerves. Additionally, as described previously, intraoperative nerve monitoring is frequently employed in an attempt to minimize risk. Nonetheless, patients
must be aware of the risk of damage to the fronto-temporal branches, which may be
encountered during the endaural approach, in addition to injury to the marginal
mandibular nerve, which may be encountered during the submandibular approach
[32]. In many cases, traction neuropraxia injuries are nearly inevitable. That being
said, in most cases, with intraoperative monitoring and careful dissection, many of
these injuries are transient and return to full function.

Infection
A comprehensive discussion regarding infections in the context of total joint replacement is beyond the scope of this article. In brief, prosthetic joint infections have
plagued orthopedic surgery for decades. These include acute and/or chronic infections. Pertaining to TJR infections involving the TMJ, multiple articles have suggested
an infection rate from 2% to 5% [31]. Many hypothesize that these infections are
related to biofilms on the prosthesis, which result in infections that become difficult to
treat with antibiotics alone. Accordingly, well-defined protocols have been elucidated,

406

A. Wandell et al.

including early wash out/debridement in the context of acute infections and removal/
replacement of the prosthesis in the case of chronic or nonresponsive infections [33].

Allergic Reactions
Metal allergies associated with TMJ prostheses are well-documented. Accordingly,
patients should be asked prior to surgery if they have had any previous metal hypersensitivity. Where there is concern, patients should be sent to an allergy/immunologist prior to the placement of the prosthesis for appropriate testing. The diagnosis
and management of allergic reactions may be difficult and should be managed in
conjunction with an allergy specialist [34].

Heterotopic Bone Formation
Heterotopic ossification is another well-documented phenomenon in the context of
TJR, both in conventional orthopedic replacement and in TMJ reconstruction. The
underlying pathophysiology is poorly understood; however bone formation that
occurs surrounding the fossa/ramus components can lead to decreased range of
motion, pain, and, in some cases, joint ankylosis [35]. Multiple modalities have
been described that aim to mitigate risk, including placement of free fat surrounding
the joint, as described above, utilizing a piezoelectric saw for resections and osseous
contouring and meticulous hemostasis. Additionally, the use of low-dose indomethacin has been proposed in high-risk cases [36]. In instances where patients have
developed heterotopic ossification and will be debrided, focused external beam
radiation to the site has been utilized with some success, combined with surgical
debridement and possible joint replacement.

Secondary Soft Tissue Management
Patients with CFM and TCS often need secondary soft tissue reconstruction to
achieve optimal esthetic results. There are a number of approaches to reconstructing
depressed/hypoplastic areas in patients with congenital malformations. These include
the use of autologous tissue grafts, allogenic tissue grafts, and alloplastic materials.
Autologous tissue grafting can be used to achieve proper contour of the face,
improving symmetry with fewer complications and shorter operating times than
microvascular free flaps [37]. Surgeons typically use the lower anterior abdominal
wall as the donor harvesting fat site. Usually, fat is infiltrated into the recipient tissue until an overcorrection is achieved in areas of under projection (Fig. 20.12). Fat

20

TMJ Total Joint Prosthesis in Treacher Collins Syndrome and Hemifacial…

407

Fig. 20.12 Autologous fat
placed in the soft tissue

injections can produce high-quality immediate postoperative results, although long-­
term success is not guaranteed. Horl et al. (1991) reported greater than 50% volume
loss when measured 6 months post injection with magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI) [38]. Postoperative physiotherapy prevents soft tissue contraction in some
cases, and additional less-invasive fat transfer can take place in the future if it is
necessary to make adjustments.
Implants made from alloplastic materials such as silicone, Medpor, and expanded
polytetrafluorethylene implants (ePTFE) can improve the soft tissue projections in
a deficient area, but each of these materials poses their own unique challenges for
congenital facial deformities. Silicone is soft and tends to change shape and shift
over time. Medpor implants are stiff and are mainly recommended for bone contour
deformities. EPTFE implants can be placed beneath the superficial temporal fascia
and over the superficial musculoaponeurotic system in the zygomatic region, mandible, and cheek. EPTFE meshes may prove promising in the future; however, like
all alloplastic materials, it poses higher risks for inflammatory cell reactions and
bacterial microfilm contamination [39].
Autologous tissue grafting remains the most effective technique to recreate soft
tissue contours and can be performed in conjunction with orthognathic and TJR
procedures.

Patient Expectations
The surgical treatment of both TCS and HFM patients requires great preparation
and surgical skill. Even in the hands of the most skilled surgeons, these cases are
difficult to treat. It is imperative to understand the goals and expectations of the
patients and their families in order to prepare them for realistic outcomes. Below are
some case examples of patients who have undergone surgical treatment of TCS and
HFM (Figs. 20.13 and 20.14).

Summary
• Total joint replacement (TJR) with concomitant orthognathic surgery has proven
to be a stable alternative to conventional distraction or osteotomies and can
improve the function/esthetics of patients with moderate to severe Treacher
Collins syndrome (TCS) and craniofacial microsomia (CFM).
• Both TJR and orthognathic surgery can be accomplished in a single operation.
• Where feasible, surgery should be delayed until skeletal maturity in patients with
TCS and CFM, so as to minimize the need for additional revision surgery.
• Virtual surgical planning (VSP) plays a critical role in creating a custom-fitted
prosthesis and planning the concomitant orthognathic surgery.
• We describe and illustrate the surgical approach and protocol for total joint
replacement (TJR) with orthognathic surgery and discuss possible
complications.

Maxillomandibular Deformities
in Treacher Collins Syndrome
E. Weston Santee and Vernon Burke

Treacher Collins syndrome is a distinct genetic disorder characterized by abnormalities in the structures of the first and second branchial arches. It is eponymously
named after Edward Treacher Collins, a renowned English ophthalmologist, who
was the first to cohesively describe the essential findings of the condition in 1900.
The condition is also known as mandibulofacial dysostosis, which is the term that
was used by Adolphe Franceschetti and David Klein when they characterized the
same condition in 1949 [1]. The clinical findings include downward sloping palpebral fissures, inferiorly positioned lateral canthi, a prominent nose, a severely convex facial profile, and long sideburns or tongues of hair extending onto the face. See
Fig. 21.1 of an individual with characteristic findings.
The extent of the abnormalities can vary, but there are characteristic maxillomandibular findings that include malar and midface hypoplasia, a hypoplastic and irregularly shaped mandible, and hypoplasia of the structures of the temporomandibular
joint. Affected individuals often have severe skeletal and dental malocclusions with
large anterior open bites. The constellation and severity of the abnormalities in the
facial skeleton create a maxillomandibular complex that has unique features and
requires an orthognathic surgical plan that is tailor-made for the individual patient.

Cephalometric Findings
Individuals with Treacher Collins syndrome have characteristic cephalometric findings. For an affected individual, the length of both the maxilla and mandible is short.
The mandible is inescapably rotated downward and backward. There is premature
occlusion of the posterior dentition due to the short ramus height and severely
enlarged mandibular plane angle. Consequently, anterior open bites are frequently
present. The nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal spaces are diminished due to the
short posterior facial height in conjunction with the aforementioned findings [2].
Basilar kyphosis has also been demonstrated as a frequent finding, which likely has
adverse effects on the upper airway spaces [3, 4]. It is important to utilize lateral
cephalograms and computer software to objectively quantify skeletal abnormalities.
The extent of hypoplasia and skeletal abnormalities can be more easily appreciated.
See Fig. 21.2a and b for an example of a traced lateral cephalogram and the accompanying cephalometric analysis data.
It appears that females tend to have more severe mandibular abnormalities and
present with more significant mandibular retrusion in relation to the relative position of the maxilla and skull base. Typically, the maxilla is quite retruded in female
subjects, as well. The changes in the growth and shape of the mandible are severe in
all dimensions. See Fig. 21.3 for a sample 3D reconstruction from a CT scan. The
vertical ramus height, length of the horizontal ramus, volume of bone in the horizontal ramus, and position of the chin prominence were all shown to be significantly
affected in a study by Chong et al. from The Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto,
Canada. Indeed, the shortened posterior facial height is one of the most notable differences when compared to controls [7].
A comprehensive assessment of cephalometric findings in 20 patients with
Treacher Collins syndrome was published in 2013 by Dr. Kapadia from Seattle
Children’s Hospital and Dr. Shetye, Dr. Grayson, and Dr. McCarthy at New York
University. They were able to present their findings on 20 unoperated patients, from
age 5 to 16 years, for whom diagnostic quality lateral cephalograms were available.
A summary of their findings can be found in Table 21.1.
Several important observations included the abnormal position of the tongue
superiorly and posteriorly secondary to severe mandibular retrognathism and a
much smaller mandibular ramus height. The mandibular length is also greatly
reduced [8]. The hypoplastic maxilla has deleterious effects on the nasal airway and
possibly causes choanal stenosis or atresia. The hypoplastic maxilla combined with
the hypoplastic mandible creates an unfavorable airway that is highly susceptible to
obstructive sleep apnea [10]. Please see Chap. 15 regarding management of the
pediatric airway for patients with Treacher Collins syndrome.
A whole host of pernicious effects of obstructive sleep apnea can plague individuals with Treacher Collins syndrome throughout childhood and adulthood.
Obstructive sleep apnea in children can manifest as behavioral and cognitive problems leading to poor performance in school. Long-term effects can cause hypertension, type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, arrhythmias,

Stability of Orthognathic Surgery
Many surgeons who have had the privilege to care for individuals with Treacher
Collins syndrome will undoubtedly relate their personal experiences with frustrating long-term stability issues. Indeed, separate and respective studies published by
Dufresne and Stelnicki confirm that even with early surgical intervention the
Treacher Collins mandible has a profound tendency to relapse [5, 6]. There seems
to be something influencing the stability of orthognathic surgery in patients with
Treacher Collins syndrome, but at this time the cause is not fully elucidated.
The surgical movements typically needed to advance the maxillomandibular
complex for an individual with TCS include maxillary advancement, mandibular
advancement, and a counterclockwise rotation of the complex, which does include
inferior movement of the posterior maxilla. A genioplasty with or without the inclusion of the genioglossus muscles is also typically performed. This is a similar treatment for individuals with a class II malocclusion with mandibular retrognathia and
an open bite. Individuals with Treacher Collins syndrome have characteristic malocclusions. See Chap. 22 for more information regarding orthodontic treatment.
Data from the 2007 publication by Proffit, Turvey, and Phillips indicated that
with rigid fixation mandibular advancement is a very stable and predictable surgical
movement. Maxillary advancement is also considered stable, but moving the

Surgery Protocol
At our institution, we strongly believe that each patient with Treacher Collins syndrome should be treated as a unique individual. The degree of psychosocial impact
of having Treacher Collins syndrome will vary among affected individuals, and
these children should ideally have access to the appropriate specialists. We recommend and invite all patients with Treacher Collins syndrome to be seen and evaluated by our ACPA-approved cleft and craniofacial team. Individuals with Treacher
Collins syndrome are candidates for specialized surgical and nonsurgical intervention from numerous specialists and are likely to benefit from being seen in a multidisciplinary team setting.

21 Definitive Correction of Associated Maxillomandibular Deformities in Treacher…

421

Fig. 21.6 Custom surgical cutting guides

In general, we adhere to the principle of postponing maxillomandibular orthognathic surgery until skeletal maturity. However, children with significant obstructive
sleep apnea are considered candidates for orthognathic surgery, knowing full well
that growth may be unpredictable and a second or even third operation may be indicated in the future. We refer children in whom we suspect obstructive sleep apnea to
a sleep medicine specialist who can help determine the severity of OSA and offer to
the child and family nonsurgical options that can be considered as stop gaps until
either growth of the mandible occurs or skeletal maturity is reached.
We recommend every patient with Treacher Collins syndrome to start seeing a
pediatric or general dentist when the primary dentition begins to erupt. Routine,
thorough evaluations should continue through early childhood, and at the appropriate age, these patients should be evaluated by an orthodontist who routinely performs surgical orthodontic treatment. Severe open bites with a reverse curve of Spee
are routinely encountered, and nearly all of these individuals will be candidates for
surgical orthodontics and bimaxillary orthognathic surgery. Fig. 21.11 shows a typical open bite malocclusion seen in a TCS individual. Please see Chap. 22 regarding
orthodontic treatment for an individual with Treacher Collins.

422

E. W. Santee and V. Burke

Fig. 21.7 Custom-designed fixation plates

Once it has been determined that a patient is a candidate for orthognathic surgery, the decision is then made to pursue a surgery-first approach or the traditional
three-stage approach with presurgical orthodontics, surgery, and post-surgery orthodontics. At our institution, in the majority of cases, we treat patients with the traditional three-stage approach.
Some form of maxillomandibular orthognathic surgery will be indicated for
these individuals. Mandibular osteotomies such as the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy and the inverted L osteotomy are two options. See Figs. 21.8, 21.9, and 21.10
for lateral and profile photos, as well as 3D recons for an individual treated with
bilateral inverted L osteotomies, LeFort I osteotomy, and genioplasty. Bicortical
fixation screws with bilateral sagittal split osteotomies may not lend themselves
well for large mandibular advancements. For patients who are having severe airway
obstruction, we will consider performing neonatal mandibular distraction. For more
on the pediatric airway, see Chap. 15 and mandibular distraction see Chap. 19.

In order to appropriately treat each patient, it is crucial to identify the severity of
the skeletal deformity and understand the limitations of the various treatment
modalities available to the patient. See Table 21.2 for a summary of our osteotomy
options. For mild deformities, we strongly consider use of more traditional bimaxillary surgery, which includes bilateral sagittal split osteotomies, LeFort I osteotomy,
and +/− genioplasty.
In individuals with a moderate degree of deformity, we opt for use of bilateral
inverted L osteotomies, in order to maximize the advancement and counterclockwise rotation. See Fig. 21.4 for a typical virtual workflow including LeFort I,
inverted L osteotomies, and a genioplasty. Sufficient ramus height is necessary, and
the stability of the TMJ is also important to consider. If the TMJ is a Kaban type I
or type IIa, then this is our preferred approach. This is done in conjunction with a
LeFort I osteotomy and a genioplasty.
Individuals with severe hypoplasia and deformity of the temporomandibular
joint complex, such as in Kaban type IIb and III joints, will benefit from total joint
replacement in conjunction with a LeFort osteotomy. We have significant concern
for further remodeling of the TMJ and for significant relapse if a large advancement
is performed without addressing the joint with a prosthetic reconstruction in these

21 Definitive Correction of Associated Maxillomandibular Deformities in Treacher…

425

Fig. 21.11 Typical open
bite for TCS

individuals. For further details regarding temporomandibular joint total joint
replacement for the patient with Treacher Collins syndrome, please see Chap. 20.
Our clinical workflow in preparation for surgery includes the following:
1. Obtain full medical history.
2. Clinical measurements.
3. CBCT.
4. Intraoral scanning.
5. Clinical photos.
6. Cephalometric evaluation.
7. Computer-aided surgical planning.
8. Fabrication of computer-designed occlusal splints, cutting guides, and patient-­
specific plates (for large advancements with inverted L osteotomy) or custom
TMJ total joint prosthesis with TMJ concepts (Ventura, CA).
In order to optimize stability for large advancements and improve bone growth
in the large gaps at the osteotomy sites, we utilize several strategies. First, appropriately rigid plates are utilized. These can either be stock recon plates that are pre-bent
off 3D printed models or can be custom-made plates. Next, allogeneic or autogenous bone grafting is performed at the osteotomy gap. Recombinant human bone
morphogenetic protein-2 (rhBMP-2) on a collagen sponge is also mixed with the
bone graft. We also use a similar technique in large maxillary advancements with
cortical blocks of bone wedged and often fixated with screws and then covered with
sheets of rhBMP-2 in a collagen sponge.

Summary
The morphologic characteristics of the maxillomandibular complex, the degree of
hypoplasia, the challenging malocclusions, and the restrictive soft tissue envelope
create a constellation of surgical challenges for the Treacher Collins patient. The
growth potential of the TCS mandible is diminished, and the mandible tends to

426

E. W. Santee and V. Burke

remain diminutive despite the pubertal growth spurt that tends to help with mandibular growth in other craniofacial syndromes [13]. It is imperative that these individuals receive treatment based on a team approach with access to the medical and
surgical specialists who can address the specific needs of the affected individual.
Obstructive sleep apnea that cannot be treated nonsurgically or psychosocial problems may expedite the need to perform surgery prior to skeletal maturity.
The goals of definitive maxillomandibular surgical treatment should include
eliminating obstructive sleep apnea, providing a functional occlusion, and creating
a facial profile that is within normal limits. Some individuals with more severe
deformities will need temporomandibular total joint reconstruction. Others will be
appropriately treated with bilateral inverted L osteotomies or bilateral sagittal split
osteotomies, with concomitant LeFort I osteotomy and genioplasty. In general, the
surgical movements are forward in the maxilla and mandible with a counterclockwise rotation.
Surgical planning should include 3D imaging with CBCT or CT scan, intra-oral
scanning, clinical photos, and clinical measurements. Computer-aided planning
should be utilized to fully appreciate the skeletal deficiencies, to plan movements
accordingly, and to appreciate vital structures (Fig. 21.5). The fabrication of custom
cutting guides and plates (Figs. 21.6 and 21.7) is widely available.
In an effort to lower the burden of care for patients and their family, the surgery-­
first approach in orthognathic surgery is an option. In select patients, the overall
treatment time can be drastically reduced. Also, it may be appropriate to consider
the surgery-first approach for individuals with severe obstructive sleep apnea who
can benefit from an expedited surgical date and realize the benefits of an expanded
airway sooner, rather than potentially years of presurgical orthodontics [14]. The
conventional approach typically takes 27 to 35 months of orthodontic treatment
[15–17]. The surgery-first approach can require on average 10 months of orthodontics [18, 19].
With technological advancements providing for a fully digital workflow with
computer-aided planning, patient-specific osteotomy cutting guides and fixation
devices, and the use of growth factors, the future is promising that more predictable
and more stable maxillomandibular surgical outcomes can be achieved for individuals with Treacher Collins syndrome.

Introduction
Treacher Collins syndrome (TCS), frequently referred to as mandibulofacial dysostosis, is a disorder of craniofacial development attributed to mutations in the “treacle” gene (TCOF1) on chromosome 5q32 (TCS-1), POLR1D gene on chromosome
13q12 (TCS-22), POLR1C gene on chromosome 6p21 (TCS-3), or POLR1B gene
on chromosome 2q14 (TCS-4) [1–4]. A vast majority of cases of TCS are due to
mutations in TCOF1, and the incidence of TCS is about 1 in 50,000 live births
[Caluseriu 2013] [5]. TCS-1 and TCS-4 are inherited as an autosomal dominant
disorder, TCS-3 is inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder, while TCS-2 can be
inherited either as autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive [1–4]. There is variable involvement of craniofacial structures derived from the first and second branchial arches [6, 7]. The involvement of craniofacial structures is usually symmetric.
TCS has a high penetrance and variable expressivity [8–10]. Those with TCS require
care from a multidisciplinary team comprised of orthodontists, pedodontists, craniofacial surgeons, oral and maxillofacial surgeons, etc. [11]. The earliest clinical
interventions could start as early as infancy, and the continuum of care could last

Orofacial Features
The phenotypic expression of TCS is highly variable [12–17]. Frequently, those
with TCS present as Class II skeletal malocclusions, marked convexity of face (due
to a prominent nasal dorsum and retrognathic mandible), and an anterior open bite.
Some of the common facial features (Fig. 22.1) include downward-slanting palpebral fissures, euryblepharon, absence of lower medial third of eyelashes, coloboma,
hypoplasia of the zygomatic arches, maxillary hypoplasia, external ear malformations, accessory skin tags, and external ear malformations [12–17]. Tessier type 6–8
clefts can also be seen in those with severe manifestations of TCS. The typical oral
features (Fig. 22.2) include anterior open bite, crowding of maxillary and mandibular arches, Class II molar relationship, ectopic eruption of maxillary first molars,
congenitally missing teeth, high-arched palate, shortened soft palate, and cleft palate (estimated to occur in 35% of patients) [12, 16–18]. About 30 to 40% of those
with TCS have velopharyngeal incompetence, and 25% have obstructive sleep
apnea [12]. The classic lateral cephalometric features include (Fig. 22.3) reduced
cranial base angle, steep mandibular plane angle, antegonial notching, clockwise
rotation of occlusal plane, short ramus, obtuse gonial angle, increased lower anterior facial height, reduced posterior facial height, and increased ANB angle [10, 19].

Principles of Orthodontic Management
Those with TCS present with occlusal/skeletal disharmony in all three dimensions,
transverse, sagittal, and vertical, and are very challenging to treat orthodontically.

Maxillary Expansion
Frequently, those with TCS tend to have a high-arched palate and about 30% have a
cleft palate [12, 16–18]. Consequently, the maxillary arch is constricted which manifests as posterior crossbites. Depending on severity of constriction, there is crowding. Some of the objectives of orthodontic treatment are to establish the maxillary
arch form, make maxillary and mandibular arch forms compatible, correct crossbites, and resolve crowding. These objectives can be realized by expansion of maxilla. The type of expansion that needs to be done is dependent on the arch form and
area of constriction (anterior versus posterior). Those with a cleft palate and alveolus tend to have collapsed arch segments in the anterior region. In such situations,
differential expansion (more expansion in the anterior region versus posterior
region) is required. On the other hand, a symmetrical expansion will be required if
there is constriction in both anterior and posterior regions. Fan-shaped expanders
are used to obtain differential expansion (Fig. 22.4). Symmetrical expansion can be
achieved by a wide variety of expansion appliances such as hyrax expanders, Haas
expanders, etc. (Fig. 22.5). Below is a step-by-step process recommended for
accomplishing maxillary expansion:
• Clinical examination: The importance of a good clinical examination cannot be
overemphasized. The severity of crossbite can range from a single tooth to

involving an entire segment. A crossbite that involves only a single tooth or a
couple of teeth typically are dental crossbites and can be effectively addressed
with orthodontic aligning/leveling and use of cross elastics. On the other hand, if
multiple teeth or an entire segment is involved, then maxillary skeletal expansion
will be required. It is vital to assess the maxillary arch form and its compatibility
with the mandibular arch. The type of expander that needs to be used is depen-

434

V. Allareddy et al.

dent on these factors. As mentioned earlier, those with TCS have Class II skeletal
and dental manifestations. Consequently, on clinical examination in maximum
intercuspation, there may not be an apparent posterior crossbite since the maxillary arch articulates with a narrower segment of the mandibular arch. It is recommended that the patient positions the mandible anteriorly (into a Canine Class I
relationship) and then the transverse relationship be examined. When the mandible is positioned anteriorly to as close as possible to the future desired position,
the maxilla articulates with a wider segment of the mandible and the true relative
maxillary/mandibular transverse discrepancy can be appreciated.
• Diagnostic aids: The amount and type of maxillary expansion that need to be
obtained are dependent on a multitude of factors such as severity of constriction
of maxillary arch, amount of arch length teeth size discrepancy (crowding), type
of maxillary arch form and its compatibility with mandibular arch, and compensations of posterior teeth (usually maxillary molars are buccally tipped while the
mandibular molars are lingually tipped). We recommend that diagnostic models
be obtained and assessed for the above factors. As mentioned in the clinical
examination step, the models should be articulated (mandible moved anteriorly
into the future desired position) in a Class I canine relationship, and then the
amount of posterior crossbite should be quantified. The degree of compensations
of the maxillary and mandibular molar teeth and amount of crowding should also
be accurately assessed, and the planned amount of expansion should be established accordingly. One other key diagnostic aid is a postero-anterior cephalometric radiograph. This enables us to assess the amount of relative skeletal
maxillary/mandibular transverse discrepancy.
• Maxillary expansion appliance designs: A wide variety of maxillary expansion
appliances are in use, and the specific design should be based on the type and
timing of expansion. Expansion can be done during the mixed dentition stages
using a simple quad-helix or W-shaped expander. Typically hyrax and Haas-type
expanders are done before the age of 15 years. Beyond this age, the median palatine suture tends to interlock, and it is difficult to obtain pure skeletal expansion.
In such scenarios, temporary anchorage device-assisted expansion appliances
can be used. As explained earlier, fan-shaped expansion appliances can be used
to obtain differential expansion (more expansion in the canine region compared
to in the molar region) (Fig. 22.6). The positioning of the fulcrum of the expansion screw in relation to the distal abutments determines the amount of anterior
versus posterior expansion. As the fulcrum is placed more anteriorly in relation
to the distal abutment, more anterior expansion relative to the posterior expansion can be achieved. We have conducted extensive lab experiments in an attempt
to compute the relative anterior and posterior expansions obtained by varying the
position of the fulcrum [20]. When the fulcrum of the expansion screw is placed
10 mm behind a line drawn from and to the central pits of the distal abutment
teeth (usually the maxillary first permanent molars), an anterior to posterior
expansion ratio of 1.95 to 1.9 is obtained. If the fulcrum is placed 5 mm behind
the distal abutment, the anterior to posterior expansion ratio is 5.20:1, and if the
fulcrum is placed 3 mm behind the distal abutment, the anterior to posterior

22

Principles of Orthodontic Management of Treacher Collins Syndrome

435

expansion is 27.33:1.9. Regardless of the type of expansion appliance used
(hyrax, Haas type, or fan-shaped), we recommend using four abutment teeth to
support the expansion appliance. We use the maxillary first molars as the distal
abutment and the maxillary first premolars (or maxillary first primary molars) as
the mesial abutments for hyrax and Haas-type expanders. For fan-shaped expanders (usually used only in those with a cleft palate), we use the maxillary first
molars as distal abutments and the primary canines as the mesial abutments.
• Activation protocol: For most patients, a rapid maxillary expansion is done. The
recommended activation protocol is one turn activation of the expansion screw
each day. We have obtained consistently good clinical outcomes with this
approach. Occasionally, we have used two activations of expansion screw each
day. The total number of activations will be dependent on the amount of expansion required. Typically, each activation will yield about 0.25 mm of expansion.
It is critical that the total amount of expansion need to correct the transverse
discrepancy be computed prior to cementing the expansion appliance. The length
of the expansion screw is dependent on this and should be taken into consideration while designing the appliance. In those with cleft palate, where there is an
increased likelihood of opening palatal fistulas with rapid expansion, we tend to
do slow expansion. We activate the expansion by one turn every 3 or 4 days to
minimize opening of large fistulas. Our rationale is that the slow expansion protocol enables the palatal tissues to adapt to the stresses placed by the expansion
appliance.
• Retention: Maxillary expansion is one of the least stable orthodontic movements, and there is significant amount of relapse. It is our practice to over-expand
by about 25% to account for possible relapse. Following completion of maxillary
expansion, we use brass wires or composite to seal the expansion screw and have
the appliance in place for about 3 months. After this, we remove the maxillary
expansion appliance and cement a fixed trans-palatal arch with mesial extension
arms (up to the maxillary canines). The trans-palatal arch is made of rigid stainless steel wire. This is in place until the commencement of comprehensive phase
of orthodontic treatment when fixed orthodontic appliances are banded/bonded.
Limited Orthodontic Treatment
A limited phase of orthodontic treatment (usually only in the maxillary arch) while
not an absolute essential is usually recommended if there are any anterior crossbites
leading to functional shifts and traumatic occlusion and to facilitate eruption of
permanent teeth. Frequently, those with TCS have hypoplastic maxilla and mandible, and there is relative arch length/teeth size discrepancies. The severe crowding
may lead to ectopic eruption of teeth and/or blocked/impacted teeth. In such situations, a limited phase of orthodontic treatment is usually done to facilitate eruption
of teeth into their appropriate positions in the arch. The case illustrated in
Figs. 22.7a–c is a female patient aged 12 years. It is evident that there is severe
crowding in the maxillary arch, constriction of the maxillary arch, posterior crossbite, premature loss of maxillary right second primary molar which resulted in the
first permanent molar drifting anteriorly, palatal eruption of maxillary second

Comprehensive Orthodontic Treatment
The degree of malformation of different structures impacted in TCS is thought to be
stable and does not worsen with age [21]. However, growth cannot be predicted
with certainty. Consequently, it is best to initiate the comprehensive phase of orthodontic treatment (with fixed appliances in both maxillary and mandibular arches)
at close to completion of growth. The primary objectives of the comprehensive
phase of orthodontic treatment are to help restore facial imbalance and correct malocclusions. More often than not, those with TCS require orthodontic treatment in
conjunction with an orthognathic surgery to address the skeletal imbalances. Those
with TCS present with a wide range of malocclusions, and reviewing every type of
orthodontic correction will be beyond the scope of this chapter. A brief overview of
orthodontic preparation for orthognathic surgeries is provided below.
Maxillary Expansion Using Temporary Anchorage Devices As mentioned earlier, it is best to correct the transverse discrepancies earlier during the mixed denti-

22

Principles of Orthodontic Management of Treacher Collins Syndrome

441

tion stage when the median palatine suture is still patent and not significantly
interlocked. Usually, the comprehensive phase of orthodontic treatment is initiated
at close to cessation of growth. As a result, the maxillary expansion appliances
which use teeth as anchorage are not very effective at obtaining skeletal expansion
of the maxillary arch. What is typically obtained is dentoalveolar bending and tipping of teeth. To overcome the dentoalveolar undesirable side effects and maximize
skeletal expansion potential, a nonsurgical miniscrew-assisted rapid palatal expansion (MARPE) technique was introduced [22]. The role of the miniscrews to provide expansion with less tipping, reducing the excessive pressure on the buccal
plates of the anchor teeth, MARPE is tooth-and-bone-borne expander. The MARPE
design is a combination of hyrax expansion appliance with four extension arms
made of 0.9 mm round rigid stainless steel soldered under the body of the jackscrew
for the accommodation of four miniscrews adjacent to the median palatine suture,
two mesial and two distal to the expanding screw (Figs. 22.14 and 22.15) [22]. The
bicortical insertion of the miniscrews is recommended to obtain anchorage in internal cortical plates of the palate and nasal fossa. The fixation in both cortical plates
is fundamental to aid the anchorage during expansion and to surpass the resistance
of maxillary bones to separation [23]. Correct selection of miniscrew location and
length by analyzing the bone thickness and height of median palatine suture is pivotal for the success of MARPE. Below is the recommended protocol for this
procedure:
• An impression or scan with the bands on the first premolars and first molars
should be obtained.
• Using CBCT, the location of the four miniscrews is selected to provide good
skeletal anchorage and stability; measurements of the bone thickness and soft
tissue thickness are essential for choosing appropriate miniscrew length. Usually
1.6 to 2 mm diameter is appropriate.

• The locations of miniscrews are transferred to the cast over which a conventional
hyrax expander is fabricated. Four rigid connectors made of stainless steel wire
with helical hooks are soldered on the base of the hyrax screw body. Two anterior
hooks are positioned on the rugae region, and the two posterior hooks are placed
on the parasagittal area. The hooks should be adjusted for passive contact with
the underlying tissues.
• The MARPE appliance is cemented on the first premolars and first molars.
Orthodontic miniscrews are placed in the center of the helical hooks under local
infiltration anesthesia.
• The activation rate of hyrax expansion screw is once a day to provide about
0.25 mm of expansion per day.
• After active expansion, the MARPE can be maintained for 3 months to allow
bone formation in the separated sutural areas.
• Since MARPE is performed during the comprehensive orthodontic phase, the
fixed orthodontic appliances with continuous main arch wire can prevent relapse.
Orthognathic Surgery Those with a TCS typically present with a skeletal Class II
malocclusion with anterior open bites. Depending on the severity of skeletal discrepancies, a single jaw or a bimaxillary surgery is required in conjunction with
orthodontic treatment. The LeFort I osteotomy can correct the transverse, anteroposterior, and posterior vertical discrepancies [10, 21]. Counterclockwise rotation
of the occlusal plane helps to improve the tooth-lip relationship while increasing the
height of the posterior maxilla which is usually short in those with TCS. The frequently performed mandibular surgery is a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy that
advances the mandible and rotates the mandible in a counterclockwise direction to
close the anterior openbite [21]. Bilateral extraoral inverted “L” ramus osteotomies
with bone grafts have also been used successfully to treat the skeletal discrepancies
in those with TCS [24].

22

Principles of Orthodontic Management of Treacher Collins Syndrome

443

Presurgical Orthodontics The goal of presurgical orthodontics is to prepare the
patient for the surgical procedure by placing the teeth in a good position relative to
their supporting bone and to arrange the teeth so they will not interfere with setting
of the jaws. This requires aligning the arches to make them compatible and establishing the anteroposterior and vertical position of the incisors [25]. Leveling of
arches is fundamental. Extrusion generally is done more easily postsurgically,
whereas intrusion must be accomplished presurgically. For those with TCS, there is
an abnormal clockwise rotation of mandible and a very steep mandibular plane.
Consequently, in those with TCS, the leveling of arches must be accomplished presurgically. Leveling of the mandibular arch should be accomplished by intrusion of
incisors. The posterior teeth should not be extruded. In those with an open bite who
will have vertical repositioning of the maxilla and multiple segment surgery, presurgical leveling of the upper arch should be done only within each segment, and then
the segments are leveled at surgery. Extrusion of anterior teeth prior to surgery must
be avoided [26, 27].
The anteroposterior position of the incisors determines where the mandible will
be placed relative to the maxilla during surgery. For mandibular advancements,
retraction of protruding lower incisors before surgery is required to provide adequate overjet for advancing the mandible. In some cases, lower first or second premolar extractions will be required. When several surgical segments are planned for
the maxilla, the axial inclination of the upper incisors and canines should be established presurgically so that major rotation of the anterior segment at operation can
be avoided [25–27].
After presurgical orthodontic preparation, minor adjustments can be made to
avoid interferences. Stabilizing wires are full-dimension edgewise wires (i.e.,
17 × 25 steel in the 18-slot appliance and 21 × 25 steel in the 22-slot appliance).
Hooks as attachments are crimped to the archwires as needed [27].
For the final surgical planning, surgical guide CBCT is used to simulate surgical
movements and evaluate the resulting soft tissue profile. When the satisfactory functional and esthetic balance has been achieved, the surgical movements are applied
in the virtual or actual model surgery, and the surgical splint is fabricated according
to the dental relationships it establishes [28].
Postsurgical Orthodontics After the initial healing, the finishing stage is initiated.
Light vertical elastics are needed initially to allow the teeth to settle into better interdigitation. Elastics should not be discontinued until a solid occlusion has been
established. Elastics can be discontinued during any further detailing of the occlusion. A TMA wire can be used for final detailing [27].
Orthodontics Retention Anterior open bite malocclusions which are typical manifestations of TCS tend to be very challenging to retain with traditional retainers
such as Hawley appliances. We recommend bonded fixed lingual retainers (canine
to canine in mandibular arch and lateral incisor to lateral incisor in maxillary arch)
along with clear retainers. The clear retainers prevent extrusion of posterior teeth

444

V. Allareddy et al.

and are ideal for retaining open bites. We recommend retainer wear (24 hours) for
the first year, and thereafter the clear retainers can be worn at night times only.
Stability Both traditional orthognathic surgeries and distraction osteogenesis can
be successfully used to correct the skeletal discrepancies of the maxilla and mandible. There is a paucity of studies that have prospectively evaluated the stability of
surgical corrections in those with TCS. Most of the published literature are either
case reports/series or retrospective evaluations [29–31]. Nguyen and colleagues
conducted a retrospective analysis of 22 patients with TCS who underwent orthognathic surgery between 1993 and 2007 [31]. Patients were followed up for 1 to
3 years. They found that superior repositioning of the maxilla is most stable followed by mandibular advancement. Mandibular counterclockwise rotations tended
to be stable over time, and there was no significant relapse of the mandibular length.
Significant relapse of the palatal plane was found. They concluded that the overall
relapse rates following bimaxillary orthognathic surgery correction of TCS were
comparable to typical Class II corrections [31]. Gursoy and colleagues examined
the long-term stability of mandibular distraction osteogenesis on the dentofacial
structure of syndromic children and concluded that while excellent short-term
results can be achieved the results are not stable during growth in syndromic children [30]. They recommended mandibular distraction osteogenesis for addressing
airway issues as opposed to for improving facial esthetics.

Hearing Loss and Aural Rehabilitation

Kevin Chow, Randi Tepper, Jaymee Frankneckt, Lauren Kaplan,

Introduction
Hearing loss is a ubiquitous manifestation of first and second pharyngeal arch dysgenesis in Treacher Collins syndrome (TCS). Malformations of the cartilaginous
auricle and temporal bone are both common and highly variable in this population.
Patients with TCS usually present with varying degrees of symmetric and bilateral
malformations of the external and middle ears, most commonly resulting in mild to
profound conductive hearing loss [1]. Early identification and diagnosis of both the
type and degree of hearing loss is crucial to facilitating speech and language development in these children. While the intellectual abilities of TCS patients are unaffected, language and speech development become impaired in the absence of timely
screening and treatment of hearing loss. It has been well-documented that

expressive and receptive language outcomes in children [2].
A multitude of unique amplification options are available which address conductive hearing loss in these patients. These should be initiated as soon as hearing loss
is identified in early childhood. Surgical correction of auricular deformities and
aural atresia is also possible in many children and typically occurs in later childhood
depending on patient-specific anatomic and hearing loss considerations.
Individualized surgical interventions may include any combination of atresiaplasty,
ossicular chain reconstruction, or placement of bone-anchored hearing implants.
Overall, optimal management of hearing loss in this patient population requires a
multidisciplinary team of specialists in neurotology, audiology, and speech language pathology.
This chapter discusses otologic manifestations of TCS, diagnostic testing, and
available treatment options for hearing loss, with an emphasis on evidence-based
audiologic and surgical options to improve language and speech development
through childhood.

Otologic Manifestations of Treacher Collins Syndrome
Outer Ear/Auricle
Both external auditory canals (EAC) and auricles are commonly dysmorphic and
malpositioned in cases of TCS (85 to 100% of cases), with a high degree of variance
existing in presentation of microtia (small or malformed) or anotia (absence) of the
auricle [3, 4]. Although microtia is typically a unilateral malformation, in TCS
microtia is often bilateral and symmetric, occurring in up to 85% of TCS patients
[3–5]. Ears may present with malformed, typically low-lying and rotated pinna,
fistulas, preauricular tags, and missing landmarks. The Marx microtia classification
is the most commonly used assessment of the auricular remnant (Fig. 23.1) and uses

presentation of microtia in TCS [5].
Congenital aural atresia, or the complete absence of the ear canal, is present in
54–78% of cases and is often bilateral (Fig. 23.2). Less frequently, stenosis or narrowing of the ear canal may occur in 22–31% of cases with bilaterally deformed
tympanic membranes [3–6].

Middle Ear
By the nature of their anatomy, patients with aural atresia have no tympanic membrane and typically have bilateral, often symmetric hypoplasia of the middle ear
cavity (Fig. 23.2). The bones of the middle ear, including the malleus, incus, and
stapes, are typically fused, malformed, or absent (22–67%) [4, 6]. Specific deformities reported in the ossicular chain include monopodal stapes, stapes ankylosis
(33–82%), underdeveloped ossicles, and fusion of the malleus and incus [6]. The
presence and condition of the ossicular chain are important factors in the evaluation
of TCS patients for surgical correction of the ear canal (e.g., atresiaplasty) (described
in more detail below). Aural atresia is often associated with aberrant paths of the

portion) [3, 7]. An understanding of the facial nerve location is crucial, as this
knowledge will influence or impede surgical decision-making in atresiaplasty.

Inner Ear
Because of their different embryologic origins, the morphology and function of the
inner ear, specifically the cochlea and semicircular canals, is largely preserved in
TCS patients. In general, the type and degree of hearing loss is guided by the anatomic malformations. Patients with TCS typically present with conductive hearing
loss (CHL) due to aural atresia and normal inner ear structures. Even in TCS patients
with normal or stenotic ear canals, CHL may result from eustachian tube dysfunction, middle ear fluid, or abnormalities of the ossicular chain [8]. About 96% of
individuals with TCS have unilateral or bilateral conductive hearing loss, usually
moderate or maximal up to 60 dB [3–6]. Because the inner ear is typically unaffected, sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) is rare but has been seen in up to 7% of
children with TCS. In all cases, the SNHL was present with an anatomic abnormality of the outer ear, resulting in a mixed (meaning combined conductive and sensorineural) hearing loss [6]. The understanding of anatomy and hearing loss has
important implications for the type and timing of treatment, influencing decisions
concerning hearing aid amplification and surgical intervention.

Radiographic Imaging
While microtia assessment is based on the physical exam, evaluation of aural atresia
and stenosis requires radiographic imaging. Temporal bone and skull base bony
anatomy is best assessed with fine cut (1 mm) non-contrast computed tomography
(CT) of the temporal bone. The analysis of CT imaging and identification of various
key middle ear structures serves as a crucial step in deciding patient candidacy for
atresiaplasty [7] (Fig. 23.3). However, this information must be used in conjunction
with a hearing assessment, as patients with SNHL may not benefit from surgical
creation of an external ear canal. Because atresiaplasty surgery is not commonly
performed until age 6–7, radiographic imaging for conductive hearing loss and
aural atresia is often deferred until approximately 5 years of age [9]. Due to the
complexity of craniofacial abnormalities in TCS, many children may obtain imaging that evaluates the temporal bone at an earlier age. Scoring systems such as the
well-known Jahrsdoerfer scale aid in surgical candidacy assessments by predicting
the likelihood of hearing improvement following atresiaplasty (Table 23.1) [5]. The
presence of a normal stapes and middle ear space demonstrates improved hearing
outcomes in comparison to their lower-scoring counterparts following atresiaplasty
[10]. Ultimately, the presence of an aerated middle ear is considered the most

Imaging may also identify the presence of a cholesteatoma, a collection of squamous epithelium that can become trapped during atypical embryologic development
and maybe associated with congenital aural stenosis in up to 20% of patients with
diameter < 2 mm [12]. External ear cholesteatoma is rare, and, while benign, it may
lead to bone erosion, ongoing infection, and various complications inside and outside the temporal bone [13]. CT imaging may be suggestive of cholesteatoma in
TCS with characteristic findings of smooth margins of erosion. Magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) is less commonly employed to delineate temporal bone anatomic

K. Chow et al.

malformations but may be used to assess for presence or abnormalities of the
cochlear nerve when sensorineural hearing loss is diagnosed. Additionally, specific
MRI sequences, including non-echo planar diffusion weighting imaging, may be
employed to detect the presence of cholesteatoma when suggested by CT findings [14].

Hearing Loss in Treacher Collins Syndrome
While the rate of being deaf or hard of hearing increases from 1.2/1000 in newborns
to 3/1000 in early school age, the incidence of hearing loss among those with Treacher
Collins syndrome (TCS) is greater. An estimated 1 in 55,000 newborns is born with
TCS with up to 97% presenting with some degree of hearing loss [6]. Access to sound
is a requisite for successful development of speech and language in young children,
and this relationship underlies the motivation for establishing universal newborn
hearing screening. The universal newborn hearing screening (UNHS) is a state-mandated standard test designed to screen newborn hearing status shortly after birth.
Ideally, screening of newborns is conducted before leaving the hospital, or before
1 month of age in cases of home births. Early detection, especially for those at risk of
hearing loss, is crucial. The Joint Committee on Infant Hearing (JCIH) 2019 stresses
the importance of early hearing detection and intervention for all infants, especially
those at risk of being deaf or hard of hearing, as well as those with risk factors for
delayed onset and progressive hearing loss [8, 15]. In all cases of TCS, ear anomalies
dictate that additional audiologic testing beyond the UNHS is required.
Because of the complexity of craniofacial anomalies in TCS, hearing loss is not
the only factor affecting speech and language development in young children.
Abnormalities of orofacial musculature, voice and breadth, suction, and chewing
and swallowing functions may all influence receptive and expressive speech acquisition. Therefore, prompt and accurate audiologic assessment and multidisciplinary
intervention, including speech language therapy, are essential to maximize speech
and hearing outcomes. For infants with TCS and bilateral conductive hearing loss,
a comprehensive evaluation of auditory function is warranted. Behavioral, electrophysiological, and acoustic immittence measures can be utilized in isolation or in
combination with one another in the evaluation process. These tests aim to determine the degree, configuration, and type of hearing loss.

Age-Based Audiological Testing
Various audiological tests are available when assessing pediatric patients, the modality of which depend on age, cognitive, and developmental abilities. Often, multiple
visits are required to obtain a complete understanding of the child’s auditory function.
For infants, the most accurate method to measure auditory function is through electrophysiological testing. This type of noninvasive testing includes auditory brainstem
response testing (ABR) and auditory steady-state response (ASSR). This testing requires

23

Hearing Loss and Aural Rehabilitation in Patients with Treacher Collins Syndrome

453

the patient to be still and quiet, ideally in a deep sleep, but can also be performed with
sedation if natural sleep cannot be achieved. Testing is typically conducted with sticker
electrodes placed on the child’s ears or mastoid bone and forehead. When there is a patent ear canal, the stimulus is presented through an inserted earphone, and the response
of the auditory nerve is measured at the site of electrode placement. Because of the
many craniofacial abnormalities associated with TCS, including atresia of the ear canal,
it is often not possible to test air conduction. As a result, only bone conduction threshold
testing is performed in most cases. This testing involves presenting a vibrating stimulus
on the child’s mastoid bone, which bypasses the outer and middle ear and directly stimulates the cochlea. Based on the combined results of air and bone conduction testing, the
type and degree of hearing loss can be determined. These results are necessary to guide
treatments pertaining to amplification selection and fitting.
As a child develops, more subjective behavioral testing techniques are preferred
over (or in combination with) electrophysiological assessment. When testing younger
children, audiologists will utilize visual reinforcement audiometry (VRA) for children 5–24 months old and conditioned play audiometry (CPA) for 2–5 year olds [16].
Of note, age ranges may vary depending on the patient’s developmental status. VRA
is an operant-conditioned response that capitalizes on a child’s natural instinct to
respond to auditory stimuli with a head turn [17]. When a child responds with a head
turn, reinforcement is provided for that response in the form of lighting and/or activation of a movie/motorized toy by the audiologist [18, 19]. While this technique for
eliciting responses to auditory stimuli is used in children aged 5–24 months, this age
range may vary depending on the patient’s developmental status. Since CPA relies on
the use of a play-based motor activity to establish a time-­locked conditioned response
to an auditory signal, the test assistant may provide the child with a positive social
reinforcement to further shape the response behavior [20]. For children aged 5 years
or older, standard adult behavioral audiometry is performed, which involves conditioning the child to raise a hand in response to a sound.
Speech audiometry is an essential component of the audiologic test battery performed at approximately 6 months developmental age and older to examine speech
awareness, speech discrimination, and speech recognition [21]. Speech audiometry
assesses a child’s ability to perceive speech or speech-like stimuli, aids in determination of pure-tone threshold reliability, and helps to monitor the child’s progress
with amplification.

Auditory Rehabilitation Options
Traditional Hearing Aid Amplification
Amplification options depend on the type and degree of hearing loss and the patient’s
ear anatomy. Hearing technology is complex. To that end, there are several different
types of hearing devices that may be appropriate for children with TCS, the first of
which is a traditional hearing aid. Simply put, this is a type of hearing aid that fits
behind the ear and is connected to a soft, plastic custom earmold that fits inside the

454

K. Chow et al.

ear. This hearing aid design can be worn by children with any type or degree of hearing loss as long as there is an ear canal that can fit and hold the earmold securely.
Traditional amplification is appropriate for children with grade 1 or 2 microtia and
a patent ear canal. Hearing aid use can begin as soon as hearing loss is diagnosed
and characterized, ideally before 3 months of age.

Bone-Anchored Hearing Amplification
In more severe cases where a patient presents with grade 3 or 4 microtia, or in cases
where there is an atretic or absent canal, traditional amplification is not an option.
In these cases, bone-anchored or bone conduction hearing aids should be recommended. This type of hearing aid is indicated for children with CHL or some forms
of mixed hearing loss (combination of sensorineural hearing loss and CHL). Use of
a bone conduction hearing device is a necessity for normal speech and language
development in children with bilateral aural atresia [9, 22]. When utilized, a bone-­
anchored hearing aid is worn behind the ear or auricular remnant. Sound is received
by the hearing aid and is transmitted through the skull directly to an intact, functioning cochlea, after which it travels along the remaining intact auditory pathway
to the cortex. Because bone-anchored implants bypass abnormal outer and middle
ear anatomy, they are frequent options for aural rehabilitation in patients with
TCS [4].
There is a myriad of surgical and non-surgical options for bone-anchored hearing
devices from multiple manufacturers. The options are highlighted below and vary
by device strength and size, in addition to surgical and wear options unique to each
manufacturer.
Non-surgical devices can be fit on children as young as newborns and involve
wearing a hearing aid on a specific type of headband (Fig. 23.4). The “softband” is
the most common non-surgical option and uses an adjustable, elastic soft band
(Fig. 23.4a). Two alternatives include the hardband SoundArc ™ (Cochlear
Americas, Englewood CO) recommended for older school-aged children and the
AdHear ™ (MEL-EL, Austria) which adheres to the skin with adhesive
(Fig. 23.4b, c).
Surgical options involve placing an implant into the calvarium, which then
osseointegrates and transmits sound from a processor to the functioning inner ear
(Fig. 23.5). Sound can be transmitted to the osseointegrated implant directly
through an abutment or transcutaneously through the skin with a magnet. Currently,
viable options include percutaneous osseointegrated bone conduction devices such
as the BAHA Connect (Cochlear, NSW, Australia) and Ponto implant (Oticon,
Copenhagen, Denmark), as well as the BoneBridge (MED-EL, North Carolina,
USA), BAHA Attract, and newer OSIA (Cochlear, NSW, Australia) (Fig. 23.5).
FDA indications for recipient age vary by device, but all begin at 5 years of age.
Although the exact details regarding surgical candidacy for the aforementioned

implants are beyond the scope of this chapter, it should be noted that additional

device, as well as the specific choice of device, is a highly individualized process.
Decision-making should be directed by the patient’s family in consultation with a
multidisciplinary care team.
Whether surgical or non-surgical, an important feature of all bone conduction
devices is the ability connect to hearing-assistive technology (HAT). This is
extremely important for children in educational settings because it helps reduce the
signal to noise ratio, thus reducing the negative effect of background noise on the
child’s learning environment. A hearing education specialist (HES) is also needed to
ensure the child’s device and HAT are paired successfully with additional technology and fully functional.

Atresiaplasty or Canalplasty
Surgical creation of an external ear canal in congenital aural atresia is guided by the
patient’s hearing assessment and temporal bone anatomy as determined by radiographic imaging. In cases of ear canal stenosis or narrowing, surgery may be necessary due to concern for cholesteatoma. Surgery in these cases is typically variable
and is guided by the degree of stenosis and amount of preserved anatomy. This
includes bony or cartilaginous ear canal remnants in addition to ossicular
involvement.
For patients with complete atresia to be considered for atresiaplasty, they must
have normal inner ear function without significant SNHL. Surgery is not recommended until the child is approximately age 6–7 years old due to the need for compliance during postoperative debridement, resolution of age-related eustachian tube
dysfunction, and decrease in bony regrowth [9]. Radiographic imaging, specifically
CT, serves as the basis of candidacy for atresia surgery. As described above, imaging should note both middle ear anatomy and facial nerve position. If the facial
nerve position traverses the planned location for the new canal or blocks ossicular
assessment and reconstruction, atresiaplasty should not be attempted [7, 9].
Recommendations for surgery in non-syndromic atresia from the International

23

Hearing Loss and Aural Rehabilitation in Patients with Treacher Collins Syndrome

457

Microtia and Atresia Workgroup (IMAW) supports the use of the Jahrsdoerfer grading scale and recommends surgery for children scoring 7 or higher [22, 24]. No
published guidelines exist for patients with TCS. Additionally, and especially in
cases of TCS, the timing of atresiaplasty must be balanced with other planned surgical interventions, including possible microtia or external ear reconstruction.

Conclusion
Children with TCS manifest a variety of otologic manifestations, the most common
and important of which is bilateral aural atresia resulting in bilateral maximal
CHL. Early and accurate audiologic assessment is crucial and should occur as soon
as possible in the newborn period to facilitate early amplification. Initiation of
amplification is crucial to assist with speech and language development in this complex syndrome. Decisions about surgical intervention are highly individualized and
are typically based on radiographic assessments of otologic anatomy. Due to the
complexity of craniofacial anomalies, these children are best managed by a multidisciplinary team with experience assessing and treating patients with TCS.

Background
Treacher Collins syndrome (TCS) has a high degree of penetrance but variable
expressivity. A range of craniofacial manifestations may be observed. This chapter
serves to discuss the identification and management of manifestations related to the
external ear. These manifestations may include periauricular anomalies like accessory appendages or pits, auricular deformities like cup ear, or malformations like
microtia or atresia (Fig. 24.1).
TCS affects the development of first and second branchial arch structures. The
external ear arises from the 6 hillocks of His, with the first 3 hillocks arising from
the first branchial arch and the second 3 hillocks arising from the second branchial
arch. The hillocks lead to development of the tragus, helix, concha cymba, antihelix,
and antitragus. Thus, any alteration in the development of the first and second branchial arch will be reflected in the mature external ear anatomy.
After diagnosis of TCS, a comprehensive physical examination should be undertaken (Fig. 24.2). It is important for the patient and family to establish care with a
reconstructive surgeon, who is a key part of the multidisciplinary team. Early identification of auricular deformities and malformations is important in providing the

Periauricular Anomalies
Periauricular Accessory Appendages
Periauricular accessory appendages occur in up to 30 to 40% of the TCS population
[2]. These anomalies may be referred to by one of several names, including accessory tragus, supernumerary tragus, accessory auricle, or ear tag. They may appear
as single or multiple (Figs. 24.3 and 24.4). They may be sessile (flat against the
skin) or pedunculated (raised by a stalk). They may be soft (with little to no cartilage) or firm (with cartilage). These appendages often involve cartilage, versus an
Fig. 24.3 An accessory
auricle located anterior to
the tragus and another at

K. P. Alfonso et al.

Fig. 24.4 Another
example of a preauricular

acrochordon, also known as a skin tag. In one study of over 1000 accessory auricles,
the authors found that 78.4% contained cartilage [8].
These appendages arise from first branchial cleft anomaly and may be located
anywhere along a triangle from the ear to the lip, along the mandible. The appendage may be pedunculated via a very thin stalk and fall off naturally as the lesion
itself becomes ischemic with growth. Generally, surgical excision under sedation
will be performed after the age of 3 due to the elective nature of the operation or in
combination with other procedures (i.e., auricular reconstruction). Earlier excision
could be considered during the first several months of life under local anesthesia.
Elliptical excision surrounding the base of the appendage, with undermining,
allows for approximation of the skin without tension. It is important to avoid deep
dissection, particularly in the preauricular area, for risk of injuring the parotid,
facial nerve, or superficial temporal artery. This method of excision generally leads
to a satisfactory aesthetic result. Use of absorbable sutures with surgical tape or glue
use improves cooperation in the postoperative period. It also prevents the need for
suture removal, which reduces patient discomfort and possible need for further
sedation.

Preauricular Pits
Preauricular pits may also be noticed at or near the root of the helix (Fig. 24.5). The
pit may have a blind-ended pouch or continue as a deeper sinus to attach to the
auricular cartilage.
Surgical excision may be offered, particularly if the patient has suffered a prior
infection of the pit or sinus. This may be done in conjunction with other procedures
or as an ambulatory procedure. An elliptical incision can be designed surrounding
the pit or sinus, after probing with a lacrimal probe. Dissection must continue along
the tract to its base, which typically inserts into cartilage. A small area of cartilage
should be removed to prevent recurrence. Primary closure is then performed.

Auricular Deformities
The auricle in the TCS patient may appear anomalous secondary to a deformity
(Fig. 24.6). Deformities may include cryptotia, prominauris, lop ear, or cup ear [16].
These anomalies are less commonly seen than microtia in the TCS population, however.

If identified early enough, auricular molding procedures can be performed.
Molding is much more successful if instituted within 1 week of birth. Due to circulating maternal exogenous estrogen, infant cartilage is more pliable. Estrogen levels
peak around 3 days after birth and then begin to fall. The manner in which estrogen
influences the auricular cartilage is due to the increase in hyaluronic acid within the
cartilage [11]. Once estrogen levels decline, the ear then becomes firmer and molding techniques are less likely to succeed.
Various materials may be used to stent the auricle into the desired shape, such as
silastic tubing with dental wire, dental wax, or an endotracheal tube stylet (Fig. 24.7).
Commercial kits are also available, including EarBuddies (Ear Buddies Ltd.,
London, UK) and EarWell (Becon Medical, Batavia, Illinois). These may be placed
by the physician or by the family. The stent should be changed at least biweekly to
allow examination of the underlying skin and ensure no breakdown or infection has
occurred. This also allows for assessment of progress. Molding will generally take
place for 2 to 6 weeks depending on how early the process was initiated.
Otoplasty may be considered in these patients if they are too old for molding
procedures. Otoplasty is generally undertaken around 5–6 years of age, once the
auricle has reached around 85–90% of adult size. Various techniques may be used
and individually designed to address the deformity.

Microtia
Microtia is the most common auricular malformation and has been reported to occur
in up to 85% of TCS patients [3]. In an assessment of Nagata’s auricular reconstruction clinic, 9.1% of the syndromic patients with microtia had TCS [17].
One commonly adopted grading system, originally described by Weerda and
simplified by Aguilar, classifies the deformity based on the appearance of the vestigial remnants. Grade 1 microtia has a mild reduction of size compared to a normal
ear. Grade 2 microtia has a volume loss with reduced cartilage and skin. Landmarks
are not as easily identified. Grade 3 microtia is also known as “peanut ear” as only

or “anotia,” with no external auricule (4). (Reprinted from Clinics in Perinatology. 45 (4). Hartzell

Elsevier)

a small remnant remains, with a lobule. Grade 4 microtia is the absence of any external ear, also known as anotia (Fig. 24.8).
The family of a TCS patient should be fully informed of the reconstructive
options. These include no intervention, prosthetics, porous polyethylene (MedPor)
implantation, or autologous rib reconstruction.

Prosthetics
Prosthetics may allow for an excellent aesthetic result without the requirement for
surgical intervention. Interested patients and families may be referred to an anaplastologist, or one may be already incorporated into the reconstructive team. An anaplastologist is a clinical specialist experienced in prosthetic design and creation for
the replacement of an absent or malformed body part.
Auricular prostheses are generally constructed from silicone after molds have
been created. The template may be the patient’s contralateral ear or that of a family
member. The prosthetic may be secured in place using adhesive or implantable
magnets or abutments. Adhesive may allow for the prosthetic use at an early age, as
young as age 3. The adhesive is typically painted onto the prosthetic, allowed to dry
partially, and then the prosthetic can be applied. Adhesive-applied prosthetics are
the most conservative method of auricular reconstruction [15]. Risks associated
with adhesives include a failure of the adhesive to hold, particularly in a humid or
hot environment, or skin reactions.
Implantable magnets or osseointegrated (bone-anchored) abutments are placed
after age 5 (Fig. 24.9). One such abutment option is the VistaFix system (Cochlear,
Sydney, Australia). It is important to consider the bone integrity, particularly in the
TCS population. These patients are more likely to have poor bone integrity or irregularity [13]. A “sleeper” screw may be helpful in case of poor osseointegration or

(right image)

potential trauma of the other screw. Additionally, a two-stage procedure is recommended in this population: the first to place the screw and the second to attach the
abutment 4 to 6 months later after osseointegration is achieved.
The surgeon must work closely with the anaplastologist in deciding the best
placement of the prosthetic and abutments. Auricular remnants may need to be
excised or altered depending on the prosthetic design. Sometimes the prosthesis can
be designed to incorporate the auricular remnant. A tragus may also need to be constructed. This can be done via cartilage harvest from the contralateral concha cavum.
The prosthetic is also an ideal option in the case of a failed porous polyethylene
implant or rib reconstruction, post-traumatic cases, and following excision of malignancies and irradiation. Limitations include daily prosthetic care, daily application
and removal of the prosthetic, and the need for prosthetic replacement every
4–5 years due to wear. The prosthetic should be removed during water activities,
bathing, and sleeping.

Implantable Reconstruction
Early alloplastic implants used for auricular reconstruction were based in silicone.
However, these had a high rate of infection and extrusion. Porous high-density polyethylene (MedPor [Stryker, Kalamazoo, MI]) implantation became available in the
1990s. The material is more resilient to trauma. Disadvantages include using

468

K. P. Alfonso et al.

nonnative tissue and there is still a risk for future infection or extrusion compared to
autologous tissue.
The surgery can be performed as early as 3–5 years old and is generally performed in a single stage. The implant requires a temporoparietal fascia (TPF) flap
for coverage. The course of the superficial temporal artery is identified using
Doppler and marked on the patient (Fig. 24.10).
The incisions are made and the skin pocket is developed. The TPF flap is raised
carefully from posterior to anterior, making sure to keep a wide base around the
vascular pedicle. By keeping a wide base, postoperative edema and risk of vascular
compression are reduced. The rudimentary cartilage is then removed from the auricle, and the implant is assembled (Fig. 24.11). The implant comes in two parts, one
as the base and one as the helix. These are customized as necessary and then secured
together with non-absorbable suture. The implant is inserted with the TPF flap providing anterior coverage (Fig. 24.12). Any area without epithelial coverage may be
reconstructed with a split or full-thickness skin graft, which may be harvested from
the postauricular region or thigh. A bolster is applied, and the patient is seen back in
the office 1 week later for removal.
