Autologous Rib Reconstruction
Autologous rib reconstruction techniques have been described by numerous surgeons, including Tanzer, Brent, Nagata and Firmin [4, 7, 14, 18]. The benefit of
using autologous tissue includes less risk of extrusion, infection, or failure due to
trauma in patients implanted over several decades. Disadvantages include donor site
morbidity, more than one procedure, and less predictable aesthetic result.
Surgery generally requires several stages, ranging from two stages in the Nagata
and Firmin techniques to four stages in the Brent technique. In our practice, the two-­
stage Firmin method is followed. The first stage combines framework construction,
lobule transposition, and tragal reconstruction. Framework elevation and postauricular skin grafting occurs in the second stage.
The first stage starts with harvest of section of costal cartilage from ribs 6 through
9. A template is designed from the contralateral ear if normal, or a previously
selected model ear, such as that of a parent. The template is drawn on radiograph
film and soaked in betadine (Fig. 24.13). Harvest may be from the ipsilateral or
contralateral chest, but preferably on the same side. The sixth and seventh ribs form
a synchondrosis which is harvested for use as the base of the construct (Fig. 24.14).
The floating eighth and ninth ribs are harvested for use as the helix, antihelix, tragus
and antitragus. A portion may also be used as a projection piece. During harvest, the

Considerations on Timing and the Patient Perspective
Patients with TCS typically present with several craniofacial anomalies, not simply
related to the external ear. Timing for surgical intervention of the external ear does
not need to be different for the patient with TCS than a non-syndromic patient [1].
However, the average TCS patient undergoes five different surgeries during their
reconstructive process [12]. A general approach to the overall operative timeline
involves airway management, oropharyngeal repair, and then midface and auricular
reconstruction [6]. Hearing should be assessed early with necessary amplification
provided during the first year of life, which has been discussed elsewhere in this text.
A study by Lodovichi et al. sought to explore the TCS patient perspective on
their ear deformity [12]. Twelve patients with TCS were divided into two groups,
those with normal ears and those without, and then asked to complete the World
Health Organization (WHO) quality-of-life questionnaire. Despite a small sample
size, the study demonstrated an intermediate quality of life for both groups without
a statistically significant difference.
The benefit of awaiting until the patient is older for auricular reconstruction is
increased maturity and cooperation with post-procedural care, increased size of ribs
(ideally a chest circumference greater than 60 cm), and patient assent for the procedure. An argument against this is the desire for repair prior to starting school when
patients may experience bullying [5]. Overall, it is most important for a patient and
family to find a reconstructive surgeon who considers their concerns and desires for
reconstruction and is comfortable with his or her skills in auricular reconstruction.

Rhinoplasty in Patients with Treacher
Collins Syndrome
Alexander P. Marston and Andrew R. Scott

Introduction
Failure of neuroepithelial proliferation as a result of mutations in the TCOF1 gene
leads to incomplete development of the first and second pharyngeal arches in individuals with Treacher Collins syndrome (TCS). Although this has a more direct
effect on the mandibular and midfacial anatomy, there are significant secondary
consequences on nasal anatomy, function, and aesthetics. The timing and order for
surgical correction of the complex TCS deformities are initially based on priorities
of airway stabilization, followed by staged procedures based on skeletal growth and
psychosocial needs [14]. Airway obstruction is most commonly due to mandibular
hypoplasia and secondary posterior positioning of the tongue base; however, choanal atresia is variably present in patients with TCS [1, 11] and may contribute to
early respiratory difficulty. If choanal atresia significantly impacts respiratory function, this may require an endonasal surgical intervention early in life. Mild cases of
choanal atresia can be surgically treated later in childhood with associated improved
outcomes and less risk of revision surgery [10, 19]. In the absence of choanal atresia, surgical nasal intervention, such as septorhinoplasty, is delayed until after skeletal maturity is achieved. As a result of multiple severe anatomic deficiencies that
take precedence over the nasal sequelae of TCS, few available studies on rhinoplasty techniques and results are published in the literature.

Nasal Anatomy
Although the nose is typically less dysplastic than the surrounding facial and cranial
anatomy in patients with TCS, intrinsic and extrinsic nasal structures can be severely
affected. There are reports of arhinia [7] and choanal atresia [1, 11], but more commonly there is moderate nasal obstruction that results from midfacial hypoplasia
[14] and septal and/or external deviation. A thorough understanding of the adjacent
dysplastic facial anatomy is an important component of rhinoplasty assessment,
planning, and patient counseling. Regardless of the severity of the facial malformations at birth, these generally remain stable into adulthood [16]. Although the facial
deformity is bilateral, there are typically asymmetric features with one side demonstrating more severe involvement. Prominent features that secondarily impact nasal
anatomy in patients with TCS result from orbitozygomatic hypoplasia, retrognathia,
and microgenia leading to relative prominence of the nasal dorsum and an overall
convex facial profile [14]. A reduced cranial base angle further contributes to the
convexity of the facial profile and apparent prominence of the nose [8]. Cephalometric
analyses demonstrate that the lower anterior facial height is long and the posterior
facial height is short due to mandibular dysplasia and chin retrusion [4]. The upper
anterior facial height is typically normal. Hypertelorism may be present, and the
globes appear protruded as a result of midfacial hypoplasia and dysplastic lateral
orbital walls. Soft tissue deficiencies of the eyelids, cheek skin, and temporal fossa
are additionally important factors to consider [4].
More careful analysis of the nasal anatomy on frontal view often reveals external
deviation of the nose due to underlying asymmetries of the midface and orbitozygomatic complexes. The width of the upper third of the nose is often increased [5]
(Fig. 25.1), and this deformity is further accentuated if hypertelorism is present. The
nasal tip may appear boxy or bulbous and is classically bifid in appearance
(Fig. 25.2) [13]. Furthermore, the alar bases are often narrow and constricted. On
profile view, there is a characteristic mid-dorsal hump composed of both bone and
cartilage (Fig. 25.3) [5]. The length of the nose from the radix to the tip is often long
with ptosis of the nasal tip and deficient projection. Underlying midfacial hypoplasia and incomplete superior rotation of the maxilla lead to a deficient and downward-­
oriented nasal spine that further contributes to nasal tip ptosis. In cases of severe
underprojection, the nasofronal angle is greater than 135 degrees (the generally
accepted upper limit of normal) (Fig. 25.4) [15]. Ptosis of the nasal tip can additionally cause an acute nasolabial angle. The nasofacial angle, represented by the intersection of a line from the nasal tip to the nasion and a vertical line from the pogonion
to the glabella, has a range of normal between 30 and 40 degrees. As a result of
micrognathia, the pogonion is posteriorly positioned, which leads to an obtuse nasofacial angle in most TCS patients. An optimal chin-nose relationship places the
pogonion and glabella along the same vertical line that is perpendicular to the
Frankfurt horizontal [3]. As a result, the retrodisplaced chin among individuals with
TCS contributes significantly to their nasal aesthetics.

Few publications are available on the specific nasal characteristics of patients
with TCS. One such report from 2015 by Plomp et al. included 11 TCS patients and
found that 73% had a dorsal hump, 55% had external nasal deviation, 55% had a
bulbous or bifid nasal tip, and 36% had under-rotation of the nasal tip [13]. On profile view, approximately one-third of patients had an under-rotated nasal tip leading
to a reported “droopy” appearance. Endonasal examination demonstrated an 82%
incidence of septal deviation (Fig. 25.5). This same study also used the Nasal
Appearance and Function Evaluation Questionnaire (NAFEQ) to assess the satisfaction of nasal function and appearance among this cohort of 11 TCS patients
compared to 151 controls. When compared to controls, TCS patients had significantly lower satisfaction scores for the following metrics: nasal position, nostril
size, color of the nose, and total nasal appearance. Nine of 11 (81%) TCS patients
indicated they were “satisfied” with their “total nasal appearance.” Interestingly, the
two individuals who were unsatisfied were the two patients who had undergone
prior rhinoplasty procedures.

Rhinoplasty
Similar to standard rhinoplasty workup and preoperative counseling, particular care
is taken to understand the patient’s priorities and expectations, appreciate the
nuances and variability of the nasal anatomy, and create a well-outlined surgical
plan. It is important to carefully advise the patient on how a potential rhinoplasty
intervention is expected to alter their facial aesthetics. Due to adjacent midfacial and
orbitozygomatic anatomic deficiencies, there are obvious limitations in how nasal
surgery will impact overall appearance among patients with TCS. Preoperative
computer-simulated morphing is a valuable way of gaining a better understanding

480

A. P. Marston and A. R. Scott

of the patient’s wishes [9], allows for demonstration of the anticipated outcome, and
depicts how the procedure might improve their overall facial form. An honest
approach to preoperative image morphing is critical in order to create realistic goals
[3]. Patients with TCS require a myriad of surgical interventions throughout their
childhood and adolescent years; rhinoplasty should be considered only after skeletal
maturity has been attained and, if necessary, orthognathic surgery has been completed [14].
Definitive rhinoplasty often requires an open approach in TCS patients to allow
for correction of external nasal deviation and severe nasoseptal obstruction. Dorsal
hump reduction typically necessitates resection of both cartilage and bone with
osteotomies and medialization of the bony vault to close the resulting open roof
deformity (Fig. 25.6). Osteotomies additionally achieve a more natural appearing
nasal width, which is increased at baseline in individuals with TCS. According to a
TCS nasal analysis paper by Farkas et al., the nasal root width should be reduced by
up to 7 mm for an ideal aesthetic result [5]. Decreased nasal tip projection and
under-rotation are best addressed with a caudal septal extension graft in the authors’
experience. Greater projection, rotation, and long-term stability can be accomplished with a caudal extension graft as compared to a floating columellar strut [2].

According the Farkas et al., the tip projection ought to be increased by up to 4 mm
in this patient population. Nasal tip definition improves as a result of increasing tip
projection and can be further refined through conservative trimming of the cephalic
margin of the lower lateral cartilages and dome suturing techniques (Fig. 25.7).
Lastly, the surgeon and patient should discuss chin retrodisplacement as a contributing factor of their nasal aesthetic and consider alloplastic chin augmentation or
genioplasty in conjunction with septorhinoplasty.

Implications of Nasal Dysfunction
Consequences of the TCS nasal deformity and dysfunction can have wide ranging
implications from speech disturbance and obstructive sleep apnea to exacerbation of
psychosocial-related outcomes. Abnormalities of speech are common among TCS
individuals, primarily due to the high incidence of cleft palate and conductive hearing loss, with a prevalence ranging between 21–33% [17, 18, 23] and 83–92% [18,
23], respectively. If one or both of these features are present, there is a significant
risk for speech delay and/or velopharyngeal insufficiency (VPI). For those with a
history of cleft palate and VPI, this is typically manifested in the form of hypernasal
speech. However, in cases of severe TCS midfacial hypoplasia and/or repaired choanal atresia, secondary constriction of the nasal cavities can actually lead to

482

A. P. Marston and A. R. Scott

hyponasality of speech [20]. Although the underlying midfacial hypoplasia is difficult to correct, septorhinoplasty can lead to an increase in nasal airflow and possible
improvement in hyponasality.
Nasal obstruction can additionally manifest as a contributing factor of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). The prevalence of OSA among pediatric and adult patients
with TCS has been reported to be 54% and 41%, respectively [12]. There is often
multilevel obstruction with the most prominent contributing factors being midfacial
hypoplasia, as well as oro- and hypo-pharyngeal collapse secondary to mandibular
deformities [12]. Nasal obstruction can further contribute to the severity of OSA
secondary to constricted nasal cavity dimensions and nasoseptal deviation. However,
surgical correction of nasal obstruction only imparts a minor benefit toward the
treatment of OSA. As previous publications have demonstrated, nasal surgery as an
isolated surgical treatment does not reliably improve OSA by objective measures
[6]. Nevertheless, subjective measures of nasal breathing and snoring often improve
following nasal surgery with a possible reduction in pressure titrations for those
treated with continuous positive airway pressure support for OSA [6]. Due to the
known high prevalence of OSA and the frequent occurrence of nasal obstruction in
individuals with TCS, septorhinoplasty interventions should aim to improve not
only nasal breathing and aesthetics but also sleep- and OSA-related metrics.
Improvements in speech and OSA severity are important potential outcomes of
nasal surgery; however, perhaps the most significant result can be observed in optimization of a patient’s psychosocial health. Patients with congenital facial deformities have been found to be significantly less satisfied with their facial appearance
[21]. This can then lead to low self-esteem and high fear of negative appearance
evaluation by others, both of which are strong determinants of psychological functioning [21]. An emphasis should be made on preoperative counseling to impart
realistic surgical expectations, but a definitive goal of the nasal procedure should
include an improvement in patient satisfaction so as to optimize their long-term
psychosocial well-being [22].

Conclusion
Although TCS nasal deformities are typically less severe than the adjacent mandibulofacial dysostosis, there are significant implications of the altered nasal function and aesthetics. Therefore, septorhinoplasty is an important aspect in the staged
surgical management of TCS patients. Narrowing of the nasal dorsal width, dorsal
hump takedown, and correction of external nasal and septal obstruction can lead to
marked improvement in nasal function and appearance.

Introduction
Similar to craniofacial microsomia described in Section 1, Treacher Collins syndrome (TCS) is an entity that affects derivatives of the first and second branchial
arches. TCS occurs in 1:50,000 live births and has no gender predilection. Sixty
percent of cases of TCS arise from de novo mutations and 40% of cases are familial
(40%) [1, 2] (Table 26.1).

Etiology and Pathogenesis
TCS most commonly results from a mutation in the treacle ribosome biogenesis
factor 1 (TCOF1) gene which leads to a defective treacle protein resulting in mass
apoptosis (death) of the neural crest cells. These neural crest progenitor cells are
responsible for the creation of the craniofacial bones, tissues, and structures residing within the first and second branchial arches. The first, or mandibular, branchial
arch gives rise to the muscles of mastication, stylohyoid, anterior belly of the digastric, tensor tympani, and tensor veli palatini muscles, the malleus, incus, and
Meckel’s cartilage, as well as the third division of the trigeminal nerve (V3). The

second, or hyoid, branchial arch provides the muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of the digastric muscle, as well as the stapes,
styloid cartilage, lesser cornu of the hyoid bone, and Reichert’s cartilage, and the

Clinical Features
The clinical features of TCS result from a hypoplasia of the orbits, midface, mandible, ears, skull base, and soft tissues of the face (Figs. 26.1a–c and 26.2a–d). More
specifically, orbito-malar/zygomatic arch hypoplasia is present in all patients with
TCS. This results in a more inferior position of the lateral canthus and thereby the
hallmark downslanting of the palpebral fissures. Coloboma, a structural defect of
the eyelid or the eye that appears as a cleft in the lid margin or the iris, while not
present in every case, is highly specific for TCS. Lacrimal system anomalies are
also common with atresia of the lacrimal puncta and cannaliculi being typical. The
mandible is also a prominent feature of the phenotype with characteristic micrognathia that features marked antegonial notching and a steep mandibular plane. The
TMJ may also be hypoplastic and/or dysplastic. The ears are typically bilaterally
involved with microtia/anotia, atresia of the auditory canal, and anomalous middle
ear ossicles leading to a bilateral conductive hearing loss. Also common are preauricular skin tags and preauricular hair displacement. Less common features include
cleft palate, maxillary hypoplasia, and an over-projected nasal dorsum. Intelligence
is usually normal in affected individuals. For a thorough discussion on this topic,
please refer to Chap. 14 from which the above excerpt was taken.

Functional Concerns
These anatomical aberrations lead to a myriad of functional concerns, which must
be considered during the initial evaluation of a newborn with suspected TCS. The
micrognathia may result in airway obstruction, feeding, and swallowing problems.
The orbito-malar hypoplasia combined with colobomas of the eyelids may result in
exposure keratopathy and visual disturbances. The auricular and ossicular anomalies typically lead to a bilateral conductive hearing loss which jeopardizes normal
speech and language development. As the child grows, these functional concerns
will need to be monitored and interventions timed and planned so as to minimize
morbidity and treatment burden and maximize benefit. Long-term dependence on

490

D. M. Yates and S. Bufford

tracheostomies and gastrostomies are not infrequent and often the focus of these
interventions. Speech and language development must be monitored along with
hearing. Jaw function should be observed as well for the impact of malocclusions
and limitations in mouth opening. Neuropsychological monitoring is essential to
support psychological and mental development and to identify any cognitive delays
or deficits [7]. For a thorough discussion on this topic, please refer to Chap. 3 under
the Treacher Collins section of this book.

Treatment Guidelines
It is important to understand that treatment of TCS requires a multidisciplinary
approach that is sequenced appropriately based upon the age and individualized
needs of the patient. The craniofacial team evaluating these patients should include
a pediatric otolaryngologist, ophthalmologist, geneticist, audiologist, a speech
pathologist, cranio-maxillo-facial surgeon, orthodontist, social worker, neuropsychologist, pediatric dentist, and care coordinator. Airway, nutrition, ocular concerns,
speech, and hearing are generally the most critical and recurrent needs in this patient
population. At every appointment, these areas should be addressed.
Guiding Principles:
1. Regular multidisciplinary craniofacial team evaluation.
2. In general, reducing the number of surgeries during active growth will result in
better functional and cosmetic outcomes (do not burn bridges).
3. Ensuring that the patient is supported and able to feed, hear, and speak as soon
as physically possible is critical to overall success.
4. Providing appropriate social and psychological support systems for the child as
they develop emotionally and physically.

Prenatal Evaluation (Second-Third Trimester)
Diagnosis of at-risk families or suspected fetuses may be accomplished by chorionic villus sampling. It is critical to determine the extent of mandibular retrognathia/micrognathia prior to delivery to prevent poor airway outcomes at birth. 3D-4D
sonographic imaging may be used to demonstrate a decreased inferior facial angle
(IFA). The IFA is a reliable predictor of retrognathia as measured on ultrasound
(US). It is measured by taking the intersection of two lines: (1) a line perpendicular
to the vertical part of the forehead, drawn at the level of the nasal and frontal bone
suture, and (2) a line from the tip of the menton and the anterior border of the more
protrusive lip. An IFA of >2 standard deviations from normal (65.5 degrees) corresponds with an angle of <50 degrees and is a reliable indicator for retrognathia. Of

26 An Overview of Treatment Recommendations for the Treacher Collins Syndrome…

491

neonates presenting with micrognathia, 54% require immediate airway support
from simple positioning to tracheotomy. If concern exists for severe micrognathia
based on an IFA, an ex utero intrapartum treatment (EXIT) procedure should be
ready to be performed at birth.

Airway
At birth if the inferior facial angle (IFA) < 50 degrees on prenatal US, prepare for an
EXIT procedure (Fig. 26.3a, b). If IFA > 50 degrees, EXIT procedure is likely
unnecessary, but it is recommended to have an airway specialist present at birth.
Immediate helpful interventions may include prone positioning, placement of a
nasal trumpet, or an oral airway with use of supplemental oxygen therapy. Should
these interventions fail to provide relief, a tongue stitch or intubation may be
required. Upon initial examination, if the patient is unable to maintain their airway
and a severe mandibular deformity is present (Kaban IIB or III), consider tracheotomy. If the mandible is a Kaban I or IIa and the patient’s airway is unable to be
maintained, judicious mandibular distraction may be considered. It is noted that

During infancy and early childhood, obstructive sleep apnea signs and symptoms
warrant evaluation with polysomnography. The craniofacial team may consider
judicious mandibular distraction if necessary. It is important to minimize mandibular surgeries – final cosmetic and functional outcome depends upon this principle.
Tracheotomy may be considered if worsening airway concerns are present which
are not able to be addressed with mandibular distraction, tonsillectomy, or other
effective surgical treatment.
In late childhood if a tracheostomy is present, consider mandibular reconstruction to obtain decannulation if possible. It is emphasized that mandibular reconstruction at this age is avoided when possible. Only airway concerns legitimize
mandibular surgery at this time (Fig. 26.5). TMJ and ramus reconstruction can be
achieved with costochondral grafting >9–10 years of age. Additionally, early (prior
to skeletal maturity) TMJ alloplastic reconstruction may be considered. Judicious
mandibular distraction may also be used to augment mandibular growth.
Once skeletal maturity is reached, definitive maxillomandibular surgery is performed which will provide adequate airway support. It is recommended to have a
yearly PSG since TCS patients represent an at-risk population.

Speech/Nutrition
During the initial evaluation at birth, it is critical for speech/nutrition to be an active
part of the team evaluating these patients. Due to the often-present significant mandibular retrognathia, it is common for patients with TCS to aspirate when feeding,
and many will suffer from failure to thrive. Adequate nutrition is key in promoting
physical development. In the neonatal period, bedside and videofluoroscopic swallow studies may be performed, and a PEG is placed if the child is unable to maintain
appropriate nutrition.
During infancy, cleft palate repair may be considered and should be performed
ideally by 18 months of age. However, airway concerns must also be taken into
account prior to repair. The use of Sign language is encouraged in this population
and careful attention to the child’s growth curve during this period are encouraged.
During early childhood, speech is encouraged, and if tracheostomy dependent,
the use of a Passy Muir is advised. The child continues speech therapy and is encouraged in the use of sign language. Growth is carefully monitored under the care of a
nutritionist on the craniofacial team.
In late childhood and adolescence, speech therapy is maximized, the use of sign
language is encouraged as needed, and the child may be a candidate for additional
speech surgeries for palatal lengthening/function which may include buccinator
flaps, pharyngeal flaps, or sphincter pharyngoplasty. Prior to any speech surgery, a

494

D. M. Yates and S. Bufford

polysomnogram should be performed to ensure that sleep apnea is appropriately
managed and not worsened.
By skeletal maturity, speech should be optimized.
For a thorough discussion on this topic, please refer to Chap. 15 under the
Treacher Collins section of this book.

At birth a hearing evaluation is performed. Since the majority of TCS patients have
significant bilateral conductive hearing loss, diagnosis and treatment are critical to
ensuring appropriate cognitive speech development. Removable BAHA softbands

Orbito/Ocular
At birth the patient is evaluated to ensure that they are able to achieve appropriate
lid closure thus providing sufficient corneal protection. If they are unable to self-­
protect their cornea due to the presence of a hypoplastic lower lid/coloboma, lubrication and/or a temporary tarsorrhaphy is performed. Pediatric ophthalmology
evaluation is performed at birth and yearly.
During infancy (6–9 months), coloboma reconstruction is undertaken for large
defects to ensure corneal protection. A lateral canthoplasty may also be undertaken

26 An Overview of Treatment Recommendations for the Treacher Collins Syndrome…

at this time. Visual rehabilitation and, if needed, epibulbar dermoid excision may be
performed if the child is symptomatic.
During late infancy (12–24 months), consider strabismus surgery, lacrimal drainage surgery, and continue visual rehabilitation.
Preschool-age children may undergo coloboma reconstruction of small to moderate defects, lateral canthoplasty, and ptosis repair.
In school-age children, one may consider all of the above surgeries and revisions,
as well as orbitozygomatic reconstruction – which is generally performed using
either malar implants or cranial bone (Figs. 26.7a–d and 26.8a–c).
Once adulthood/skeletal maturity is reached, revisional surgeries may be performed as needed. Fat grafting around the orbits is frequently helpful in softening
the appearance of the reconstructed orbitozygomatic complex.

Dental/Orthodontic
Children with TCS are at a much higher risk of dental caries secondary to parotid
dysgenesis, ectopic eruption, and dental malformations. We recommend regular
establishment of a dental home at the eruption of the first primary tooth with regular
visits every 3–6 months.
Orthodontic care is established at the first craniofacial team visit, and the patient
is regularly followed. During the mixed dentition period, maxillary expansion is
frequently needed to correct posterior cross bites and establish compatible arch
forms. At this time, a limited phase of orthodontic treatment may be undertaken to
facilitate eruption of permanent teeth and correct traumatic occlusions.
Once permanent dentition is in place, comprehensive orthodontic therapy is
undertaken – many times in conjunction with orthognathic surgery. Careful planning and combined decision-making are required between the cranio-maxillo-facial
surgeon and the orthodontist.
For a thorough discussion on this topic, please refer to Chap. 22 under the
Treacher Collins section of this book.

Soft Tissue Concerns
Tessier VII clefting resulting in macrostomia is frequently present in TCS patients.
Correction is undertaken less frequently than in patients with CFM, likely due to the
bilateral nature of clefting in the TCS patient population and the lack of eye-­catching
asymmetry.
Fat grafting around the orbits is frequently helpful in softening the appearance of
the reconstructed orbito-malar-zygomatic complex.

500

D. M. Yates and S. Bufford

Maxillomandibular Treatment
Mandibular management is critical in the reconstruction of TCS patients. Treatment
protocols vary based upon age and stage of dental development. The specific surgical techniques, methods, and materials vary with the severity of the individual
deformity but may involve orthodontic intervention, orthognathic surgical procedures, distraction osteogenesis (DO), and TMJ reconstruction with costochondral
grafting, vascularized flaps (e.g., fibula), or alloplastic joint replacement. In general,
reducing the number of procedures performed will result in a more cosmetic and
functional final outcome.
The first decision is made prenatally. If there is a family history of TCS, the
mother should be under the care of a maternal fetal medicine doctor, and during
sonographic exams, the inferior facial angle (IFA) is calculated (Fig. 26.3a, b). If the
IFA is less than 50 degrees, an EXIT procedure is planned. If greater than 50
degrees, likely the baby will not require an emergency airway – however, an airway
specialist is present at delivery ready to intervene if necessary. Likely, conservative
measures (i.e., prone positioning, nasal trumpet, oral airway, or a tongue stitch) will
be sufficient to maintain the airway.
Upon initial examination, if the patient is unable to maintain their airway and a
severe mandibular deformity is present (Kaban IIB or III), consider tracheotomy. If
the mandible is a Kaban I or IIa and the patient’s airway is unable to be maintained,
judicious mandibular distraction may be considered. It is noted that mandibular
distraction in Treacher Collins patients is much less reliable than in the straightforward Pierre Robin sequence population. This is likely secondary to the U-shaped
mandible often present and the lack of mandibular stop secondary to a hypoplastic
cranial base in the region of the glenoid fossa (Fig. 26.4a, b).
During the preschool- and early-school-age years, attention is directed toward
maintaining healthy dentition. Due to their deformity and difficulty with oral
hygiene, as well as parotid dysgenesis, TCS patients are at a greater risk of dental
caries. Occasionally, additional distraction versus tracheostomy is needed as the
child continues to grow if struggling with progressive sleep apnea and/or other manifestations of hypoxia.
School-age children (9–14 years) may be candidates for TMJ and mandibular
ramus reconstruction. Judicious mandibular distraction may be performed only if
airway/sleep apnea demands it. Reconstruction with costochondral grafts or “early”
(prior to skeletal maturity) TMJ alloplastic reconstruction may be considered for
Kaban/Pruzansky Types IIB and III.
Once skeletal maturity is reached, the maxillomandibular complex may be
addressed in its totality. In mild cases, a LeFort I/bilateral sagittal split ramus osteotomy with counterclockwise rotation may be all that is needed for surgical success.
In moderate to severe cases, additional considerations need to be taken into account.
Key to successful reconstruction is building off a stable temporomandibular joint

26 An Overview of Treatment Recommendations for the Treacher Collins Syndrome…

501

complex. In severe cases, this may be achieved with successful costochondral grafting bilaterally or with the placement of alloplastic temporomandibular joints. Once
TMJ stability has been achieved, significant counterclockwise rotation of the maxillomandibular complex must occur. The midface deformity, steep mandibular plane
angle, and severe retrognathia must be addressed (Fig. 26.9). This has been done
with the combination of a Kufner osteotomy (Modified LeFort III) followed by a
LeFort I in the maxilla and inverted L plus a genioplasty in the mandible (Fig. 26.8d–
g). It may also be accomplished with a LeFort III osteotomy/mandibular osteotomies followed by counterclockwise distraction.
The maxilla/mandibular maxillomandibular instead of maxilla/mandibular
deformity associated with TCS is among the most difficult issues confronted in their
complex care. Key treatment concepts include (1) maintenance of the airway and
monitoring of sleep apnea, (2) reducing the number of maxillomandibular surgeries
performed which will result in an improved final cosmetic and functional outcome,
and (3) successful reconstruction being dependent on building off a stable temporomandibular joint complex.
For a thorough discussion on this topic, please refer to Chaps. 19–21 under the
Treacher Collins section of this book.

Nasal Deformity
TCS characteristically presents with a constricted nasal airway and may present at
birth with choanal atresia. Useful exams to determine the extent of the nasal deformity include attempted passage of a 5 French orogastric tube through nasal cavity,
nasendoscopy, and CT maxillofacial. If choanal atresia is present, surgical correction is performed.
The typical nasal deformity seen in TCS includes septal deviation, prominent
dorsal hump, nasal tip ptosis, bulbous tip, external tip deviation, and a narrowed alar
base (Fig. 26.10a, b). Definitive nasoseptorhinoplasty is performed at the cessation

tip-defining sutures

of nasal growth and ideally after completion of midface advancement as early as

For a thorough discussion on this topic, please refer to Chap. 25 under the

Conclusions
It must be recognized that there is no complete consensus on diagnosis and/or management of TCS. Therefore, evidence-based decisions are difficult; often decisions
are based upon the existing low-level evidence and/or the individual practitioner’s
experience. There is certainly controversy about the preferred treatments and timing. Standardizing treatment algorithms is difficult due to the varying severity of
phenotypes present. Individualized treatment planning in the team setting is the
most ideal while adhering to certain guiding principles.
Guiding Principles:
1. Regular craniofacial team evaluation.
2. In general, reducing the number of surgeries during active growth will result in
better functional and cosmetic outcomes.

504

D. M. Yates and S. Bufford

3. Ensuring that the patient is supported and able to feed, hear, and speak as soon
as physically possible is critical to overall success.
4. Providing appropriate social and psychological support systems for the child as
they develop emotionally and physically.
Case Studies:
1. This case study importantly illustrates the value of appropriate treatment planning and how it can save lives, prevent unpleasant experiences for patients and
their families, and ensure that care is delivered in the correct treatment
environment.
Term infant with prenatal care – not referred for EXIT procedure though inferior facial angle is clearly <50 degrees corresponding to severe mandibular
hypoplasia. Patient was born without any planning for an EXIT procedure.
Neonatologist present at birth immediately identified the life-threatening airway
situation. Due to the extreme micrognathia, visualization of the laryngeal cords
was not possible. The neonatologist present was unable to intubate; however the
baby was able to be ventilated secondary to supraglottic placement of an ET tube
nasally and orally (Fig. 26.11a). The patient was immediately transferred via
ambulance to the local children’s hospital where a pediatric ENT, pediatric
OMFS, neonatologist, pediatric anesthesiologist, and pediatric surgeon were all
assembled in the operating room (OR). The patient was brought into the OR, and
using a rigid pediatric ventilating bronchoscope, a bougie was used to slide past
the vocal cords and an endotracheal tube was slid over the bougie to intubate.
A CT scan was then obtained to determine if the patient was a candidate for
mandibular distraction to assist in avoiding a tracheotomy (Fig. 26.11b).
Unfortunately, due to the lack of a condylar stop at the temporal bone and the
severe hypoplasia of the mandibular condyle/ramus complex, the patient was not
a ­candidate for neonatal mandibular distraction at that time. The patient underwent a successful tracheotomy.
2. A 2-year-old male presented with Treacher Collins syndrome. The patient was
hospitalized every month for the preceding 10 months secondary to multiple
bouts of aspiration pneumonia. Born full term, he necessitated a NICU stay secondary to breathing and feeding difficulty x 2 weeks in Peru. Swallow study
demonstrated aspiration present. Patient was underweight secondary to chronic
malnutrition secondary to feeding difficulties. He presented with severe sleep
apnea and frequent aspiration when feeding. The patient at this point did not
have a g-tube or tracheostomy present and was an excellent candidate for mandibular distraction secondary to Kaban IIa mandible (glenoid fossa present,
mandibular condyle present but diminutive) (Fig. 26.12a). Mandibular distraction was performed, and the mandible was advanced at a rate of 1 mm/day ×
20 days (Fig. 26.12b, c). The patient did well after surgery – he gained weight
and tolerated feedings without further aspiration, and his sleep apnea significantly improved (Fig. 26.12d, e). Upon team evaluation, the patient was found to
be one of the 7% of patients with TCS with sensorineural hearing loss and underwent cochlear implant placement.
